title: களிற்றியானைநிரை 0-20
theme: The invocation to Shiva and Akananuru 1 to 20 in the anthology's fixed order of lands: paalai poems of men leaving or turning back for wealth and of mothers whose daughters eloped, Kapilar's hill courtships in which the friend presses for marriage, mullai homecomings at evening, neythal shores closed by gossip, and marutham quarrels over the husband's women. Chola, Chera, Pandya and lesser chiefs' names (Thithan's Uranthai, Thondi, Kodai, Avi's Pothini, Nannan's Pazhi) serve as measures of private beauty, guard and loss.

title: கடவுள் வாழ்த்து
reading: The god wears fresh konrai blossom as garland and chaplet, a fine thread on his chest, an unwinking eye on his brow, axe and pick in hand and a three-pointed spear; he rides the bull with Umai beside him, red as the evening sky, with crescent-white teeth, flame-bright matted hair lit by the young moon, a tiger's hide and a dark throat, and the world rests in the shade of his flawless feet, an old order no god or sage has fathomed.
nuance: The poem is a list of possessions in short clauses (மார்பினஃதே, நுதலது, கையது, ஊர்ந்தது, சேர்ந்தோள்) and gives its only verb of the world at the end: the whole world has stopped (தவிர்ந்தன்று) in the shade of his feet. Unlike the Purananuru's opening by a poet of the same name, it sets Umai beside him rather than inside him, a fitting choice for an anthology of love.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the god, கடவுள் வாழ்த்து (porul 2.27)

comparisons.tenor: the god's body, red as the evening sky
his white curved teeth, like the bright crescent
his bright twisted matted hair, like rising flame

tamil: நிழல் தேய்ந்து உலறிய மரத்த; அறை காய்பு,
reading: The woman asks her friend whether he has forgotten his word that they would never part, a bond he likened to stone set with lac at Avi's Pothini, now that he has left, her shoulders slackening, to fetch gold from a far country across a forest where the sun has stripped the trees of shade, dried the springs, parches spilt grain, emptied the road even of robbers, and where wind-tossed murungai blossom looks like sea spray.
nuance: She does not accuse; she asks whether he forgot (மறந்தனர் கொல்லோ), which keeps the fault in memory rather than in will. The promise was itself a simile of permanence, stone fixed with lac, set against a land where everything is coming loose: shade, water, people. Line 5 recurs verbatim in Akananuru 356.

thinai_evidence.note: the woman speaks of a man gone across the waste for wealth

comparisons.tenor: the lovers' promised bond, like stone set fast with lac
the sun's rays, burning like fire
the white murungai blossom blown up by the wind, like the spray of breaking waves
the blossom-swept forest, looking like the sea

reading: The friend tells the hill lord that on his slopes a male monkey drinks without knowing it the wine that ripe jackfruit and plantain have made in a rock pool, cannot climb the pepper-twined sandal tree and sleeps content on the flowered slope; if beasts there find unplanned joy so easily, how can the joy he plans be hard for him, when the girl's heart cannot be held back and he may yet come at night, slipping past her father's watchmen, though the vengai has burst into flower and the full moon has risen.
nuance: The friend states the moral of the monkey herself (குறியா இன்பம் ... குறித்த இன்பம்), so this is an open comparison, not ullurai; a traditional further reading makes the drunk monkey that cannot climb the lover who will not rise to marriage. The closing signs are a warning dressed as permission: the vengai's flowering is the season of the girl's confinement and the moon lights the path he would take by night.

thinai_evidence.note: secret meeting under the father's watch, on the hill slopes

comparisons.tenor: the monkey's unplanned joy set beside the joy the hero plans and delays

reading: The man tells his heart, which showed him the long road through the waste and pushed him from behind toward wealth, that its lie, which looks like truth, cannot lift his grief when on that far road the glance of the girl with the red mouth and sweet speech, eyes that rival her curved earrings, comes across his way; and the road is the one where a red-eared vulture, to feed its mate weak from laying in the omai tree, ceaselessly tears like looters at the rotting wild cow a tiger killed and left.
nuance: The heart stands behind and drives (பின்நின்று துரக்கும்), the very phrase another paalai poet uses for a heart that stays behind and holds back (Akananuru 19). The vulture that forages for a nesting mate is the man's own errand seen from the road, and its carrion feast makes the wealth he is promised look like plunder.

colophon.thurai: முன்னொரு காலத்து நெஞ்சினாற் பொருள்வலிக்கப்பட்டுப் பிரிந்தான் தலைமகன்; பிரிந்து இடைச்சுரத்தினின்று அவள் நலநயந்து மீளலுற்ற நெஞ்சினைக் கழறிப்போய்ப் பொருண் முடித்துவந்தவன் பின்னும் பொருள்வலிக்கப்பட்ட நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லிச் செலவழுங்கியது.

thinai_evidence.note: a man argues with the heart that drives him across the waste for wealth

comparisons.tenor: the dark rough bark of the omai, like a crocodile's back
the vulture tearing at carrion, like plunderers
the heart's promise, a lie that looks like truth
her red mouth, like the coral-tree petal

iraicchi.act: the male vulture flies out hungry to bring food to its mate, who has laid and lies weak in the nest
iraicchi.sense: a male's errand is for the mate he leaves weak at home, which is the very claim of the heart's errand for wealth and the reason the man turns back to her

reading: The friend shows the woman the season: jasmine has put out its tips, konrai buds open, the stag with horns like twisted iron leaps into the gravel hollows and rain has made the forest lovely; look, there comes the chariot of the lord of the low hills, its reins drawn taut as lute-strings and its bell-tongues tied so as not to startle the nectar birds asleep with their mates in the flowering boughs, as he comes thinking of her beauty, fragrant as the kanthal opening on the tall hill east of festive Uranthai.
nuance: The man's tying of the bells is the poem's proof of his tenderness: a man who will not wake sleeping pairs of birds is hurrying to his own pair. The rain does the promising before he arrives (கார்செய்தன்றே), as the friend's argument requires.

thinai_evidence.note: the rains have come to the jasmine forest, the season of his promised return

comparisons.tenor: the stag's dark horns, like twisted iron
the drawn reins, taut as strung lute-strings
her beauty, fragrant as the opening kanthal

iraicchi.act: the nectar birds sleep in the flowering boughs together with their mates
iraicchi.sense: the man who will not wake a pair asleep is coming home to rest with his own wife

reading: The man tells his heart why he gave up the journey: when he thought of crossing the stony, useless forest where gooseberries fall like dice on the rock and sharp stones cut the toes, she came near unasked, with a faint forced smile, said nothing but stood like a painting as if assenting to the old saying that such leaving is not the way of right, and when, eyes swimming, she sighed over the garland on the head of the son held to her breast, its bright flower lost its colour; seeing that he stayed, for she grieves even with him beside her and would not live if they parted.
nuance: Her whole argument is unspoken: she refuses by looking (முன்னம் காட்டி, முகத்தின் உரையா), and the decisive sign is not on her but on the child, the garland withering under her breath. The old maxim she seems to accept, அறத்தாறு அன்று, is the poem's only statement of a rule, and it is attributed to tradition, not to her.

colophon.thurai: பொருள் வயிற் பிரியக் கருதிய தலைமகன் தன்னெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லிச் செலவழுங்கியது.

thinai_evidence.note: a man weighs crossing the waste for wealth and gives it up

comparisons.tenor: the fallen gooseberries on the rock, like gaming dice heaped up
the blunted points of the stones, as if worn down
the ridged sharp stones, set in rows like garden beds
her silence, as if she said 'so be it' to the old saying
her stillness, like a painted figure

reading: The wife tells the husband back from a courtesan that yesterday he bathed with his beloved in the Kaveri flood at Uranthai of the generous Thithan, clasping a white reed raft, faces bright like the Poozhiyar's elephant in a pond, his garland crushed on his chest; today he comes and repeats lies about 'the mother of his son, of spotless chastity', mocking her age, which she lets pass: her youth, like Mathi's Kazhar where the otter that fed on vaalai fish among the vallai creepers goes back to rest in the old cane thicket, is long gone, so what can sweet lies do for her.
nuance: The otter that feasts in the lotus field and then returns to the old thorny cane is set inside the simile for her lost youth: she pictures him eating among new flowers and sheltering in the old thicket, which is herself. The praise he offers (மாசில் கற்பின், புதல்வன் தாய்) is the true wifely title, and she calls it a lie because it is said to placate her.

colophon.thurai: பரத்தையிற் பிரிந்து வந்த தலைமகற்குக் கிழத்தி கூறியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife's quarrel with a husband who has been with another woman

comparisons.tenor: the lovers' delighted faces in the water, like the Poozhiyar's elephant in a pond
her youth, rich and gone like Mathi's Kazhar
the husband, who feasts among new women and returns to the old wife

ullurai.tenor: the husband, his courtesan and his aging wife

pairs.situation: he has feasted on a new woman
he has tangled the household's order
he comes back to shelter with the old wife

ullurai.speaker_fit: the wife uses the otter of the marutham fields of her own town, a thing she knows (porul 7.26)

reading: The foster mother, following her daughter who has eloped, recalls her warnings (your breasts have formed, you are no child now, keep away from the old town's spirits and do not go out), and asks a doe with its herd, and a hill girl wearing a tiger-tooth tali who gathers the jackfruit seeds the grazing stag drops, whether they have seen her girl, who fled like a hind that sees a net, with a youth of white spear into this waste, while robbers raiding a cattle-pen have blocked her pursuit.
nuance: The first lines quote the very prohibitions the girl escaped; the mother's list of the signs of puberty is also her account of why the girl left. Her questions go to a doe and to a hill girl like her daughter, as if the wild had become the only household left to ask.

colophon.thurai: மகட் போக்கிய செவிலித்தாய் பின் சென்று தான் கானகத்தே கண்டதோர் மகளைக் கண்டு சொல்லியது; நவ்விப் பிணாக்கண்டு சொல்லியதூஉமாம்.

thinai_evidence.note: a girl has gone with her lover across the waste

thurai_akam.speaker: sevili

occasion.words: தான் கானகத்தே கண்டதோர் மகளைக் கண்டு சொல்லியது

thurai_akam.note: a girl of the forest

thurai_akam.speaker: sevili
thurai_akam.note: a doe

comparisons.tenor: the daughter fleeing the house, like a hind that has seen a net

reading: The woman tells her friend, while her lover stands unseen nearby, that even the midnight when the bear clawing termites from the wet anthill makes snakes lose their strength would not be hard to face, if only someone would ask him: in your land, where the tiger drags the boar it killed so the jackfruit slope reeks of flesh and the cow elephant breaks a great tree to ease her mate trapped in a pit, do you who led her off the path even know this road, where she came by lightning flashes without losing her way, gathering her rain-wet hair over her back and wringing it?
nuance: She wants the danger she has run spoken to him by someone else; the poem is overheard reproach. The cow elephant crashing down a tree for her mate in the pit is the one tender act among the beasts, and it is what she herself has been doing.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் சிறைப்புறத்தானாகத் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லுவாளாய்த் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: a midnight tryst on the hill slopes

iraicchi.act: the cow elephant breaks a great tree to ease the pain of her mate fallen into a pit
iraicchi.sense: she braves the night for him as the cow labours for her trapped mate, while he does not see what it costs her

reading: Returning with his work done, the man tells his heart, the charioteer listening, that it raced ahead of the sleepless chariot past the iruppai-strewn red path and the hill where pestle songs echo with the owl, and asks whether it has already reached her, standing at a corner of the tall house in the evening when calves come home, praying at every chirp of the lizard, and crept up with hand unraised to cover her eyes, touch her braid and stroke her bangled arm.
nuance: The man's homecoming is imagined from her side: the evening, the lizard's omen, the game of covering her eyes, all happen in the heart before the body arrives. The road's iruppai and red earth belong to the waste, but the poem's situation is the mullai return and the woman waiting at dusk.

colophon.thurai: வினைமுற்றி மீண்ட தலைமகன் தேர்ப்பாகன் கேட்பச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the work is done and she waits at evening for his return; the waste is only the road

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the charioteer overhears

comparisons.tenor: the iruppai buds, like arrow points
the soft hollow iruppai flowers, like butter
the red hill slope, like coral
her braid, like a cow elephant's trunk

reading: The friend stops the shore lord leaving after a night meeting and tells him, lord of the coast where birds settle on the old punnai whose buds look like fish eyes, that if he means to part and make the girl's neythal eyes weep he has taken on a hard thing; he must marry her properly and take her, for her beauty is like rich Thondi, where fishermen with new nets share out the horned fish on the sandy shore of the fragrant hamlet.
nuance: The friend values the girl in the currency of a Chera port: a public, famous, prosperous town, the opposite of a secret meeting. The fishermen's sharing of the catch is a picture of open, rightful taking, which is what she asks of him (உரிதினின் கொண்டு).

colophon.thurai: இரவுக் குறிவந்து தலைமகளைக் கண்ணுற்று நீங்குந் தலைமகனை எதிர்ப்பட்டு நின்று தோழி சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the punnai, the fishermen and the lord of the shore

occasion.words: இரவுக் குறிவந்து தலைமகளைக் கண்ணுற்று நீங்குந் தலைமகனை

comparisons.tenor: the punnai buds, like fish eyes

reading: The woman tells her friend that had he taken her with him through the sun-scorched forest where the leafless silk-cotton blooms like rows of festival lamps and the pools have turned to dust, he too would have had her close embrace on the sandbank of the forest stream under the drooping flowered boughs, and her eyes, which now weep every night like dripping flowers as if to fill a dry tank, would have slept.
nuance: She turns the usual argument round: the road is not too hard for her; it is the place where their embrace could have been. The colophon reads the poem as her assurance that she will bear up, but what it says is that she does not: the assurance lies in her saying it calmly, not in its content.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பொருள்வயிற் பிரிந்தவிடத்து ஆற்றாளாய தலைமகள் வேறுபாடுகண்டு ஆற்றாளாய தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் ஆற்றுவல் என்பதுபடச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the sun-burned forest the man has crossed without her

comparisons.tenor: the sun's disc, red as fire
the silk-cotton in flower, like long rows of festival lamps
the heaped sand of the stream bank, like spread cloth
the embrace, as if body entered body
her streaming eyes, like flowers dripping water
her nightly weeping, as if to fill a dried tank

tamil: யாமே, பிரிவு இன்று இயைந்த துவரா நட்பின்,
reading: The friend tells the hill lord that the girl's mother loves her more than her own eyes, her father cannot bear her small feet on hard ground, and the two of them are one life like the two-headed bird; on his hill, where an elephant takes the vengai flowers strewn over the hunters' hut for a tiger and flees through the bamboo, if he comes (by night) the gentle girl will not survive.
nuance: The household's love is given as the guard itself: the closer they hold her, the less she can slip away. The elephant that bolts from vengai blossom mistaken for a tiger is a hill scene of false alarm; a reader may hear in it the danger of discovery, but it maps to no stated situation. Whether 'we' (யாமே) are the girl and her friend or the girl and her lover is open.

colophon.thurai: "பகற்குறி வாரா நின்ற தலைமகன் தோழியாற் செறிப்பறிவுறுக்கப்பட்டு இரவுக்குறி வாரா வரைவல் என்றாற்கு, அதுவும் மறுத்து வரைவு கடாயது.

thinai_evidence.note: millet guards, hill hunters and the vengai of the hill

occasion.words: இரவுக்குறி வாரா வரைவல் என்றாற்கு, அதுவும் மறுத்து வரைவு கடாயது

comparisons.tenor: the two women (or the two lovers), one life like the two-headed bird

reading: The friend tells the man that even if the wealth he would earn were as great as the fruitful sacrifice of the Pandya's warrior, lord of Kodai, who wears the pearl of his sea and the sandal of his hill and gives to suppliants without limit except the short while it takes to teach a pit-caught elephant to obey, he should not leave his gentle companion in these days of cold dew, when the lonely north wind sways the forked paddy in the wide fields and makes the white heron on the sugarcane cry; let the wealth go, and the nights in a clean bed without embrace.
nuance: The patron's limitless giving is the measure, and the friend uses it to set a ceiling: no wealth, not even such a man's, is worth a winter apart. The two clauses of wishing (நோய் இன்றாக செய்பொருள்; கவவுஇன் புறாமைக் கழிக) can be read as bitter dismissal or as a blessing on his going, which is why the colophon allows that she consented.

colophon.thurai: பொருள் வயிற் பிரியலுற்ற தலைமகனைத் தோழி செலவழங்கு வித்தது; உடம்பட்டதூஉமாம்.

thinai_evidence.note: the friend argues against a departure for wealth

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: she consents to his going

comparisons.tenor: the wealth he would earn, measured against the patron's great sacrifice
the paddy's young blades, like flame tips

reading: The bard tells his companions that the wife said to him, 'if he does not remember us even in this evening, when the stag nuzzles its doe and leaps grazing on the red-earth road strewn with kaya flowers, herders deck themselves in the jasmine land and good cows, udders dripping, low for their calves as they crowd into the common, what will become of us by morning, bard?'; unable to answer, he played his lute, praised the god, steadied his grief and went toward the husband, and now he has seen his tall chariot coming, wheels roaring like thunder-clouds.
nuance: The bard's own answer to her question is not words but music and prayer, and then a sighting; the poem moves from her evening to his seeing. Evening in the jasmine land is the hour when everything returns to its pair, which is why it is the measure of his forgetting.

thinai_evidence.note: evening in the jasmine land, the herders and cows coming home

thurai_akam.note: those close to him

the hills, like coral studded with gems
the roar of the chariot wheels, like thunder of rain clouds

iraicchi.sense: in this season even the stag keeps to its mate, yet the husband has not come home to his

reading: The mother whose daughter has eloped wishes that, if her fierce longing can be granted, the old town of the man's many hamlets may know how to welcome her, as the Kosar's Thulu country, with its peacock groves, shelters empty-handed travellers; for her soft-shouldered dear one, leaving her friends and mother lonely, has slipped the strict guard of a house like Nannan's fortress Pazhi and gone with him on the road where bears scatter the iruppai flowers and konrai pods, set on her sweet companion.
nuance: Her grief turns into a blessing on the stranger's town. The house is likened to Nannan's guarded Pazhi so that the breach looks like the fall of a fort; the girl's resolve (இன்துணைப் படர்ந்த கொள்கை) is acknowledged, not condemned.

thinai_evidence.note: the daughter has gone with her lover across the waste

thurai_akam.speaker: nartaay
thurai_akam.note: no one is addressed

comparisons.tenor: the man's old town, hoped to be as hospitable as the Kosar's Thulu country
the guarded house, like Nannan's fortress Pazhi
her shoulders, rounded like hill bamboo

tamil: 'வருக மாள, என் உயிர்!' எனப் பெரிது உவந்து
reading: The wife tells her husband, who claims he knows no other woman, that she saw a sharp-toothed girl find their little son alone in the chariot street, lift him to her ornamented breast crying 'come, my life!' when no one was looking; she went up and asked 'why so flustered, spotless girl? are you his mother too?', embraced her, and watched her bow her head, scratch the ground and stand ashamed like one caught in a secret; and so, she asks, did she not treat her kindly, since that goddess-like woman is fit to be his son's mother?
nuance: The proof against his denial is the courtesan's love for the child, and the wife's weapon is courtesy: she embraces the rival and then, with full irony, ranks her as fit to be the son's mother, which is the title the husband had denied anyone else could claim.

colophon.thurai: பரத்தையர் சேரியினின்றும் வந்த தலைமகன் யாரையும் அறியேனென்றாற்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife's quarrel over a rival, with the son between them

comparisons.tenor: the child's spotless palm, like a lotus petal
the child's mouth, like coral-red gem
the courtesan's shame, like one who has owned to a theft
the courtesan, like an unapproachable goddess of the sky

reading: The foster mother remembers that her girl, if she threw a ball a little or played jacks with her friends, would say 'mother, I am tired' and lie in her arms with sweat on her brow; now, forgetting kin and nurse, she has crossed her proud father's strict guard and given her whole heart to a stranger, and the nurse asks whether those little anklet feet can walk the waterless waste where salt-carters' calls echo in the hills and the falling silk-cotton flowers flicker like festival lamps or like stars at dawn, under the dark hill that bars the way.
nuance: The whole poem rests on one contrast: a girl too tired for a ball game now walking the waste. The silk-cotton flowers like lamps in an old town's festival bring the home town into the wilderness, the place she has left as a light falling on her road.

reading: The friend asks the hill lord whether anyone comes here at midnight, crossing like a fierce boar the dreadful ford of the forest torrent, its water hidden under fallen flowers, where crocodiles sleep in the eddies and the flood drags off a wild elephant; if her friend suffers harm even for a day she will not live after, and even on safe paths those who go often slip, so they live in fear; let him come by day and meet her in the kanthal grove below the honey-combed hill of their garden, and hold the soft shoulders, like bamboo, that her mother reared.
nuance: She does not forbid the meeting; she moves it. The danger she names is the road's, but the argument is also about discovery: the frequent traveller slips (பயில வழங்குநர் ... இழுக்குவர்), and a secret repeated becomes known.

tamil: வருந்தினை- வாழி, என் நெஞ்சே!- பருந்து இருந்து
reading: The man, on his way for wealth, tells his heart that it neither stayed with her then nor will cross the hills with him now, where the kite cries wearily from the tall yaa and the owl hoots like a drum; if it means to stay behind, let it go back, prosper, and not forget him, once it has embraced the tired drooping back of his love, who sits unmoving with a lamp for company, her dark lily eyelids gone red and burning with every thought of him, hot tears falling, bangles slipping from her wrist, wilting like a creeper that has shed its flowers.

nuance: The list of shore games is a portrait of a girlhood now closed by gossip, and it is spoken for the hidden lover to hear: the last line names his chariot as the cause, so the report is also a summons to marry.

title: களிற்றியானைநிரை 21-40
theme: Akananuru 21 to 40, in the anthology's fixed order of lands: ten paalai poems of men on the road to wealth arguing with their hearts and women counting seasons, set beside hill courtships at the millet field, marutham quarrels settled by a child or sharpened by gossip, mullai camps and homecomings, and neythal evenings. Puram fame (Alankanam, Thithiyan, Kari's Pennai, Korkai, Kolli) supplies the similes for private feeling.
source_issues: 22, 24, 37: the colophon thurai is numbered (1) but gives no second alternative.
25: line 7 reads படுநா விளியா னடுநின்று, which looks corrupt (the word division and the sense are unclear).
31: the colophon thurai breaks off (…பிறர் சொல்லக் கேட்டு) without the speaker or the verb; the speaker is inferred from the poem.
32: the text flag notes a printed line number 51 standing on line 15, a stray number in the base text.
38: line 15 has ஐ.தேங்கு with a stray full stop, and line 17 கணஃது; both look corrupt.
39: the record has no colophon thurai and no poet (the flags say the colophon and verse block were not found in the commentary section).
21, 39: stray or unbalanced opening quotation marks at line 1.

tamil: எழுஇனி, வாழி என் நெஞ்சே!- புரி இணர்

nuance: The roles are reversed from the usual quarrel: the man had argued for staying, the heart for going, and now he holds the heart to its own choice. The goal is named as மனைநக, that the house may laugh, so the journey is cast as a gift to the home rather than flight from it.

reading: The girl recalls the midnight rite her mother held to cure her: old women said Murugan's power had seized her, the velan sacrificed and scattered red millet with blood, and in that very night her lover slipped past the house guards like a hunting tiger, so that in his embrace she laughed at an offering wasted on a stranger priest while the true cure of her sickness had come.
nuance: She speaks to defend the man her friend has just blamed, and the defence is a confession: he risked the guarded house on the night of the rite. Her laughter judges the rite only as a diagnosis; it does not deny the god, whose fierce presence (அணங்கு, உருகெழு) the poem keeps.

reading: The rains have spent themselves, the forest is fragrant with opening jasmine and pidavam, and in the hollows the stag, done grazing, embraces his doe, drinks the cool water and lies down; the woman asks her friend whether this is the time her man meant when he pointed to the jasmine on the house's nochi and said he would return by then from the wealth he went to earn.

reading: Seeing her weep that spring, with its sandbanks of kaanji pollen and its cuckoos calling in turn, is surely the sign her man set for his return, her friend promises that he who crossed the hills whose falls sound like the music of Thithiyan, lord of Pothiyil, will come quickly with soft words of sorrow for her tears.
nuance: The friend puts apology into the absent man's mouth before he has come (நோவல், குறுமகள்), so her comfort is a script for his return. The spring is described as a season that even scorners cannot scorn, which makes his absence from it harder to excuse.

reading: The wife asks her friend how she could sulk with her husband: once he praised her breasts and would not stop embracing, but lately he held back for fear of spilling the milk meant for their son, so she turned to the boy in the nurse's arms saying he suits the good women and she suits the son, and at that he said he too loved the child, held her from behind and wept, melting like ploughed red earth in the rain.
nuance: The child decides the quarrel twice: he is her reason to withdraw and the man's way back to her. The rain-on-ploughed-field simile gives the melting to him, so her question (புலத்தல் கூடுமோ) means that his tears have left her no ground for sulking.

reading: The friend tells the girl, who has paled on hearing that her man will leave to fetch wealth across the tiger's forest, that she is naive: even if her red mouth with teeth like the pearls of Korkai does not hold him, how could her eyes, which outdo the blue lily and fight like a victorious spear swinging with blood, let him go?
nuance: The friend argues from the girl's own beauty, which is a comfort and a reproach at once: her body should be his reason to stay. The pearl simile carries a whole Pandya world (the Venkatam elephant, Korkai guarded by aram) into a two-line image of her teeth.

tamil: உறற்கு அரிது ஆகும், அவன் மலர்ந்த மார்பே!
reading: With the man listening nearby, the friend warns the girl that the millet ears are bowing and harvested stalks are showing in the fields: if she, content with her hunter, does not rise and scare the parrots, her mother will say she cannot guard the crop and send others, and then his broad chest will be hard to reach.
nuance: The warning is meant for the overhearing man: the ripening millet dates the end of the field meetings, so he must turn the secret love into marriage before the harvest closes it.

reading: Back from his work, the man answers his wife, who asks with a fading smile whether he forgot her: he left vowing that a day without thinking of her eyes would not be worth living, and in the burning waste where elephants chase mirages and wilt like boats in dried water, only his body stayed there, bound by shame to finish the task, while his foolish heart was always with her.
nuance: He splits himself to answer the charge: the body (உடம்பு) was held by நாண், the shame of an unfinished task, and the heart (நெஞ்சம்) never left. The tiger that will not eat prey fallen on its left side measures his resolve by a hunter's code of honour.

reading: The friend tells the lord of a shore where fishermen haul in their catch together like ploughmen at a threshing floor, fling fish to fill the empty pots of those who beg, and sleep on the high dunes, that greatness is not lost by coming one day to the cool punnai grove and asking how she fares, and implies that to ask once and leave is no greatness.
nuance: The two closing lines can be read as a plea (would your greatness suffer if you came and asked?) or as a reproach (is it greatness to come once, ask, and go?); the generosity of his own fishermen is set before him as a standard either way.

reading: Hearing it said that she cannot bear the parting, the woman tells her friend of the road her man took: a season of failed rain when the fiery sun scorched the land, where bowmen of the rock forts shoot travellers whose eyes the vultures pluck, beyond which lie the many hills of the land of changed speech, outside the rule of the three Tamil kings.

reading: She tells her friend how yesterday a jewelled man, looking like a patron but pleading like a suppliant, came to the millet field, called her a hill goddess who had stricken him and held her from behind; melting inside but afraid he would see it, she broke free like a startled doe and stood firm, and he went off like an elephant parted from its herd, so now she proposes they go and laugh at the gracious man who keeps trying, not knowing her shoulders are his alone.
nuance: Puram's pair of giver and receiver (புரவலன், இரவல்) is turned inside out: the man who looks like a patron begs. The plan to laugh at him is an assent in disguise, since in the same breath she says the claim to her shoulders is his.

reading: On the road the man tells his heart, which wants to turn back: it chose to leave the virtuous wife and to cross the land where a kite calls its mate, and now, halfway over the gravel hills, it would be better never to have parted from her with shoulders like the bamboo of Vanavan's Kolli; but to break off the work now would only win the laughter of others.
nuance: The poem does not deny the heart's longing; it concedes that never leaving would have been good (நன்றுமற் றில்ல) and then argues that turning back now is worse. Shame before others (பிறர்நகு) is the last argument, not wealth.

reading: A mother whose daughter has run off with a man prays: the girl, forgetting those who bore and raised her, left the high-walled house desolate and dared the flesh-smelling road where bowmen honour hero-stones with peacock feathers, drums and toddy; may the stranger who became her companion in an unknown land adorn her again and again and put her to sleep on his chest, her curled hair like the fine ripples of Kari's Pennai river.
nuance: The prayer hands the stranger her own office: அணிந்து அணிந்து, adorning again and again, is what a mother does. The road is marked by offerings to the dead, so the daughter's path into marriage is drawn through a landscape of graves.

reading: The wife tells her husband, lord of a town where a great striped varal fish swallows the hook, tears the water-lily leaves, crushes the blue lilies, tangles the vallai creeper and will not come to the angler's pull, raging like a roped bull as it churns the pond each day, that the gossip of his wedding with a young girl in the marutham grove on the Vaigai's sands is louder than the shout of Chezhiyan's warriors on the day he crushed seven kings at Alankanam.
nuance: The gossip is measured by the most famous victory shout the audience knew, so a private wrong is given the volume of a public war. The fish's scene is the wife's hidden charge; the battle simile is her open one.

tamil: மறந்து, அவண் அமையார் ஆயினும், கறங்கு இசைக்
reading: Breaking down under her friend's reassurance, the woman says that even if he has not forgotten her, this is the lovely spring: farmers thresh all night under dust like mist, rise at dawn to pluck mangoes green as parrots, drink new brew from leaf cups like oxen at a pond, eat horsegram and lentil porridge with milk, and rest at noon with their oxen in the marutham shade, a sweet season only for those who have partners to enjoy.
nuance: The farmers' full day, from night threshing to noon's rest with the oxen, is a picture of shared life; only the last line turns the whole landscape into her lack.

thinai_evidence.note: a woman without her partner in the spring

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the addressee, the friend who gave the reassurance, is inferred

comparisons.tenor: the threshing dust, like a misty sky hiding the quarters
the farmers drinking deep, like oxen plunging into a pond
the white porridge, like drawn rods of silver

reading: The friend imagines the hill-man, garlanded with vengai and blue lily, bow in hand, coming to the old meeting places and finding the swing on the ashoka abandoned, the pool where lilies open like eyes, and the harvested millet field, and wonders whether he will turn back grieving, since she forgot to tell him that their village is the one on the high hill crowned by the white waterfall.
nuance: 'I forgot to tell him our village' is the real message for the overhearing man: the field trysts are over, and the way to her now runs through the village, that is, through marriage. Line 15 (ஐ.தேங்கு) looks corrupt.

colophon.thurai: (1) தோழி தலைமகன் குறைகூறியது. (2) பகலே சிறைப்புறமாகத் தோழி தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லுவாளாய்த் தலைமகன் கேட்பச் சொல்லியதூஉமாம். (3) தோழி குறிபெயர்த்திட்டுச் சொல்லியதூஉமாம்.

thinai_evidence.note: hill flowers, a harvested millet field and the hill-man

occasion.words: பகலே சிறைப்புறமாகத் தோழி தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லுவாளாய்த் தலைமகன் கேட்பச் சொல்லியதூஉமாம்

comparisons.tenor: the long-petalled blue lilies of the pool, opening like eyes

reading: The returned man tells his wife not to speak like a stranger, asking whether he ever thought of her: in a vast forest swept by a wildfire from rubbing bamboo, where travellers lost the path and elephants fled a tiger, he lay at sunset thinking of her and dreamed he found her brooding with loose bangles, stroked her brow and smoothed her hair asking why she sulked, and the false dream left him with empty hands; it is she who has not cared for his distress.
nuance: He turns her charge round: her sulk is answered by his dream of answering her sulk, so the dispute is already rehearsed in the dream, and the empty hand he woke to is his evidence that he thought of her.

thinai_evidence.note: a wildfire across the great forest on the road

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the record has no colophon thurai; speaker and situation are inferred from the poem (the returned man answers her complaint)

reading: At evening on the shore, as the backwater flowers close, the sea roars and herons crowd into the punnai nests, the woman tells her friend that though her man has gone without pity and left her heart in grief, may his friendship never break, and may her heart, which went to his breast of sweet sleep, not tire of staying there for want of kindness and come back.
nuance: She blesses the bond in the same breath as she names its cruelty. The heron that flees the reapers' drum to roost in the palmyra's inner frond is the picture of her own heart, which fled the evening's pain to his breast.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பொருள்வயிற் பிரிந்துழிக் கிழத்தி தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the seashore at evening

comparisons.tenor: the heron's cry, like the horn blown at the sluice

ullurai.tenor: the woman's heart and her absent husband

pairs.situation: her heart is frightened by the evening's pain
her heart has gone to rest on his breast

ullurai.speaker_fit: the wife uses a heron of her husband's shore, near her own home and known to her (porul 7.26)

title: களிற்றியானைநிரை 41-60
theme: Akananuru 41 to 60, in the anthology's fixed order of lands: ten paalai poems of men away for wealth and women and mothers left behind, set beside hill courtships moving toward disclosure and marriage, marutham quarrels over the husband's other women, mullai homecomings and neythal pleas. Puram names (Venni, Musiri, Kurukkai, Pazhaiyan, Pannan) are used throughout as similes for private grief and joy.
source_issues: 44: the colophon thinai is the numbering rule's முல்லை; the commentary edition gives பாலை. The poem (a man returning from finished war to his wife) fits mullai.
47: the base text numbers the last line 15 though the poem has 19 lines, as the commentary edition shows; a misprinted number.
55: the colophon thurai reads தலமகட்கு, a misprint for தலைமகட்கு.
56: the colophon thurai has the corrupt word *வந்தசனாக, presumably வந்தானாக (the bard came to her house).
57: the base text has 19 lines and the commentary edition (pmuni0490_01) 18; marked as the base text stands.

reading: Away on his errand for wealth, the man looks at a dawn countryside in full beauty, the palasa ablaze with flowers, bees humming and ploughmen calling over the fields, and asks whether the dark-skinned, freckled woman he left is wasting, her shoulders slackening, in the loneliness of his absence.
nuance: The landscape gains its beauty (காடுஅணி கொண்ட) in the very lines where she loses hers (நலம் செலச் சாஅய்); the season that adorns the land is the measure of what parting takes from her, and he can only guess it with a question (கொல்லோ).

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பொருள்வயிற் பிரிந்த விடத்துக் கிழத்தியை நினைந்து சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the man speaks from inside a parting he chose; the fields around him are marutham

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named: he speaks his thought aloud

comparisons.tenor: the palasa's flowering branches, as fire
the fine freckles on her dark skin, like pollen spray on tender leaves

reading: The friend tells the heroine that the joy of a whole people when heavy rain at dawn fills a dried-out tank after a long drought has all been poured into her, because the lord of the sky-touching hills has come.
nuance: The friend speaks of her own joy, not the heroine's; the drought image measures how long the waiting for marriage had become, and the whole land rejoicing hints that the marriage will be public, the opposite of secret love.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் வரைவு மலிந்தமை தோழி தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill lord's coming to marry decides it; the drought and tank belong to the simile

comparisons.tenor: the red-cornered eyes, against the red back of jasmine buds
the tank's high banks, like hills

comparisons.vehicle: பல்லோர் உவந்த உவகை எல்லாம் என்னுள் பெய்தந் தற்று
comparisons.tenor: the friend's joy at the hill lord's coming, like the people's joy at rain after drought

reading: The man tells the heart that urged him to go for wealth that the monsoon has come, the clouds joining land and sky so that only water-clock keepers know where the sun is, and he has held his mullai-scented wife; pitiable are those who, without kindness, leave their sweet companion for a stranger's wealth.
nuance: He calls the wealth-seeker's departure மடமை, folly, the word usually kept for the woman's innocence; the cow elephant, worn by summer and now bathing with her bull in the flood, is the rains' gift to the paired, and he places himself with the pair.

thinai_evidence.note: the situation is a refused departure for wealth; the land and season are mullai's

iraicchi.act: the cow elephant, worn by the summer heat, goes into the flood to bathe together with her bull
iraicchi.sense: the rains bring the parted together, and the man who has stayed to hold his wife is doing what the elephants do

reading: The king's war is done and the enemy has paid tribute, so the man bids his charioteer drive ahead of the column, that he may sleep on the breast of a wife who is like Kudavayil, a town as rich as Chenni's Azhumbil; Chenni is the king who, unable to bear the sight of Pazhaiyan's fall, when the chiefs Nannan, Etrai, Atti, Kangan, Katti and Punthurai had massed their camp, captured Kanaiyan and took Kazhumalam.
nuance: The catalogue of chiefs and the fall of Pazhaiyan fill lines 7 to 17, and the wife is reached only through a chain of likenesses, a king, his town, another town; the war that kept him away is also the stock from which he praises her. Who fought whom in lines 7 to 14 is compressed, and this reading of it is offered with caution.

colophon.thurai: வினை முற்றி மீளுந் தலைமகன் தேர்ப்பாகற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the man returns from finished work to the waiting wife

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is the charioteer

comparisons.tenor: Kudavayil's unfailing wealth, like Chenni's Azhumbil
the wife, like the cool, rich town of Kudavayil

reading: Told to bear up, the heroine says her lover has crossed a summer forest where dry pods rattle like dancing-floor drums and the tiger springs on the waterless track; her skin must pale like peerkku flowers, the gossip is louder than the bards' clamour the day Anni cut down Thithiyan's punnai at Kurukkai, and she will wander distraught like Aathimanthi, sleepless as a broken fort shaken by the Chera's assault.
nuance: Every likeness she reaches for is a public disaster: a battlefield's din, a famous madwoman, a sacked fort. Her private loss is told in the scale of puram events, which is how she answers the friend's claim that it can be borne.

thinai_evidence.note: the lover has gone through the forest and she cannot bear it

comparisons.tenor: the rattling of dry uzhinjil pods, like the dancing-floor drum
her pallor, like the peerkku flower
the gossip, louder than the bards' clamour at Kurukkai
her sleepless dread, like a broken-walled fort under assault

reading: The friend refuses the man entry: he is lord of a town where a red-eyed buffalo, tired of the mud, breaks its tether in the sleeping night, pushes through the thorn fence, scatters the fish and grazes the lotus; they say he has brought another woman home and married her, and the friend will not say it herself, but her bangle, like Chezhiyan's Allur, may slip if it must; go, lord, who is stopping you?
nuance: The refusal is made as a release: யாரையோ நிற் புலக்கேம் (who are we to quarrel with you) and நிற் றகைக்குநர் யாரோ (who is there to stop you) deny her any claim on him, which is the sharpest claim she can make. The report of the wedding is put in others' mouths (என்ப).

colophon.thurai: வாயில் வேண்டிச் சென்ற தலைமகற்குத் தோழி வாயின் மறுத்தது.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife's side quarrels with a husband who has taken another woman

comparisons.tenor: the husband who breaks the household's bond for a new woman
the speaker's bright bangle, rich and fine as Chezhiyan's town Allur

ullurai.tenor: the husband and the new wife he has brought home

pairs.situation: he breaks the bond of his household
he does it secretly, while the town sleeps
the household is thrown into disorder
he enjoys the new woman

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses a buffalo of the marutham fields in a marutham poem, without leaving the land (porul 7.27)

reading: The man tells his faltering heart to rise quickly now the work is done, cross the hot wilderness where wind-whipped bamboo catches fire, the flames leap the crags and cracking joints scatter the stags, and at dusk, when lamps are lit and the male dove calls its mate in the tall house, reach her who weeps asking where he is, and embrace many times her bamboo-smooth shoulders, fragrant with the koothalam of Chezhiyan's Sirumalai.
nuance: He pictures the dusk at home before he has crossed the fire: the lamps, the calling dove and her question 'யாண்டு உளர்கொல்?' are what make the burning road crossable.

thinai_evidence.note: the hot wilderness to be crossed on the way home

iraicchi.act: at lamp-lighting the red-legged male dove calls to its beloved mate in the tall house
iraicchi.sense: at the hour when even the dove calls its mate home, the husband's absence is felt most, and his return is owed

reading: The friend answers the foster mother, who asks why her daughter will not drink milk and has paled: when the girls went to pick vengai flowers and someone cried 'tiger', a garlanded young hunter came asking which way the beast went, asked if such girls could lie, gazed long at her daughter's eyes and drove away, and at sunset the daughter looked where he had gone and said 'he is a man indeed'; the wise can measure the rest.
nuance: The friend never names love. She gives the scene and the daughter's one sentence and leaves the inference to the foster mother (மதிவல் லோர்க்கே), a disclosure that keeps the girl's modesty. His question about lies plays on their silence: they hid and did not answer where the beast went.

thinai_evidence.note: a first meeting with the hill lord on the slope

comparisons.tenor: the red water-lily petals of his garland, like eyes

reading: The foster mother grieves at home: she had seen the girl who loved her parrot, ball and play-seeds grow unlike herself, had come close, stroked her forehead and held her, and the girl had embraced her again and again; had she known the girl would go, praising the tall man, through a forest where tired deer chew withered marul in the rainless shade, she would have followed her like her own shadow wherever she played in her father's house.
nuance: Her regret is not that she failed to stop the girl but that she was not near enough: the shadow image (மெய்ந்நிழல் போல) makes her wish to have gone along. The girl's many embraces, read now, were a farewell the mother did not understand.

colophon.thurai: உடன் போயின தலைமகளை நினைந்து செவிலித்தாய் மனையின்கண் வருந்தியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the girl has gone with her lover through the forest

thurai_akam.speaker: sevili
thurai_akam.note: she grieves alone at home; no hearer is named

comparisons.tenor: the foster mother watching the girl's back, like a cow tied with its calf
the foster mother following the girl everywhere, like the body's shadow

reading: The friend tells the bard that the shore lord once came often, even by day, despite the leaping fish of the backwater and the red-mouthed women's gossip, and now stays away; she asks him to go secretly to the old town and tell the hero what the bright-browed girl says as she hides her tears: 'see, the anril on the palmyra by the house cannot sleep at night if parted from its mate even once; what shall I do?'
nuance: The anril is the girl's own message, not an image the poem lodges: she uses the bird to say that she cannot sleep, so it carries the sense openly rather than as iraicchi. The friend, not the girl, chooses the bard as carrier, and asks him to go secretly.

thinai_evidence.note: the backwater and the shore lord

reading: The man tells his heart, which urged him to leave, that in the peopleless summer wilderness where a male vulture with flesh-red ears sits scorched on a burnt yaa tree gazing at its hungry mate, the wealth he would toil for is not worth having if it comes only by parting from his wife: better to stay, hold her close so her jewels jingle, and be glad in the household's work.
nuance: The hinge is the play on புணர்வு: wealth is 'joined' only by parting, and staying is the other joining, with her. The vulture stays by its mate in the burning tree; the hearth (மனைமுதல் வினை) is set against the work (செய்வினை) abroad.

thinai_evidence.note: the summer wilderness he refuses to cross

comparisons.tenor: the vulture's red ears, like flesh stuck on

iraicchi.act: the male vulture, its wings scorched, stays on the burning tree looking at the face of its hungry mate
iraicchi.sense: even the vulture in the fire does not leave its mate, which is the choice the man makes against his heart

reading: The heroine tells her friend that the two-sided question, whether to tell mother of the hill lord whose wide chest their heart loves, a lord of a land where a girl's cry for vengai flowers brings the men running with bows for a cattle-seizing tiger, has been settled one way: even if her life leaves her body, the friend must not say that her pallor is love-sickness.
nuance: The colophon says she speaks knowing the friend will disclose; her forbidding is modesty speaking, and the oath (இன்உயிர் கழிவது ஆயினும்) shows the cost she sets on silence. The false alarm on the hill, a girl's cry taken for a tiger's threat, is how secrets get out in this land.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகள் வேறுபட்டமையறிந்த செவிலித்தாய்க்குத் தோழி அறத்தொடு நிற்குமெனத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill slope and the hill lord

comparisons.tenor: the new vengai flowers, like gold

reading: The heroine tells the friend who urges patience that she does not know: he has crossed the waterless wilderness of drumstick flowers and cactus, where a red dog rests with its starving mate in the shade of a lettered hero-stone, because his heart cannot hide what it has when the needy say they have nothing; his love is for wealth more than for her, and the friend calls it grace.
nuance: She grants him the virtue and turns it against her: the inability to refuse the poor is what takes him away, so his generosity and his desertion are the same act. The last two lines set காதல் against காதல் and பொருள் against அருள்.

thinai_evidence.note: the waterless wilderness he crossed

iraicchi.act: the red dog, itself hungry, keeps with its starving mate and rests beside her in the hero-stone's shade
iraicchi.sense: even the wild dog of that waste stays with its hungry mate, while the man has left his for wealth

reading: The guest kings have paid tribute and the king's anger has cooled, the rains have come, so the man bids his charioteer drive over the red earth that the cochineal beetles make like a painting: at dusk, when the cattle hurry home to their calves with the cowherds behind, he wants to see his wife beckon the young moon with her finger, prattling sweet as water after gooseberries from the garden of Pannan, who lives for others, promising it milk if it brings their son a gold tali.
nuance: What he hurries home to is not her waiting but her play: the mother tricking the child with the moon (புதல்வற் பொய்க்கும்). The village whose gooseberry gives the simile is that of Pannan, praised in one line as தனக்கென வாழாப் பிறர்க்கு உரியாளன், a puram patron lodged inside an akam homecoming.

thinai_evidence.note: the rains, the evening and the cowherds driving cattle home

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is the charioteer

comparisons.tenor: the red earth strewn with velvet mites, like a painting
her sweet prattle, like water to one who has eaten green gooseberry

iraicchi.act: at dusk the milch cows, udders full, hurry lowing to the homes where their tethered calves wait
iraicchi.sense: the man's return at the same hour is the cattle's return to their young: he goes home to his wife and son

reading: The mother tells the neighbour women who console her that she does not grieve that her daughter went with a youth strong as an elephant across the sun-cracked waste; she lies sleepless, breathing hot like a forge's bellows, and quarrels with her own life, which will not leave her to go after the girl as the noble men who heard Cheralathan, shamed by his back wound at Venni, sit facing north, died to go with him.
nuance: She accepts the match (கழிந்ததற்கு அழிந்தன்றோ இலனே) and turns her anger on her own life for staying. The puram image is chosen for its followers, not its king: the companions who chose death with him are what her life refuses to be.

colophon.thurai: புணர்ந்துடன் போன தலமகட்கு இரங்கிய தாய் தெருட்டும் அயலிலாட்டியர்க்கு உரைத்தது.

thinai_evidence.note: the daughter has gone with her lover across the waste

thurai_akam.speaker: nartaay
thurai_akam.note: the addressees are the neighbour women who console her

comparisons.tenor: the youth, strong as an elephant
her hot inward breathing, like a forge's bellows

comparisons.vehicle: சான்றோர் அரும்பெறல் உலகத்து அவனொடு செலீஇயர் பெரும்பிறிது ஆகி யாங்கு
comparisons.tenor: her life, which will not follow her daughter as the noble men followed their king into death

reading: The heroine laughs to her friend that yesterday the bard of the lord of the cool ford, where a black-horned buffalo stirs the gem-clear pond, gorges on lilies and comes home dusted with kaanji pollen, was hurrying to bring new brides to the lord's chest when a newly calved cow charged him; he dropped his lute and ran into her house, and when she hid her mirth and said 'this is not your house, that one is', he stood bewildered with folded hands.
nuance: The laugh is the weapon: by sending the bard to 'your house' she names the courtesan's house as his true home and her husband's errand-runner as a stranger in hers. The joy she hides (மெய்ம்மலி உவகை மறையினென்) is a joy in his discomfiture.

colophon.thurai: பரத்தைமனைக்குச் செல்கின்ற பாணன் தன் மனைக்கு *வந்தசனாகத் தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the husband's new women and the bard who serves them

comparisons.tenor: the clear pond, like a gem
the buffalo's black horns, like wrought iron
the husband who takes many new women and comes home marked by them

ullurai.tenor: the husband and his new brides

pairs.situation: he takes many new women
he comes home bearing their marks
the household's calm is troubled

ullurai.speaker_fit: the heroine uses the buffalo at the pond of her own town, a thing she knows (porul 7.26)

reading: On the summer road among the hills, where a small green-feathered female bird crosses the sky in the heat, finds no fruit on the bare fig whose roots hang like an elephant's trunk, and faints remembering the days of plenty, the man, alone, wonders whether his wife's beauty, bright as the full moon, has turned to the colour of peerkku flowers, as she weeps night and day like the wounded in Chezhiyan's siege of Musiri.
nuance: The bird comes to a tree that once fed it and finds it empty, as the man imagines his wife finding the days of their life together gone; the war simile of the wounded at Musiri makes her grief a casualty of the same world of kings and wealth that took him away.

colophon.thurai: பொருள் வயிற் பிரிந்த தலைமகன் கிழத்தியை நினைந்து சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the long summer road

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named

comparisons.tenor: the fig's hanging roots, like an elephant's raised trunk
her beauty, like the full moon
her paled colour, like peerkku flowers
her suffering, like that of the gravely wounded at Musiri

iraicchi.act: the female bird comes back to the fig that once fed her, finds no fruit, and wilts remembering the days of plenty
iraicchi.sense: the wife, left alone, remembers the full days together and finds them gone

reading: The heroine tells the hill lord, whose land is one where at midnight in cold-season rain the hunter father of the hill girls, finding no game, keeps to his house on a tiger-skin bed, that it is sweet when her arms clasp his back on his chest; but the cold north wind, which torments her whenever she thinks of him in his absence, waits long outside at midnight, bending the house tree, looking for its chance.
nuance: The father kept home by the rain is the danger to their meeting, and the wind that waits outside is like the lover who stood outside; the close of the poem (நெடும்புற நிலையே) may be his long waiting or the wind's, and the reading turns on which.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill lord and the midnight of the cold season

reading: The friend tells the heroine, whose eyes have lost their flower-like beauty, that on the road taken by the man who went far for wealth a bull elephant bends a tall yaa tree with his head so his young mate can eat its shoots, as Maal trod down a tree on the Yamuna's sands to give the cowherd girls leaf-skirts; yet those men do not remember even the mornings when they praised her back, lovely as the water-lily of Murugan's Parankunram, and have left her shoulders to slacken.
nuance: The comfort is double: the elephant who feeds his mate is meant to promise the man's return, while the friend also admits he does not think of her. The god's image of a tree bent for women's sake makes the elephant's care a divine habit.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பிரிவின்கண் வேறுபட்ட கிழத்திக்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the man has left for wealth in a far land

comparisons.tenor: the bull elephant bending the yaa tree for his mate, like Maal treading down a tree for the cowherd girls

iraicchi.act: the bull elephant bends the tall yaa tree with his head so that his young mate can eat its shoots, and fans the bees from his cheek
iraicchi.sense: on the very road the man took, the male feeds his mate, so he too will remember and come back to care for her

reading: The friend tells the hero: do not crush our bright bangle, fine as Porayan's Tondi where a fisher girl brings her father rice bartered for salt, tamarind fish stew and fat fish; if the mother, who flushes at nothing and says 'playing in the sand with your friends wears away your glow', sees anything, she will shut the girl in more closely than the Chola guards the tribute stored at Kudanthai.
nuance: The threat of confinement is the argument for marriage: the friend never asks him to marry but makes the mother's guarded house the alternative. The fisher girl feeding her father in the opening is the life of the shore the heroine is about to lose.

thinai_evidence.note: the sea, the fishing boats and the shore

comparisons.tenor: the heroine's bright bangle, rich and fine as Porayan's Tondi
the mother's confinement of the girl, closer than the Chola's guarded tribute at Kudanthai

title: களிற்றியானைநிரை 61-80
theme: Akananuru 61 to 80, in the anthology's order of lands: ten paalai poems of men leaving or refusing to leave for wealth, women and mothers left behind and an elopement, set beside hill trysts at night, mullai waiting and homecoming, a marutham husband held at home by his son and a courtesan's boast, and neythal pleas for open marriage. Puram fame (Pulli, Udhiyan Cheral, the Moriyar, Aay, Pittan, Paari with Kapilar, Rama at Kodi) is drawn on throughout as likeness.
source_issues: 67: lines 10 and 11 repeat Akananuru 131 lines 11 and 12 word for word (the hero-stone couplet), as the text flag notes; marked as the base text stands.
70: line 9 carries a repaired character (an unassigned code point after ஞ் read as ஞா in ஞாழல்), per the text flag.

71: the colophon says the friend speaks to the heroine, but the poem speaks of என் உயிர் and addresses the friend (வாழி, தோழி), which fits the heroine as speaker; thurai_akam keeps the colophon's speaker.
72: the colophon thurai is numbered (1) but gives no second alternative.

73: the colophon thurai reads as two sentences and names no speaker (தலைமகன் பொருள்வயிற் பிரிகின்றான். குறித்த பருவவரவு கண்டு அழிந்த தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லியது.); the poem itself addresses காதல்அம் தோழி and speaks of என்அழிபு, which suggests the heroine as speaker. The rain-cloud of the promised season makes the poem mullai on its own evidence, against the colophon's பாலை.

reading: The friend tells the heroine not to waste away watching the wall where she scratches off the days since her man left for a distant land, driven by the saying that those who fall at others' hands rather than to Death are blessed; even if he won Pulli's festive Venkatam, where bowmen barter elephant tusks and drink their daily toddy, he could not stay there forgetting her breast, rich as Avi's golden Pothini.
nuance: The man's journey is justified with a warriors' maxim about dying in battle rather than of sickness, so a search for wealth is dressed as heroic striving; the friend answers not by disputing the maxim but by setting a famous prize (Venkatam) against a famous city (Pothini) and letting the woman's body outweigh both.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பொருள்வயிற்பிரிய வேறுபட்ட தலைமகட்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the man has gone to a far land and she counts the days

comparisons.tenor: the heroine's adorned breast and chest

reading: After a tryst that failed, the man tells his heart how the dark girl of their secret union, when talk broke it as loud as a war drum and meeting grew hard, yesterday clasped him to end her trembling as if she were plunging into the whirling Kaveri flood, she whose innocence is as perfect as the image the god made on the bright slopes of Poraiyan's Kolli.
nuance: Tonight's failure is answered with yesterday's embrace: the poem is a memory held against a broken tryst, and the closing likeness to a god-made image on Kolli sets the girl at once beyond reach and beyond blame.

thinai_evidence.note: a secret union of the hills, kept and broken by talk

comparisons.tenor: the talk that broke their union

reading: The foster mother tells her own daughter that she does not grieve that the girl left the great house and crossed the mountain with her lover; she grieves that her peacock-gentle child, sheltering for the night in a raiders' noisy hamlet in an old woman's rotting hut, will lie awake on his shoulder listening for the drum of cattle thieves.
nuance: She accepts the elopement in a single clause and spends the poem on a night she imagines in detail; at dawn on that road the red quail cock and his small hen bathe in the dust together, a pair at ease where the mother can see only danger.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகள் புணர்ந்துடன் செல்லச் செவிலி தன் மகளுக்குச் சொல்லியது.

comparisons.tenor: the girl's soft gait and innocence

reading: Returning with his task done, the man urges his charioteer through the wet red country of the rains: at this hour the bull with earth on its horns leads the young heifer home and the cows' clear bells fill the village common, and she who waits for him is undone each time she hears them in the lonely evening.
nuance: The sound that marks every other homecoming (the cows' bells at dusk) is the sound that torments her, so his haste is set against a sound she hears without him.

thinai_evidence.note: rain season and evening, with a herd coming home

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is the charioteer (பாக, line 1)

comparisons.tenor: the speed of the plumed horses

reading: The friend tells the heroine to rejoice like the bards who went singing to Udhiyan Cheral, for they are free of the suspicious mother and the lying women of the street: the man has today set out with them on the very journey he once put off, saying the hard road over the hills, lit with bamboo fires like fishing boats' lamps at sea and guarded by a tusker, was too hard for women.
nuance: The friend quotes his old refusal in full, the road's beauty and danger included, so the elopement is told as his change of mind; the bards' joy before a famous giver is the measure of the girls' release.

colophon.thurai: வேறுபட்ட தலைமகட்குத் தலைமகன் உடன்போக்கு வலித்தமை தோழி சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the lovers set out together across the waste

comparisons.tenor: the girls' joy at going with him
the fires bamboo friction kindles on the hills

reading: The heroine tells the friend who came on her husband's behalf that the old saying (sons bring fame here and a clean passage hereafter) has proved true: yesterday, dressed to wed another, he stopped his chariot when their little son ran out to see him, could not hand the crying boy back, came into the house with him, and, held by the memory of the kindness he once showed her among the girls at play, gave up the wedding though its drums kept calling him.
nuance: The proverb about sons is a puram commonplace about fame and the next world; she tests it on a household quarrel and finds it true in a way the proverb never meant, since the son's merit is that he keeps his father at home. Her own part is comic and rueful: ashamed to seem the cause, she makes a show of beating the boy.

colophon.thurai: பரத்தையிற் பிரிந்த தலைமகற்கு வாயிலாய்ப்புக்க தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது.

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the friend has come as the husband's go-between

comparisons.tenor: the boy who stops his father
the wedding drums seeming to call him

reading: The heroine asks her friend what she can do, when they say the road her man took is a rainless gravel waste where marauders rush at night, hero-stones crowned with peacock feathers stand like a battle front, stone heaps mark where men fell, and the gravel glitters like fireflies beside a ghost's mirage.
nuance: Everything she describes is hearsay (என்ப): the dread comes from report, and the poem's last line puts the road beside the beauty he gave up to travel it.

colophon.thurai: பொருள்வயிற் பிரிந்தவழி வற்புறுத்துந் தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the cloud withholds its rain from a gravel upland

the stone heaps over the fallen

tamil: கேட்டியோ? வாழி, வேண்டு அன்னை! நம் படப்பை
reading: The friend tells the heroine how, testing whether their mother slept, she asked her whether she had heard the waterfall shaking the koothalam and the thunder that split the asoka where their swing hangs; the mother, hearing nothing, sank into sleep, all creatures slept, and the man, as their hearts had hoped, came through the cold road of torrents, crying elephants and pythons.
nuance: The friend's innocent-sounding questions are a sleep test, and the noise of the night (falls, thunder, flood) is both the cover for his coming and the danger he braved to come.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் இரவுக்குறி வந்தமையறிந்த தோழி தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the lover comes by night while the house sleeps

comparisons.tenor: the swing's rope, struck as if it were a snake

reading: The friend tells the heroine, wasted and dimmed in eye and colour, to stop weeping: though the man, wanting the joy of giving, has gone past the rock the Moriyar's chariot wheels cut, through summer wastes where deer herds strip the nelli, he will not stay long forgetting sweet sleep on her breast, fragrant as the first-day blossom of Aay's forest.
nuance: The friend grants his motive full dignity (he went for wealth to give, ஈதல் இன்பம்), and uses that dignity as her argument: a man moved by giving will not hoard his absence.

colophon.thurai: பொருள்வயிற் பிரிந்து நீட்டித்தான் தலைமகன் எனக் கவன்ற தலைமகட்கு வருவரென்பதுபடச் சொல்லித் தோழி ஆற்றுவித்தது.

thinai_evidence.note: he has gone to earn wealth

comparisons.tenor: her eyes, which have lost the dark flower's loveliness

reading: The friend tells the heroine that their love for the lord of the fishing shore, once broadcast by gossiping women, is now crowned by the wedding, and the noisy town has fallen silent, like the banyan whose birds Rama, victor in war, hushed for his secret counsel at the ancient Kodi of the Kavuriyar.
nuance: Gossip, the force that drives so many akam poems, is here simply shut off by marriage; the Rama legend supplies the image of a silence imposed on a whole clamorous tree.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் வரைவு மலிந்தமை தோழி தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: fishers, the neythal flower and the shore grove

reading: In the evening that ends the day, when bees leave pool flowers for branch flowers like graceless men who drop the poor, deer stand bewildered and the sky blooms like cooling gold, the speaker tells her friend that the evening's pain strikes like spearmen aiming at a wounded man's vital spot, her strength thins like breath in a furnace, and asks if this is the hour her life will leave her like a bird quitting a tree in a gale.
nuance: The opening simile is about bees, but its vehicle (men who leave those who are no longer useful) falls on the absent lover without naming him.

colophon.thurai: பொருள்வயிற் பிரிந்த விடத்து ஆற்றாளாய தலைமகட்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது,

thinai_evidence.note: the pain of a lover gone

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives the friend as speaker, but the poem speaks of என் உயிர் and addresses the friend

comparisons.tenor: the bees leaving pool flowers for branch flowers

reading: With the man standing outside at the night tryst, the heroine tells her friend that the road he came by at midnight in the rain is fearful (lightning on the anthills where a bear digs, rivers with crocodiles, a tiger that killed an elephant for its pregnant mate, paths like walking a sword's edge), and that he who came with a loving heart and only a spear for company is not cruel, nor is the friend who brought him at fault: the fault is hers.
nuance: Spoken for his ears, the self-blame is a plea: by listing the road's terrors and taking the guilt on herself she tells him the night visits must end in marriage.

colophon.thurai: (1) தலைமகன் இரவுக்குறிக்கண் சிறைப்புறத்தானாகத் தலைமகள் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது.

nuance: The rain cloud is both comfort and accusation: it is the season he named for his return, seen over his country, not yet over hers.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பொருள்வயிற் பிரிகின்றான். குறித்த பருவவரவு கண்டு அழிந்த தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லியது.

comparisons.tenor: the gleam of the single pearl string

reading: The heroine tells the friend who keeps assuring her that the man, his task won, will see the startled doe of the stag in the rain-washed scrub, think of her and order his charioteer to hurry, that she could hold firm on that comfort if only the cowherds' small harsh flute did not torment her in the evening.
nuance: Almost the whole poem is the friend's comfort, quoted back; the last three lines undo it with a single sound of her own mullai land.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பிரிவின்கண் அழிந்த கிழத்தி வற்புறுத்துந் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது.

comparisons.tenor: the red mites on the road
her own startled eyes, which he will recall

tamil: தருநரும் உளரோ, இவ் உலகத் தான்?, என-
reading: Answering the woman's fear that he will leave, the man recalls the saying that effort, not grace, is a man's wealth, says that those who follow it across burnt hills only grieve ever after for beauty that wasted unembraced and that no one in this world can give back, and asks whether he could ever plan to leave her, so hard a prize to win.
nuance: The opening maxim is quoted to be refuted, and the refutation turns on a pun: the vision that decided on wealth is பொருள்அல் காட்சி, a view that misses the point (பொருள்) even as it pursues wealth (பொருள்).

colophon.thurai: பொருள்வயிற் பிரிவரென வேறுபட்ட தலைமகட்குப் பிரியேனெனத் தலைமகன் சொல்லியது.

reading: Told that the wife's people rail at her, the courtesan says within their hearing that his women may keep on clamouring like bards' drums at a patron's morning feast; as Aathi Manthi wandered distraught asking who had seen her curly-haired dancer and the cool Kaveri held him, so she has resolved to seize the man and hold him fast.
nuance: The courtesan borrows the Aathi Manthi legend and takes the river's part in it, leaving the wife the role of the bereaved queen.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகளை நயப்பித்துக் கொண்டாளென்று கழறக்கேட்ட பரத்தை தலைமகள் பாங்காயினார் கேட்பச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the lord of the ford town visits the courtesans' street

thurai_akam.speaker: parathai
thurai_akam.note: spoken so that the heroine's companions (பாங்காயினார்) hear

comparisons.tenor: her seizing and holding the man

reading: The man tells his heart that if it plots to cross the forest for wealth though her brow pale, it plots ill: past ruined villages where vultures pull out the guts of fallen warriors, at the dark evening in a hamlet's ithi shade, her tear-filled eyes will wound him like the spear Pittan, Chera's generous warrior, raised against hostile kings.
nuance: The parting is stopped in the imagination: the man pictures the evening of the journey, and what decides is not the road's danger but her eyes as he will remember them.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பிரியக் கருதிய நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லி, செலவழுங்குவித்தது.

thinai_evidence.note: the man weighs leaving her to earn wealth

comparisons.tenor: the vulture pulling out the guts of the dead

reading: The friend asks the hill-lord, back from his absence, whether in his few days away he ever once thought of them in the cold dewy season, when the tusker on the slope, afraid of the yali, wraps his trembling pregnant mate in his trunk; and she says the girl's brow smells of the new flowers of Paari's pool, Paari who with Kapilar beside him held out for years and drove the kings away.
nuance: The friend puts the right thought into his mouth (how will they fare, poor things, alone in our town?) and then asks if he ever had it; the brow fragrant as Paari's pool makes the girl a prize kings could not take.

colophon.thurai: களவுக் காலத்துப் பிரிந்து வந்த தலைமகற்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: hill folk, kaanthal and the mountain slope

comparisons.tenor: the fragrance of the girl's brow

iraicchi.act: the tusker, fearing the yali, clasps his trembling pregnant mate in his trunk to shelter her
iraicchi.sense: the man should guard the girl who trembles alone through the cold season, as the beast of his own hill guards his mate, instead of leaving her

reading: Midway across the waste, the man tells his heart that it has suffered for wealth that never stays, crossing the hard ground of stone-cut wells, the red dust of the Kongar herds rushing to water, and the long road where the kite's mate calls while the Eyinar bowmen go out raiding to their drum.
nuance: The last word is the charge: the wealth that drew him is நில்லாப் பொருள், wealth that does not stay, so the hardship is spent on something already slipping away.

colophon.thurai: பொருள்வயிற் பிரிந்த தலைமகன் இடைச் சுரத்துத் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: he has left her, bound by the desire for wealth

reading: The friend tells the lord of the cool shore that he has truly come by night, swimming the dark backwater where crocodiles and sharks move; asking whether they are so hard for him to reach, she says they spend the day driving birds from their father's drying fish, and bids him drive his chariot over the adumbu creepers and come by day to the punnai grove.
nuance: The invitation by day is a refusal of the night: a chariot that cuts the shore creepers leaves a track everyone can see, so the friend is asking for a courtship in the open.

thinai_evidence.note: crocodiles of the backwater and the punnai grove of the shore

title: களிற்றியானைநிரை 81-100
theme: Akananuru 81 to 100 in the anthology's fixed order of lands: ten paalai poems of men crossing the waste for wealth, of their return, and of a girl's elopement seen by her foster mother and by her lover; hill courtships under watch and a veriyattu rite; marutham marriage and infidelity, from a wedding night remembered to gossip loud as a Chola victory; mullai war camps and homecomings; and neythal confinement and pressure for marriage. Kings and towns of puram (Pulli's Venkatam, Kuttuvan's Kudanadu, Uraiyur, Koodal, Karuvur, Paruvur, Viyalur, Puranthai) serve as measures of distance, wealth and noise.
source_issues: 81: the base text numbers the last line 13 though the poem has 15 lines (flagged); a misprinted number.
84 line 12: அரிஞ்ர் is not a word; read அரிநர் (reapers), the word the sense needs.
86 line 31: மா அ யோளே is split by stray spaces; read மாஅயோளே.
89 lines 7 to 8 (காழியர் கவ்வைப் பரப்பின் வெவ்வுவர்ப்பு ஒழிய): rare words whose sense is not secure; the reading of the poem does not turn on them.
90 line 14: பாசிலை விலையே is obscure (a green-leaf courtship gift, or the girl's worth); the verse is marked uncertain.
93 line 17: a stray space before the comma (கடாஅத்து ,).
95: the colophon reads போக்குடன் பட்ட தலைமகன் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது, but the speaker is the woman (என் தளிர்புரை மேனி; the mother says என் மகட்கு of her); read தலைமகள்.
96 line 7: வீஞ்குபு is not a word; read வீங்குபு (swelling).
97: the colophon's வற்புறுந்துந் is a misprint for வற்புறுத்தும்.
98 line 22: பெண்டிற்க்கு is misspelt for பெண்டிர்க்கு.
99: the colophon thurai ends with a comma instead of a full stop.
85 line 2, 92 line 2 and 96 line 18 recur in 147, 108 and 368 (flagged): formulaic lines, not errors.

reading: The friend, having read the woman's heart, asks the man who has announced his going whether he will really cross the long burning waste for wealth made by going away, where a bear tired of sweet iruppai fruit digs out a termite mound and a kite pines alone on a sun-scorched maraa tree, while her lovely kohl-dark eyes, fair as Kadalan's town Vilangil, run with tears.
nuance: The question is put in the plural of respect (ஐய! சேறிரோ) and closes on the wealth itself, அகன்றுசெய் பொருள், wealth that is made by leaving: the friend names the price inside the word for the prize. The bear that turns from sweet fruit when it is sated to dig in a hard mound for a meal could be read as the man who leaves a sweet home for hard-won wealth, but the poem draws no pairing, so it is left as scene.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவுணர்த்திய தலைமகற்குத் தோழி தலைமகள் குறிப்பறிந்து வந்து சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the summer waste where the earth cracks is the road he means to take

thurai_akam.note: the friend speaks for the woman, having read her mind (குறிப்பறிந்து)
