her kohl-dark lovely eyes, as fair as Kadalan's town

reading: The woman tells her friend that the hill man's country is a stage where wind in bored bamboo is the flute, the waterfall the drum, the stag's call the horn and the bees the lute, the monkeys an amazed audience and the peacock a dancer; many saw him standing at the gap of the millet field with his bow, asking after the elephant he had hunted, so why should she alone lie through the dark night with streaming eyes and slackened arms?
nuance: Telling the friend this is the first step of disclosure (அறத்தொடு நிற்றல்): she admits she met him, but in the form of a complaint that many saw him and only she suffers. The hill's whole orchestra plays to an audience of monkeys, and the one hearer it truly moves is she, alone at night.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill slope, the millet field and the hunter with bow fix the hill land

comparisons.tenor: the west wind in the bored bamboo, as a flute
the waterfall's sound, as a drum
the humming bees, as a lute
the female monkeys, as the assembly watching a performance
the dancing peacock, like a dancer entering the stage

reading: On the road, the man tells his heart that though he has passed the Venkatam hill of Pulli, chief of the unlettered young men who wear maraa flowers, tear an elephant calf from its wailing mother and tie it at the toddy-houses of their flag-lined town in exchange for drink, his love's virtues, her rain-moist eyes like an opening neythal flower, did not count the distance and have come all the way to reach him.
nuance: Paalai usually makes the woman the one whom memory reaches; here her qualities (குணனே) are the travellers, driven by love (அன்புமிகக் கடைஇ) across the frontier he has just crossed. The cow elephant crying in the forest for the calf the young men have taken sits behind his thought of the woman he left, but the poem does not draw the pairing.

thinai_evidence.note: he has gone far from her beyond the frontier hill and is still on the road

reading: In the war camp the man says that the rains have come, a rainbow on the hill and drum-voiced clouds pouring till the directions vanish, and she of the bright brow is in her small village on the frontier woodland where mullai flowers drop on a sleeping boar's back; while he is in the camp of a garlanded king who, angry, will not accept even the rare tribute of a fortress set among rich fields of reapers and toddy-drinking labourers, and moves his army on to fight.
nuance: Two lands face each other across the poem: her mullai woodland in the promised rains, and the enemy's marutham fields where the harvest goes on. The rains that should send him home have come; what keeps him is the king's anger, which turns down the very tribute that would end the war (அருந்திறை கொடுப்பவும் கொள்ளான்).

thinai_evidence.note: the rains have come over her mullai woodland while he is held at war

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named: he speaks his thought in the camp

comparisons.tenor: the many red flowers of the fields, like fire

reading: The friend tells the woman not to weep in reproach that the man who left them is without virtue while her brow pales and her arms waste: he assured them he would come back in the cool rains, when on the slopes of Thiraiyan's tall Venkatam hill the bull elephant breaks young bamboo shoots to feed the hungry calf of his soft-stepping mate, and the peacock, bathed in vengai pollen, calls its mate from the kurunthu branch; that is the season, and the rain has spread.
nuance: The comfort is built from his own words: the friend quotes the promise, scene and all, and then points to the sky. The elephant feeding his mate's calf is inside that promise, so the man himself had chosen the image of a male who provides.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பிரிய வேறுபட்ட தலைமகளைத் தோழி வற்புறுத்தியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the heart of the poem is waiting for a return promised for the rains, which is mullai's situation

iraicchi.act: the bull elephant breaks young bamboo shoots and feeds them to the hungry calf of his mate, who has lately given birth
iraicchi.sense: the man who named this scene in his promise is one who provides for his own, so his word to return can be trusted

reading: The man recalls the wedding: rice cooked with black gram heaped high, sand spread under the cool pandal, lamps and garlands, the auspicious dawn when the moon stood free of the evil planet; matrons with pots and bowls passing things in order; four mothers of sons pouring water with petals and paddy on her hair and blessing her never to fail in chastity and to love the man who took her; her kin then giving her as lady of the great house; and the first night, when she lay curled in her new cloth with her face hidden, and asked what her heart felt, she only bowed her head in deep joy.
nuance: The blessing (கற்பினின் வழாஅ, நற்பல உதவிப் பெற்றோற் பெட்கும் பிணையை ஆக) is the karpu ideal spoken by women who have kept it. By the colophon's first reading the man tells all this to the friend who has shut the door on him, so the memory of the wedding becomes his plea against a quarrel the poem never names. Her answer to his question is a gesture, not a word.

colophon.thurai: வாயில் மறுத்த தோழிக்கு தலைமகன் சொல்லியது தலைமகளைக் கூடி இன்புற்றிருந்த தலைமகன் பண்டு நிகழ்ந்தது சொற்று இன்புற்றிருந்ததூஉமாம்.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem is a household wedding with no landscape; its situation is union, and the marutham placement rests on the colophon's door refused

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: with his wife, recalling the first night

comparisons.tenor: her shy, wondering glance, as a deer's

reading: Coming home with his work done, the man tells his heart that it suffered long on the road, lodging for the night in a poor hamlet of grass huts where a calf sucks the churning stick hung in the yard, leaving at the cock's first call, and passing hill forks where the drum of fierce marauders from their rock forts makes travellers' hearts quake; now let it rejoice, for they will praise her breasts and lie in her bamboo-smooth arms in their tall house where the lamp burns all night.
nuance: The hamlet's small homely detail, a calf mouthing the curd-stick under a creeper pandal, is the first sight of a home on the way back and foreshadows his own; the heart, not the man, is the traveller who suffered (நனிநீடு உழந்தனை).

colophon.thurai: வினைமுற்றி மீளுந் தலைமகன் இடைச்சுரத்துத் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem looks back on the waste road of marauders he has crossed

comparisons.tenor: her arms, smooth and long as bamboo

reading: With the man listening outside, the friend wonders whether the good man who came guided by the torch a hunter had set on his platform to watch for the boar stealing to the red millet, and who ended their trembling grief, has gone back by that path no one can tread, where a tiger-killing elephant's musth draws bees whose hum the asunam takes for a lute, where snakes crowd the bamboo thicket and the bear digs at deep anthills.
nuance: The catalogue of dangers is spoken for the listener outside: a road this perilous cannot be walked every night, and only marriage ends the need. The torch set to catch a thief is the light the lover came by.

colophon.thurai: இரவுக்குறி வந்த தலைமகன் சிறைப்புறத்தானாகத் தோழி சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: millet field, hunter and hill fix the land

reading: The foster mother, after the girl has gone off with her man, asks whether she can walk on her soft red feet across the wide burning land where the rains failed and the mirage runs, where the owl booms like struck stone in the crevices, cicadas shrill in the thorn trees, and marauders who have eaten pale meat cut down the guards of a donkey caravan and share out the loot to the beat of the drum, she who would not drink honeyed milk even when coaxed and played under the sand-strewn pandal.
nuance: The road is all violence and the man does not appear at all: the mother can only measure the girl's feet against the land. The last lines bring the reader back into the house, to the milk she refused and the pandal where she played, so the loss is set in the very place the girl has left.

thinai_evidence.note: a girl gone off with her lover through the waste, grieved by the mother left behind

thurai_akam.speaker: sevili
thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named

reading: The friend meets the man leaving after a day tryst on the shore where white-crested waves like old men wreck the sand houses of the young girls, and tells him that gossip of their union, known to few, has risen and the girl has been shut up at home; she cannot tell him to go away while he suffers so, but her people would not take even the rich market of the dark-eyed Kosar east of Chellur as enough for her.
nuance: The waves likened to old men (மூத்தோர் அன்ன) that break the play-houses of the young are the elders who have shut the girl in and broken off the lovers' meetings, and the friend never says so. The closing bride-price line turns on பாசிலை, whose sense here (a green leaf of a courtship gift, or her worth) the text does not settle.

colophon.thurai: பகற்குறி வந்து கண்ணுற்று நீங்கும் தலைமகனைத் தோழி எதிர்ப்பட்டு நின்று இற்செறிப்பு அறிவுறீஇயது.

thinai_evidence.note: the waves, the screwpine grove and the shore ford fix the seashore

comparisons.tenor: the Kosar market's noise, as the roar of the sea

ullurai.tenor: the girl's elders, who have shut her in and ended the meetings

pairs.situation: the old ones of her house
they break up the young lovers' play of meeting

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses the waves of their own shore, without leaving the land (porul 7.27)

reading: The friend tells the wasting woman that though the man left for rare wealth across a waste where the sun has dried the falls, and an elephant that found no water in the dread pool ate moss and shrank together with his hungry mate, he has great love: even if he gained Kuttuvan's Kudanadu beyond the marauders' scrub, a land of drums that knows no hunger, where the buffalo tired of lotus rests in the shade of old jackfruit trees, he would not stay there forgetting her beauty.
nuance: The wealth the man went for is measured by the richest land the friend can name, and the claim is that he would refuse it. The elephant pair is on his road, the buffalo in the land he would refuse.

thinai_evidence.note: the falls have dried and the wide land shimmers in the heat

iraicchi.act: finding no water, the elephant eats moss and shrinks together with his hungry mate
iraicchi.sense: even beasts in the drought keep together, so the man who crossed that land has not stopped loving her

reading: The friend tells the man not to come on such nights, when lightning blinds the slopes and in the pouring midnight rain a striped tiger strikes an elephant and roars; tomorrow she and the girl will be guarding millet, and in a grove so thick that not even the monkeys know it, by a cool fall where red kanthal has opened, he may have the sleep of her soft dark hair, by the light of a gem from a snake that thunder has struck.
nuance: The day tryst she offers is made of impossibilities, a grove unknown to monkeys and a lamp from a thunder-killed snake's gem, so that the man hears what the colophon says she means: marriage, not meetings (வரைவு கடாயது).

colophon.thurai: இரவுக்குறிச் சென்று தலைமகளைக் கண்ணுற்று நீங்குத் தலைமகனைப் பகற்குறி நேர்ந்த வாய்பாட்டால் தோழி வரைவு கடாயது.

thinai_evidence.note: millet guarding and the kanthal by the fall fix the hill

comparisons.tenor: the snake's gem, as a lamp

reading: Coming home with his work done, the man tells his heart: to end the kin's ruin, feed the relatives and make friends of strangers, he went with zeal for effort and won rare treasure as fine as the just assembly of the Cholas at Uraiyur; now let them go and embrace, more times than the sands heaped on the banks of the Porunai at Kothai's Karuvur, the dark woman whose brow smells like the morning market of Vazhuthi's Koodal, in their sky-high house on a bed soft as gathered foam by the tall lamp, till her ornaments print their marks on her.
nuance: The opening gives the paalai journey a household reason: wealth is for the kin, the relatives and the stranger made friend. The three crowned houses each lend one simile: the Chola court for wealth, the Pandya market for her scent, the Chera river's sands for the count of embraces.

colophon.thurai: வினைமுற்றி மீளலுறுந் தலைமகன் இடைச்சுரத்துத் தன்னெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem is the return from a parting for wealth

comparisons.tenor: the rare treasure he has won
their tall house, as if carved from a mountain
the soft flower bed, like gathered foam

reading: Returning, the man tells his charioteer that her town, the town of the woman of thick dark hair and loving gentleness, lies in the hard woodland country where at midnight the musundai blooms white like the sky, a goatherd with a leather bag, wearing a dripping garland of mullai and thondri, warms his palms at a sputtering brand and whistles long into the dark where the jackal howls, together with the black horn the field-guards blow to drive off herds of boar.
nuance: Her town is reached through its night sounds, the herdsman's whistle and the guards' horn, heard as one; the herdsman out in the dark, warming his hands far from home, is a figure of the man himself.

colophon.thurai: வினைமுற்றி மீளுந் தலைமகன் தேர்ப்பாகற்குச் சொல்லியது தலைமகன் பாங்கற்குச் சொற்றதூஉமாம்.

thinai_evidence.note: the herdsman, the mullai garland and the woodland country

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is the charioteer

comparisons.tenor: the musundai's white flowers, as the starry sky

tamil: புரைய அல்ல, என் மகட்கு' எனப் பரைஇ,
reading: The woman tells her friend that her brow has paled, her leaf-tender body thinned and her grief shows for all to see, and thinking can end it only with her life; the town, fond of gossip, will not say she grieves for one who crossed the wastes where a bear and her cubs carry off the hail-like iruppai flowers, and her mother has answered the women of the town that their harsh words do not fit her daughter: before such a mother, who understands and is calm, what can she do in this state?
nuance: The mother here does not scold; she defends the girl against the town, and that is what the girl cannot bear, since the mother's trust is what she is about to betray. The colophon says the speaker is தலைமகன், but the poem's first person is the woman (என் தளிர்புரை மேனி, என் மகட்கு in the mother's mouth).

thinai_evidence.note: the iruppai and the bear of the wastes he crossed

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon reads தலைமகன் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது, but the speaker is plainly the woman; see source_issues

comparisons.tenor: her body, tender as young leaves
the hollow iruppai flowers, like hailstones

reading: The friend, refusing the man entry, calls him lord of a kaanji town where in the field-pond prawns leap like a bow sprung loose, and a thorny cane, its long stem toothed like a file, catches the broad leaves of the water lily and, swung by the north wind, swells and slackens like a forge's bellows; they say he has chosen one young girl out of all the bangled band, and that news has spread through many mouths like the uproar of elephants taken on the day the Chola, father of Aqthai, beat both great kings on the battlefield of Paruvur.
nuance: The friend matches his private conquest to a royal victory's din: what he thought hidden is as public as a war. The cane that catches the lily and swells and slackens with every wind is his way with women.

thinai_evidence.note: field pond, paddy land and kaanji town

reading: The woman answers her friend, who tells her not to weep thinking of the cruel man who crossed a waste where the spotted stag's horns fall in the drought and vultures and kites gather at a stench the tiger left, like marauders cutting up meat in rock clefts after a night raid on cattle: how can she easily stop her tears, hearing the sated koel call in spring, when the kuravam blooms, the cold season is over, marutham trees crowd the river ford and new mango flowers crown the boughs under smoky mist?
nuance: The friend's comfort carries a compliment (her bosom fair as Nannan's Viyalur, a court that cherished bards), and the answer sets against it the joy of spring: the koel is நுகர்குயில், a bird that has had its fill, and it is the season's plenty, not the waste, that makes tears impossible to stop.

thinai_evidence.note: she weeps for the man gone across the waste

comparisons.tenor: the vultures and kites crowding at the carrion
the mist creeping over the mango boughs

tamil: பண்டையின் சிறக்க, என் மகட்கு' எனப் பரைஇ,
reading: With the man standing by, the girl tells her friend that her mother does not know the ache of his withheld grace can be eased only on his chest; seeing her bangles slip, the mother asked the old lying women, who said it was Murugan's seizure, and so a velan dances in the decorated pandal to restore her beauty: if after all that her wasted body does not recover the secret will become gossip, and worse, if the god relieves her and the hill man hears that her sickness was something else, living will be harder still.
nuance: The rite is described with care and mocked in the same breath (மையற் பெண்டிற்க்கு நொவ்வல்): the women are deluded, the velan dangles like a puppet. Her deepest fear is not exposure but that the rite might work, and the man conclude she never pined for him.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் சிறைப்புறத்தானாகத் தோழி தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லுவாளாய்ச் சொல்லியது. தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லிய தூஉமாம்.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill lord and Murugan's rite fix the hill land

comparisons.tenor: the well-made house, like a painting
her admired beauty, like a doll's
the velan dangling in his dance

reading: Leading the girl who has gone off with him, the man coaxes her to look at the forest, strewn with palasa buds red as a tiger's claws, kongam opening like jewelled breasts, athiral and paathiri petals and maraa blossoms, lovely as the flower-strewn town of a dread god, and asks whether it also has hills of all heights that look like her father's war elephants, tusk-rings broken, crowded by their mates.
nuance: This is the same kind of road that the foster mother of 89 fills with marauders; the lover makes it a temple town of flowers. His last question teases and reassures at once: even the hills are her father's elephants, so she has not left home behind.

colophon.thurai: உடன் போகிய தலைமகளைத் தலைமகன் மருட்டிச் சொல்லியது,

reading: The friend tells the man that it is sweet to her too that he comes, wipes off his sandal, embraces the girl till her breast is marked, and leaves in the dark; but the gossip has come true, loud as a newly arrived flock of storks at the punnai-grove ford of Puranthai, town of the bards' patron Periyan, where fishers' lamps on the stilled sea at night shine like the face-lamps of a king's dancing war elephants; theirs is a sorrowing town of screwpine gardens where the buffalo that went out at cold dawn feeds on fresh neythal flowers.
nuance: Line 4 is irony: what is sweet to the friend is exactly what she is ending. The buffalo that goes out at dawn and grazes the fresh neythal flower of their own town is the man who takes the girl's youth and leaves before light.

thinai_evidence.note: the punnai shore grove, screwpine and fishing fix the seashore

comparisons.tenor: the fishers' bright lamps on the night sea

title: களிற்றியானைநிரை 101-120
theme: Akananuru 101 to 120, in the களிற்றியானைநிரை section: ten paalai poems of roads through raider country, a heroine doubting an old proverb, two mothers grieving for eloped daughters, set beside kurinji night trysts pressed toward marriage, marutham quarrels measured against Chezhiyan's wars, two mullai homecomings and two neythal scenes. Puram names (Ezhini, Evvi, Erumai, Ahthai and the Kosar, Vaanan, Chezhiyan at Koodal) serve as similes and settings for private grief.
source_issues: 110: line 20 reads பல்லோர் ருள்ளும், a word split by a stray space and doubled consonant; read பல்லோருள்ளும். Line 1 recurs as Akananuru 218 line 18 (a formula).
111: the colophon thurai reads தலைமளை, a misprint for தலைமகளை.
114 and 117: the poet's name is not preserved (the commentary edition prints dots).
118: the colophon thurai breaks off at வரைவு; it presumably ended வரைவு கடாயது.
120: the colophon thurai breaks off after வந்து, without saying to whom the friend speaks; the poem's பெரும (line 9) shows it is the hero.
115: line 7 recurs as Akananuru 227 line 13 (a formula).
103: line 11 was repaired (a stray space before a dead consonant).

reading: The heroine asks her friend whether the old proverb that no harm comes in this life to those who do good has turned false today, since the man who crossed the many dewy hills, by a vast forest where red-eyed Mazhavar raiders with fire-sticks and bows drive off herds with their calves and where the whirling midday wind shakes the murungai's spent flowers down like cold hail, has gone though she did nothing to deserve his displeasure.
nuance: The proverb is about this life (இம்மை), not a reward hereafter: she asks whether right conduct protects anyone now. The image of cool hail made out of flowers shaken down by scorching wind turns the comfort of rain into a sign of heat.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவிடை வேறுபட்ட கிழத்தி, தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது; தோழி கிழத்திக்குச் சொல்லியதூஉமாம்.

thinai_evidence.note: she speaks of a man who has crossed the waste and left her

comparisons.tenor: the raiders' curled matted hair, like a ram's horn
the sun crossing the wide sky like a boat
the murungai's spent flowers dropping in the hot wind like cold hail

reading: Speaking to her friend so that the hero standing outside will hear, the heroine recalls how the man of the country where a fierce young elephant falls suddenly asleep to a hill girl's kurinji song, while the millet watcher lies drunk on his platform, came softly past the guards through the unbarred door, bees humming on his sandal-smeared chest, embraced her and left with sweet words; and she asks what this pallor is that has now come over her brow along with the gossip, because he has not given her more.
nuance: The speech is aimed at the overhearer: the night visit is told as past and tender, the pallor and gossip as the present cost. The fierce elephant lulled by the girl's song and the drunk watchman asleep set a hill where every guard is off duty, which is what made the visits possible; a reader may also hear in the lulled elephant the hero lulled out of his purpose, but no part-by-part match is stated.

colophon.thurai: இரவுக் குறிக்கண் சிறைப்புறமாகத் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லுவாளாய்த் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: a secret night meeting that evades the guards

reading: The heroine tells her friend that, thinking the man would have finished his work and come back across the hot, hard waste, past a cattle village whose people have left the tall wide hill, she lay at midnight with pallor as her only companion, and asks whether the one they love will not give back the beauty that went away with him of its own accord.
nuance: She does not ask for him but for her beauty, which she says went with him of itself (தம்மொடு தானே சென்ற நலனும்); the deserted cattle village on his road mirrors her own emptied state. Lines 1 to 4 (the spotted cock and what it watches) are obscure in our text.

thinai_evidence.note: the shadeless waste the man must cross

comparisons.tenor: the bird's fine spots, as if sprinkled on it

reading: The friend blesses the hero who, his king's war finished, drove his swift four-horsed chariot through the cool, bee-loud woodland, leaving behind many small villages where white kids with hollow bellies like empty avarai pods and drooping ears frisk with the children and nibble the aar tree's shoots on the common, and arrived at evening to set flowers in the hair of his bangled wife, who had lived in tears and many reproaches.
nuance: The friend praises the return by one act (இனிதுசெய் தனையால்): setting flowers in the wife's hair, the ornament she had given up while he was away. The playful kids of the small villages show the settled domestic life he rides through to reach his own.

thinai_evidence.note: the woodland and the evening of the homecoming

comparisons.tenor: the kids' hollow bellies, like empty avarai pods
the kids' long ears, drooping as if wilted

reading: The mother wonders how her daughter, who would not drink the sweet milk her nurses held to her in a jewelled bowl and gave no thought to the family's wealth in their great house cool as a shaded pool, but believed false words, will manage the many-pathed summer journey with the hill man who praises her and weaves her a garland of vengai leaves, through a scorched forest of hot stones where bowmen fulfilling the commission of Ezhini of many spears and the rhythmic-stepping horse drink honeyed toddy and drive off herds of full-uddered cattle across the frontier.
nuance: The mother's doubt is about fitness, not morals: a girl who would not even take milk from her nurses now walks a road of cattle raiders. பொய்ம்மருண்டு (deceived by falsehood) is the mother's only judgment of the lover, and the vengai garland he weaves is a hill thing carried into the waste.

thinai_evidence.note: the daughter's journey away with her man

thurai_akam.speaker: nartaay
thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named

comparisons.tenor: the family's great house, cool and rich like a shaded pool
the horse's rhythmic steps, like a bouncing ball

reading: Hearing that the wife of the man of the bright ford, where an old kingfisher too spent to fly rests on fragrant lotus leaves in a fire-red lotus pond, waiting to eat small fish that leap like popped rice, quarrels with her husband on their account, the courtesan tells her friend that since they cannot escape the blame though they did nothing, they should go there swinging their tight bangles and stroll a little, and let the wife beat her own belly like the drum the bard, who is fed on elephants, beats each time Chezhiyan of the shining-sword army wins a battle.
nuance: The courtesan's mockery is in the landscape before it is in her words: the old kingfisher that cannot fly and only waits for the leaping fish is her picture of the wife. Chezhiyan's war drum, beaten at every victory, turns the curse into a public spectacle.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகள் தன்னைப் புறங்கூறினாளாகக் கேட்ட பரத்தை அவட்குப் பாங்காயினார் கேட்பச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife's sulking quarrel over the husband's other women

thurai_akam.speaker: parathai
thurai_akam.note: the courtesan addresses her own friend; the overhearers are the wife's companions

comparisons.tenor: the small fish leaping like popped rice
the wife beating her own belly, like the bard's drumhead
the aging wife, too slow to follow her husband among the lively women

ullurai.tenor: the hero's wife and the young women around her husband, as the courtesan sees them

pairs.situation: the wife, past her youth, can no longer go after her husband
the many lively young women who draw him away
she can only sit at home and sulk

ullurai.speaker_fit: the courtesan is neither heroine nor friend and may use any thing (porul 7.29); the kingfisher and fish are of the marutham pond of the poem

reading: The friend tells the hero, who is preparing to leave, that to end the grief she has borne each time she heard of his going, her friend with thick parted hair will go with him: across the hard frontier of the Vadukar, men of strange long speech with fierce dogs who eat white rice cooked with fat on teak leaves, where travelers rejoice at venison a tiger left on the black rock, past the steep slope where a lamed ox left alone is fed iluppai flowers by boys of a hill hamlet who drive the deer off with their bows, she will be his sweet companion at evening, and at dawn the forest will smell like a wedding house as fresh blossoms fall on the gravel.
nuance: The friend turns the paalai road into a feast and a wedding: travelers' venison, the Vadukar's rice, a hamlet's evening and a forest that smells like a marriage house. The lamed ox left alone yet fed by strangers stands quietly against the fear of being left behind, though the poem does not draw that sense.

colophon.thurai: தோழி தலைமகள் குறிப்பறிந்து வந்து தலைமகற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the hero's departure and the heroine's going with him

comparisons.tenor: the forest at dawn, fragrant as a wedding house

reading: Speaking to the heroine so that the hero outside will hear, the friend says that pitying the pain of those one has joined is fitting for those who understand, yet the lord of the cloud-capped mountain, where kaanthal flowers rise like cobras spreading their hoods at a peacock and a bee at their pollen looks like a spinning top, shows no such pity, for he comes alone through midnight dark of pelting rain, where hail struck from an elephant's face streams on the rock like scattered pearls, lightning flashes like sparks of a whirled firebrand, and beasts of prey roam.
nuance: The friend turns his courage into a want of kindness (அருளான்): by braving the night path he makes the women suffer fear for him, so true pity would be to stop coming that way, that is, to marry. The snake-hooded kaanthal carries the path's dread into the closing praise of his hill.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் சிறைப்புறத்தானாகத் தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லுவாளாய்த் தோழி சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the mountain lord and the midnight tryst

comparisons.tenor: the hailstones scattered on the rock, like pearls at a hill's foot
the hail streaming down the rock, like crystal poured
the lightning, like sparks flying from a firebrand
the kaanthal's flower clusters, like snakes spreading their hoods at a peacock
the bee circling the kaanthal, like a top spun by hand

reading: Halfway along the road, the man tells his heart that the town where she lives, she of soft eyes like many-petalled flowers and words as sweet as a well-tuned yazh string, is now cut off by many dry hills: a wide land of tall groves and bamboo where herds of tusk-ploughing elephants gather, forked tracks heaped with countless cairns over men felled by white-tipped arrows, where travelers are killed though they carry nothing, and which a king without aram rules, taking great tusks and striped hides.
nuance: Three lines give her, twelve give the road; the killing ground is described so fully that it explains why the hills 'lie across' (விலங்கின) his way back. Lines 11 to 13 (whether the robbers kill to stop witnesses escaping, and whether the king takes tusks and hides as tribute) are hard to fix.

thinai_evidence.note: the waste and the dry hills between him and her town

comparisons.tenor: her eyes, like soft many-petalled flowers
her sweet words, like the sound of a good yazh string

reading: Disclosing the secret to the foster mother, the friend says let the mother know and let the gossiping street hear, and swears before the god of the whirling river mouth that there was nothing else: while the girls rested after bathing in the sea, building sand houses and heaping play rice, a man came, said the day was done and he was very tired, and asked whether he might eat with them on spread leaves and stay in their noisy hamlet; they, heads bowed, said the fish food was not fit for him; when the others ran off, crying that a ship with a tall flag was in sight, he looked at her alone and asked, 'Bright-browed one, shall I stay?', and when she said 'go', he stood holding the pole of his tall chariot, gazing — and she says he seems to stand so before her eyes even today.
nuance: The friend tells the meeting in her own first person (என்னே குறித்த நோக்கமொடு, என் கட்கே), as if the man had looked at her; whether she speaks for the heroine or shields her by taking the story on herself is left open. The oath before the river-mouth god and the girls' modest refusal (இவைநுமக்கு உரிய அல்ல) are the proofs offered that nothing improper happened.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore games, fish food and ships of the meeting place

reading: The friend assures the heroine that the man who crossed the sky-touching hills will not stay content where he is and, ashamed of the scornful words of hostile men, will come back; she pictures his road, where a spider's web on a withered nemai tree swings in the hot wind like the cloth banner on a royal elephant, weary elephants mistake it for a rain-cloud and breathe through their aching trunks like the pipes of performers, and vultures feeding on a boar the red dog has killed show red ears like the lamps carried at night over a battlefield to search out the wounded.
nuance: The comfort rests on shame, not longing: he will return because staying away invites scorn. The thirsty elephants deceived by a cobweb into hoping for rain sit uneasily beside a promise of return. Lines 1 to 3 (whose mockery, and why he would be ashamed) can be read more than one way.

thinai_evidence.note: the hot wind and the waste road he travels

comparisons.tenor: the spider's web swinging in the wind, like a royal elephant's cloth banner
the weary elephants breathing through their trunks, like performers' pipes
the vultures' red ears, like lamps searching the wounded on a night battlefield

reading: Meeting the hero who has come at night, the friend tells him he has done wrong to come here, not thinking of them alone, through the cold dark grove where at midnight a hunchbacked bear tears open a termite mound and a tiger whose mate is hungry after giving birth kills a tusked elephant and roars; if a day passes without him her friend will not live, and he too desires her embrace, but the worthy, however deep in love, do not want a pleasure that comes with blame, so why not marry? Then, not knowing of the union already made, they will watch the ancient rite and see her new shyness like strangers come as guests.
nuance: The closing joke turns the secret into a performance: at the wedding the friend will pretend, like a stranger, not to know that the union already happened, and enjoy the bride's shyness. The maxim on the worthy (சான்றோர் பழியொடு வரூஉம் இன்பம் வெஃகார்) is the friend's lever.

colophon.thurai: இரவுக்குறி வந்த தலைமகனை யெதிர்ப்பட்டு நின்று தோழி சொல்லி வரைவு கடாயது.

thinai_evidence.note: the night tryst and the friend's demand for marriage

occasion.words: இரவுக்குறி வந்த தலைமகனை யெதிர்ப்பட்டு நின்று தோழி சொல்லி வரைவு கடாயது

comparisons.tenor: the friend and her circle watching the bride's new shyness, like strangers come as wedding guests

iraicchi.act: the tiger, its mate weak and hungry after giving birth, kills a tusked elephant to feed her
iraicchi.sense: even the fierce tiger provides for its mate; the hero, who braves the same dark for stolen meetings, should take her home as his wife and provide for her

reading: The heroine tells her friend that the man who joined her shoulders, as rich as the good land of the Kosar (those of many spears who, never swerving from friendship even in bad times, follow and guard Ahthai, giver of elephants), with its neythal fields fragrant of new toddy, abandoned her without kindness while the old town raised its gossip, and is now said to be far off beyond the land of Paanan, past a shrunken stream where enemies who killed travelers washed their weapons; so that her helpless heart may be eased and she can stay without weeping, she wishes her life would leave her body here and go to where he works, as a bird leaves its nest on a swaying branch when the place grows empty.
nuance: The Kosar's loyalty 'even in bad times' frames, by contrast, a man who would not stay kind; the body left here like an empty nest is her image of herself. Lines 10 to 16, on the far land and its people, are hard to construe in our text.

thinai_evidence.note: the lover who left and is far away

comparisons.tenor: her shoulders, rich as the Kosar's good land
the rich meats, as if a festival were held

comparisons.vehicle: குடம்பை புல்லெனப் புலம்பெயர் மருங்கிற் புள்எழுந் தாங்கு
comparisons.tenor: her life leaving her body for him, like a bird leaving its emptied nest

reading: The returning hero, imagining his wife telling her friend that he does not remember them even in the small dull evening when the weakened sun sinks behind the hill like the moon swallowed by the snake, bids his charioteer, learned in the craft, drive on to end her sorrow: there the tall flags wave on the sky-touching walls of the old guarded town where the watchmen's lamps shine like stars, and they will see the beautiful woman of faultless chastity, with red-streaked rain-dark eyes and shoulders like bamboo.
nuance: Lines 1 to 7 are the wife's complaint as the hero imagines it, addressed to her friend (கேளாய், எல்ல! தோழி!); the poem thus holds both voices, hers at home and his on the road. Evening, which makes her grieve, is the hour he races against.

colophon.thurai: வினை முற்றி மீளுந் தலைமகன் தேர்ப்பாகற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the wet woodland at evening on the way home

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the charioteer (பாகன், வலவ in line 8)

comparisons.tenor: the woodland strewn with mixed blossoms, like the ground of the Velan's rite
the setting sun vanishing like the moon swallowed by the snake
the watchmen's lamps on the walls, like stars

reading: The heroine tells the friend who urges patience: let the old town of endless festivals gossip though we are blameless, let the harsh-tongued women of the street mock, let my beauty, like the Kudanadu of Erumai of fine ornaments, waste away — only let my lover be free of illness always, he who, bound by the need for wealth, stays far from us across the long road where the konrai's ripe pods, curved like the yazh necks the bards broke off and laid down in worship at the battle where Evvi of the true sword fell, lie strewn on the rock, and where tusked elephants with tusks like the crescent moon hide their herd in fear of a fierce leaping beast.
nuance: Her wish is for his health, not his return; she gives up name, mockery and beauty in three concessive clauses (எள்ளினும் எள்ளுக, தொலையினும் தொலைக). The Evvi simile brings a patron's death and the bards' mourning rite into a love poem, so the very pods on his road recall broken harps.

thinai_evidence.note: the man away for wealth and the woman left

comparisons.tenor: her beauty, like Erumai's rich Kudanadu
the konrai's curved ripe pods, like the harp necks laid down by the bards
the elephant's white tusks, like the crescent moon

reading: The friend refuses the man of the town of rushing water, where field workers reaping red paddy amid flame-red lotuses prop the toddy cart sunk in the mire with adumpu creepers, telling him he has no shame: people say that yesterday he played in the river with a woman of bright brow, short flower-decked hair, soft eyes and full breasts, at the wide ford where punku flowers open like popped rice; and though they hid it behind lies, the gossip slipped from their hands and grew louder than the shout on the wide field of Koodal when Chezhiyan of the elephant army routed the sea-like hosts of two great kings who had risen together and saw them flee, leaving their drums.
nuance: The friend admits the women tried to hide his conduct with lies (பொய்புறம் பொதிந்துயாம் கரப்பவும்), so the refusal is also a confession that the household's loyalty has been spent. The cart sunk in mire and propped with creepers is a scene of the marutham fields; a reader may see the hidden affair being shored up in it, but no part-by-part match is anchored.

thinai_evidence.note: the refusal of the husband over his river-play with another woman

comparisons.tenor: the opening punku flowers, like popped rice
the two kings' great army, like the sea
the gossip about him, louder than the victory shout at Koodal

reading: The foster mother grieves for the girl who, trusting a stranger's false words and forgetting the nochchi that flowers with jasmine and her playmates, left the rich house desolate and went, bangles jingling and anklets ringing on her red feet, through a waste of fearful forked paths where a white-headed kite on a black-stemmed omai calls its mate; she asks whether, since the girl would not let her wash her hair with tagaram when she combed and parted it, that hair, now that her lover as fine as she weaves fragrant flowers into it, falls over her back like the bright ripples of the sweet forest river north of Vaanan's Sirukudi, where a crooked-legged tortoise and its young snatch ripe white mangoes in the encircling pond.
nuance: The foster mother's grief is jealous of a task: she combed and dressed the hair the girl would not let her wash, and now pictures the lover doing it. The kite calling its mate on the waste, 'so that pity comes' (அருள்வர), is the pair the girl has become.

thinai_evidence.note: the daughter's elopement through the waste

thurai_akam.speaker: sevili
thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named

comparisons.tenor: the lover, equal to the girl in worth
the girl's dark hair falling over her back, like the bright ripples of the forest river

reading: The friend tells the hero, who is handsome as Murugan himself, that if he comes by day, his strong hunting dogs behind him, to the small hill village by the roaring white waterfall where women wearing honey-scented vengai flowers dance in the street to the tondakam drum, they fear the gossip, and they fear still more his coming alone at pitch-dark midnight when the tiger that missed the great elephant hurrying with its mate and calf lies in wait; what will become of her friend, who has even stopped singing the parrot-scaring songs in the ripening millet where they met for many days — pitiable, she has nothing but his grace.
nuance: Both trysts are closed in turn, day by gossip and night by the tiger, and the millet field is closed too, since she no longer guards it; only marriage is left, though the friend never names it. The elephant that takes its mate and calf out of the tiger's reach is the path's danger here; the poem does not turn it on the hero.

thinai_evidence.note: the vengai, the millet field and its parrot-scaring of the hill tryst

reading: Told that he will leave, the heroine (or, in the colophon's second reading, the friend) asks whether the man who looked closely and said 'she will suffer, her brow, shoulders and spotted waist losing colour, beauty and lines', and still goes without thinking marriage good, will truly venture, with a peacock-feathered spear broad-bladed like a neythal petal as his only companion, along a mountain road of dry tracks where pirandai vines cut by travelers wither by the path like the green pieces of a snake struck by thunder, where bow-strong Mazhavar roast meat on the abandoned hearth stones of salt caravans, and where a great elephant whose head the tiger gashed dips its trunk in a dry spring and sighs.
nuance: He foresaw her wasting in detail and still did not choose marriage (வரைவுநன்று என்னாது): the complaint is that his knowledge did not change his act. The wounded elephant at the dry spring and the spear as his only companion make the road a place where even strength is alone and thirsty.

colophon.thurai: செலவுணர்த்திய தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொற்றது. தோழி தலைமகட்குச் சொற்றதூஉமாம்.

thinai_evidence.note: the dry road and waterless spring he will take

comparisons.tenor: the cut pirandai withering by the road, like pieces of a thunder-struck snake
the spear's broad bright blade, shaped like a neythal petal

reading: Having brought the heroine home from the daytime meeting, the friend tells the hero that the sun has sunk in the west as green-legged herons, flying in a line like the garland on tall Murugan's chest, cross the red sky after fish, and her friend, her proud rain-dark eyes in tears and her fragrant beauty spoiled, has begun to burn with longing; so would anything be lost if, rather than setting out at night with his bowmen and his mule, its leg wounded by a backwater shark and worn out by the long waters, he stayed and then went from their country of the great backwater, where palmyras rise in white-sand gardens, the anril calls and small-budded neythal grows?
nuance: The invitation is phrased as a harmless question (சிதைகுவது உண்டோ): staying one night would cost him nothing, while her weeping has already begun. The anril, the bird of pairs that cannot part, calls in the last lines; the poem leaves it as the sound of the place.

thinai_evidence.note: the backwater shore at sunset

comparisons.tenor: the line of herons across the red sky, like the garland on Murugan's chest

title: மணிமிடைபவளம் 121-140
theme: Akananuru 121 to 140, from the மணிமிடைபவளம் section: paalai partings argued with the heart or comforted by the friend, kurinji night-tryst poems spoken for an overhearing lover (the sleepless town, the dangerous path, the mother's Murugu rite), three mullai returns in the rains, a neythal pair of men smitten by a girl's eyes, and a full wedding night recalled in marutham, with puram fame (Karikal at Vaakai, Anni and Thithiyan, Cheralathan, Kazhuvul's Kamur, Thithan's Uranthai) used as the scale of comparison.
source_issues: akananuru:122: flagged repair: a stray copy of the first line of poem 121 stood as line 1 and was dropped; the printed line numbers then fit.
akananuru:123: lineation flag: the last line is numbered 12 though the poem has 14 lines.

akananuru:125: the colophon thurai begins with a stray digit (2தலைமகன்) and has தலைமகட்கச் for தலைமகட்குச்; copied as is in `colophon`. The colophon's speaker (the friend, on learning he has returned) does not fit the poem, which addresses the north wind and makes the return conditional (வல்வரின்).

akananuru:129: the quotation marks of the base text open at line 1, close at line 1, and open again at line 3 with no clear close before line 16, so the boundary between the man's quoted words and the friend's is uncertain.
akananuru:131: numbering flag: the poem is printed with the number 130.
akananuru:132: lineation flag: a printed line number 5 stands on line 10.
akananuru:140: line 12 மாமூ தள்ளல் is a sandhi split of மாமூது அள்ளல் (the old deep mire); not an error, but the word division is misleading.

reading: The man tells his heart they have cause for joy: the girl of broad soft shoulders, they say, will come with him into the summer forest of black-faced langurs, where a bull elephant washes his young mate's head with the muddy water of a dug pit in a shrunken pond and rests in the striped shade of a kadamba, and where a startled beast calls to a traveller's white rice-bundle blown by the wind, taking it for its mate.
nuance: The road is shown at its worst (the shrunken pond, the travellers killed by Mazhavar raiders, their food parcels blowing loose), so the joy of the first line is the measure of what she is willing to cross with him. The beast that mistakes a dead man's rice-bundle for its mate turns the image of companionship into one of loss.

colophon.thurai: தோழியால் தலைமகளை உடன்வருமெனக் கேட்ட தலைமகன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: she is to leave home with him across the dry land, the parting of udanpokku

occasion.words: தோழியால் தலைமகளை உடன்வருமெனக் கேட்ட தலைமகன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது

iraicchi.act: in the drought the bull elephant washes his young mate's head and rests with her in the shade
iraicchi.sense: as the tusker tends his mate on the parched road, so the man will tend the girl who crosses it with him

reading: With her lover listening outside, the girl tells her friend that their secret love has as many hindrances as the old stony outskirts of Thithan's Uranthai: the noisy town never sleeps, and when it does the mother does not, then the watchmen, the young spearmen, the dog, the bright moon, the owl at the ghost-hour and the cock each keep watch in turn, and on the one night when all are asleep he does not come.
nuance: The poem is a chain: each sleeper hands the watch to the next, and the last link is the lover's own absence, so the complaint aimed at the overhearing man is that he is the final obstacle. The listing presses him toward marriage without saying so.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் சிறைப்புறத்தானாகத் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லுவாளாய்த் தலைமகள் சொற்றது. தோழி சொல்லெடுப்பத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியதூஉமாம்.

thinai_evidence.note: the obstacles to a night meeting in secret love

occasion.words: தலைமகன் சிறைப்புறத்தானாகத் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லுவாளாய்த் தலைமகள் சொற்றது

comparisons.tenor: their secret love, beset on every side

reading: In the middle of the desert the man rebukes his heart: you cannot cross the hills where elephants, gaunt like fasting ascetics, file along narrow paths and bring back wealth, yet if you stay embracing her you fear poverty; like the tide at the Chola's Kaveri mouth that comes in with prawns and goes out with garlands, you hold to neither, so be ruined.
nuance: The tide image is exact: the heart neither goes nor stays but swings between the two each day. The elephants likened to ascetics who neither eat nor bathe make the road itself a place of renunciation.

thinai_evidence.note: the man torn on the road between going on for wealth and turning back

comparisons.tenor: the starving elephants filing along the path
the gleam of the Chola spear-blades
the heart that swings between going and staying

reading: The man, his campaign ending, tells the charioteer that if the enemy bring tribute and elephants and bow and ask the king to go, the king's army will enter today; so, to end the camp's hardship and gladden their beloved in the mansion, he must drive the swift horses with harness like lightning down the long road fragrant with rain-opened mullai, scattering the bees, and reach by morning the walled town where the evening drum sounds.
nuance: The man's homecoming waits on the enemy's surrender: the puram event decides the akam one, and he plans the drive before the tribute has even come.

thinai_evidence.note: the rain-opened mullai along the road of return

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is the charioteer (பாகன்)

comparisons.tenor: the gold-wrought harness of the horses

reading: Addressing the north wind, the speaker says that while he is away for wealth, and the rain-clouds that have emptied themselves roam the sky like an elephant past its must, the wind torments the lonely in the cold midnight; but if the man gone on his worthy work comes back soon, the wind will flee like the nine kings without honour who left their nine umbrellas at midday on the Vaakai field before great Karikal.
nuance: The colophon gives the friend speaking to the heroine on hearing he has returned, but the poem itself is spoken to the wind in the first person plural (எமக்கே), and the return is still conditional (வல்வரின்). The defeated kings are made a measure of disgrace: the wind will run as they ran.

colophon.thurai: 2தலைமகன் வினைமுற்றி மீண்டமை யுணர்ந்த தோழி தலைமகட்கச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: waiting through the rains for the man gone on his work

comparisons.tenor: the ripe buds of the eengai
the white eengai flowers strewn about
the cloud that has poured and is empty
the north wind put to flight

reading: The man tells his heart, which will not stop following the young girl with a parrot's prattle, kayal eyes, cloud-dark hair and lightning waist, that besides its own long sorrow it may perish like Anni, who would not be held back by the kind counsel of Evvi, lord of a rich Kaveri land where a bard's daughter refuses old paddy for the vaalai fish her brothers caught by night and takes pearls instead, and who fought Thithiyan for his punnai tree.
nuance: The Anni story is a warning of ruin from obstinate desire, and Evvi's rejected counsel stands for the advice the heart will not take. Nothing in the poem fixes whether the girl is a wife in sulking (alternative 1 of the colophon) or a girl not yet won (alternatives 2 and 3).

colophon.thurai: (1) உணர்ப்புவயின் வாரா ஊடற்கண் தலைமகன் தன்னெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது. (2) அல்ல குறிப்பட் டழிந்ததுமாம். (3) தோழியைப் பின்னின்ற தலைமகன் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியதுமாம்.

thinai_evidence.note: river, vaalai fish and paddy of the watered land, though they belong to the Evvi simile

occasion.words: உணர்ப்புவயின் வாரா ஊடற்கண் தலைமகன் தன்னெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது
தோழியைப் பின்னின்ற தலைமகன் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியதுமாம்

comparisons.tenor: the pearls the bard's daughter receives
the heart that may perish for its desire
her dark hair falling down her back

reading: The friend comforts the wasting girl: even if in a single day he could win treasure like the hoard of tribute that Cheralathan, who drove off the sea-foe, cut the kadamba and carved his bow on the Himalaya, heaped at Maanthai and left for the earth to eat, he would not stay a day longer in that land of strange speech where bowmen crowned with kadamba wait at the forks of the road.
nuance: The argument runs by scale: the largest wealth the hearers know, a king's buried tribute, would not hold him one extra day, so he will surely come. The kadamba appears twice, once as the enemy's guardian tree that Cheralathan felled and once as the wild bowmen's crown.

thinai_evidence.note: the dangerous forks of the road in a land of another tongue

comparisons.tenor: the wealth he might win in a single day

reading: With her lover outside, the girl tells her friend that the village has fallen silent and midnight comes on cruel as a killer, and her love overflows its banks like a sea; why then does her heart, without consulting either of them, go out tonight to the narrow path over the rocks, narrow as the rope on an elephant's back, slippery with rain and full of hidden pits, to watch his steps and hold up his faltering feet as he comes wearing kuvalai from the mountain spring?
nuance: The fear is turned around: the girl is anxious not for herself but for him on the night path, and since he is listening, the danger she describes is the argument for ending the night meetings by marriage.

colophon.thurai: இரவுக்குறி வந்ததலைமகன் சிறைப்புறத்தானாகத் தலைமகள்தோழிக்குச் சொல்லுவாளாய்ச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the mountain path at midnight

comparisons.tenor: the cruelty of the midnight hour
the narrow path along the rock ridge

reading: The friend tells the girl that the man who shared her trembling nights and said one must keep her in mind after parting cannot forget her, for, his heart opening, he said that the hard desert, where a stag calls its doe to rice fallen from the bamboo, where in a ruined border hamlet a bird feeds its mate young cotton bolls and poor women gather the burst seed, and where raiders who ate fat cattle crowd the clear spring, would not be hard to cross with her.
nuance: Two creatures feed their mates in his description of the road (the stag calling its doe to food, the bird feeding its mate), and the friend sets them before the girl as his own words. The quotation marks of the base text are unclear at lines 1 and 3, so which words are the man's and which the friend's is not fixed.

thinai_evidence.note: the hard dry track with its raiders

iraicchi.act: the bird feeds young cotton bolls to its mate in the ruined hamlet
iraicchi.sense: the man who noticed a bird feeding its mate on that road will not forget to care for the girl

reading: The man answers the friends who rebuke him: had you seen her face to face you would not rebuke me, for the bold look of that young woman's bright face, her painted eyes that put to shame the bee-opened neythal of the curving backwater, at the harbour of Korkai of chariot-lord Vazhuthi, where thaazhai guards its white flowers and horses' hooves crush the pearls the waves bring in.
nuance: The whole shore of Korkai is laid out as the setting of a single look: the pearls trodden underfoot by horses tell how rich the place is, and the girl's eyes defeat even the flowers of such a shore.

thinai_evidence.note: the screw-pine, the neythal flower and the sandy shore

comparisons.tenor: her painted eyes, which the flowers turn their backs to

reading: The man refuses his heart, which says that giving is worth more than the girl with bee-dark hanging hair and a cool garland, and bids him come through the dread forest where the hero-stones of men who died recovering cattle driven off at dawn by bowmen, crowned with peacock feathers and inscribed with name and fame, stand along every path like a hostile front of planted spears and shields: I will not come, heart; may your work succeed.
nuance: The heart argues from a puram value (ஈதல், the giving that needs wealth), and the man answers with the price of that value, the hero-stones of men killed on the road. The dismissal, வாய்க்கநின் வினையே, turns the usual blessing on the departing man into an ironic farewell to his own heart.

thinai_evidence.note: the hot dread track lined with hero-stones

comparisons.tenor: the rows of hero-stones along the path

reading: Meeting the lover after leading the girl home, the friend tells him that the millet is harvested, the girl's forehead has lost its beauty to lovesickness and the town eyes her and talks; so if he loves this hunters' sister with bamboo shoulders and rain-cool eyes, let him take her away to his own town walled by great hills, where a small-winged bee that opened the buds by the spring sips the vengai, sleeps in the honeyed kaanthal and dreams of the elephant's must.
nuance: The harvest of the millet ends the daytime meetings in the field, which is why the friend speaks now. A traditional reading takes the bee that moves from vengai to kaanthal as a hint at the lover; the poem gives only one correspondence, so it is left as scene.

thinai_evidence.note: millet, vengai and kaanthal of the hills

reading: The girl tells her worried friend that he once asked her, in vain, whether she could come with him to drink the wind-blown spray of a flower-laden forest stream in a rain-fresh pasture land of vengai, kaayaa and ilavam where white clouds drift like bow-beaten cotton; now he has crossed alone the wild Milai track where a twisted-horned stag keeps his young doe that chews the marul grass.
nuance: The remembered invitation is all mullai freshness, the present road is paalai; she sets the land he offered her against the one he took alone. The colophon says she means to show she can bear it, but கொன் ('in vain') carries a reproach.

thinai_evidence.note: he has crossed the forest without her

iraicchi.act: the stag keeps beside its young doe as she grazes
iraicchi.sense: even the stag of that forest stays with its mate, yet he crossed it without her

reading: Returning with his work done, the man tells the charioteer that the rains have come and the forest is lovely, with sapphire-blue poovai, red velvet-mites and fallen mullai on red soil like a master's painting; let the horses step softly and forget the goad, for if the twisted-horned stag and his doe in their loving union hear the swift chariot, [they will be parted], and still a midnight meeting can be theirs at home.
nuance: The man spares the mating deer the noise of his chariot on his way to his own reunion; his care for them is the tenderness he brings home. The syntax of the last two lines is compressed, and whose union the midnight meeting is (the deer's restored, or his with his wife) is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: the forest pasture in the rains

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is the charioteer (பாகன்)

comparisons.tenor: the red-soil pasture strewn with flowers

iraicchi.act: the stag and doe lie together in loving union
iraicchi.sense: the deer's union is the one the man is hurrying home to, and the care he takes not to break it is the care he brings to his wife

reading: The girl tells her friend that her skin has lost its tender sheen, her forehead is spread with pallor like the peerkku flower, her eyes weep, and her mind is changed like Aathi Manthi's; her lover has crossed the forest where iruppai flowers fall on the rock like dice in the burning wind, and her heart that trusted him is shaken like Kazhuvul's Kamur when fourteen Velir of undying fame attacked it together.
nuance: Two legendary disasters frame her state: Aathi Manthi who lost her husband to the river and went mad, and the siege of Kamur by fourteen chiefs at once. Her trust (தெளிந்த) is the fortress that has fallen.

thinai_evidence.note: he has crossed the sun-scorched forest

comparisons.tenor: her mind gone strange with grief
the iruppai flowers fallen on the rock
her heart that trusted him, now shaken

reading: The man, kept out by his wife's unyielding sulk, recalls to his heart their wedding: the feast of ghee-rich rice, the good omens and the moon in Rohini, the drums, the bathing of the bride, the arugu and vaakai garland tied with white thread, the sand-strewn pandal; and on the first night, when he asked her to loosen the cloth that made her forehead sweat and pulled the covering, her body flashed like a sword from its sheath, and not knowing how to hide she bowed her head in shame and hid in the darkness of her flowered hair.
nuance: This is the fullest account of a wedding in the anthology. The sulk of the colophon is not in the poem: the man answers present refusal only by remembering her first shyness, and the poem ends inside the memory.

colophon.thurai: உணர்ப்புவயின் வாராஊடற்கண் தலைமகன் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem gives no landscape; the colophon's sulk decides it

occasion.words: உணர்ப்புவயின் வாராஊடற்கண் தலைமகன் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது

comparisons.tenor: the dark petals of the arugu buds
the sand strewn thick under the pandal

reading: The friend tells the girl who fears he will leave that although he has not even set out for the forest track where a tusker, longing for his mate, follows her footprints past the travellers' mud wells, her forehead has already become a waste like the empty theatre with cold hearths in the grove at the Chola's Uranthai the day after the Panguni festival, and her shoulders, once like the tall bamboo on Chezhiyan's hill, have lost their old beauty: I grieve.
nuance: The friend's point is the girl's haste: she wastes for a parting that has not happened. The tusker following its mate's tracks on the very road she fears quietly answers her fear.

thinai_evidence.note: the dry forest track with its mud wells

comparisons.tenor: her shoulders in their old beauty

iraicchi.act: the tusker, longing for his mate, follows her footprints as he crosses the track
iraicchi.sense: on the road she fears he will take, even the tusker cannot be parted from his mate, so he will not leave her

reading: With her lover outside, the girl tells her friend that when she wept for no cause her mother suspected something else and every night, wearing neem and blue lily, with music like the Pothiyil falls of the Pandya, has Murugu brought into the house and sings of the kadamba and the elephant, searching for the cause: is that good? Her own heart thinks only of the long hard way by which the hill lord comes at midnight, over the peak where in pitch darkness a dragonfly sipping kaanthal is bewildered by the colour of a snake that has spat its jewel.
nuance: The mother's veriyaattu is described in full (Murugu brought into the house, the kadamba and the elephant sung) and dismissed by the girl as a vain search; aimed at the listening lover, it warns that the household is already looking for the cause.

thinai_evidence.note: the hilltop at midnight, the hour of the tryst

comparisons.tenor: the sweet music of the rite

reading: The wasting girl tells her friend that the rains have had their last day of darkening, flashing and roaring, the empty clouds play on the high hills at dawn, the stag has drunk and grazed and rests with his lovely mate in the pidavam shade, and red velvet-mites shine by the running water; if he still does not come, what has become of him, for was this not the thundering season in which he said he would come?
nuance: The landscape is all fulfilment (the rain spent, the stag at rest with its mate), so the only thing missing is the man. The last two lines can be read as 'this is not the season he named' (a comfort she tries on herself) or 'was it not this season' (the broken promise); the second fits her fear in line 17.

thinai_evidence.note: waiting through the rains for a man who promised to return with them

comparisons.tenor: the red velvet-mites spread by the water

iraicchi.act: the stag, fed and watered, rests at ease beside his mate in the shade
iraicchi.sense: the season has brought every creature home to its mate, so the man's absence has no excuse

reading: After his first meeting with her, the man tells his companion that the salt-merchant's young daughter, crying 'white salt for the same measure of paddy!' through the street with her bangles jingling, startled by a barking house dog, turned on him eyes like fighting kayal fish, and they have become a sickness that makes him strain and breathe hot like the ox yoked to her father's cart sunk in deep old mud.
nuance: The simile turns on her own family: the man compares himself to the beast that pulls her father's salt cart out of the mire, so his love has already yoked him to her household.

thinai_evidence.note: the fishermen's salt pans in the backwater

comparisons.tenor: the man labouring in his lovesickness

title: மணிமிடைபவளம் 141-160
theme: Akananuru 141 to 160, in the anthology's fixed order of lands: ten paalai poems weigh wealth against parting from both sides (men who go, one who stays, women who consent, resolve to follow, or scorn the stay-at-home), two foster mothers mourn eloped girls, hill poems move secret meetings between day and night, and neythal and marutham poems press for marriage. Puram fame (Minjili and the fallen Eyinan, Kurukkai's punnai, Muziri's trade, Pittan, Nannan, Nalli, Aay) is used throughout as the measure of private feeling.
source_issues: 143: the colophon thurai reads தலைகனைத், a misprint for தலைமகனைத்.
146: line 6 reads ஒள்ளிமழை, apparently a misprint for ஒள்ளிழை (bright-jewelled); line 8 reads அனியள், apparently for அளியள் (pitiable). Marked as the poem plainly means.
147: the base text has 14 lines and the commentary edition (pmuni0523_01) 13; marked as the base text stands.
155: line 15 reads வடுவில், where a comparison (வடுவின்) seems meant; recorded as a comparison without a marker.
157: the base text numbers the last line 15 though the poem has 14 lines; a misprinted number.

reading: Answering a friend who fears she cannot bear the parting, the woman says her dreams are sweet night after night, the house birds give good omens and her heart is eager: may he come back for the town's festival of lamps on the full-moon midnight of the six stars, he who crossed the Vengadam desert to bring wealth as famous as Karikal's town Idaiyaru.
nuance: Her answer to the friend's worry is a date, not resignation: she has fixed the Karthigai full moon as the night of his return. The wealth he went for is pictured not as gold but as a Chola town's household plenty (a new bride fed in her house, girls pounding fresh rice, a pregnant heron startled by the pestle), so even his errand is imagined as home.

thinai_evidence.note: she waits for a man who has crossed the desert for wealth

comparisons.tenor: the famous wealth he went to bring

reading: Leaving the night tryst, the man tells his heart to rejoice like the needy who carried full vessels away from Poraiyan Kadungo of Maantharam: she came at midnight, slowly, fearing that many would know, her dark hair swaying, walking like a doll that had learned to move, and embraced him till her bangle left its mark, speaking words sweet as tuned strings.
nuance: Lines 7 to 14 set a puram battle (Minjili killing Athikan, 'a protection to the birds', at Nannan's Paazhi) beside her coming, but how the battle attaches to the sentence is not clear in our text: it may measure his joy or her daring. The patron simile is pointed: he is a suppliant who has received.

colophon.thurai: இரவுக்குறி வந்துநீங்குந் தலைமகன் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: a midnight meeting in secret love

comparisons.tenor: the red tongues of the noble praisers
the heart's fullness after her coming
the pollen dropping from her rain-soaked garland

reading: The friend tells the man that when he said, 'We will go, crossing the burning hills where the sun has stripped the teak and wind-fed fire roars in the clefts', at that small word the woman's eyes ran with tears like the blue lilies opened by spray in a pool on Kudhirai hill of Pittan, the Chera's warrior who showers fine vessels on those who live by hope; and the friend grieves.
nuance: The long, vivid account of the road is the man's own speech, quoted back; the friend's reply is one phrase, 'small word', and the tears. The colophon says it worked: he gave up the journey.

colophon.thurai: பொருள்வயிற் பிரியக்கருதிய தலைகனைத் தோழி தலைமகளது ஆற்றாமை கண்டுசெலவழுங்குவித்தது.

thinai_evidence.note: a man proposes to leave for work across the desert

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon does not say whether this is before or after marriage

reading: His war done, the man tells his heart (for the charioteer to hear) that his wife may say the days he promised have proved false, her tears will not stop, he forgets her hair bare of mullai garlands, he has no fear of wrong; but on the day his people hurry home to tell of the wealth won in battle, from a camp where the rutting elephant trumpets back at the thunder, she will rejoice as if she already had the embrace that ends all sulking.
nuance: He imagines her complaint in her own words before he imagines her joy, and her joy comes from the news before he arrives: the report of the victory does the work of the embrace (துனிதீர் முயக்கம் பெற்றோள் போல).

thinai_evidence.note: a wife waiting through the rains for a man at war

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is the charioteer (பாகன்), spoken to as if to his own heart

comparisons.tenor: her joy at the news of victory
the blood glittering here and there on the field

reading: The foster mother hears that her girl has crossed with her man the empty, sun-stripped forest where cicadas shrill like chariot bells and a tiger-wounded elephant roars like thunder; and she curses her own hand, which in the rich father's house once seized the girl's small hair and beat her till the stick broke: may it come to harsh ruin like the punnai felled at Kurukkai in the war of Anni and Thithiyan.
nuance: The curse falls on her own hand, not on the man who took the girl: the elopement is read back as the result of her harshness at home. The girl who tired after a single step in her father's house is set against the road she has now crossed.

thinai_evidence.note: a girl has left with her lover across the desert

thurai_akam.speaker: sevili
thurai_akam.note: she grieves aloud; no hearer is named

comparisons.tenor: the hand that beat the girl, cursed to ruin

reading: Refusing the bard sent to plead for her husband, the woman says that if his tall belled chariot will not stop going for days on end to the street of the bright-jewelled women, then whoever she is, the woman who now trusts that deceiving philanderer's word as she once did will weep like a wind-shaken flower dripping dew, go pale, and give up the beauty her mother guarded.
nuance: She speaks of the new woman with pity rather than anger (அளியள்), and the pity is self-description: எம்போல், like me. The opening buffalo, which spends the day in the flowered pond and then lies down by a young cow near the garden, carries the charge without her stating it.

colophon.thurai: வாயில் வேண்டிச் சென்றபாணற்குத் தலைமகள் வாயில் மறுத்தது.

thinai_evidence.note: a wife refuses her husband's go-between over his other women

comparisons.tenor: the new woman's tears dropping on her breast
the new woman who trusts him as the speaker once did

ullurai.tenor: the husband and the new young woman he has taken up

pairs.situation: he spends his days roaming the courtesans' quarter
he takes up a young new woman
he settles near the home but not in it

ullurai.speaker_fit: the wife uses the buffalo of her own town's fields, a thing she knows (porul 7.26)

tamil: செலவு அயர்ந் திசினால் யானே; பல புலந்து,
reading: Told by her friend that the man is leaving, the woman says that, like Velli Veethi, she has made herself ready to go on that endless forked road where a spotted tiger listens for the stag's call to feed his mate, starving in a rock cleft after bearing three cubs; wasting unfed, her shoulders losing their beauty, grieving daily for his return, she has no will to stay behind, since there is no other medicine.
nuance: Velli Veethi is the name of a woman poet (Akananuru 45 is under her name); the heroine claims her as a precedent for a woman who goes after the man. The hungry tigress fed by her mate, and the woman who does not eat (உண்ணா உயக்கம்), stand a few lines apart.

thinai_evidence.note: a woman about to be left resolves to follow on the desert road

comparisons.tenor: her own resolve to go after the man

iraicchi.act: the male tiger hunts for his mate, who is starving in her cleft after giving birth
iraicchi.sense: on the very road he will take, the beast provides for its mate in her need, while he leaves her to waste unfed

reading: To the man of the land where a rutting elephant, after smashing trees and goring a tiger, raids the millet field, the friend says the girl's distress is great, like the owl that, ashamed when Aay Eyinan fell fighting Minjili, does not go abroad in broad day; so he must come at nightfall, by the small stony path where the great tusker grazes shoots.
nuance: The owl's shame belongs to the Eyinan legend in which the birds shaded the fallen hero from the sun: the night bird could not join them. The friend turns that daylight shame into the reason the meetings must move from day to night. The raiding elephant of the address may hint at his daytime visits to the field she guards, but the poem never makes the match.

thinai_evidence.note: hill slopes, millet fields and elephants

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon does not name the speaker; the friend speaks of the girl as இவள்

comparisons.tenor: the girl's distress at day meetings

reading: The man tells his heart he will not go down the long desert road, where bears raid the iruppai blossoms when tired of termites, even if the precious wealth that is hard to win came easily, for it would fill with tears her eyes, which are like the paired blue lilies of the deep pool on the Tall One's hill west of Koodal, the city of Chezhiyan, who stormed Muziri where Yavana ships come with gold and leave with pepper.
nuance: He refuses not hard-won wealth but wealth gained easily, the strongest form of the refusal. Muziri's trade, gold in and pepper out, stands in the same sentence, so the richest wealth the poet knows is weighed against one woman's tears.

thinai_evidence.note: a man gives up the journey for wealth across the desert

tamil: தார் ஆர் மார்ப! நீ தணந்த ஞான்றே!
reading: The friend tells the man who comes for day meetings that the mother, seeing the girl's hair now loosed from its braid, the gold spots budding on her chest and her breasts rising, praised her, held her close, thought long, and put her under strict guard; and since he left, every time the girl sees the backwater and the shore grove where neythal closes at evening and opens with the kaavi at morning, she grieves, asking whether he will not come.
nuance: The mother's praise and embrace are themselves the act of confinement: the signs of the girl's coming of age are what close the house to her. The flowers that close at dusk and open at dawn mark the days she counts.

colophon.thurai: பகற்குறி வந்துகண்ணுற்று நீங்கும் தலைமகனைத் தோழி தலைமகளை இடத்துய்த்து வந்து, செறிப்பறிவுறீஇ வரைவு கடாயது.

thinai_evidence.note: backwater, shore grove and neythal flowers

comparisons.tenor: the pallor spots on her chest

reading: The woman tells her friend that the man, holding that the poor cannot support those who depend on them nor laugh at ease among their kin, has a heart set on great wealth for which grace counts for nothing, and has crossed the forest where uzhinjil pods rattle like a dancer's drum in the wind, and a small red-tongued lizard by a cairn's withered shade tells travellers what will befall them.
nuance: She quotes his reason fairly before judging it: the maxim is about duty to dependants and kin, not greed, and her complaint is only that it leaves no room for grace (அருள் பிறிது). The cairn and the omen-lizard put death and chance on the road his reason sends him down.

thinai_evidence.note: a man has crossed the forest in search of wealth

comparisons.tenor: the forked branches of the uzhinjil
the rattling of the dry pods

reading: Leaving the night tryst, the man tells his heart that the woman who came to end his trembling grief and is now going home to her small hill village, her curled hair like the peacock's train on the Ezhil hill at Nannan's Paazhi, her shoulders fragrant beyond the kaandhal of Nalli's slopes and smooth as the bamboo on the crags of Aay's forest, still gives him trembling pain though she is far away.
nuance: The chain of patrons (Thithan Veliyan's shore, Pindan defeated by Nannan, Nalli, Aay) is used only to grade her beauty: every great man's land supplies one feature. The phrase about Aay, who gives to all who come 'whether able or not', is a patron's praise carried whole into a love poem.

thinai_evidence.note: hill village, kaandhal and bamboo

reading: The foster mother grieves that the girl, who used to tire even chasing a ball with her sweet-voiced friends, has now trusted a hard man's chest and sweet words and gone without a thought for their sorrow into the summer forest where wind-struck bamboo throws up sparks and fire; she asks whether those soft feet can bear the barren desert under the dark hill, where at night kongu flowers fall like lamps let slip from the hand against a starry sky.
nuance: The only beauty in the poem is at the end, and it is a night image of falling lights on the hill the girl must pass under: the mother's fear and her eye for the land are in the same line.

thinai_evidence.note: the scorched summer forest and the barren way

thurai_akam.speaker: sevili
thurai_akam.note: she grieves aloud; no hearer is named

comparisons.tenor: the hill crest strewn with lit kongu flowers at night

reading: His work done, the man bids the charioteer drive fast over the rain-washed woodland, where frogs croak like many small instruments, pidavu blossoms streak the red sand, kodal buds open like a cobra's raised hood, and the twist-horned stag drinks clear water and rests in safety with his mate, so they may hasten to the lovely woman whose ways are bent on him.
nuance: The stag drinks and rests 'in safety' (ஏமுற) with his mate: the word for the beasts' ease is the word another homecoming poem uses for the man's own heart (Akananuru 34).

thinai_evidence.note: rain-washed woodland on the road home

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is the charioteer (பாகன், வலவ)

iraicchi.act: the stag drinks clear water and rests in safety beside his mate
iraicchi.sense: the man, his work done, means to come home and rest with his wife as the stag does with his mate
