reading: The woman tells her friend that the man who stroked her hair saying 'A life that never comes to the door of wrong, and wealth that never goes to another's door: both come from wealth, my jewelled one' may finish his work though she suffers; he has crossed the hills where the marul withers, where in Paan country the tiger's pugmarks in an elephant's footprint by a herdsmen's dried well look like finger marks pressed into a drum's head.
nuance: She consents in his own words, and the consent is real (தாந்தம் செய்வினை முடிக்க), but the two goods his maxim names are virtue and independence; the pleasure of the household, which his going costs, is not among them.

thinai_evidence.note: a woman endures a man's absence on his errand for wealth

comparisons.tenor: the tiger's pugmarks in the elephant's footprint

reading: The friend tells the lord of the town, where guards fence the drooping rice ears from an old cow with gourd vines and cotton, that since she and the girl, playing in the fields in leaf skirts of ambal, met him, the girl's gem-dark skin has turned gold with pallor, and her mother, weeping and finding no cure, offers toddy, garlands and a white goat to the god of the ford: was it their fault?
nuance: The mother treats the pallor as a god's seizure and sacrifices for it; the friend lets the man know that only he can cure it. Line 12 (நின்நகாப் பிழைத்த தவறே) is hard and we cannot fix whose laughing or not laughing is the fault. The guarded rice may point to the girl's guarded youth, but the poem does not name the guarding, so it is left as scene.

colophon.thurai: தலை மகளைஇடத்துய்த்துவந்த தோழி தலைமகனை வரைவு கடாயது

thinai_evidence.note: rice fields, ford and the town lord; the human situation is courtship, not quarrel

reading: The woman tells her friend that men who mean to go alone down the fearful road, where red-eyed bowmen drunk on palm toddy roar for war and a forest elephant at dawn eats the athiral creeper that bloomed by night over the cairns of the slain, would speak such heart-consuming words only to women able to stay home, withering like a ruined painted doll in the deserted square of a raided village.
nuance: She defines the woman who can be left as a thing already ruined, a doll rotted by rain and sun in an emptied village; by implication she is not that woman, and his words are wasted on her.

thinai_evidence.note: the bandit road with cairns of the slain

comparisons.tenor: the woman who can stay behind, withering

reading: With the man listening nearby, the friend tells the foster mother not to torment the girl for what she says she saw at midnight after the storm, earrings flashing like lightning, swaying like a peacock coming down a hill: on their garden hill spirits come in any form they please and dreams fool sleepers like waking truth, and this girl shivers alone without a lamp, runs for shelter when the owl hoots in the kadamba, and with their fierce father away would she ever dare such a thing?
nuance: The defence offers two explanations (a hill spirit, a dream) and a character witness (her timidity), and every word of it also reaches the hidden lover: the mother has seen, and the night meetings cannot go on.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன்சிறைப்புறத்தானாகத் தோழி செவிலித்தாய்க்குச்சொல்லுவாளாய்த் தலைமகன் கேட்பச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: midnight after rain on the hill

comparisons.tenor: the father's pack of hunting dogs

reading: The friend tells the woman not to grieve that her lover has crossed the forked road where bowmen, back from raiding cattle on the frontier, cook meat to the beat of the tudi beside the cold hearth stones left by salt carters; even if he reached Aamur with its high walls east of Vaanavan's hill, where that king broke the tusks of elephants, he is not a man to stay there and forget her breast.
nuance: The road's dangers are named only to be set aside: the comfort rests not on the road being safe but on the man's attachment outlasting even a famous city.

thinai_evidence.note: the friend comforts a woman whose man has crossed the desert

reading: The friend asks the girl whether her heart too is trembling: the chariot of the lord of the shore, where the open-mouthed male turtle guards the eggs his mate buried in the white sand until they hatch, used to come at night, the driver easing the horse through the backwater so the wheel cut the neythal buds, which rose like snakes' raised heads; now it has come by day, openly, with shouting young men, for the noisy little village to see.
nuance: Night against day, hiding against showing (கரவாது): the chariot's daylight arrival is the public sign of marriage, and the village whose gossip was the danger is now the witness.

thinai_evidence.note: backwater, turtle and neythal on the shore

iraicchi.act: the male turtle guards the eggs his mate buried in the sand until they hatch
iraicchi.sense: the man who now comes openly will guard her and their household as the turtle guards its brood

title: மணிமிடைபவளம் 161-180
theme: Manimidaipavalam 161-180: separation for wealth and war argued from both sides of the road, the friend's dissuasions and comforts, the marutham quarrel heard from wife and other woman, and the press toward marriage in the hills.
source_issues: 161: line 9 reads தோழ் தாழ்பு, probably for தோள் தாழ்பு (hair falling to the shoulders); the flag also records line 3 as repaired from a joined line.
162: lines 1 and 2 (கொளக்குறை படாஅக் கோடுவளர் குட்டத்து அளப்பு அரிது ஆகிய குவைஇருந் தோன்றல) are obscure in word division and sense.
164: a printed line number 5 stands on line 10 (flag); line 6 ends with a stray closing quotation mark, and line 7 வெறியேன் றன்றே looks mis-divided.
165: the base text has 13 lines, the commentary edition 12 (flag); line 3 ஒய்யென எந்த is unclear (perhaps ஏந்த).
166: the colophon thurai has a stray digit before பரத்தை (கேட்ட 3பரத்தைதன்).
168: the colophon says இரவுக்குறி வந்ததலைமகளை, but the poem addresses the hero (வெற்ப!); தலைமகனை looks intended.
169: line 14 (வருந்துமால், அளியள் திருந்திழை தானே) is repeated as Akananuru 224 line 18 (flag).
175, 180: the colophons give a second speech situation (…உமாம்) without numbering; 175's is split as சொற்றதூ உமாம்.
178: line 19 closes a quotation (…அரிது' எனக்) that never opens.

reading: The friend asks the man what this leaving for work can mean: has the girl already heard that he means to cross, for wealth, the frightening forest where hard-eyed archers kill travellers and the red-eared vulture calls its kin to the carrion, since her many-petalled eyes are already pouring tears onto her young breasts?
nuance: The friend never reports the departure to the girl; she argues that the girl has read it in him before any word was spoken, so her tears are the friend's whole case for stopping him. The forest is given as the man's own reported resolve (பொருள் புரிந்து இறப்ப எண்ணினர்), set inside quotation, as if overheard.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவுணர்த்தியதோழி, தலைமகளதுவேறுபாடு கண்டு முன்னமேஉணர்ந்தாள் நம்பெருமாட்டியென்று தலைமகனைச்செலவு விலக்கியது.

thinai_evidence.note: a man resolved to cross the waste for wealth

comparisons.tenor: her young breasts, risen as if a tormenting power

reading: Leaving after a night meeting, the man tells his heart how, at midnight in a storm whose lightning split a sky like the sea, he stood by one corner of her father's guarded house until the guards slackened, and she came, trembling like a shoot in the wind, and held him till his sickness eased: she who is as hard to win as the goddesses of the high slope where waterfalls shine like the Pandiyan's flag, on the hill of Athigan who never fails a suppliant.
nuance: The danger he braved (the storm, the guards, the father's house) is the proof of love he offers his own heart, and the closing image places her among the hill goddesses, beyond reach even while just embraced. Lines 1 and 2 are obscure: they seem to describe the unmeasurable dark mass of cloud drawn from the deep, but the word division is uncertain.

colophon.thurai: இரவுக்குறிக்கண்தலைமகளைக் கண்ணுற்று நீங்கிய தலைமகன் தன்நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: a secret night meeting at her father's house in the hills

comparisons.tenor: the wide sky, like the sea
lightning, like a creeper of flame
her hair, gleaming like rippled dark sand
her rain-cool eyes, like flowers in her bright face
her white teeth, like a row of buds
her trembling, like a tender shoot in the wind
the shining waterfalls, like the Pandiyan's victorious flag on his elephants
the girl, as hard to win as the goddesses of the slope

reading: Alone at the end of the rains, bangles slipping as she thinks of the man who went, the woman turns on the cold north wind of the early-dew midnight, whose spray like an elephant's breath scorches the lotus: it seems to have come for her alone, so let it go, as unrelenting as she is, to the land where the cruel one went; those eager in their work may yet remember.
nuance: She sends her tormentor as her messenger: the wind that melts her heart like a heap of fine sand in a stream is told to do the same to him. The last line is a hope that slips out under the anger: men intent on work also remember.

thinai_evidence.note: she waits at home at the turn of the season, watching for his return

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the poem itself addresses the north wind

comparisons.tenor: the wind's spray, like an elephant's breath
the cold of the north wind, as if a hill had melted
her heart dissolving like a heap of fine sand laid by a stream

reading: In the war camp the man tells his heart that the rains have restored the sun-cracked land, bees hum over mullai and glory lilies and the forest is fragrant: this is the season when she who lives in pain, eyes dripping, wondering how he fares, would regain her old beauty, if only the fierce king would release them from the work of his fort-breaking elephants.
nuance: The season he promised has come and he is held by another's war: the elephant that smashes forts and snaps its tethering post is the king's power, and also an image of the restraint he himself cannot break.

thinai_evidence.note: mullai flowers in the first heavy rains

comparisons.tenor: the sun's rays as hands that draw up the land's yield

reading: Onlookers describe the house after the daughter has gone off across many lands with her lover: her playmates have put off their ornaments and mourn, and the mother, crying 'give me your sweet shoulder, let my life end', strokes eyes and brow, rests in the striped shade of the nochi the girl used to touch, crowns her doll with fading kuvalai from the water-pot and embraces it weeping, 'this doll lying in the sand is my precious daughter'.
nuance: Lines 1 to 5 describe the lands the girl crossed: an elephant calf, frightened by the male's trumpeting when its mother fell into a pit, drinking from a buffalo's udder in an old town. Read as a hidden sense (the young parted from its mother and fed at another's breast) it would mirror the daughter, but the syntax of line 3 (எந்த) is unclear, so it is left as scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the daughter has left with her lover across many lands

thurai_akam.speaker: kandor
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names no addressee

comparisons.tenor: the doll taken for the daughter herself

reading: The other woman mocks the husband who soothes his wife with an oath ('may the fearsome god at the gate of Velur strike me if I was ever at that woman's shoulder'): if that is he, then who was it, friend, that yesterday clasped the head-float with us and, decked as for a wedding, bathed in the Kaveri's new flood?
nuance: She speaks so that the wife's people will hear, turning the god he swore by against him; the oath is set at Velur, where broken toddy jars chill the street like rain, so the shrine's grandeur makes the perjury worse.

colophon.thurai: பரத்தையொடு புனல்ஆடிய தலைமகன் தலைமகளிடைப் புக்கு யான்-ஆடிற்றிலன் என்று சூளுற்றான் என்பது கேட்ட 3பரத்தைதன் பாங்காயினார் கேட்பச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the husband's affair and his false oath to his wife

thurai_akam.speaker: parathai
thurai_akam.note: the parathai addresses her own friend so that the wife's people overhear

comparisons.tenor: the street chilled by spilt toddy as by drizzling rain

reading: Pressed by his heart to go for wealth, the man asks it: after tonight, spent sweetly with his dark-skinned wife in a sky-touching mansion, shall they tomorrow lie sleepless in the ruined public hall of a village the people fled for fear of caravan-raiding archers, where an elephant rubbing its back has toppled the brick wall, the doves have left, the painted god has gone and the unswept floor forgets its offerings, and termites roof the rafters? So he gives up the journey.
nuance: The ruin is built point by point against the bedroom: gems against termites, a made bed against a cracked floor, a full house against one even its god has deserted. The desolation of the road is what keeps him home, not her plea.

thinai_evidence.note: the deserted village of the robber-haunted waste

reading: The friend tells the hill-man that, having spent the night watch with him, they are left love-sick with wet eyes, and he must stop: will he still come at night, when the hunters sleep, down the narrow deer-path of the great slope where waterfalls roar like the kitchen of Udhiyan at Kuzhumur, where a male elephant, embracing the female who has just calved, guards the sleep of their swaying calf, and a fierce striped tiger roars in its cave?
nuance: The path is drawn to frighten (the tiger, the dark) and to instruct (the elephant family): the danger argues against night visits, the guarded calf argues for a household.

colophon.thurai: இரவுக்குறி வந்ததலைமகளை இரவுக்குறி விலக்கி வரைவு கடாயது.

thinai_evidence.note: the friend ends the lovers' night meetings in the hills

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon has தலைமகளை, but the poem addresses the hero (வெற்ப)

comparisons.tenor: the roar of the waterfalls, like the din of Udhiyan's kitchen

iraicchi.act: the male elephant embraces the female who has just calved and guards their calf's sleep
iraicchi.sense: the man who crosses this slope sees what he should be: a mate keeping a household, not a night visitor

reading: Halfway across the waste the man tells his heart how she must be suffering: on a burnt clearing where hunters roast on a fire-drill blaze the elephant meat a tiger left and salt-carriers cook rice with spring water and the sea's nectar, he has crossed many such wastes, while she, pale and thinking long in the lonely dimming evening, fingers to her brow, tears running, shoulders wasted, grieves.
nuance: Both halves are pictures of evening: the travellers' camp fire on the road and her vigil at home, so the man sees his own night and hers at once. The tears 'like water a kayal fish spits' turn her fish-shaped eyes into the simile's source.

thinai_evidence.note: the scorched waste he has crossed

comparisons.tenor: salt, as the nectar the sea grows
her tears, like water a kayal fish spits

reading: With no one else to carry her word (the grove, the backwater and the punnai will not speak), the woman begs the crab to tell the lord of the shore, where bees drunk on neythal scent falter in flight, that at midnight, while the small sea-crow wearied on the thazhai bough dreams of prawns beside its mate, she asks whether the one who cured his pain must now swim through her own.
nuance: Her message turns on a reversal: she once relieved his distress, and he leaves her to drown in hers. The bees that sip and then falter echo the lord of the shore himself.

thinai_evidence.note: punnai, neythal and the shore lord of the backwaters

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: she addresses the crab (அலவ)

comparisons.tenor: the neythal blooms of the backwater, like eyes
the bees take the neythal's scent as nectar

iraicchi.act: the small sea-crow rests through midnight beside its mate on the thazhai bough
iraicchi.sense: even the weary crow sleeps paired while she lies awake alone, which is the wrong he has done her

reading: The friend tells the woman not to grieve endlessly that her brow pales, her shoulders lose their bamboo-like beauty and she thinks of him daily: he will come back to her, the man who, set on wealth, crossed the waste where, because hill villagers roam with bows to hear the tiger's call, the bear leaves the honey below and climbs the black iruppai to eat its sweet flowers like fruit.
nuance: The bear that changes its food for fear of the hunters is only the road, but it shows a creature adapting to danger, which is what the friend asks of her.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பிரிவின்கண் வேறுபட்ட தலைமகளைத் தோழி வற்புறீஇயது.

thinai_evidence.note: he crossed the waste for wealth and she must bear it

comparisons.tenor: her shoulders, with the beauty of chosen bamboo
the iruppai's pulpy flowers, like fruit

reading: The friend tells the hill-man that on his slopes, where a honeyed waterfall sounds like drums, the iron-armed hunter kills an elephant, plants its tusk at his grass hut and feasts with his kin on jackfruit liquor and meat roasted on sandal brands; she never knew he was loveless, and had she known, gold-coloured pallor would not have spread over the girl's gem-like beauty.
nuance: The hunter's catalogue is of a man who takes, keeps and celebrates with his kin; the friend's reproach is that the hill-man has done only the taking. The reproach is aimed at marriage, as the colophon says.

colophon.thurai: தோழி தலைமகளை இடத்துஉய்த்துவந்து தலைமகனை வரைவு கடாயது.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill hunter and his slopes

comparisons.tenor: the waterfall's sound, like resounding drums
the hunter's black arm, like wrought iron

reading: The friend tells the woman he will come: set on his work, he said that never straying from dharma and propping up kin in their misfortunes are not for those who sit at ease, asked her to bear the hard sorrow a few days and straightened her bangles; then he crossed the gold-bearing slopes of Nannan's sky-touching range, where deer flee the salt-carriers' shouts and drought-split bamboo throws out pearls like kazhangu seeds.
nuance: The comfort is built on the man's own maxim: wealth is what makes dharma and help to kin possible, so his going is a duty, and the gesture of straightening her bangles seals the promise.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பிரிவின்கண் வேறுபட்ட தலைமகளைத் தோழி வற்புறுத்தியது.

thinai_evidence.note: he has gone across the hills for work

comparisons.tenor: the bamboo pearls, shining like kazhangu seeds

reading: In the war camp, having declared that victory now rests with the side that can turn back the attacking army with one force and set aside the drum that calls men to take the battle-flower, the man tells his heart she does not know he is coming: as the mullai sprouts under the morning rain, at every thunder she must shrink, helpless and resentful, pale with sorrow, she with spots on her breast like ripe vengai flowers and soft few steps on the sand.
nuance: The reading of lines 1 to 5 is uncertain: they may mean that he has declined the call to further battle and is going home, or that he went to war without her knowing. Either way the poem's present is her not knowing, while the rain she reads as betrayal is the season of his return.

thinai_evidence.note: the mullai creeper under the rain clouds

comparisons.tenor: the spots on her breast, like ripe vengai flowers

reading: The woman reminds her friend that the man who crossed the hot waste, where archers' whistling arrows take travellers' lives and vultures call their flock to the carrion, swore hard vows, held her bangled wrist and said he would come back with the work done when the cool clouds came down, flashing more often than the spear Chezhiyan raised after winning at Alangaanam, thundering like drums, the rainbow arched like the garland on the wheel-bearing god's chest, and the earth's yield flowering: and that time is now.
nuance: The poem calls the lover's promise a வஞ்சினம், the word for a warrior's vow, and frames the season of its testing with a king's victory and a god's garland, so a private promise is measured against the public oaths of puram. Against the friend's comfort she sets the season itself as evidence.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவின்கண்வற்புறுக்குந் தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது.பிரிவின்கண் வேறுபட்ட தலைமகள் தோழிக்குச்சொற்றதூ உமாம்.

thinai_evidence.note: she waits for the return promised for the rains, which have come

comparisons.tenor: the lightning, flashing more often than Chezhiyan's raised spear

reading: The friend refuses the husband at the door: lord of a town where, in a lotus pond wide as the sea, a long-eyed water crab, afraid of the white heron hunting for food, runs across the mud and hides in its water-filled hole, has your new beloved turned angry because you let go her bangled hand in the festival dance, so you come here? what does she owe, she who has borne no son and does not keep your house as we do? she weeps her painted face away, snaps her fingers red and blunts her teeth: go, so that she who tells the whole town about you may see you.
nuance: The crab's flight from the heron into its hole is the husband's flight from the other woman's rage into his wife's house, which the friend reads aloud only by refusing him entry. Lines 16 to 26 are dense and partly uncertain, especially who owes what in line 21.

thinai_evidence.note: a husband's affair and the wife's side refusing him

the hollow lotus stalks, like bamboo
the lotus leaves, like elephant ears
the plump buds, like raised stakes
the many flowers, like smiling faces
the crab's eyes, like neem buds
the crab's tracks in the mud, like the streaks of skin spots

tamil: இன்னும் வாரார்: இனி எவன் செய்கு? எனப்,
reading: The friend tells the woman not to despair that her old beauty is gone and he still does not come: though the man who went across the forest (where the sun withers the wazhai on bamboo slopes and a heavy-bellied peahen, craving red paagal fruit, cries like a horn on the Ayiri's bank) has stayed long, he will surely hurry back, remembering the painted designs among the spots on her breasts, budded like the shoots of the tall mango by the shaded pond on the Kaveri's north bank, in the land of Pannan whose spear stopped the hill-like elephants of his foes.
nuance: The comfort rests on his desire rather than his word: what will bring him back is the memory of her body, and the land the friend borrows to praise it is a warrior-patron's fertile riverbank.

thinai_evidence.note: he has crossed the forest and delays

comparisons.tenor: her oiled, bound tresses, like a female elephant's trunk
the peahen's cry, like a horn
her breast, like the mango's tender shoots

reading: The friend, glad that marriage is settled, tells the woman she joined knowingly with the lord of a good hill where a boar with diamond-sharp tusks drinks from a drum-round spring, gorges on chempu tubers, ambles down a rock shaped like a lying elephant, brushes pollen from the koothalam's flowers and, having grazed the millet, sleeps content: may she live with him for ever, her shoulders unspoiled, for he says nights alone in the cold dew are hard, knows no parting even in dreams, and by his nature loves her more than on the day he first saw her.
nuance: The boar that eats from the guarded millet field and then sleeps easy can be read as the man whose secret love is now made safe, but the poem gives no anchor for that, so it is left as scene. The friend quotes the man's own words as the guarantee.

thinai_evidence.note: the millet and the lord of the hills

comparisons.tenor: its coarse bristles, like bamboo roots
the full spring, like a drum's face
the chempu's broad leaves, like sapphire
the rock, like a lying female elephant
the seeping water, like a river
the white koothalam flowers, like herons perched on a green bush
the fallen pollen, like gold streaked on a touchstone

reading: The friend asks the man who has announced his going: if he wants to cross the waste of the sky-touching peak, where the mirage runs, fire has spread, the elephant raises its trunk to the sky and finds no water, the paths are lined with stones carved with archers' stances and no one quells the robbers' uproar, can he bear to live away from home while she of the sweet smile, quill-like teeth, kuvalai eyes and moon-bright brow is left alone?
nuance: The road's hero-stones are given as a plain warning of death on the path; the friend sets them beside the woman's face, feature by feature, and leaves the choice as a question.

thinai_evidence.note: the man means to leave home across the waste

comparisons.tenor: her massed sharp teeth, like peacock-quill tips
her kohl eyes, like fresh kuvalai flowers
her bright brow, like the moon

reading: It is laughable, friend: while we played at sand houses on the dunes of the grove, one man drove up in his chariot, needlessly hung a bee-thronged wreath of pond kuvalai down her braided back, gazed at her breasts, thought long and left without a word; and for that alone this noisy town now looks at the gold pollen of the bent punnai in the garden and looks at me too.
nuance: Under the mockery the friend is reporting a suitor's first approach and testing the girl's response, as the colophon says (குறைநயப்ப); the town's gaze at the pollen and at her is the first stir of gossip.

colophon.thurai: இரந்து பின்னின்றதலைமகற்குக் குறைநேர்ந்த தோழி தலைமகளைக்குறைநயப்பக் கூறியது. தலைமகன்சிறைப்புறத்தானாகத் தோழிக்குச்சொல்லியதூஉமாம்.

thinai_evidence.note: the thazhai and punnai of the backwater grove

comparisons.tenor: the punnai's fine pollen, like gold

title: மணிமிடைபவளம் 181-200
theme: Akananuru 181 to 200 in the anthology's fixed cycle of lands: ten paalai poems in which men argue with their hearts about going for wealth, three of them giving up the journey, and mothers mourn eloped daughters; around them hill trysts ruled by the weather and the harvest, a marutham quarrel told by both courtesan and wife, waiting in the promised rains, and neythal disclosure and invitation. Puram names (Minjili and Eyinan, Pazhaiyan of Por, Thithiyan and Anni Minjili, Kannan Ezhini, Nannan and Narmudi Cheral) serve as measures for private feeling.
source_issues: 183, 194: my inferred thinai (mullai for 183) differs from the colophon's paalai; both poems are the waiting wife at the arrival of the promised rains.
187: the colophon thurai gives a second alternative (…சொல்லியதூஉமாம்) without numbering the first.
189: lines 6 and 7 carry stray single quotation marks ('கவாஅன் … சுட்டிப்') that mark no speech.
192: the colophon thurai has a stray footnote numeral, 1செறிப்புஅறிவுறீஇ.
194: line 1 reads வகைறை, apparently a misprint for வைகறை.
199: line 10 reads பூளையன், apparently a misprint for பூளையின்.
190: line 17 (சேர்ந்தன்றே இலனே) is hard to construe; the reading of the rescue's end is uncertain.
183, 191: unbalanced quotation marks (183 line 1 opens a quotation that never closes; 191 line 16 closes one that never opens).

reading: A man on the road tells his heart, which cannot face the hard forest and wants to turn back, to go and report his state to the girl who lives on a great sand dune in a fragrant street of Pukar, a town of high walls, a Shiva shrine and a ford where women leave their dolls.
nuance: Most of the poem is the address of the girl's home, built up as a chain of places; the fall of Aay Eyinan to Minjili, with a flock of birds massing over the field and hiding the sun, is set beside the Kaveri's heaped white sand, so a battle memory becomes the measure of how thick that sand lies. The heart is not rebuked into going on, as in Akananuru 21; it is sent back as a messenger while the man goes forward.

thinai_evidence.note: a man mid-journey whose heart wants to turn back to the woman

comparisons.tenor: the Kaveri's sand, gathered and heaped into white dunes

reading: The friend tells the man of the hill country, where the hunter drinks jackfruit toddy and kills a porcupine, that the girl weeps every night thinking of him coming alone through midnight storms that strike down snakes, so he must come by full daylight instead.
nuance: The opening hunter, who returns with his kill through bloodied grass, is the hill's ordinary daytime courage set against the man's lonely night journey; the closing slope strewn with alari petals is likened to the velan's ground of possession, a hint of the mother's suspicion that the friend does not voice.

thinai_evidence.note: hill hunters, vengai and jackfruit, and a night tryst

comparisons.tenor: the slope strewn with fallen alari petals where the stag leaps

reading: The woman tells her friend that she was promised he would not stay long, though he went far across the waste; now the rain clouds, having drunk the sea, have come up from the west like herds of she-elephants, the cold wind spreads the scent of opening pidavu buds, and she asks whether those who are parted do not suffer.
nuance: The season he named has arrived on time while he has not, so the clouds prove the friend's comfort false; the clouds are described as a herd of pregnant she-elephants gathering with their kin, a picture of fullness and company set against her solitude.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் குறித்த பருவவரவு கண்டு தலைமகள் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the heroine waits through the promised rains; the road is only mentioned

comparisons.tenor: the dark rain clouds appearing here and there
her eyes, dark and wet like the blue water lily

reading: The friend greets the returning man: his coming at red dusk, his chariot bells ringing like a waterfall on rock, past fields where pidavu and jasmine bloom and the stag rests with its doe, is sweet not only to his wife, the light of the house who bore him a son, but to her too.
nuance: The friend's blessing 'may your life flourish' and her claim that the joy is hers as well make the welcome public; the wife is praised as mother and as 'light of the clan' before anything is said of her love, the karpu household seen from outside.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் வினைவயிற்பிரிந்து வந்து எய்தியவிடத்து தோழி புல்லுமகிழ்வு உரைத்தது.

thinai_evidence.note: jasmine, pidavu, the scrub and the deer at evening with the hero returned

comparisons.tenor: the ringing of the chariot's many bells

iraicchi.act: the stag, having drunk clear water, stays at rest beside its spotted doe
iraicchi.sense: the man who has finished his hard work now stays with his wife, as the stag on his road stays with its doe

reading: The woman tells her friend that her bangles slip and her shoulders lose their beauty while her lover, as if his life were made of iron, has hardened himself and crossed the scorched summer hills where bamboo bursts like a warrior's bowstring and leafless ilavam blazes like the lamps of a great festival.
nuance: Her only accusation is the iron simile: he is not cruel but able, வலித்து வல்லினர, to will the parting, and that ability is what she cannot match; the festival lamps on the bare ilavam are a celebration seen from inside her loss.

thinai_evidence.note: the summer waste with failed rain and leafless ilavam

comparisons.tenor: her lover, who could steel himself to leave
the dry bamboo bursting with a crack
the leafless ilavam trees in full red flower

reading: The courtesan, speaking so that the wife's companions hear, says the gossip about her and the lord of the town is loud, though their bond was only a bathing friendship on a raft of reed; he is now with another woman, and if the wife quarrels with her, let her know that it is her own husband, who leaves women pale, that is the enemy living in her house.
nuance: The courtesan both disowns and boasts: he has never broken her bangles, which stand firm like Pazhaiyan's fort of Por, so she is not the one he leaves; the lotus leaf that flaps like an elephant's ear at every gust may be read as his fickleness, but the poem does not make the match itself.

thinai_evidence.note: lotus pond, reed raft and the lord of the town

thurai_akam.speaker: parathai
thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named; she speaks within the wife's hearing, to the heroine's companions (பாங்காயினார்), recorded as overhearer thozhi

comparisons.tenor: the broad lotus leaf swaying at each gust
her close-set bangles, which he has never broken

reading: The woman asks her friend whether their sanded courtyard, lovely as the first day of a warrior festival, will grow lonely now that her lover, ashamed to prolong their hidden union, has gone for wealth to a far land, across hills where a sleeping elephant looks like a fishing boat at rest on the sea.
nuance: The union was hidden and long, and he leaves out of shame at its length (நாண் உடைமையின்) and with thoughts of 'our standing' (நம் உயர்வு): the journey is for the marriage that will end the secrecy. The road is drawn in detail, a deserted country emptied by raids and a hamlet that shelters guests at night.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவுணர்த்தியதோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது. தலைமகன்பிரிவின்கண் தலைமகட்குத் தோழி சொல்லியதூஉமாம்.

thinai_evidence.note: summer forest drying and the hard road of the parting

comparisons.tenor: the bright sanded courtyard of their house
the forked bright young leaves of the yaa tree
the elephant asleep with its trunk curled under the dark hill

reading: The friend, at night and within the hidden lover's hearing, scolds the thundering, lightning-flashing cloud for raging to no purpose, and asks it whether it will also bring to an end the millet field the hill girl guards with her companions, wearing vengai flowers and scaring birds.
nuance: Addressing the cloud is a way of speaking to the man: the rain will ripen the millet, the harvest will end the guarding, and with it the day meetings, so he should act. The cloud's lightning is likened to the swords of just kings' warriors, a puram image used to scare a lover.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill girl guarding the millet with her rattle under vengai

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: she addresses the rain cloud (மழையே)

reading: The foster mother laments that the little girl has gone off with the youth across the scorched hills, where a tusker clutching his mate breaks a path, and has become another's; she herself wanders bewildered at home, and the town, whose streets ring with music, has lost the thing it loved.
nuance: Her grief widens from herself to the town: the girl was the town's treasure, so the loss is public. The tusker that shelters its young mate and treads a path through the drought answers her fear with a picture of a guarded crossing; on our reading that is the sense the poem lets rise without saying it.

thinai_evidence.note: the parched summer road of an elopement

thurai_akam.speaker: sevili
thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named; she laments aloud

comparisons.tenor: the tusker lifting its trunk as it leads its mate

iraicchi.act: the tusker keeps his young she-elephant close and treads a track for her through the dry hills
iraicchi.sense: the youth who has taken the girl across the same land may guard and lead her as the tusker does its mate

reading: The friend tells the foster mother not to fret over the town's gossip about the girl and the lord of the shore: one evening, as the wind-driven sea beat the bay, a fierce shark struck in the estuary, he speared it, and with his tired horses he came and rested by them on the sand at dusk.
nuance: This is the friend's disclosure (அறத்தொடு நிற்றல): she presents the bond as born of a rescue at sea, which gives the family an honourable reason to accept him. The closing words சேர்ந்தன்றே இலனே are hard to construe, so who came to whom, and whether he stayed, is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: salt heaps, fishing boats, punnai and the seaside grove

reading: The man tells his heart that if, having gone, it plans to stay away for wealth across the hot road where the salt-carriers' bullock bells tell travellers they are safe, it should first be able to say firmly to the woman with soft hair like rippled sand that she will bear it.
nuance: He does not refuse the journey outright; he sets the heart a test it cannot pass, telling her to her face, and so gives up going. The bells of the salt-carriers, which reassure travellers, are the reassurance he cannot give her.

thinai_evidence.note: the long hot road of the wealth journey

comparisons.tenor: the chain of bells on the salt-carriers' bullocks

reading: The friend tells the man of the high hills that the girl's moon-bright forehead has turned the colour of gold with longing; the millet has been reaped by parrots and junglefowl, and a snake-spat gem washed down by the falls lights up the village street, so if he comes at midnight she has lost even the night, and pity her.
nuance: Each detail closes a way: the end of the harvest ends her days in the field, and the street lit by the gem ends the dark that hid night visits; the friend says this to turn him from secret meeting toward marriage without naming it.

thinai_evidence.note: the millet field, parrots, waterfall and hill hamlet

comparisons.tenor: the pallor that has come over her forehead
the green ring on the small parrot's neck

reading: The man, giving up the journey his heart had settled on, says the road would be easy, a waste where hunters with bows leave blood on the field, a red-eared vulture feeds its young in a yaa tree and dropped flesh becomes an old jackal's meal; what he cannot do is leave the sweet sleep on the shoulders of his young wife.
nuance: The danger of the road is granted and then dismissed: the waste is 'easy for us'; the only hardship that counts is the bed at home. The vulture feeding its chick is the road's one image of care, and the scraps falling to the jackal show how that care spills over to others.

thinai_evidence.note: vulture, yaa tree and jackal on the hard road

reading: The woman tells her friend that this is the very rainy season he named when he promised to come driving his chariot: rain has soaked the ploughed red furrows, the sown seed has sprouted like a spread herd of deer, and a peacock on a kurundhu branch calls like girls shooing parrots.
nuance: The whole description is of a working field (ploughing, weeding to the beat of a drum, the varagu harvest), so the season is fixed by labour as much as by rain; the peacock's call, compared to girls' shouts in the millet field, is the only sound, and it calls no one home.

thinai_evidence.note: the promised rains, varagu fields and kurundhu

comparisons.tenor: the red ridges of the deep furrows
the sprouting seed scattered over the field

reading: The mother says the other mother will gladly paint her walls and spread sand for the return of her son with the girl, while she herself, who combed the girl's hair and carried her on her hip, asks the diviner with his staff and his molucca beads whether the youth will bring the girl first to her house or take her straight to his own.
nuance: Her claim is not on the youth's love but on her own care for the girl; she knows she has no right to his kindness (அருளான் ஆயினும்) and asks only for a sight of her daughter. The velan is called here not to cure lovesickness but to read the eloped pair's road home.

thinai_evidence.note: the daughter has crossed the hard road with the youth

thurai_akam.speaker: nartaay
thurai_akam.note: she addresses the diviner (வேல)

reading: The wife tells the man of the town, where women at dawn bring hot rice and cane fruit on lily leaves to husbands asleep after eating varaal fish and drinking, that he must not come near or touch her, since his chest has embraced the woman fit for him who walks as proud as Anni Minjili after Thithiyan killed the Kosar.
nuance: The comparison is barbed: Anni Minjili's pride was won by revenge for her father's blinding, so the rival is cast as a woman triumphant over the wife. The opening scene of men who forget their fishing after a feast while their women still feed them at dawn may be heard as the wife's own household, but the poem leaves it as the town's picture.

thinai_evidence.note: varaal fish, water-lily leaves and the lord of the town

comparisons.tenor: the rival woman, proud in her gait
the round thick slices of fish

reading: The friend tells the grieving woman not to despair: though her lover has crossed Kannan Ezhini's Themuthu hill, he will not stay long, for on that cold road a tusker sleeps embracing his pregnant mate while their calf climbs on and slides off him, as a small son clambers on the chest of a father who holds his wife.
nuance: The simile runs backwards: the human family is the vehicle and the elephants the tenor, so the man on the road is shown his own household in the beasts. The friend's comfort rests on that sight: a man who has seen it cannot linger.

thinai_evidence.note: the friend's reassurance during the man's absence across the hills

comparisons.vehicle: மடவோள் தழீஇய விறலோன் மார்பில் புன்தலைப் புதல்வன் ஊர்புஇழிந் தாங்கு
comparisons.tenor: the elephant calf climbing on and sliding off the tusker who embraces his pregnant mate

iraicchi.act: the tusker embraces his pregnant mate and lets their calf climb on him as they rest together
iraicchi.sense: the man who passes this family on the road will think of his wife and child and hurry home

reading: The man tells his heart that the girl who, trusting his words, came at midnight through the rain with her anklets hushed, embraced him while the town slept and went away, was not a mere woman of perfect virtue but surely the dread maiden who lives in the flower-filled spring on the peak called Kaviram in Aay's southern land.
nuance: The awe follows the union, not first sight: having held her, he still cannot think her mortal. The peacock wreathed in young cloud gives her coming its look, while the spirit of the mountain spring gives it its danger, and both images belong to the hill.

colophon.thurai: புணர்ந்து நீங்கியதலைமகளது போக்கு நோக்கிய தலைமகன் தன்நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: a midnight tryst in the hills

comparisons.tenor: the girl coming through the rain with her dark fragrant hair
the girl who came and went in the night

reading: The man tells his heart, which urges him to go for wealth like other men, that it may go, but he will not leave his wife with her bamboo-smooth shoulders, not even for riches as great as the land Narmudi Cheral won back when Nannan fell at the battle of Vakai.
nuance: The road is drawn as a place of failing care: the thirsty elephant mistakes falling flowers for rain, the wild dogs scatter the deer, and only the stag at sunset calls its lost herd back with a male cry. That stag is the one creature doing what the man chooses to do.

thinai_evidence.note: thirsty elephant, wild dogs and bare trees of the waste

comparisons.tenor: the white mara flowers falling from the hill trees

iraicchi.act: at sunset the stag calls with a male cry to bring back its scattered herd
iraicchi.sense: even the stag on the road gathers its own at nightfall, so the man who stays with his wife is doing what the road itself shows

reading: The friend, having read the girl's wish, invites the man of the shore to their fishing hamlet of thatched huts that smells of fish and is hardly a town, yet makes anyone who stays one day forget his own city; he may yoke his chariot and go by evening, but if he stays, they too will welcome him as far as their station allows.
nuance: The invitation is made through modesty about the village (புலால்அம் சேரி, a fish-smelling settlement) and a boast that it makes guests forget home, so the friend accepts his suit while stating the gap in rank (எம்வரை அளவையின்) that he must accept with it.

thinai_evidence.note: the fish-smelling hamlet on the sand by the sea

comparisons.tenor: the sand of the street, shining

title: மணிமிடைபவளம் 201-220
theme: Manimidai pavalam 201-220: friends answer women left for the desert road, mothers of eloped daughters grieve, friends press lovers from night meetings toward marriage, and puram fame (Alankanam, Ori's Kolli, Eyinan's fall, Mathi's ford, Chellur) serves as the measure of gossip and beauty.

tamil: ஆண்டு அமைந்து உறைகுநர் அல்லர்- முனா அது
reading: The friend asks the grieving woman why she despairs that gossip has filled the common ground like the sea swelling at full moon off the Pandya's Korkai and that her mother lies sleepless and sighing: the man who crossed the long summer desert, where a male bear sports with his she-bear and their cub on the hill slope, would not settle there even if he were given the rich rice country of the Cholas.
nuance: The friend first repeats the woman's own complaint (lines 1 to 11) and only then answers it, so the gossip and the mother's sighing are given in the woman's voice. The comfort rests on a hyperbole of refusal (not even the Chola land) rather than on a promise of his return date.

thinai_evidence.note: the friend comforts a woman whose man has crossed the summer desert

comparisons.tenor: the gossip that has filled the common ground
the thick fur of the bear cub

iraicchi.act: the male bear stays and sports with his she-bear, whose cub is with them, on the hill slope of the desert road
iraicchi.sense: the man who saw even the bear keep to its mate and young on that road will not stay away from his own woman

reading: The friend tells the lover who leaves after a night meeting that in his hill, where a wounded tusker that beat off a tiger lifts its trunk and sighs among its young she-elephants and the vengai blossoms fly up like a smith's sparks onto the dark bushes, she wonders whether anyone but themselves suffers as they do while he comes at midnight, spear for company, down the dark stony path where thunder splits the hooded snake.
nuance: The question 'are there others besides us?' turns the women's fear for him into pressure to marry: the colophon says she is urging marriage, and the poem does it only by counting the dangers. A traditional reading takes the wounded tusker among its she-elephants as the lover who braves the night to reach the girl; it is left as scene here because only one correspondence (danger overcome) is clear.

colophon.thurai: இரவுக் குறிக்கண் வந்து நீங்கும் தலைமகற்குத் தோழி சொல்லி வரைவு கடாயது.

thinai_evidence.note: a lover comes to the night meeting through the hill path

comparisons.tenor: the vengai blossoms settling on the dark bushes

tamil: யாய் அறிந்து உணர்க' என்னார், தீ வாய்
எனக்கு எளிது ஆகல் இல்' எனக், கழற்கால்
reading: The mother whose daughter has eloped says that she kept silent when the gossiping women told her day after day what the girl was doing, sparing her shame, but the girl feared her mother would know and left with her spear-bearing young man across the hills; may it prove that she was not such a mother, and may she herself be the housewife of the lonely hill hamlet with its nochi hedge who takes the girl in as a passing guest when she arrives safe.
nuance: Her wish is not that the girl come back but that she be the stranger on the road who shelters her: a mother's care transferred to the place the daughter has chosen. Her silence, meant as kindness, is what the daughter read as danger, so the poem turns on a misunderstanding between them.

thinai_evidence.note: the daughter has left with her lover across the desert hills

reading: The man, his work done in the Pandya's great camp, tells his charioteer that the evening of the rains has come over the grassland, with bee swarms humming at the fragrant mullai, so he must drive fast to reach the shoulders of his bright-bangled wife, whose hair smells like the groves of Vaanan's Sirukudi where the reapers' drums scare birds from the flowered pools.
nuance: The season he promised to return in has arrived on its own (உதுக்காண் வந்தன்று பொழுதே), so his haste is the keeping of a word. The camp opens with the king's world-shading umbrella and sea-like army; the close sets that public scene against a farming village's fragrance in his wife's hair.

thinai_evidence.note: the rains, the grassland and the jasmine evening of return

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is the charioteer (பாகன்)

comparisons.tenor: the fragrance of the wife's hair

reading: The woman tells the friend who urges her to bear up that her lover, who swore with a lying heart that he would never leave her, like those joined in an old flawless friendship of mingled lives, has gone and left her weeping; even so, may he easily gain wealth enough to feed guests in a house as rich as Killi's Kaveri port, as he crosses the hill path of strange speech in the cool season where an elephant's musth runs and the male monkey calls and leaps on the high branch.
nuance: The reproach and the blessing come in one breath: she names his oath a lie and still wishes his errand success, and what she wishes him is wealth for hospitality, the householder's duty, not riches for himself.

thinai_evidence.note: he has left her to cross the desert for wealth

comparisons.vehicle: உயிர்கலந்து ஒன்றிய தொன்றுபடு நட்பின் செயிர்தீர் நெஞ்சமொடு செறிந்தோர்
comparisons.tenor: the lover as he spoke his promise
the rich house she wishes him

reading: The woman, refusing the go-between, asks her friend what this will be called: the lord of a town where small boys climb the dark back of a buffalo whose twisted horns spread as ludicrously as a dancer's gestures, looking from afar like monkeys on a boulder, delights in marrying women with mango-sprout skin in his festive city, and sulking at it her broad soft shoulders have melted like the salt heaps of Veerai in heavy rain.
nuance: The mockery is in the image: the great buffalo carries boys about like a toy and looks absurd, and so does he, ridden by every woman. Her own body, not her words, gives the refusal its force: the shoulders that waste like rained-on salt.

colophon.thurai: வாயில் வேண்டிச் சென்றவிறலிக்குத் தலைமகள் வாயில் மறுத்து.

thinai_evidence.note: she sulks at the husband's new marriages

comparisons.tenor: the spreading twisted horns of the buffalo
the boys on the buffalo's back seen from afar
the skin of the women he marries

comparisons.vehicle: நெடுவெள் உப்பின் நிரம்பாக் குப்பை பெரும் பெயற்கு உருகி யா அங்கு

ullurai.tenor: the husband and the women who make free with him

pairs.situation: lesser women climb onto the man as boys climb the buffalo
his conduct makes him ridiculous
the town sees it from afar and names it (என்னெனப் படுங்கொல்)

ullurai.speaker_fit: the heroine uses the buffalo of her own marutham town, a thing she knows (porul 7.26)

reading: The mother whose daughter eloped wonders whether the girl, who refused with a sick heart the sweet milk mixed with honey that her mother held out while combing her hair and coaxing her, has drunk, sighing and with sweat on her crescent brow, the brackish pot of water her heartless lover drew from a well dug where a sun-scorched tusker had rolled, on the dread forked desert path cut by the hooves of the salt traders' grey donkeys.
nuance: The road is built from the salt trade, carried from the sea to the western uplands, so the desert here is a merchant road, not wild land. The poem's last image is of the girl at home refusing milk, so the mother's question about the well water is also about the comfort she failed to give.

thinai_evidence.note: the scorched desert road the girl has taken

reading: The lover, leaving after their meeting, blesses the girl of fine dark hair, fragrant as the flowers of Ori's Kolli, who came and gave herself with a desire that shame could not hold back, like a flood the salt-pan bank cannot stop and like Akuthai who brought back the kin after the outcry of the Vel women when Aay Eyinan fell to Minjili at Paazhi and Nannan would not look on the field.
nuance: Most of the poem is a puram story told inside a single simile: Eyinan the generous, killed at noon, the birds that should have shaded him, Nannan's refusal to see. What it measures is the girl's boldness, a thing usually blamed in akam, here blessed. Line 18 (அகுதை கிளைதந்தாங்கு) is obscure, and the turn of the Nannan episode is uncertain.

thinai_evidence.note: the hero rejoices after a secret union

comparisons.vehicle: வசைவிடக் கடக்கும் வயங்குபெருந் தானை அகுதை கிளைதந் தாங்கு

comparisons.tenor: her desire that shame could not hold

reading: The friend tells the woman not to weep that her shoulders have lost their beauty, her mother grieves and the gossip is louder than the roar at Alankanam when Chezhiyan beat the seven: though her man has gone beyond Pulli's Vengadam, he cannot forget her beauty, which is like the statue set up by the god on Kolli, the hill Kaari of Mullur gave to the Cheras after killing Ori.
nuance: The friend first speaks the woman's complaint in her own words and then answers it, as in 201. Both measures in the poem come from puram: a Pandya victory for the gossip, a Kolli statue that outlived the change of its lords for her beauty, which is the friend's point: his love will last as the statue did.

thinai_evidence.note: he has crossed the rocky land beyond Vengadam

comparisons.vehicle: கொல்லி நிலைபெறு கடவுள் ஆக்கிய பலர்புகழ் பாவை

reading: The friend, knowing the lover stands by unseen, tells the woman that the lord of the shore, where a great fish struck by the fishermen's harpoon stains the sea with its blood, arcs through the waves like a rainbow and follows the boats with its strength gone, once came at midnight thinking of her shoulders and praised their seaside grove endlessly, and now, they hear, says the screw-pine thickets block his chariot and the way is hard.
nuance: The friend sets his first praise of their shore against his present excuse about the same shore, and lets him overhear the comparison. The wounded fish that still follows the boats is sometimes read as a hidden image of a lover hurt yet clinging; it is left as scene because its matching to the people is not fixed by the poem.

thinai_evidence.note: fishermen, the seaside grove and screw-pine

comparisons.tenor: the wounded fish arcing through the waves

reading: The friend, seeing the woman changed, tells her that though her man is in the land of strange speech beyond Vengadam, where a tusker rubbing against the maraam scatters its lime-white blossoms like hail onto the rock where farmers dry their rice seed, he will be kind and return, he who left her weeping with gossip roaring like the water at Mathi's stony ford, where Ezhini's teeth were set into the gate of Venmani.
nuance: The gossip is again measured by a war story, here a grim trophy: a fallen raider's teeth driven into a fortress door. Lines 9 to 15 compress the Ezhini episode so tightly that its sequence (the cattle, the outcry, the king's command) cannot be fixed.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவின்கண் வேறுபட்டதலைமகளது வேறுபாடு கண்டு தோழி சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: he has gone to a far land leaving her in tears

reading: The lover, after a meeting that failed, curses his heart: desiring a girl whose beauty is like a golden statue holding the young sunlight, whose teeth are like the shoots of reed tubers in sand and whose speech is like the music of a lute played in sevvazhi, it never thought she was hard to win and crossed the bitter waste every day, bringing him endless pain; may its keen pride be broken as the sea was when Kuttuvan's tempered spear drove it back.
nuance: The curse runs through a puram image, the Chera who besieged the ocean itself; the heart's pride is set against the sea's, and both are pierced. Line 9 (the water troubled by the elephant herd) is unclear in its connection.

thinai_evidence.note: the lover's longing for a girl who is hard to meet

comparisons.vehicle: தாஇல் நன்பொன் தைஇய பாவை விண்தவழ் இளவெயிற் கொண்டுநின் றன்ன
நாணற் கிழங்கு மணற்கு ஈன்ற முளைஓ ரன்ன

reading: The friend tells the woman that though her man chose to cross the shadeless waterless waste beyond the Tondaiyar's Vengadam, into the land of the Vadugar who wear wilted athiral in their curly hair and offer toddy to the cattle they raid, he will not linger there even if he were given the world of the worthy together with its nectar, forgetting to join her shoulders like the bamboo of Kolli and her hair rippled like Kaveri sand.
nuance: The friend's hyperbole goes past any kingdom to heaven itself: not even the gods' world and its nectar outweighs the woman's embrace. The road is drawn from its people, a raiding folk with their own rites, which makes the distance cultural as well as physical.

thinai_evidence.note: the waterless, shadeless desert he crossed

comparisons.tenor: the gems shining in the field

reading: In the war camp, where the rain pours ceaselessly from a sky that has hidden the day, chilling the elephant herds, and the king, eager for glory, does not sleep, the man tells his heart that the war is their duty, and asks how she of thick hair, who knew him as her own, will fare as she hears alone in the rainy evening the sad sevvazhi lute and the flute of cowherds driving home cattle with bells.
nuance: The colophon gives the speech to the woman, but the speaker is in the camp and says the war is ours (அமரும் நம்வயினதுவே), so it can only be the man; he imagines her evening, not his own. The music that wounds her is his invention, placed in her hearing.

thinai_evidence.note: the rains, the evening and the cowherds of the waiting season

reading: The friend tells the man, who stands ready with spear in hand to cross the hills for work in a land of other tongues, that wishing him a swift and successful going would be well enough for those who could bear to stay behind grieving for the absent, on a road where bowmen who bite the finger that missed its mark raise dread stone heaps over men they kill and a red-beaked male vulture picks the eyes from the heads of corpses and drops them for his mate.
nuance: The blessing is withheld by a conditional: it would be fine to say 'go well', but only to someone able to stay behind, which the woman is not. The vulture feeding its mate is the poem's sharpest stroke: on a road of killing, even the carrion bird provides for its partner without leaving her.

colophon.thurai: செலவுணர்த்திய தோழி தலைமகள் குறிப்பறிந்து தலைமகனைச் செலவழுங்குவித்தது.

thinai_evidence.note: the robbers' road of stone heaps and vultures

iraicchi.act: the male vulture gathers what it finds on the killing ground and brings it to its mate
iraicchi.sense: even the vulture of that road provides for its mate without leaving her, so the man need not part from his wife to provide

reading: The courtesan, speaking so that the wife's women will hear, says the wives of the lord of the cool-ford town, where a bard's daughter fishes with a fine rod and roasts the varaal on vanji wood for her toddy-drinking father, are said to talk of her as they please; if she is caught in that gossip, so be it, but if she goes to their street they will suffer like the great tusker when the Chelli lord's white spear struck Aathan Ezhini's chest.
nuance: Her threat is to visit, not to fight; she makes her mere presence in their street a wound. The simile's referents are uncertain: whether the suffering tusker is Ezhini's own elephant or Ezhini himself called a tusker cannot be settled from the line.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகட்குப் பாங்காயினார் கேட்பத் தனக்குப் பாங்காயினார்க்குப் பரத்தை சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the courtesan's quarrel with the wives of the town's lord

reading: Told of the coming parting, the woman says that now the cold season has come, with white rain-clouds like carded cotton, cane flowers swaying, pakandrai blooming white, avarai and thondri opening, herons crying in every field and women at the ford shivering without their ornaments, she will proclaim to every couple 'whatever wealth you gain, do not part', for her body is ruined by the lover who took her beauty and left, and she shivers in the hard cold with chattering teeth.
nuance: Her answer to news of his going is a public maxim addressed to all lovers, made from her own case. The long catalogue of the cold season is not decoration: every flower and bird marks the time he should be home, and the women shivering at the ford are a picture of her own state.

thinai_evidence.note: the threatened parting is what she answers

tamil: படாஅ வாகும், எம் கண் என, நீயும்
reading: The friend tells the lover, who said his eyes would not close except on her shoulders on nights when the storm cloud flashes and thunders over the peaks, after the tusker has fed sprouts and fodder to his herd, and who thinks it easy to come at midnight through the mountain clefts where the tiger waits for travellers, that if they cannot embrace his chest even one day they too will waste; let mother know and the old town gossip: let him come by day to the cool slope where vengai and thondri smell sweet.
nuance: Moving the meeting to daytime is a dare: the friend accepts the risk of discovery (let mother know, let the town hear) rather than his risk on the night path, which forces the matter toward marriage. She quotes his own lover's oath back to him before setting her terms.

colophon.thurai: தோழி தலைமகளை இடத்துய்த்து வந்து பகற்குறிநேர்ந்த வாய் பாட்டால் தலைமகனை வரைவுகடாயது.

thinai_evidence.note: the friend arranges a day meeting for the lovers

iraicchi.act: the tusker who cherishes his herd feeds them sprouts and the fodder they want
iraicchi.sense: as the tusker openly provides for his own, the lover should take up the care of the girl in marriage rather than steal visits by night

reading: The mother whose daughter has gone grieves that the girl who ran ringing her anklets through their great house and played ball with her friends, whom she fed from a bowl of milk like a white pakandrai flower brimming with dew ('drink your father's share too'), and adorned from birth, has gone with a heartless man; she cannot forget and wonders whether the girl walks, wasting, the long waterless road where a stag flees the red dog and the hot wind in the dry vila pods sounds to cowherds like a flute.
nuance: The feeding scene is told in the mother's own coaxing words, which makes the loss concrete: the voice that coaxed is still speaking, with no child to hear it. The flute that the cowherds imagine in the wind is the road's one sound of home, and it is false.

thinai_evidence.note: the waterless road and the hot wind

comparisons.tenor: the wind in the dry vila pods

reading: The friend, meeting the lover as he leaves the night tryst, tells him that while gossip rises in town and street he goes about in his chariot and speaks humbly, shivering whenever he thinks of her body, unapproachable as the guarded pillar of the sacrifice the axe-bearing tall one completed at Chellur; he stands outside and suffers, and should instead, like the great bird at Oonur by the sea, settle in a steady union and speak the words that protect her beauty, so that they may be at ease.
nuance: The sacrificial pillar roped at its waist, which none may approach, makes the girl's guarded state a sacred enclosure that only a public rite can open: the friend is asking for marriage. Several phrases (நோலா இரும்புள், the whole of lines 10 to 21) are obscure and the reading is tentative.

colophon.thurai: இரவுக்குறிவந்து நீங்குச் தலைமகனை யெதிர்ப்பட்டுத் தோழி சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the sea tide, backwaters and shore grove

comparisons.tenor: the steady union the lover should enter

title: மணிமிடைபவளம் 221-240
theme: Akananuru 221 to 240, from the மணிமிடைபவளம் section: half the poems are paalai partings and comforts in which the friend argues from memory, glory or the lover's body that the man will return, set among kurinji night-tryst poems pressing for marriage, two mullai homecomings, two marutham reproaches and two neythal meetings, with puram fame (Kazhar, Uranthai, Unur, Uthiyan Cheral's feast, Nalli) used repeatedly as a scale of comparison.
source_issues: akananuru:224: line 13 reads குரலிசைப் கடுப்ப; the doubled ப் before க is not regular sandhi and is probably a misprint for குரலிசை கடுப்ப.
akananuru:225: the flag reports 17 lines in our base text against 18 in the commentary edition (pmuni0523_02); the poem reads complete as it stands, but the lineation differs.
akananuru:230: lineation flag: a printed line number 5 stands on line 10 of the base text.
akananuru:234: the colophon thurai has தலைமமகன், a doubled ம, for தலைமகன்; copied as is in `colophon`.
akananuru:236: line 5 இடைனில is probably இடைநில, and line 10 உய்ர்த்தனென் is probably உயிர்த்தனென்.
akananuru:238: line 10 பெருகல் நாட is probably பெருங்கல் நாட, the usual epithet of the hill lord.

reading: The friend tells the girl that, since their people have begun the wedding rites with toddy and heaped sand, she has arranged for her to leave with the dark-bearded young man of the new spear, who will crown her hair with kadamba blossoms, along the hard forest track where a tiger that missed its elephant roars and the she-elephant bolts.
nuance: The poem never says whom the kin mean to marry her to; that the wedding is not to her lover is the colophon's reading (போக்குடன்பட), and it is what makes the friend's arrangement urgent. The kadamba spray the young man will pick for her hair is a small wedding of their own set against the kin's wedding at home.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகற்குப் போக்குடன்பட்ட தோழி, தலைமகட்குப் போக்குடன்படச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the girl is to leave home with her lover over the dry track, the parting of udanpokku

reading: With the hill lord listening, the friend says that since the sickness he caused is wasting her beauty she will speak out: let us go, along the river cold with many nights of thunder and rain, to win a fame like Maruthi's, who showed Aathi Manthi her lover taken by the Kaveri at the Kazhar festival and then went into the sea.
nuance: The friend borrows a known story of love and drowning to hint at a desperate act; aimed at the overhearing hero, the hint presses him to marry rather than keep coming by the flooded night path. The Maruthi part of the legend is told only here in this chapter; poem 236 uses the same story from Manthi's side.

thinai_evidence.note: the great hill of the hero's country and the night rain on his path

comparisons.tenor: the fame the friend hopes the two of them will win

reading: The friend tells the grieving girl not to fear that the man who could leave her will forget her: though he has crossed the long shadeless waterless track where wind-tossed flame-of-the-forest pods curved like a boar's tusk blaze like a fire-spouting elephant, how could he sleep forgetting the sleep he found in her garlanded hair?
nuance: The comfort rests on his memory of her hair, which he once gathered over her shoulders and decked with athiral and kuvalai; the friend argues from the body's habit, not from his promise.

thinai_evidence.note: the shadeless, waterless long track he has crossed

comparisons.tenor: the long curved pods of the flame-of-the-forest
the wind-lifted mass of red murukku blossom

reading: The hero, his task done, tells his charioteer to drive on as the day ends, horses breathing hot as a smith's bellows and flecked with milk-white froth, the wheel cutting the sand with the sound of a housewife's quern, while he pictures his wife pushing back her bangles and looking again and again toward the gate, asking whether he is coming.
nuance: The two domestic similes, the smith's bellows and the quern turned by a housewife, bring the home into the journey before he reaches it; the wife he imagines speaks only one line, and it is a question.

thinai_evidence.note: a wife waits at home for the returning husband, in the woodland after the heat has gone

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is the charioteer (பாகன்)

comparisons.tenor: the white froth on the horses
the sound of the wheel in the sand

reading: The hero asks his heart whether, after being one with her today in love, innocence and gentle speech, they will lodge tomorrow in a rainless hamlet on the hard track, where wind through bee-bored bamboo sounds like a herdsman's flute and iruppai flowers drop like loosened pearls, thinking of her anguished look and her sulking.
nuance: Today and tomorrow (இன்றே, நாளை) frame the poem: the whole journey is imagined from inside the embrace. The music of the bamboo is the one soft thing on the track, and it belongs to the herders' land, not the desert.

thinai_evidence.note: the hard track and the hamlet the rain has forgotten

comparisons.tenor: the wind sounding through the bored bamboo
the iruppai flowers falling on the red ground

reading: The friend refuses the lord of the rich town his tricks: his bathing yesterday in the Kaveri's dawn flood at Matthi's Kazhar ford with the woman he desires has raised more uproar than the shout when Katti fled without a fight on hearing the kinai drum at Thithan Veliyan's court in Uranthai.
nuance: The scale is the joke: a private bathe is measured against a famous rout, and the hero is mocked by being set beside a king who ran. The women scaring herons with sedge in the karanthai fields are the town's ordinary life, which has now seen him.

thinai_evidence.note: the husband's bathing with another woman, the sulking of the marutham house

reading: The friend tells the girl to stop brooding over her pale forehead and slack shoulders: though he has crossed many tracks where a lone tusker in musth tears at a vengai and roars like warriors taking a field, may our lover stay well, he who left with a clamour like the bright market of Marungur beyond Thazhumban's Unur.
nuance: The friend's blessing, நோய்இலராக, turns comfort into a wish for the absent man. Thazhumban is praised for a drum that brought Tamil under it (தமிழ் அகப்படுத்த), an early use of தமிழ் for a land or people; line 17's பிடிமிதி வழுதுணை is obscure to us.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பிரிவின்கண் வேறுபட்ட தலைமகட்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது. பிரிவின்கண் வேறுபட்ட தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியதூஉமாம்.

thinai_evidence.note: the red-dust tracks the tusker roams

occasion.words: தலைமகன் பிரிவின்கண் வேறுபட்ட தலைமகட்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது

reading: With the hero listening, the friend says it would be well enough if he spent the days with them bathing in the kuvalai pool under the cold slope, and went home at night; but on the moonlit path to his hamlet the vengai blossoms look like a tiger's spots and the she-elephant bolts.
nuance: The danger is an illusion of moonlight, yet the friend uses it to turn him from night meetings to day ones, and in the end toward marriage. The she-elephant fleeing a flowering tree it takes for a tiger is a traditional candidate for a hidden sense (the girl's fears for him); it does not pass the act condition here, so it stays scene.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் சிறைப்புறத்தானாகத் தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லுவாளாய்த் தோழி சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the cold hill slope and the moonlit night

occasion.words: தலைமகன் சிறைப்புறத்தானாகத் தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லுவாளாய்த் தோழி சொல்லியது

reading: The girl answers her friend's comfort: you tell me not to grieve as tears blur my eyes and gold-like pallor spreads, yet he who crossed the far hills of a waterless track where starving she-elephants stand like huts of a deserted village, and promised to come at once, has not come even in the sweet young spring when the cuckoo calls from the mango.
nuance: The spring is the proof: the cuckoo's call marks the season by which he promised to be back, so the beauty of the season is itself the evidence against him. The poem gives his own words, இன்னே வருதும், only to set them against the calendar.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பிரிவின்கண் வேறுபட்ட தலைமகளை வற்புறுத்துந் தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் வன்புறை யெதிரழிந்து சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the waterless long track he crossed

occasion.words: தலைமகன் பிரிவின்கண் வேறுபட்ட தலைமகளை வற்புறுத்துந் தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் வன்புறை யெதிரழிந்து சொல்லியது

reading: The hero tells his heart how he asked the shore girl in her leaf skirt, gathering punnai pollen like gold with her playmates, whether any harm would come if the right of this house were joined to him, and how, as his chariot drew near, she held back her tears and bowed her head a little, leaving him in great pain.
nuance: Her answer is a gesture, not a word: the bowed head and checked tears can be read as consent or as refusal, and the hero's pain comes from not knowing which. His proposal is couched in the language of household right (மனைக் கிழமை), unusual in a first meeting.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகளைக் கண்ணுற்று நீங்கும் தலைமகன் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the backwater, its neythal flowers and the punnai pollen on the sand

occasion.words: தலைமகளைக் கண்ணுற்று நீங்கும் தலைமகன் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது

comparisons.tenor: the large flowers of her leaf skirt

reading: The friend tells the girl that men who prize fame, holding that crushing foes and helping kin in need are not for those who stay home, have crossed the dreaded track of hunters' victims under stone heaps, yet they will come back with melting hearts, those who lay in her bee-loud hair, which is like the Pandyan's famed Koodal.
nuance: The friend argues with a puram value: glory is earned away from home, so the parting is honourable, and the same honour guarantees the return. The stone heaps over men killed by forest bowmen are the road's reminder of what that glory costs.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பிரிவின்கண் வேறுபட்ட தலைமகட்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the hot track lined with the graves of travellers

occasion.words: தலைமகன் பிரிவின்கண் வேறுபட்ட தலைமகட்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது

comparisons.tenor: her hair, or her as its wearer

reading: With the hero listening, the friend tells the girl that her bond with the lord of the rock country, where an elephant takes midnight thunder for a tiger and flees, has now brought on the season when mother, guarding the house, has the velan come, saying it is Murugu, with mixed flower offerings, in a courtyard strewn with vengai gold like a festival ground where the kuravar women dance.
nuance: The velan's rite shows the secret is close to discovery: the mother reads the girl's lovesickness as Murugu's seizure. The elephant mistaking thunder for a tiger matches the mother mistaking love for possession; we leave it as scene because only one correspondence holds firmly.

colophon.thurai: தோழி, தலைமகன் சிறைப்புறத்தானாகத் தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லுவாளாய்ச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the vengai, the hill people and their kuravai dance

reading: The friend tells the weeping girl that though he has crossed a summer track of fire-blackened land where lean elephants languish and short and tall hills crowd together like the host of ghouls gathered at Uthiyan Cheral's great feast, he will not linger over wealth, forgetting the sweet sleep of her dark hair.
nuance: The Cheral's great feast, a puram fame, is turned into a picture of the landscape: the hills crowd like the ghoulish guests. The friend's assurance turns on the same memory of sleep in her hair that poem 223 uses.

thinai_evidence.note: summer, and the track where the rain has gone

comparisons.tenor: the short and tall hills crowded together

reading: The hero tells his charioteer to drive the swan-swift horses fast over the rain-washed sand, so that by dusk, when the doe frolics with the stag and bees hum at the mullai, he may reach the pleasant woodland town where his pale, tear-eyed wife can at last undo her braid.
nuance: The braid is a sign: she bound her hair at his leaving and will loosen it at his return, so his speed is measured by her hair. The doe at play with the stag is what the arrival will be.

thinai_evidence.note: the rains, the evening and the mullai flower

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is the charioteer (பாகன்)

iraicchi.act: the young doe, tired of browsing, frolics unharmed in the joy of joining the stag
iraicchi.sense: the wife's release at his return will be as glad and as safe as the doe's play with her mate

reading: The girl asks her friend whether, set on wealth, he has not thought of them, or thinking has forgotten for his greater work, while the cold north wind and the drizzling east cloud open the thonri like a lamp and the musundai like stars on the grass, the crab hides in its hole, and the graceless wind torments her at evening, he who never asked what would become of her, pale and wasted.
nuance: The season is the rains and the cold wind, and the torment is the evening: by the Tholkappiyam's times this is mullai waiting, though the colophon files the poem as paalai because he went for wealth.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பிரிவின்கண் வேறுபட்ட தலைமகள் ஆற்றாமைமீதூரத் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: a woman waits through the rains and suffers the evening; she is not on the road

comparisons.tenor: the white musundai flowers on the grass

reading: The girl tells her friend that, not knowing how great the town lord's love was, she suffered: last night, not knowing he lay among bejewelled women, she went about with a broken heart telling her trouble, like Aathi Manthi who lost her lover and asked land after land whether anyone had seen Attan Atthi, crying that the sea had taken him, the flood had hidden him.
nuance: The phrase about the greatness of his love is bitter: the love she did not know was his love for others. She casts herself as the tragic Manthi while he was safe among other women, and the gap between the legend and his conduct is the reproach.

colophon.thurai: ஆற்றாமை வாயிலாகப் புக்க தலைமகன் நீக்கத்துக்கண் புக்க தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the husband's night among other women and the wife's reproach

occasion.words: ஆற்றாமை வாயிலாகப் புக்க தலைமகன் நீக்கத்துக்கண் புக்க தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது

reading: The friend tells the girl to stop grieving that the spring nights, with paathiri flowers on the sand and the south wind in the kuravam, pass sleepless: even if he reached rich Uranthai, where roast meat, millet, cane syrup and milk-soaked rice flakes are shared out, he would not stay there for his work's sake, away from the sweetness of her mouth.
nuance: The friend answers spring with plenty: the feast-town of Uranthai is the strongest temptation she can name, and she sets the girl's mouth above it.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பிரிவின்கண் வேறுபட்ட தலைமகளைத் தோழி வற்புறீஇயது.

thinai_evidence.note: the man is away on his work through the spring

occasion.words: தலைமகன் பிரிவின்கண் வேறுபட்ட தலைமகளைத் தோழி வற்புறீஇயது

reading: The friend asks the hill lord who has come by night, where a tiger rises at midnight to fetch food for his mate weak after bearing young, kills a bull gaur and drags it reddening the rock, whether, if he parts from her, he has any cure for her forehead, fragrant as the kaanthal on the slopes of Nalli, whose giving pours like rain.
nuance: Kapilar sets the tiger's care for his new mother against the hero's night visits: the beast provides, and the question is whether the man will. Nalli's generosity, praised in passing, gives the girl's fragrance a patron's fame.

thinai_evidence.note: midnight on the hill slope

iraicchi.act: the tiger goes out at midnight to bring prey to his mate, weak and hungry after giving birth
iraicchi.sense: the man who comes by night should, like the tiger, take on the care of the woman rather than leave her

reading: Leaving for wealth, the hero tells his heart how pitiable is the fine town of the little girl who only yesterday, with long and short sulks and many sweet words, asked whether he would not stay long away, crossing rivers of strange lands on tracks where red-eyed raiders roaring like tigers seize cattle at night, while the women here worship the crescent at dusk.
