thinai_evidence.note: the youth has led the girl away across the wasteland

comparisons.tenor: the red wound in the omai's bark

reading: Wasting with longing, the girl speaks to the flooding stream from her lover's hill: she reproaches it for slipping away ashamed under his hill's flowers instead of telling him of her pallor and tears, and asks what harm there would be if it rested a while in her father's flowering forest, before going back to the country where a spent elephant groans as it embraces its tired mate.
nuance: The stream is a messenger from his hill that she blames for his silence, and she offers it the hospitality she cannot offer him. The elephant that, wounded and spent, still holds its mate is the care his land knows and he withholds. Several lines (9 to 16) are hard to construe.

colophon.thurai: காமமிக்க கழிபடர் கிளவியால் (விரைவிடத்துக்கண்) தலைமகள் தலைமகன் வரையினின்றும் போந்த ஆற்றொடு புலந்து சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill country, its vengai and elephants

iraicchi.act: the elephant, spent and wounded from fighting a tiger, still embraces its tired mate
iraicchi.sense: even the elephants of his hill hold their mates in distress, yet their lord leaves her to waste

reading: The friend tells the wife, whose hair smells like the Himalayan forest, that her husband will not stay away without coming back to embrace her as if drinking her in, though he crossed sun-scorched hills where a doe, chewing nelli fruit, listens to the lonely notes of herders' bamboo flutes as they rest their cattle in konrai shade.
nuance: The herders' flute is called lonely (புலம்புகொள்) and the doe listens to it: the road he is on is full of sounds of solitude that will turn him home.

thinai_evidence.note: the husband is away across the hills

reading: After the wedding the friend tells the bride it is laughable now that they once feared gossip even if she ran off with him: the day the lord of the shore came, his strong chariot racing over milk-white sand and mud like water down a ford, their old town of palmyras by the roaring sea looked new, the neythal buds opening and smelling of new toddy.
nuance: The chariot passage is the same apparatus akam uses for the lover's secret night visits, here driven openly to the wedding, so speed now means eagerness rather than stealth. The town that gossiped (அழுங்கல் ஊர்) is the town that looks new.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் வரைந் தெய்திய பின்றைத் தோழி தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore grove, the neythal flower and the palmyras

occasion.words: தலைமகன் வரைந் தெய்திய பின்றைத் தோழி தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லியது

title: புறநானூறு 1-20
theme: Poems 1-20 open with the invocation to the god of the konrai and then praise and counsel the three crowned lines: counsel (செவியறிவுறூஉ) on giving, impartiality and guarding the realm like a child, vanji poems that boast of burned enemy fields, questions about gifts paid for by conquest, and Kudapulaviyanar's argument that the king who stores water gives life.
source_issues: 1: the colophon has no thinai or thurai (both null); the poem is the anthology's invocation (கடவுள் வாழ்த்து), marked here as paadaan. The patron field reads இறைவன், a description, not a name.
2 line 23: விளக்கிற், றுஞ்சும் puts a comma inside a sandhi join (விளக்கின் + துஞ்சும் gives விளக்கிற் றுஞ்சும்); the comma belongs after துஞ்சும் or nowhere.
Stray full stops in mid-sentence: 3 line 10 (மருங்கில்.), 11 line 15 (பாண் மகனும்மே.) and 19 line 10 (துமிந்து.).
5: the thurai was repaired from வெவியறிவுறூஉ to செவியறிவுறூஉ (purananuru:5:r1) and is copied as repaired; colophon_raw still carries a modern note after the thurai (சிறப்பு: ...).
8: the patron field carries an editorial remark after the name (சேரமான் செல்வக் கடுங்கோ வாழியாதன் என்பவனும் இவனே).

9 and 17: the review's table says sangamtamil.com lacks our line 1 in both; each is needed (9 line 1 begins the list of those to be warned with ஆவும்; 17 line 1 gives the southern and northern bounds before line 2's seas), so the site has dropped a line.
10 line 12: நெய்தருங் கானல், where the patron is நெய்தலங் கானல் இளஞ்சேட் சென்னி; the line probably should read நெய்தலங் கானல். Marked as it stands; the town entity keeps the line's form.
15: poet and patron were repaired from poem 14's repeated colophon (purananuru:15:r1, r2); the thinai and thurai were kept, as both editions give them as for 14.
18: the thurai field carries an editor's variant note (பொருண்மொழிக் காஞ்சி எனவும் பாடம்); both names are given in puram_thurai.
20: the patron field carries a note after the name (மாந்தரஞ் சேரல் எனவும் குறிப்பர்).

title: இறைவனின் திருவுள்ளம்!
reading: An invocation that names the god only by his marks: a wreath and garland of konrai, the white bull as mount and banner, the dark stain on the throat that Vedic brahmins speak of, a woman's form that is one part of him and that he may also hide within himself, the crescent on his brow praised by the eighteen hosts, and the ever-full water pot and hanging matted locks of the great ascetic who is a refuge to all living beings.
nuance: Each mark is stated and then given a second clause that raises it (the stain is also spoken of by the brahmins; the crescent is also praised by the hosts), so the poem is built in pairs. The woman-form clause goes further than the usual half-woman image: the god can also conceal her within himself (கரக்கினும் கரக்கும்). The name Siva is never used.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a god by his marks, the கடவுள் வாழ்த்து that porul 2.27 sets under paadaan

title: போரும் சோறும்!
reading: Murinjiyur Mudinagarayar praises the Chera Uthiyan Cheralathan, whose forbearance, breadth of counsel, strength, fierceness and grace match the nature of the five elements, in whose sea the sun rises and in whose western sea it sets, who gave food without limit while the hundred fought the five until they fell; he wishes him to stand unshaken with his unwavering kin, even if milk turns sour, day turns dark and the Vedas' way changes, like the Himalaya and Pothiyam where deer sleep by the light of the brahmins' evening fires.
nuance: Lines 13 to 16 tie the patron's name (பெருஞ்சோறு, great food) to the war of the five and the hundred, the earliest Tamil reference to that war; the poem says only that he gave food without limit until the hundred fell, not to whom. The blessing works by impossibilities (milk souring, day darkening, the Veda's path changing), so the king's steadiness is set beyond the order of nature itself.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king's giving with a blessing that he endure

comparisons.tenor: the king's forbearance, counsel, strength, fierceness and grace
the king standing unshaken with his kin

title: வன்மையும் வண்மையும்!
reading: Irumpidarthalaiyar praises the Pandya Vazhuthi of the black hand and bright sword, scion of the Kauriyar, whose white umbrella like the full moon shades the sea-girt earth and whose word does not move even if the earth moves, and counsels him that suppliants come longing for him across waterless, townless roads where bowmen in ambush shoot travellers and kites sit grieving on their fresh stone-heaps, so that his true strength is to read their need from their faces and end their poverty.
nuance: The counsel is compressed into the last two and a half lines, and its weight falls on line 25: the giver should know the need from the face before it is spoken. The road passage (lines 17 to 23) does work for the counsel: it is the price the suppliants have already paid to come. The kites on the fresh cairns are a scene, not an image of the king.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king closing in counsel on giving to suppliants

title: தாயற்ற குழந்தை!
reading: Paranar describes the Chola's war gear after battle, each in a simile (swords red like the evening sky, feet like the horns of a killing bull, shields pierced like a fixed target, horses red-mouthed like a tiger that has seized a neck, elephants with blunted tusks like Death that eats lives), sets the king on his golden chariot like the red sun rising from the sea, and ends that the lands of those who angered him cry without ceasing like a child its mother has not fed.
nuance: The poem is a chain of seven comparisons, five of them in the same frame (thing, its battle mark, போன்றன), so the king is approached through his gear before he is named as the sun. Only the last simile turns from the victor to the victim: the enemy country as an unfed infant, which is the lament that gives the thurai its name.

thinai_evidence.note: the king's battle and the wailing of the enemy's land after his invasion

comparisons.tenor: the king's legs, their anklets worn in battle
the shields pierced again and again by arrows
the horses with mouths reddened by the bit
the elephants that battered the gates
the king on his golden chariot

title: அருளும் அருமையும்!
reading: Nariveruuthalaiyar tells the Chera, lord of a forest land where elephants spread like cattle among black rocks like buffaloes, that since he is such a man he will say one thing: do not side with those who cast off grace and love and take a hell that never leaves; guard the realm as those who rear a child, for that guarding is a thing of grace and hard to come by.
nuance: The opening picture is double: rocks like buffaloes and elephants like cattle make the wild forest a pasture, which prepares the counsel that the king should be a herdsman and nurse. The comparisons in lines 2 and 7 use the comparative -இன் (ஆனிற், பவரின்) rather than அன்ன or போல. What அது in line 8 refers to (the guarding, the realm, or the reward of guarding) is not fixed by the syntax.

thinai_evidence.note: counsel spoken to the king, the செவியறிவுறூஉ of paadaan

comparisons.tenor: the elephants spreading among the rocks

title: தண்ணிலவும் வெங்கதிரும்!
reading: Karikizhar wishes the Pandya Mudukudumi, whose form and fame reach from beyond the Himalaya to below Kumari, from sea to sea and from the waters below to the world above, that he may lean to no side like the beam of a balance, that his umbrella bow only in circling the three-eyed god's shrine, his head only before the raised hands of the Vedic sages, his garland wilt only in the smoke of burned enemy lands and his anger yield only to his women's sulking faces, and that he abide on earth like the cool moon and the burning sun.
nuance: Four optative clauses (பணியியர், இறைஞ்சுக, வாடுக, செலிஇயர்) map where the king should give way and where he should not; the paired moon and sun at the close repeat the split between mildness and heat. The giving of captured jewels to bards in due order (வரிசையின்) is placed inside the praise of conquest, so the plunder is legitimated by its distribution.

thinai_evidence.note: blessing and counsel to a king

comparisons.tenor: the king, who should hold to no one side
the king abiding on earth, cool to his own
the king abiding on earth, burning to his foes

title: வளநாடும் வற்றிவிடும்!
reading: Karunkuzhal Athanar praises Karikalan, whose feet drive elephants, whose hand is bent from the bow and whose chest has turned back horses, for taking no account of day or night and delighting in plunder amid the wailing in the light of burning enemy towns, so that the good things are no more in others' wide, rich lands where cool floods spread and are held back by fish.
nuance: The praise has a sting: நல்ல இல்ல ஆகுபவால் (the good things come to be gone) is said to the king, and the last three lines spend their richest description on the lands he ruins. The exact sense of lines 11 and 12 (a flood held back not by earth but by fish) is a hyperbole of plenty whose syntax is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: the king's raid, burning towns and taking plunder

title: கதிர்நிகர் ஆகாக் காவலன்!
patron: சேரமான் கடுங்கோ வாழியாதன் : சேரமான் செல்வக் கடுங்கோ வாழியாதன் என்பவனும் இவனே
reading: Kapilar asks the sun how it could equal Cheralathan, whom the world's kings obey, who will not bear the earth being called common to others and finds it too small, of unshrinking heart and unsparing gifts: the sun keeps set hours, turns its back and goes, comes back changed, hides behind the hills, and shines only by day.
nuance: The comparison is denied: each of the sun's motions (keeping hours, turning away, changing, hiding, shining only by day) becomes a lack set against the king's constancy. ஊக்கம் is named in line 3 as the drive that finds the earth too small (இடம் சிறிது), a praise that also admits his ambition.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king by refusing him a comparison

comparisons.tenor: Cheralathan, whom the sun cannot match

title: ஆற்றுமணலும் வாழ்நாளும்!
reading: Nettimaiyar blesses the Pandya Kudumi, who before battle proclaims the way of dharma, telling cows, brahmin-natured men, women, the sick and those without sons to perform the rites for the ancestors to go to shelter before he lets fly his arrows, and wishes him years more than the sands of the Pahruli river of the ancient Pandya Nediyon, who gave fresh gold to dancers at the sea festival.
nuance: The opening quotation is the king's own war proclamation, and its list defines who is outside war: animals of the household, priests, women, the sick, and men whose line would end with them. The blessing reaches back to Nediyon and the Pahruli, linking this Pandya to a legendary ancestor's generosity.

thinai_evidence.note: praise and blessing of the king's righteous conduct of war

comparisons.tenor: sons who can perform the rites for the ancestors
the years the poet wishes the king

title: குற்றமும் தண்டனையும்!
reading: Oonpothi Pasunkudaiyar praises the Chola of Neythalankanal, who knows well those who serve him, does not believe those who slander others, punishes a proven wrong after weighing it fairly and lessens the penalty when the offender comes and stands at his feet, whose house feeds all comers, and whose chest only women now fight with since warriors have given up fighting him; the poet has come to him to praise him at length.
nuance: The chest that only women 'fight' (மலைத்தல், also to wear or embrace) while warriors have stopped fighting it is a pun that sets love-quarrel against war. Mercy here follows submission, not rank: the softened penalty is for the one who comes and holds the king's feet.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king's justice and hospitality by a poet come to him

title: பெற்றனர்! பெற்றிலேன்!
reading: Peymagal Ilaveyiniyar tells how, by the cool Porunai where girls with fine jewels pick flowers for their sand dolls and plunge into the water, the Chera king worthy of the vanji song crossed a fierce fortress and saw his enemies' backs; the singer who sang that valour received fine gold jewels, and her partner the bard, skilled in tune, received a gold lotus strung on silver thread.
nuance: The poem never asks; it lists who received what (the king, the enemy's backs; the singer, jewels; the bard, the lotus), and the request is left for the next link, the poet herself, which is how பரிசில் கடாநிலை works here. விறல்வஞ்சிப் பாடல் is the vanji song of victory, not the Chera town Vanji.

thinai_evidence.note: a chain of gifts received from the king, which asks for a gift by telling of others'

title: அறம் இதுதானோ?
reading: Nettimaiyar asks the Pandya Kudumi whether it is dharma that bards wear gold lotuses and poets are given chariots with elephants, when he takes others' land so that it is painful to them and does what is sweet before those who love him.
nuance: The five lines can be read as playful praise (so generous it is almost wrong) or as a real question about gifts paid for by conquest; the poem gives no answer, and the pairing இன்னா ... இனிய holds the two sides of the same act together.

thinai_evidence.note: address to a king about his gifts

title: நோயின்றிச் செல்க!
reading: Mudamosiyar answers someone who asks who the man is: the one on the Death-like elephant, his armour torn by arrows, while the elephant, like a ship on the sea and the moon among many stars, surrounded by swordsmen like a shoal of sharks, has gone wild beyond its keepers' control; may he return unharmed, the lord of a land of water-fenced fields where ploughmen gather dropped peacock feathers with their sheaves and fish and toddy abound.
nuance: The poem turns from danger to plenty without transition: the last four lines describe the king's home country so richly that the wish for his return becomes a picture of what he must return to. Who asks 'who is he?' and where the elephant has run are not stated in the poem.

thinai_evidence.note: a blessing for a king's safe return

comparisons.tenor: the elephant moving through the army
the king on his elephant among his soldiers

title: மென்மையும்! வன்மையும்!
reading: Kapilar tells the Chera that his knee-long hands are hard, since they drive the elephant to break the crossbars, rein the horses at the deep moat, are scarred by the bowstring and give rare jewels to suppliants, while the hands of the poets who sing him are very soft, since they know no work but eating meat smoked with fragrant smoke, mashed meat and rice with curry.
nuance: The contrast is playful self-mockery: the king's hands are praised through the softness of the poets' own, which is the proof of his feeding. The hard hands do four labours, and the last of them is giving, so generosity is counted among the toils of war.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king's deeds and gifts through the poets' own hands

comparisons.tenor: the king's firmness toward his foes
the king as Murugan in battle

title: எதனிற் சிறந்தாய்?
reading: Nettimaiyar asks the Pandya Kudumi which are more: the enemies who came wanting to take the head of his vanguard and went away living in shame, or the wide fields where he planted sacrificial posts after completing Vedic sacrifices with ghee offerings, after he had ploughed their walled towns with white-mouthed donkeys, driven his chariots over their bird-loud fields and bathed his elephants in their guarded tanks.
nuance: The closing question (யாபல கொல்லோ) leaves war and sacrifice uncounted and equal, so the Vedic rite and the razing of cities are praised in one breath. Ploughing a conquered town with donkeys is a rite of ruin, the opposite of the ploughing that founds a field.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king that sets his wars against his sacrifices

title: செவ்வானும் சுடுநெருப்பும்!
reading: Pandarangannanar tells the Chola Perunarkilli that his army, with swift horses and shields spread like clouds, broke the enemy front, fed on their ripe fields, burned their house-beams as firewood, bathed elephants at their guarded ghats and lit fires glowing like the setting sun, so that the great cool fields that knew no wood but sugarcane, with vallai, ambal, pakanrai and pagal, became waste, and his elephants fought as one.
nuance: The fields are described at their richest (a land whose only 'forest' is sugarcane) in the same breath as they are made waste, so the beauty of the enemy's land is the measure of the king's might. The water plants are listed as what was there before the burning.

thinai_evidence.note: the invasion and burning of an enemy's farmland

comparisons.tenor: the glow of the burning fires

title: யானையும் வேந்தனும்!
reading: Kurunkozhiyur Kizhar praises the Chera Irumporai, heir of kings who ruled the whole land from Kumari to the northern mountain and from sea to sea with a straight sceptre, lord of cool Thondi of screwpine, fields, sandy groves and backwaters, who escaped his great distress as a tusker fallen into a covered pit breaks its bank and rejoins its rejoicing herd, so that enemy kings, fearing to lose their walls and moats, began to submit; the poet has come to see the king of the Kudavar, with shields like clouds, elephants like hills, an army like the sea and a drum like thunder.
nuance: The pit simile (lines 14 to 21) implies a captivity or reverse from which the king broke free, but the poem names neither; the enemy kings' two quoted thoughts (we might regain our land if he is pleased; we shall lose our walls, he looked at us in anger) are a rare piece of the defeated's reasoning.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a king's might and the submission of rival kings

comparisons.tenor: the king escaping his distress to his kin's joy
the great elephants on which bees build

title: நீரும் நிலனும்!
reading: Kudapulaviyanar blesses the Pandya Nedunchezhiyan, lord of an old city with a moat full of fish and a wall the sky fears, and tells him that whether he wants wealth in the next world, sole rule over the kings of this one, or lasting fame, he should hear what is fitting: bodies cannot live without water, food makes the body, food is land joined with water, so those who join land and water give body and life; land that sows and waits on the sky does not help its ruler however wide, so he should quickly build up tanks where the land dips, for those who bind water here have bound those goals, and those who do not have not.
nuance: The argument is a chain (water, food, body, life) closed by a pun on தட்டோர்: those who dammed (water) are those who secured (the three goals), and those who did not, did not. All three royal ambitions of lines 13 to 16, including heaven, are made to depend on irrigation.

colophon.thurai: முதுமொழிக் காஞ்சி : பொருண்மொழிக் காஞ்சி எனவும் பாடம்

thinai_evidence.note: counsel of general truth to a king, the காஞ்சி that the later scheme files under pothuviyal

title: எழுவரை வென்ற ஒருவன்!
reading: Kudapulaviyanar recalls, before the Pandya who defeated the seven at Thalaiyalanganam, where Tamils clashed and he alone was weighed against Death, that he embraced the king's chest thinking it like a stone deadfall set by a tiger-hunter, and describes the dreadful field where elephants with severed trunks rolled like ploughs and the women of old houses wept, 'our little sons lie with our fathers: is such valour ours?', so that Death fled ashamed; he asks if this is the chest wearing the bright garland.
nuance: Line 3 weighs the king against Death (the many lives against Death's singleness), and line 16 has Death flee ashamed, so the battle is told as a contest the king won against Death itself. The mothers' cry, 'is there such valour for us?', joins grief and pride in one sentence, and the poem lets them stand together.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king's victory in a named battle

comparisons.vehicle: இரும்புலி வேட்டுவன் பொறிஅறிந்து மாட்டிய பெருங்கல் அடாரும்

comparisons.tenor: the arrows lodged in the elephant
the severed elephant trunks rolling on the ground

title: மண்ணும் உண்பர்!
patron: சேரமான் யானைக்கட்சேய் மாந்தரஞ் சேரல் இரும்பொறை; மாந்தரஞ் சேரல் எனவும் குறிப்பர்
tamil: பிறிது தெறல் அறியார் நின் நிழல்வாழ் வோரே;
reading: Kurunkozhiyur Kizhar tells the Chera that though one might measure the sea's depth, the earth's breadth, the wind's ways and the empty sky, his knowledge, compassion and kindness are beyond measure; those in his shade know no burning but the cooking fire and the sun, no bow but the rainbow, no weapon but the plough; enemies never eat his land's soil, which only craving pregnant women eat; his fortress lets arrows sleep and his sceptre lets dharma rest; his guard is not shaken by omen birds coming or going; so all living beings fear for him.
nuance: The poem works by exclusions (no burning but..., no bow but the rainbow, திருவில் against கொலைவில்), so the realm's peace is described through what its people do not know. The last line, மன்னுயிர் எல்லாம் நின் அஞ்சும், can mean all beings fear you or fear for you; the praise of a peaceful realm favours the second.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a king's qualities and the peace of his realm rather than a victory

title: புறநானூறு 21-40
theme: Poems 21-40 are court poems to three kings: the Pandya Nedunchezhiyan of Talaiyalanganam and his predecessor at Kanapper fort (21-26), the Chola Nalankilli (27-33) and the Chola Killivalavan (34-40), with one Chera (22). Victory poems that make the fort, the battle sacrifice and the burned enemy land into praise sit beside kaanchi poems that turn the same kings toward transience, the three aims and grace, and counsel poems that tie a king's victories to the plough, his umbrella to his subjects and his fame to easy access and sweet speech.
source_issues: 22 line 38: சோறுயட looks like the review's யடு-for-யொடு fault (சோறொடு), though the sense of the line ('leading the army with food') is uncertain either way; marked as it stands.
24 line 8: கன்ணி is a misprint for கண்ணி; line 18 ஒம்பா for ஓம்பா.
29 line 2: அடர்ந்ற looks like a misprint for அடர்ந்த.
34 line 1: ஆன்மலை should be ஆன்முலை (cows' udders), as the list of crimes requires; the karu form is copied as printed.
35 line 15: முறைவெண்டு is a misprint for முறைவேண்டு; line 17: கொண்டுமூ looks like a misprint for கொண்மூ (cloud).

28 and 36: the review's line table says sangamtamil.com lacks our opening lines (28 lines 1-2, 36 lines 1-2); 28's lines begin the maxim the rest applies and 36's are the address the poem turns on, so they are part of the poems; all lines are marked.
30: the review says sangamtamil.com lacks our line 2 (அஞ் ஞாயிற்றுப் பரிப்பும்); it fits the list of measured heavens and is marked.

37: the colophon thurai is a note of variants (அரச வாகை, with குற்றுழிஞை and முதல் வஞ்சி as other readings), and the thinai has உழிஞை as a variant; copied exactly; our thinai agrees with the உழிஞை reading.
27 line 15 and 35 line 23 are flagged as repeated in 57 and 64; both are formulae, not copying errors.

title: புகழ்சால் தோன்றல்!
reading: The poet praises the Pandya who took Kanapper fort, whose moat, sky-high wall, star-like battlements and sunless guard forest made it as hard to win back as water that hot iron has drunk, and blesses his spear to flourish in fame while those who scorn him perish with their name.
nuance: The fort is described at length only to be the measure of the man who took it: every defence is listed and then cancelled by the single word கடந்த of the colophon and the poem's 'hard to recover'. வேங்கை மார்பின் (line 9) reads best as the name of the fort's lord, Vengaimarpan, made to grieve; taken as 'tiger-chested' it would describe the victor instead.

thinai_evidence.note: the deed praised is the taking of a fortified town, which is siege, though the colophon files it as the king's excellence

comparisons.tenor: the fort, as hard to win back once lost

title: ஈகையும் நாவும்!
patron: சேரமான் யானைக்கட் சேஎய் மாந்தரஞ் சேரல் இரும்பொறை
tamil: புத்தேள் உலகத்து அற்று’ எனக் கேட்டு, வந்து
reading: The poet, having come to see the land of Mantharam Cheral Irumporai said to be like the world of the gods, praises his musth elephants at their posts, his moon-white umbrella under whose shade the unarmed sleep safe, his open war camp loud with the thumbai-crowned warriors' kuravai, and his giving to the kin of those who bring tribute, and says the king never wearies of leading his army into enemy land because he does not sleep.
nuance: The camp is called வாய் காவாது பரந்து பட்ட, spread wide with its entrance unguarded: the king's safety is shown by a camp that needs no watch, and the sleepers 'without a sword at their side' sleep under his guard. The closing turn makes his sleeplessness the reason the kingdom is heaven-like.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises a king's excellence in his calling as guardian and leader of a camp

comparisons.tenor: the elephant's head swarming with bees at its musth
the camp's huts roofed with paddy and cane

title: நண்ணார் நாணுவர்!
reading: Kalladanar tells Nedunchezhiyan, the victor of Alankanam, that he has seen his work in the enemy country: fords churned by bathing elephants, fields stripped by his Murugan-like bowmen, guarded trees felled in every grove, fine houses burned, a land where even the foe says he will do more, and a forest turned to a waste where a doe with her fawn, her stag killed by a tiger, nibbles white velai flowers.
nuance: The closing picture is not drawn as a comparison, but a doe left with her young after the stag's death, eating the flowers of a frightening field, is placed exactly where the poem's catalogue of ruin ends; it reads as the enemy's widowed households without saying so. The poet presents the devastation as what he has seen on his way to the king (கண்டனென் வருவல்).

thinai_evidence.note: felling the guarded tree and burning the enemy's towns are the deeds of invasion

comparisons.vehicle: எழிற்கலை புலிப்பால் பட்டெனச் சிறுமறி தழீஇய தெறிநடை மடப்பிணை
comparisons.tenor: the bereaved households of the conquered land (a reading; not stated)

title: வல்லுனர் வாழ்ந்தோர்!
reading: Mangudi Kizhar pictures Nedunchezhiyan's land, where reapers cool off in the sea, fishermen drink and dance, and women drink palm, cane and screw-pine waters, names Evvi's Mizhalai and the Velir's Muthooru among his gains, blesses his star and curses his enemies', bids him live in joy among his warriors, suppliants and women, and closes with the saying that the only ones who truly lived are those whose fame stays when they die.
nuance: Sea-shore and field are run together on purpose: the reapers of the paddy plunge into the southern sea and the women drink 'three waters' and bathe in the 'three waters' (முந்நீர், the sea), so the Pandya land is shown as one where marutham and neythal meet. The joyful blessing is a setting for the closing maxim, which turns the poem toward kaanchi: enjoy, but be among those who 'did not go as the many go'.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem ends on the maxim that only lasting fame outlives death, the world that does not stay

comparisons.tenor: the warriors of old families who have grown old with the king

title: கூந்தலும் வேலும்!
tamil: ஈண்டு செலல் மரபின் தன் இயல் வழாஅது,
reading: Kalladanar tells Chezhiyan that when two allied kings came against him like the sun and the moon come down to earth together, he wasted them on the battlefield and took their drums, and asks whether his spear, which had broken firm ranks, did not stop short of further ruin when he saw the widowed women beating their breasts and shearing their dark hair.
nuance: The poem's turn is a question about the spear (சிதைதல் உய்ந்தன்றோ), and whether it means the spear itself escaped damage or was spared further slaughter at the sight of the widows is not certain; on the second reading the victory poem ends in the victor's restraint. The widows shearing their hair is the plain statement of what the same poet left as an image at the end of 23.

thinai_evidence.note: the deed is a pitched battle won against two kings and the seizing of their drums

comparisons.vehicle: உருகெழு ஞாயிறு நிலவுத்திகழ் மதியமொடு நிலஞ்சேர்ந் தாஅங்கு
comparisons.tenor: the two allied kings coming against him together

title: நோற்றார் நின் பகைவர்!
poet: மாங்குடி கிழவர்; மாங்குடி மருதனார் எனவும் பாடம்
reading: Mangudi Kizhar praises Chezhiyan, whose elephants clear the field like wind-driven ships on the sea, who killed kings and took their drums and cooked a battlefield sacrifice with crowned heads for a hearth, blood for water and bangled arms for ladles, and who also completed the Vedic sacrifices among learned Brahmins with kings serving him, and says his enemies must have done penance, since by being called his foes they now live in the other world.
nuance: The two sacrifices are set side by side with the same verb: அடுகளம் வேட்ட (he sacrificed the killing field) and வேள்வி முற்றிய (he completed the rite). The ending's compliment is grim: the enemies were lucky, because dying at his hand earned them heaven.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises the king's excellence in both war and rite

comparisons.tenor: the elephants charging through the battlefield

comparisons.vehicle: முடித் தலை அடுப் பாகப் புனல் குருதி உலைக் கொளீஇத் தொடித்தோள் துடுப்பின்
comparisons.tenor: the battlefield as a sacrificial kitchen

title: புலவர் பாடும் புகழ்!
tamil: சேற்று வளர் தாமரை பயந்த, ஒண் கேழ்,
நூற் றிதழ் அலரின் நிறை கண் டன்ன,
எய்துப என்ப, தம் செய்வினை முடித்து’ எனக்
reading: Among those born in flawless lines like the full hundred-petalled lotus and seated on thrones, the poet tells Nalankilli, few have fame in prose and song while many perish like lotus leaves; he has heard that those whom poets praise reach a sky-car no charioteer drives, so in this world where the moon shows everyone waning, waxing, dying and being born, Nalankilli should show grace to all who come in need, skilled or not, and leave ungiving to his enemies.
nuance: One plant gives both images: the full lotus flower for the few of noble birth who are remembered and its leaf, which rots unnoticed, for the many who are not. The moon's phases are offered as the plain proof of mortality that even the unlearned can see. The heaven-for-the-praised belief is reported as hearsay (என்ப ... எனக் கேட்பல்), not asserted by the poet.

thinai_evidence.note: the counsel rests on the world that does not stay

comparisons.tenor: every life, which wanes, dies and is born

title: போற்றாமையும் ஆற்றாமையும்!
tamil: அதன் திறம் அத்தை யான் உரைக்க வந்தது:-
reading: Citing the ancients' saying that the eight defective births bring their bearers nothing but folly, the poet tells Nalankilli that his enemies now live in jungles where the jungle-cock wakes the millet-watchers, while his own heartland, where thrown cane-stalks crush lotus buds, looks like a dancers' floor; so his wealth can achieve virtue, wealth and pleasure, and failing to do so would be only his own neglect.
nuance: The argument seems to be that a man born whole and rich, unlike the eight kinds of defective birth, has no excuse: if the three aims are not achieved, the fault is his own neglect (போற்றாமை). The link between the opening list and the rest is compressed, and line 11 (புறஞ்சிறை மாக்கட்கு அறங்குறித்து) is hard to place, so this reading is offered with doubt.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem is counsel addressed to the king, செவியறிவுறூஉ in kind, though the colophon names it a maxim kaanchi

comparisons.tenor: the king's heartland strewn with cane and lotus

title: நண்பின் பண்பினன் ஆகுக!
tamil: புனை விளைப் பொலிந்த பொலன் நறுந் தெரியல்
தோள் முற்றுக, நின் சாந்துபுலர் அகலம்! ஆங்க
reading: The poet blesses Nalankilli: may bards throng his court, then women embrace him; may he punish the wicked and protect the good without slackening and never side with those who say good and evil bear no fruit; may his soldiers who enjoy his rich land and his deeds be kind to those who come; and in a world where people pass in turn like the players at a festival, may his kin be his joy and his stored wealth turn into fame.
nuance: The poem names and rejects a view: 'there is no good in good and no evil in evil' (lines 11, 12), a denial of moral consequence, so the anthology already knows such a doctrine to argue against it. Lines 17 to 22 are syntactically difficult, and whose kindness and whose small huts are meant is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: the blessings rest on a world where all pass in turn

comparisons.tenor: the people of this world who pass one after another

title: எங்ஙனம் பாடுவர்?
reading: There are people who speak of the sun's path and motion, the circle it moves in, the quarters the wind blows and the empty sky as if they had gone and measured them, the poet tells Nalankilli, but his strength is hidden like the stone an elephant holds in its cheek, so how can poets sing it openly, lord of the land where great ships enter Puhar without striking mast or sail and pour out the sea's goods on the roads?
nuance: The praise works by contrast: the heavens can be measured, but this king cannot. The image of the elephant's cheek-stone (kept hidden until it is thrown) makes the hidden strength a weapon held back, not a lack.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem is praise that declares the king beyond praise

comparisons.tenor: those who speak with certainty of the heavens

title: வடநாட்டார் தூங்கார்!
tamil: இரு குடை பின்பட ஓங்கி ஒரு குடை
கடிமதில் பாயும் நின் களிறு அடங் கலவே;
குண கடல் பின்ன தாகக், குட கடல்
வெண் தலைப் புணரி நின் மான்குளம்பு அலைப்ப,
reading: As wealth and pleasure follow behind virtue, the poet tells Nalankilli, the other two kings' umbrellas follow behind his single umbrella shining like the moon; seeking fame he will stay only in a war camp, his elephants never rest from charging forts, his warriors never call any land too far, and so the northern kings lie awake in dread that he will march round from the eastern sea to the western.
nuance: The opening simile takes the ordering of the three aims (virtue first, wealth and pleasure following) and uses it to rank the three crowned kings, so an ethical doctrine is made into the vehicle of a political claim. The march 'with the eastern sea behind' and the horses' hooves in the western surf is a circuit of conquest round the land.

thinai_evidence.note: the fear of the northern kings is fear of an invasion

comparisons.tenor: the two other kings' umbrellas following his

title: பூவிலையும் மாடமதுரையும்!
reading: The poet calls the gift-seekers to come and sing Nalankilli with him, since he will give Vanji (a 'vanji that bears no flowers') to fill their cooking pots and towered Madurai so the viralis may get the price of flowers; and by ancient right this cool land is in his hand like the fresh clay the potter's boys set on the wheel.
nuance: பூவா வஞ்சி is a pun: not the flowering vanji creeper but the Chera capital Vanji. The potter's clay image says the land is his to shape as he likes; the generosity promised is a conquest promised.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem summons the gift-seekers to praise a giver

comparisons.vehicle: வேட்கோச் சிறாஅர் தேர்க்கால் வைத்த பசுமண் குரூஉத்திரள்
comparisons.tenor: the land in the king's hand

title: புதுப்பூம் பள்ளி!
reading: Even in the Pandya's country, where the hunter's basket of venison and the herdgirl's pot of curds are filled with white paddy by the ploughmen's women, the poet tells Nalankilli, he broke the doors of seven forts and carved his tiger emblem, and his fierce war camp, where bards sing vanji and the bards' families are fed heaps of meat and rice like balls of unopened flowers, outdoes all the festivals he held in his flowering groves.
nuance: The opening shows the barter of three lands (hill meat, pasture curds, field paddy) as a picture of a settled, prosperous country, which makes the conquest larger. Lines 16 to 22 on the festival groves are hard to construe, and the subject of the doll simile and of the rams slaughtered at every gate is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises the king's excellence in war and in feeding his people at the camp

comparisons.tenor: the heaps of meat and rice
the beauty of the festival dancers or lovers

title: செய்தி கொன்றவர்க்கு உய்தி இல்லை!
reading: Dharma says there is expiation for those who cut a cow's udders, destroy women's unborn children or wrong their elders, but none, even if the earth is overturned, for those who kill a benefit; so, the poet tells Killivalavan, if he did not sing the king who made the bards rich after they ate millet with milk and honey and roast hare, the sun would not rise; and he blesses him to live more years than the drops the Himalayan rain-cloud pours.
nuance: The poem quotes a rule of dharma in order to apply it to the poet himself: not to praise his benefactor would be the one sin with no atonement. The poet calls himself தஞ்சம் (a humble, dependent man), and the cosmic oath (the sun would not rise) raises his debt of gratitude to the order of nature.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem is the praise of a patron, framed as the poet's duty of gratitude

comparisons.tenor: the years wished for the king

title: உழுபடையும் பொருபடையும்!
reading: The poet tells Killivalavan that among the three Tamil kings kingship is his and the Kaveri-fed land is his, then counsels him: in the land of the just sceptre where the humble can reach the king when they seek justice, rain comes when it is sought; his tall umbrella is not for shade but to shelter suffering subjects; his victories are the fruit of the plough's furrow; the world blames kings when rains fail or harvests drop, so he should ignore the talk of malcontents, bear the burden of those who rear the plough-oxen and protect his people, and even the unsubmitting will bow at his feet.
nuance: Two causal claims carry the counsel: just rule brings rain, and victory in battle grows out of the furrow. The question about the umbrella (is it to keep off the sun? no) turns the most visible royal emblem into a duty of shelter. The poem also warns that kings are blamed even for drought, whether or not they caused it.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem is counsel addressed to a king

comparisons.tenor: the white flowers of the jointed cane

comparisons.vehicle: ஞாயிறு சுமந்த கோடுதிரள் கொண்டுமூ மாக விசும்பின் நடுவுநின்

comparisons.tenor: the elephants lying dead on the battlefield

title: நீயே அறிந்து செய்க!
tamil: நீ அளந் தறிதி நின் புரைமை; வார்தோல்,
reading: Whether he kills or releases the enemy, the poet tells Killivalavan, he knows his own worth: while the sound of his smiths' axes felling the guarded trees on the Porunai's banks, where girls once played with gold stones on the sand, echoes into the walled palace where the other king sits at ease, and Valavan's drum roars here, to say he fought such a king is a matter of shame.
nuance: The poem praises by rebuke: it says nothing against the siege's power, only that a king who will not come out is no fit opponent, so the honour of continuing the war is gone. The girls' play on the river sand, ruined by the felling, is a small picture of what the war destroys.

thinai_evidence.note: the felling of the guarded trees of another king's land is the work of an invading army

title: புறவும் போரும்!
reading: Descendant of the Chembiyan who relieved a bird's distress, with an army that strikes like the thunderbolt that hits the hill cleft a five-headed cobra has entered, the poet tells Killivalavan, he is able to wreck in battle the old town walled like copper, with its crocodile-filled moat where the beasts snap at the torch-shadows of the night watch, without sparing it as 'fine', because a king with decked elephants is inside.
nuance: Lineage and conduct are set against each other: the king is first named by his ancestor's famous mercy to a bird, and then praised for showing no mercy to a fine old town, because a rival king shelters in it. The poem neither blames nor excuses the destruction.

colophon.thurai: அரச வாகை குற்றுழிஞை எனவும், முதல் வஞ்சி எனவும் பாடம்

thinai_evidence.note: the deed is the storming of a walled and moated town

comparisons.tenor: the king's army striking the foe sheltering in his fort

title: வேண்டியது விளைக்கும் வேந்தன்!
reading: The poet tells Killivalavan, whose angry glance spreads fire and whose loving glance makes gold bloom, and who could bring moonlight out of the sun or sunshine out of the moon, that those born and raised in his shade cannot measure him, and that gift-seekers even in enemy lands think of his country, because heaven, where people only enjoy what their deeds earned and where no one gives or asks, is lacking, while here the same enjoyment is had along with giving.
nuance: The poem ranks the king's land above heaven on one ground: in heaven there is neither giving nor asking, so the gift-relation itself, which bards live by, is what earth has that heaven lacks. The comparison of the two worlds is put in the bards' mouths.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem is praise of a king as the giver bards long for

title: புகழினும் சிறந்த சிறப்பு!
reading: Descendant of the king who entered the ivory-beamed scale for a dove's sake, the poet tells Killivalavan, giving is not his own fame; with ancestors who destroyed the hanging fort, killing is not his fame; with justice standing firm in the Chola court at Urantai, justice is not his fame; so how can he praise him, except by singing the might that withered the unwithering Vanji when the Chera of the Himalaya-carved bow fell?
nuance: Each inherited virtue is set aside as the family's, not his, which leaves one deed that is his alone: the defeat of the Chera. வாடா வஞ்சி வாட்டும் is a pun, the vanji (creeper, and the Chera capital) that does not wither, made to wither.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem is praise that searches for what is the king's own

title: ஒரு பிடியும் எழு களிரும்!
reading: The poet tells Killivalavan, who took others' guarded forts and wears anklets made of the gold of their crowns, that his poets wish to see him always as today, so that his detractors bow their necks and his praisers shine, and asks him to be sweet of speech and easy to reach, lord of the land where the small spot one cow-elephant lies on feeds seven bull elephants.
nuance: The counsel is two words long, இன்சொல் and எண்பதம் (ease of access), and it is given to a conqueror at the height of his strength, as the condition for his praise lasting.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem is counsel to a king

title: புறநானூறு 41-60
theme: Poems 41-60 are poems to the three crowns: Kovur Kizhar's interventions with Chola kings (omens before a march, a siege, a war between kinsmen, children before the elephant, a bard under suspicion), guide and praise poems for Chera kings, and Pandya poems that rank righteous rule above the army, liken the king to the gods and to sun and moon, and close with a Chola-Pandya alliance and a parasol mistaken for the moon. The recurring argument is restraint: poets use ancestry, shame and gain to hold kings back from cruelty and division.
source_issues: 41 line 12: stray punctuation 'முன்ப,!'.
42 line 18 is flagged as repeated in 209 line 6; it is a formula for the watered country, not a copying error.
43 line 5: 'ஏறுகுறித், தொரீஇத்' splits one word (ஏறுகுறித்தொரீஇ) with a stray comma.
46 line 8: 'கெட்டனை' (you are ruined) does not fit; probably a misprint for கேட்டனை (having heard); marked on the second reading and flagged uncertain.
47 line 4: 'மகழ்ந்தும்' is a misprint for மகிழ்ந்தும்.
48: show flags line 5 (அஃதுஎம் ஊரே; அவன்எம் இறைவன்) as absent from Duraisamy Pillai's edition, and the review's table says sangamtamil.com has a line 6 we lack; marked as it stands.
49 and 57: the review's table says sangamtamil.com lacks our opening line; in both, line 1 is integral (49's run of questions, 57's 'skilled or not' that line 2 completes), so all lines are marked.
51: the colophon poet field reads 'ஐயூர் முடவனார்!' with an exclamation mark where a separator is meant.
55: 23 lines against 21 in Duraisamy Pillai's edition; the short lines 7 to 10 are broken differently. Line 14 ends with a double comma.
56 line 24: 'போல்வும்' is a misprint for போலவும். Line 6 'புல்கொடி' may stand for புட்கொடி (bird banner); marked as the bird-bannered god.

58 line 1: 'இவளே' where the parallel line 9 has இவனே for the Pandya; probably a misprint. Line 4 has a full stop in mid-sentence. The review's table says the site lacks our lines 1 and 26 and we lack three of its lines near 25-27; our text reads continuously and is marked as it stands.

title: காலனுக்கு மேலோன்!
reading: Death itself waits for its moment, but this Chola strikes whenever he wishes; in the lands of those who angered him every evil sign appears, in the sky, in the trees, in birdcalls and in dreams, and the people, dazed and defenceless, kiss their children and grieve with their wives in a great uproar.
nuance: The praise works entirely through the victims: a native list of portents (meteors in all eight directions, a leafless branch catching fire, teeth falling out, an oil bath and riding an elephant in dreams) makes the coming defeat look already decided, and the king is greater than Death because he does not wait. Several of the dream signs in lines 8 to 10 are obscure.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem is about the enemy country awaiting the king's march, the matter of an invasion

comparisons.tenor: the king, who unlike Death does not wait for a fit time

title: ஈகையும் வாகையும்!
tamil: ஆனா ஈகை, அடு போர், அண்ணல்! நின்
reading: The Chola's elephants loom like hills, his army roars like the sea and his spears flash like lightning, so every king trembles; yet under his unbending sceptre his own fertile country hears no cry of war, only the noise of floods, and feeds guests from the dry lands; poets flow to him as rivers to the sea, while he turns on the land of the two rival kings with the force of angry Death.
nuance: The poem sets two kinds of பூசல் (clamour) against each other: inside the kingdom only the noise of rising water, never the cry of a raid; the peace within is the other face of the terror without. The catalogue of plenty (fish taken by reapers, tortoises turned up by the plough, honey from the cane, lilies plucked by water-carrying women) is offered as food for guests, so the land's wealth is measured by its hospitality. Line 18 recurs in poem 209, a formula for the watered country.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises the king's excellence as ruler, his protection and might

comparisons.tenor: the country guarded by his sceptre
all the poets turning to the king
the king's might against rival kings

title: பிறப்பும் சிறப்பும்!
reading: The poet addresses a Chola prince of the line of the king who entered the scales to save a dove from a hawk: he admits he spoke in anger, asking whether hurting brahmins befits a son of such ancestors, and that the prince, instead of resenting it, was ashamed as if he himself had erred, showing that his house bears with those who wrong it; so the poet declares the fault his own and wishes the prince more years than the sands of the Kaveri.
nuance: The dove story is used twice: the poet invokes the ancestor's sacrifice for a weak bird to rebuke the prince, and the prince's forbearance turns the same family standard back on the poet, who ends with யானே பிழைத்தனென் (it is I who erred). The poem does not say what the quarrel was about; பார்ப்பார் நோவன in line 14 implies that the poet speaks as a brahmin who felt wronged.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises the prince's excellence in forbearance and shame, a king's virtue

comparisons.tenor: the prince's shame at the poet's fault
the years the poet wishes the prince

title: அறமும் மறமும்!
reading: Inside the besieged fort the elephants, unbathed and unfed, rub against their posts and roar like thunder, babies cry for milk, women tie up hair without flowers and the houses cry out for water; it is bitter to sit here at ease: if you are righteous, open the gate saying it is theirs; if you are brave, open it with battle; being neither, to cower behind shut doors in a corner of the long wall is shameful.
nuance: The poet gives the besieged king exactly two honourable exits, yielding as an act of aram or fighting as an act of maram, and names the third, waiting behind the wall, as the shameful one. The suffering of elephants, infants and women is the argument: counsel here works by making the cost of delay visible.

thinai_evidence.note: the king addressed is holding a shut fort under siege, the defender's side of the siege

comparisons.tenor: the trumpeting of the starved elephant

title: தோற்பது நும் குடியே!
reading: Neither of you wears the Chera's palmyra leaf or the Pandya's neem; both your garlands are of aar, so if either of you loses, it is your own house that loses, and both cannot win; this fight does not befit your clan, and it will only give deep delight to other kings like you with bannered chariots.
nuance: The argument is made through garlands, the emblems of the three houses: because both kings wear the same aar, the war can have no winner, only a losing house, and the only gain goes to dynasties outside. The appeal is to lineage and to the rivals' delight, not to compassion.

thinai_evidence.note: the matter is a battle between two kings of equal rank already joined; the colophon's thunai vanji names the poet's peacemaking

comparisons.tenor: the rival dynasties who will enjoy the Cholas' quarrel

title: அருளும் பகையும்!
reading: The poet reminds the Chola that he descends from the king who relieved the dove's distress and many others' troubles, and points to children of a house that shares its own food for fear of the hardship of those who live by learning; these small boys, who have stopped crying at the sight of the elephant, now stare bewildered at the assembly in a new distress; having heard this, the king may do as he wishes.
nuance: Two lineages are set face to face, the king's, famous for saving a dove, and the children's, famous for sharing with the learned; the verdict is left to the king, so cruelty would be a betrayal of his own ancestry. The children's having stopped crying at the elephant and now staring at the court shows a fear too young to understand what is happening. The syntax of lines 3 and 4 and the reading of line 8 (see source_issues) are not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem's act is a plea to a king, counsel on his own ancestry, not an invasion

comparisons.tenor: the protection a generous house gives the learned

title: புலவரைக் காத்த புலவர்!
reading: The bard's life of gifts, flying to patrons like birds, crossing wastes without counting them long, singing as well as an untrained tongue allows, rejoicing in what it gets, feeding its kin, spending without saving and giving without stint, troubled only about due honour, knows no harm to anyone; it walks with head high so that its rivals are shamed, and has a dignity like that of kings who rule the earth.
nuance: The poem answers a charge it never names: by insisting that the wandering bard harms no one, it lets us infer that a man who crosses frontiers from court to court could be suspected of serving the enemy. It then claims for the bard a pride equal to the king's, so the defence ends as a statement of rank.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises the excellence of the bard's own calling (porul 2.16)

title: 'கண்டனம்' என நினை!
reading: Thondi of the seaside grove smells of honey from the garland on Kothai's chest, from the garlands of the women who embrace him and from the neytal flowers of the great backwater; that is our town and he is our lord; old-tongued suppliant, if you go to him, remember us too, and tell him: we saw the man whose fame rises whenever battle rises.
nuance: The pun on கோதை, the king's name and a garland, runs through the first two lines, so the king, his garland and the garlands of the women who embrace him all perfume one town. The request to be remembered turns the guide poem into a message the suppliant carries back to the patron.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem directs a suppliant to a patron, praise in the form of a guide poem

title: எங்ஙனம் மொழிவேன்?
reading: Shall I call Kothai of the raised sword lord of the hills, lord of the towns, or lord of the cold shore where the sea roars? How can I name him, when the millet-watchers beat their rattles and the birds rise together from the nearby fields of bending ears and from the shining shore?
nuance: நாடன், ஊரன் and சேர்ப்பன் are the akam titles of the lords of hill, field and shore, and the answer is a single picture: one rattle in the millet patch lifts the birds of the paddy and of the shore at once, so the three landscapes lie close enough for one sound to cross them. Unlike 48, the poem gives no direction to a suppliant, so the colophon's guide-poem thurai fits it only by its pairing with 48.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem is praise of the king through the extent of his land

title: கவரி வீசிய காவலன்!
reading: Before the blood-thirsty war drum, strapped tight and decked with peacock plumes, a garland of gems and golden uzhinai, had come back from its ritual bath, the poet unknowingly lay down on its soft couch, white as foam of oil; instead of cutting him in two with his sword, which would itself have proved that he knew all good Tamil, the king came near and fanned him with his drum-like arm, as if he had heard that only the famous have a dwelling in the higher world.
nuance: Two graces are graded: sparing the trespasser on the sacred drum would have been enough to show the king's learning in Tamil, but he went further and fanned the sleeper. The closing question explains the act by belief in fame as the passport to the higher world, so mercy is presented as the king's investment in his name.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises one gracious act of the king

title: ஈசலும் எதிர்ந்தோரும் !
poet: ஐயூர் முடவனார்! ஐயூர் கிழார் எனவும் பாடம்
tamil: ‘தண் தமிழ் பொது’ எனப் பொறாஅன், போர் எதிர்ந்து,
reading: As nothing dams a flood, no shade shelters from overgrown fire and no strength stands against a gale, so nothing stands against angry Vazhuthi, who will not bear the claim that the cool Tamil land is shared; the kings who gave him tribute when he asked are free from fear, but pitiable are those who lost his favour, fluttering for a one-day life like the winged termites rising from the red mound the tiny termites built with toil.
nuance: 'தண் தமிழ் பொது' is quoted as a claim the king will not bear, that the Tamil land is common to the three crowns, so the poem praises a bid for sole rule. The termite image is double: the colony's long labour builds the mound, and the winged ones that leave it live a single day.

thinai_evidence.note: the king goes to war to take tribute from other kings, the matter of invasion

comparisons.tenor: the kings who lost his favour

title: ஊன் விரும்பிய புலி !
poet: மருதன் இளநாகனார்; மருதிள நாகனார் என்பதும் பாடம்
reading: Like a strong male tiger that tires of its cave in the haunted peak, stretches with a groan and, driven by hunger, goes out to hunt where it pleases, Vazhuthi sets out to make the northern kings wither; if that is his aim, pitiable are those whose rich towns, where fish-smoke clings to creepers on the marutha trees, will turn to jungle, the common hall abandoned by its god and offerings, a forest fowl laying eggs in the dice holes the grey elders carved.
nuance: Praise is delivered as pity for the enemy: most of the poem pictures the after-state, the common hall emptied of its god and of its elders' game, with a jungle fowl nesting in the dice holes, so the king's glory is measured by the ruin it will make.

thinai_evidence.note: the king sets out against the northern kings, the matter of invasion

title: செந்நாவும் சேரன் புகழும்!
reading: To Poraiyan of the war elephants and swift horses, who ended the distress of Vilankil, the pearl-strewn town where bangled women play on the terraces of gem-bright mansions: your fame widens if spelled out and is still unfinished if summed up, beyond the grasp of bewildered minds like mine; yet in a world where the great were born one cannot refuse to sing, and since you wished that Kapilan of the flawless verse were alive today, I will sing your conquests as your rank deserves.
nuance: The poet measures himself against a famous predecessor whom the king himself named: the king's wish for Kapilar sets the standard, and the poet accepts it only by promising to sing to the measure of the king's rank. It is early evidence that a poet's name outlived him at court.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem's act is the poet's undertaking to praise, which is paadaan

title: எளிதும் கடிதும்!
reading: For suppliants like us it is easy to walk straight, as if we owned it, into the noisy old town where our lord sits and enter his court with heads high; but to the boastful kings who rose against Kothai, who gives without stint until the rain-cloud is ashamed, his land is like a wide tiger-haunted pasture that a herdsman with a leaf garland, grimy cloth and whistling lips will not approach with his small-headed flock.
nuance: The open gate of the court and the closed frontier of the land are made one fact: the ease with which bards walk in is the other side of the dread that keeps rival kings out. The herdsman with his leaf garland and grimy cloth is an everyday figure used to measure royal danger.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises the king's giving and his dread among foes

comparisons.tenor: the king's land as enemy kings see it

title: மூன்று அறங்கள்!
reading: Maran, foremost among kings as the single eye shines on the forehead of the blue-throated god who strung the mountain bow with a snake and burned the three forts with one arrow: though elephants, horses, chariots and warriors make an army, a king's victory has the righteous way at its root; so do not bend the sceptre for your own or kill merit because it is another's; be like the sun in valour, the moon in gentleness and the rain-cloud in giving, so that the needy want nothing, and live longer than the sands the wind heaps at Senthil.
nuance: The four-limbed army is listed and then ranked below conduct, and conduct is defined as impartiality both ways: not bending the rod for 'ours', not destroying merit because it is 'theirs'. The three similes give the king one face for enemies, one for subjects and one for suppliants.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem is counsel to a king (செவியறிவுறூஉ, porul 2.29)

comparisons.tenor: the years wished for the king

title: கடவுளரும் காவலனும்!
poet: மதுரைக் கணக்காயனார் மகனார் நக்கீரனார்; (மதுரை மருதன் இளநாகனார் எனவும் பாடம்)
reading: Of the four gods who guard the world, the bull-bannered one with the axe and the dark throat, the conch-white one with the plough and palmyra banner, the sapphire-dark one with the bird banner and the peacock-bannered rider of the elephant, the Pandya equals the first in wrath, the second in strength, the third in fame and the fourth in achieving what he sets out to do; so let him give rare treasures to suppliants, drink cool Yavana wine poured in gold cups by bangled women, live happily, and endure with the world like the sun and the moon.
nuance: The likening to gods is systematic: four gods, each identified by banner, weapon and colour, each lending one quality. The counsel to enjoy life (இனிது ஒழுகுமதி) comes only after the command to give to suppliants, and the Yavana wine is a sign of foreign trade at a Pandya court.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises the king by likening him to the gods (பூவை நிலை)

comparisons.tenor: the white body of the plough-bearing god
the dark body of the bird-bannered god
the king's achieving what he intends

title: காவன்மரமும் கட்டுத்தறியும்!
tamil: மின்னு நிமிர்ந் தன்ன நின்ஒளிறு இலங்கு நெடுவேல்
reading: Maran, whom all praisers, skilled or not, liken to Mayon: when you take another's land, let your young men plunder its fields of bending grain, let fire waste its wide towns, let your lightning-bright spear kill your foes if it will, but whatever you do, spare their guardian trees, for they will not serve as posts for your tall elephants.
nuance: The counsel allows plunder, burning and killing and draws its one line at the enemy's guardian tree, the emblem a house protects; the reason given is a practical irony, that such a tree makes no tethering post, which lets the poet restrain the king without preaching.

thinai_evidence.note: the counsel concerns the conduct of an invasion

title: புலியும் கயலும்!
patron: சோழன் குராப்பள்ளித் துஞ்சிய பெருந் திருமா வளவனும் பாண்டியன் வெள்ளியம் பலத்துத் துஞ்சிய பெரு வழுதியும்
tamil: காதல் நெஞ்சின் நும் இடை புகற்கு அலமரும்
இன்றே போல்க நும் புணர்ச்சி; வென்று வென்று
reading: To the Chola, lord of the Kaveri and of Urandai, and the Pandya of Tamil Koodal, the young bull of the Panchavas who upheld his ancient house when the elders died as aerial roots hold up a banyan whose trunk has perished: standing together you shine like the white god of the palmyra banner and the blue god of the wheel; help each other, and if you never break your union the sea-girt earth will surely be yours; do not heed outsiders who, seeming good and kind and loyal to old ways, are eager to come between you; may your union stay as it is today, your spears rise in victory and other kings' hill-countries bear your tiger and carp on their peaks.
nuance: The address is balanced exactly, நீயே and இவனே twice, a line of praise for each, before the two are joined in one image of two gods standing together. The danger named is not war but go-betweens, described by three 'seeming' (போலவும்) phrases; the closing wish to carve tiger and carp together on others' hills makes the alliance a programme of conquest. Lines 6 and 7 (the young thunder and the snake) are obscure.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises two kings standing together and counsels them to stay so

comparisons.tenor: the young Pandya upholding his ancient house
the young Pandya who cannot bear old enemies

title: பாவலரும் பகைவரும்!
reading: Vazhuthi with the garland on your chest and arms that reach your knees, you are truly skilled at protecting with love and you know no falsehood; to your enemies you are like the sun that rises from the sea with unabating heat, to people like us you are like the moon.
nuance: The poem compresses the double simile of 55 into two lines, and the turn is in எம்மனோர்க்கே: the poet places himself among those who receive the moon's coolness.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem is praise of the king's two faces

comparisons.tenor: the king toward his own people

title: மதியும் குடையும்!
patron: சோழன் குராப்பள்ளித் துஞ்சிய பெருந் திருமா வளவன்
reading: The poet and the virali, who had reached the edge of the wasteland like peahens, saw the full moon at the zenith, among twinkling red stars like a fishing boat's lamp in mid-sea, and hurried to worship it many times, because it looked like the white parasol of their lord Valavan of the true sword, a king like the strong ox that drags a salt cart's sunken wheel out of the rut on the road from the backwaters to the hill country.
nuance: The usual simile is reversed: the bards worship the moon because it resembles the king's parasol, not the other way round. The ox that hauls a salt cart out of a rut gives the king a working animal's image, strength shown when the load sinks.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises the king's parasol, the sign of his protection

comparisons.tenor: the full moon among the stars
Valavan bearing the burden of rule

title: புறநானூறு 61-80
theme: Poems 61 to 80 praise Chola and Pandya kings and test what kingship is worth: the double death of two kings in one battle, the honour death after Venni and a poet ranking the loser over the victor, guide poems sending hungry bards to Chola patrons, three royal vows that stake justice, friendship, fame and giving, a captive king's refusal to beg, a king on the lightness of the throne, and the boy-king Neduncheliyan's single victory over seven.
source_issues: 72 line 1 reads நகுதத் கனரே; the word is very likely நகுதக் கனரே (a doubled த for க). Left as it stands.
69 line 7: the text flag records முழுவதுடன் against முழுதுடன் in the two editions; the metre favours முழுதுடன். Our reading kept.

77 line 13: the text flag records இகழ்ந்தன்றும் against மலிந்தன்றும் (TVU) and மலிந்தன்று (Duraisamy Pillai). Marked as it stands; the sense 'neither rejoiced nor gloated' is close either way. Line 1 also reads ஓண் கழல், probably for ஒண் கழல்.
77: the review's line table gives our text 10 lines against the site's 13, but our current text has 13 lines; the table looks out of date for this poem.

64, 72, 74: the review notes the site lacks our opening line; in all three our line 1 is needed for the sense (the packing of the instruments in 64, the mockery in 72, the dead child in 74), so the loss is the site's.
65: the colophon patron field holds a sentence on the circumstance (that he fought Karikal, was wounded in the back and sat north), not only a name.
78: the colophon has no patron; the poem names none either, and the king is Neduncheliyan only by the run of 76 to 79 by the same poet.
61: the poet's name reads எறிச்சிலுர், probably for எறிச்சிலூர்.
63 line 12 repeats in 352 line 5 (the text flag); it is a shared formula, not an error.

title: மலைந்தோரும் பணிந்தோரும்!
patron: சோழன் இலவந்திகைப் பள்ளித் துஞ்சிய நலங்கிள்ளி சேட்சென்னி
reading: The poet paints the plenty of Chenni's farmland, where weeding women eat fresh rice with thick slices of fish and the labourers' children, tired of coconuts, climb the straw stacks to reach for palmyra fruit, and then says that whoever challenges this king learns his fate: no one who fought him has been seen to live, and no one who bowed at his feet has been seen to suffer.
nuance: The last lines set two fates side by side: those who fight him do not live, and those who come to fit themselves to his feet (திருந்து அடி பொருந்த) do not suffer. The praise of might is also an offer of protection, and the farm scene of children too full to want coconuts is what that protection yields.

thinai_evidence.note: the deed praised is the king's sure victory over all who fight him

title: போரும் சீரும்!
patron: சேரமான் குடக்கோ நெடுஞ்சேரலாதன்; சோழன் வேற்பஃறடக் கைப் பெருவிறற் கிள்ளி
reading: Asking what victory there can be in such a war, the poet describes a field where both kings, who fought by the rule of right, have died together with their armies: demon women dance with bloodied hands to the drum, the umbrellas shake, the drums are silent, no one is left to claim the field, the queens refuse the widow's greens and cold bath and lie down on their husbands' breasts, and only the gods in their unfading world gain guests; the poet ends 'may your fame flourish'.
nuance: The opening question (அமர்மிகல் யாவது?) and the closing blessing frame the poem as counsel against such war: the only party that gains is heaven, which gets its guests. The queens who neither eat the widow's greens nor take the cold bath but settle on their husbands' breasts are, on the plain sense, dying with them; the poem states it without comment.

thinai_evidence.note: a battle in which both sides fell, which is the thumbai situation of the whole field destroyed

title: என்னாவது கொல்?
patron: சோழன் வேற்பஃறடக்கைப் பெருவிறற் கிள்ளி; சேரமான் குடக்கோ நெடுஞ்சேரலாதன்
reading: After a battle in which the elephants, horses, warriors and drums are all lost and both kings have fallen on the field, the poet asks what will now become of their wide, rich lands, where women with bangles of lily stalk eat fresh flattened rice and dive into cool water.
nuance: Each line of the catalogue ends on a verb of ending (ஒழிந்தனவே, பட்டனவே, மாய்ந்தனரே, விளிந்தனவே), and the drums die 'for want of anyone to carry them'. The question at the end turns from the dead to the living land, which now has no king; the poem counts the cost to the country rather than the glory.

thinai_evidence.note: both kings died in the fight, the thumbai matter of mutual destruction

title: புற்கை நீத்து வரலாம்!
reading: The speaker urges a dancing woman with few bangles to pack her lute and small drums and set out with him to see Kudumi, the king of great honour who stays on in the enemy's land on the battlefield where elephant herds fought and vultures wheel over the fresh flesh, so that they may leave behind their thin watery gruel.
nuance: The gift is never named; it is implied by what the travellers will leave behind, their watery gruel. The king is to be found not in his capital but in the enemy's country, so the dancer is sent to a war camp.

thinai_evidence.note: a performer directs a dancer to a king's gift, the guide-poem form of praise

title: நாணமும் பாசமும்!
patron: சேரமான் பெருஞ்சேரலாதன்; இவன் கரிகாற் பெருவளத்தானோடு பொருது புறப்புண்பட்டு, வடக்கிருந்தபோது பாடியது
reading: The drums and lutes are forgotten, the great pots are overturned and the butter gone, kin forget the toddy, the ploughmen's call and the village festivals are forgotten, because, as at the full moon when sun and moon face each other and one sinks behind the hill in the sad evening, the warrior king, ashamed of a wound in his back from a king his equal, has sat facing north with his sword to die; here the days no longer pass as days.
nuance: The full-moon image fits the event closely: two lights of equal rank face each other and one goes down, as two equal kings met and one withdrew. The shame named is of the wound's place (புறப்புண், a wound on the back), not of losing, and the five 'forgets' (மறப்ப) show a whole country stopping its music, food and work.

thinai_evidence.note: a lament over a king's chosen death, which the Tholkappiyam places with the passing of the world (kaanchi), though the colophon files it under pothuviyal

comparisons.tenor: the king withdrawing to die while his equal remains

title: நல்லவனோ அவன்!
poet: வெண்ணிக் குயத்தியார்: வெண்ணிற் குயத்தியார் எனவும் பாடம்
tamil: சென்று, அமர்க் கடந்த நின் ஆற்றல் தோன்ற
reading: Addressing Karikal Valavan, descendant of the one who drove ships over the sea by mastering the wind, the poet grants that he went and won and showed his strength, then asks whether the king who, ashamed of a wound on his back at the field of Venni, sat facing north and reached the world of great fame is not a better man than he.
nuance: The praise is real for four lines and then turns: the victor is told to his face that the defeated king, by his death, is the better man. The poem does not name him; the colophon of 65 and the line புறப்புண் நாணி, shared with 65, identify him as Cheralathan.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem weighs excellence in war, the matter of vaakai, and gives the palm to the loser

title: அன்னச் சேவலே!
reading: In an evening when the moon with joined horns shines like the bright face of the victorious lord who guards the land and the poet is helpless with longing, he asks a swan, if it flies north after eating fish at the ford of Kumari and passes through the Chola country, to alight on the high mansion at Kozhi, enter the palace without waiting at the gate, and say within the hearing of the great king Killi that it serves at the feet of Pisir Aandhai; then the king will give it his own beloved jewels for its mate to wear.
nuance: The bird messenger and the helpless evening are akam devices, here turned to a poet's longing for a king. The only credential the swan is to carry is the poet's name, and the poet is sure it will open the palace without a wait at the gate; the poem shows the bond by what it expects the name to do.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises the king's regard for the poet, which is iyanmozhi praise

title: மறவரும் மறக்களிரும்!
tamil: உடும்பு உரித்து அன்ன என்பு எழு மருங்கின்
அம் பகட்டு எழிலிய செம் பொறி ஆகத்து
reading: The poet asks a bard, whose kin have ribs that stand out like a skinned monitor lizard's and who is weary of patrons who barely listen, why he lingers here, and tells him of the lord at Uranthai, gentle to women and binding men by strength, whose Kaveri nourishes the people like a mother's milk to a newborn, where warriors with no war to go to beat their shoulders and the drum sounds, and elephants wallow in mud of spilled toddy; if the bard goes, the lord will give so much that he forgets other men's doors.
nuance: Lines 11 and 12 are hard: the warriors seem to complain that, inner enmity having been settled, the king will not send them against foes, so they will die idle; the sense of புட்பகை is not certain. Either way the warriors' frustration is praise of a peaceful land. பிறன்கடை மறப்ப names the bard's real wish: an end to going from door to door.

thinai_evidence.note: a poet directs a hungry bard to a patron, the guide-poem form of praise

comparisons.tenor: the bard's family, their ribs showing from hunger

title: காலமும் வேண்டாம்!
tamil: பகைப் புலம் படர்தலும் உரியன் ; தகைத் தார்
நெடுங் கடை நிற்றலும் இலையே; கடும் பகல்
reading: To a bard with a lute in hand, hunger in his body for want of patrons and a patched rag at his waist, whose large family is wan like the body of a man with no resolve, the poet says: go to Killi Valavan of Uranthai of tall mansions, whose army made the battle camp a field of flesh; you will not even wait at his gate, and once you have seen him in his court where he gives away chariots, you will not fail to wear a golden lotus that no bee hums over.
nuance: The opening inventory (கையது, மெய்யது, அரையது: in the hand, in the body, at the waist) makes the bard's poverty a list of possessions, the last of them hunger. The lotus that no bee visits is a gold lotus, the bard's ornament from the king.

thinai_evidence.note: a poet directs a hungry bard to a patron, the guide-poem form of praise

title: குளிர்நீரும் குறையாத சோறும்
tamil: இனிய காண்க; இவண் தணிக எனக் கூறி;
reading: The poet tells a bard who keeps asking whether his drum will at last be heard with pleasure and his hunger eased that if he goes slowly with his dancer, past the village of Pannan the open-handed where bees hum over the white lily, to Killi Valavan, whose city's food never runs low however much is taken, like a cool pond in the month of Thai, and which knows only the cooking fire and never the fire that burns towns, he will arrive; his giving is no windfall like woodcutters stumbling on gold, so the bard need not doubt it.
nuance: அடுதீ அல்லது சுடுதீ அறியாது, only the fire that cooks and never the fire that burns, makes the king's land a land without war. The last comparison is a negated one: the gift is not like a lucky find, because a lucky find cannot be counted on; the poem praises the giver's reliability, not only his wealth. Pannan, another patron, is named in passing on the road.

thinai_evidence.note: a poet directs a bard to a patron, the guide-poem form of praise

comparisons.tenor: the kinai drum, its frame braced with fine rods
the city's store of food that never lessens
the king's giving, said to be unlike a windfall

title: இவளையும் பிரிவேன்!
reading: Boothappandiyan vows that if he does not strike the kings who, raging like lions, say they have joined to fight him, and see their backs as they flee with their chariots, he may be parted from his wife of wide painted eyes, may become a king who in his assembly put an incapable man in office out of fondness and wielded a weak sceptre against right, and may lose the joy of his friends, the lord of Maiyal, Maavan, Aanthai, Anthuvan Saathan, Aathan Azhisi, Iyakkan and the rest, and be born to guard others' harsh lands instead of the southern land of his line.
nuance: The curses form a ranked set of the three things a king holds dear: his wife, his justice and his friends, and then his birthright. The friends are named one by one; the poem keeps a roll of a Pandya court's companions. The lion comparison uses the comparative case ending (மடங்கலின், 'than / like a lion') rather than அன்ன or போல.

thinai_evidence.note: a king's vow that stakes everything he holds, which the colophons place under kaanchi

title: இனியோனின் வஞ்சினம்!
reading: Neduncheliyan vows that if he does not shatter and capture with their drums the angry kings who mocked him as a boy and, trusting their elephants, chariots, horses and warriors, spoke small words, then may his people, finding no cool shade under his umbrella, weep and blame him as a cruel king; may the poets led by Maangudi Maruthan cease to sing of his land; and may he know the poverty of having nothing to give suppliants while those he keeps suffer.
nuance: What the king stakes is telling: not death or defeat but his people's tears and blame, the silence of poets, and the inability to give. A king's worst fate is to be a cruel sceptre, unsung and ungiving. The mockery 'he is young' (இளையன் இவன்) recurs as the enemies' boast in 78.

thinai_evidence.note: a king's vow that stakes his justice, fame and giving, which the colophons place under kaanchi

comparisons.tenor: the protection of the king's rule

title: உயிரும் தருகுவன்!
