reading: Nalankilli says that if men come gently, touch his feet and ask, the kingdom he inherited with its drums is a small thing to give and he would give even his life; but the fool who ignored the strength of the strong and scorned him will hardly escape alive, like a blind man who has stumbled on a sleeping tiger; and if he does not crush them like a hard bamboo shoot caught under the foot of a cane-eating elephant, may his garland wither in the reluctant embrace of women who feel no love.
nuance: The vow sets giving and fighting as two answers to the same kingdom: asked humbly, the king gives it away, even with his life; taken by scorn, he defends it. The curse he accepts is the embrace of women who do not love him, a shame of pleasure rather than of war.

thinai_evidence.note: a king's vow, which the colophons place under kaanchi

comparisons.tenor: the fool who scorned the king

comparisons.vehicle: கழைதின் யானைக் கால் அகப் பட்ட வன்றிணி நீண்முளை
comparisons.tenor: the enemies the king will crush

title: வேந்தனின் உள்ளம்!
reading: The poet-king asks whether a warrior line that will not let even a child who dies, or a lump of flesh born dead, go without the sword's cut, saying it did not die a man's death, would ever bear a son like him, who, held in trouble like a chained dog, without strength, begs to quench the fire in his belly a little water given in charity by men who are no kin.
nuance: The poem leaves its subject implicit and puts it as a question: the speaker is the one who begs, and the question says such a lineage could not have borne him. The colophon here gives no circumstance; the chain and the begging for a drink are in the poem, but who holds him is not said. The sword-cut given to the dead child shows a code in which even death must be a warrior's.

thinai_evidence.note: a statement of the shame of a life kept by begging, a kaanchi matter of honour above life, though the colophon files it under pothuviyal

title: அரச பாரம்!
reading: When the elders have gone to death and the ancient heritage of rule comes by right, a petty man of blunt manhood who thinks 'we have gained greatness' and begs dues from his people will think it a great thing, but if a worthy man whose strong legs bear the brunt of battle gets it, the fortune of kings with drums and sky-high white umbrella is as light as the dry stick of the white kidai plant withered by summer beside a dried-up pond.
nuance: The petty heir's mark is that he 'begs' from his own people (குடிபுரவு இரக்கும்): taxing is named as asking. The worthy man's lightness about the throne is not renunciation; it comes from his strength in war, the நோன்தாள் that bears battle.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem defines the excellent king against the petty one, a vaakai matter of excelling in one's part, though the colophon files it under pothuviyal

comparisons.tenor: the royal fortune in the eyes of the worthy heir

title: அதுதான் புதுமை!
reading: Killing one another and being killed is nothing new; it is the way of this world; but never till today had we heard of this: seven kings with ornate anklets, not knowing the might and greatness of Cheliyan, who wears a honey-dripping garland of neem shoots twined with uzhinai and goes to the sound of the clear kinai drum, came together saying 'we will fight', and he alone fought and destroyed their strength on the field.
nuance: The opening concedes that killing is commonplace so that the novelty of one against seven stands out: the wonder the poem names is of the new (இன்றின் ஊங்கோ கேளலம்). The neem is the Pandya's emblem and the uzhinai the flower of siege.

thinai_evidence.note: the king's single victory over seven is the excellence in war that vaakai praises

title: யார்? அவன் வாழ்க!
reading: Who is this who stands gracing the front of his tall chariot, the warrior's anklet on legs that have only just shed a child's tinkling anklets, neem shoots and uzhinai on a brow just shorn of its tuft, a bow in a hand just stripped of small bangles? Long live his garland! He has put on the garland but not yet taken off the child's amulet; weaned from milk, he ate rice only today; he neither marvelled at nor looked down on the fresh warriors who came at him from every side, and when he seized them and killed them so they fell to the ground he neither rejoiced nor scorned them.
nuance: Each line pairs a child's thing just removed with a warrior's thing just put on, so the boy's age is told entirely through objects. The praise ends on his evenness of mind: no wonder at the enemy, no contempt, no gloating after the kill.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises a young king's excellence in battle

title: அவர் ஊர் சென்று அழித்தவன்!
reading: The new warriors who came scorning my lord, whose broad chest rises to battle like a tiger leaving its den for prey, saying 'we are great and many, the fighter is young and the plunder large', went back with dull eyes and turned their backs; not content to kill them here, he followed them to their fathers' town and, to the sound of the clear drum, killed them there, so that their jewelled women passed away in shame.
nuance: The enemies' boast (பொருநனும் இளையன், 'the fighter is young too') answers to the taunt in 72; here it is reported from the other side and punished. Pursuing them to their fathers' town makes the defeat a shame for their families, not only for themselves.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises the king's victory over those who scorned his youth

comparisons.tenor: the king's chest rising to battle

title: பகலோ சிறிது!
reading: Having bathed in the cool pond at the gate of the old town and put on bright neem leaves from the common tree, walking like an elephant before the clear kinai drum, Cheliyan of the fierce war has come; the new warriors facing him are many; will any of them be left, when the day is far too short?
nuance: The question at the end is a boast put as worry: the day is too short for him to kill so many, not too short for them to beat him. The ritual bath and the neem from the common tree (மன்ற வேம்பு) show the king's going to war as a public rite.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises the king's certain victory

comparisons.tenor: Cheliyan's gait as he goes to battle

title: காணாய் இதனை!
reading: At Amur of sweet strong toddy the wrestler crushed the might of a mighty wrestler, pressing one leg on his chest and with the other bracing against his rush; let Tittan, whether he looks kindly on him or not, see how the wrestler who enters the field conquers and kills, bending his foe at both ends like a hungry elephant trying to break a bamboo.
nuance: The poem wants a particular witness: Tittan, 'whether he grants or not' (நல்கினும் நல்கான் ஆயினும்), so the hero's standing with Tittan is in question and the fight is offered as proof. The poem does not say what Tittan is to the hero; the colophon names the hero as Perunarkilli.

thinai_evidence.note: single combat to the death is a thumbai matter

title: புறநானூறு 81-100
theme: Poems 81-100 open with praise of the Chola Porvaikko Perunarkilli, including Nakkannaiyar's three poems of a woman's one-sided love for him, and a mother's boast that her son will be found on the battlefield; the rest is Avvaiyar's run on Athiyaman Neduman Anji: warnings to his foes, the nelli fruit of long life, her poems as a child's prattle, his used and broken spears, his wounds, his threat of tribute and his unabated anger.
source_issues: 84 line 1: என்ஜ is a corrupt spelling of என்னை (my lord); read as என்னை.
89 line 2: வாள்நதல் is a misprint for வாள்நுதல் (bright forehead).
93 line 10: நீழ் கழல் is a misprint for நீள் கழல்.
98 line 2: பொர்க் is a misprint for போர்க்.
81 line 3: the semicolon in ஆர்; நார்ச் splits the phrase ஆர் நார் (aathi fibre) that runs into line 4's garland; read without the break.
83's poet is spelled நாய்கண் and 84 and 85's நாய்கன்; one spelling should be chosen.
86: the poet field holds a variant note and a stray heading (காவற் பெண்டு காதற்பெண்டு எனவும் பாடம். பாடப்பட்டோன்) and the patron is None; the poet is காவற் பெண்டு, the rest is not a colophon fact.
99: poet, patron, thinai and thurai are filled from Duraisamy Pillai's edition (show reports FILLED_FROM_DURAISAMY_PILLAI).
98: the colophon gives two thinais (வாகை; வஞ்சியும்) and two thurais (அரச வாகை; கொற்றவள்ளையுமாம்); copied as they stand, both recorded in puram_thurai.

The review's line table lists 83, 86 and 88 as lacking a site line and 95, 99 and 100 as having opening lines the site lacks; our 83, 86 and 88 now have six full lines each and read complete, and the opening lines of 95, 99 and 100 are integral to the syntax (subject, simile or catalogue), so all lines are marked. The review lists 100 among poems with stray glyphs; none remain in the current text.
Patron spelling varies between நெடுமானஞ்சி (87, 88) and நெடுமான் அஞ்சி (89 to 100); spacing only.

title: யார்கொல் அளியர்?
tamil: ஆர்ப்பு எழு கடலினும் பெரிது; அவன் களிறே
reading: The poet says Killi's battle cry is louder than the roaring sea and his elephants trumpet without pause like the thunder of the monsoon, and asks who could be more pitiable than those who fall into the hands of this open-handed warrior with his tightly strung aathi garland.
nuance: The poem never shows a fight: it measures the king entirely by sound (sea, thunder) and then turns, in a single question, to the victims, so praise is made out of the dread it implies.

thinai_evidence.note: it praises the king's overwhelming strength in war, the matter of arasa vaakai

title: ஊசி வேகமும் போர் வேகமும்!
reading: Killi's fight with the champion who came to take his town was over quicker than the needle in the hand of a leather-worker stitching a cot when the festival has begun, his wife is in labour and the rain has come down as the sun sets.
nuance: The simile stacks three pressures on one low-status craftsman (the festival trade, the birth, the failing light and rain), so the king's speed is measured by a working man's desperate haste, a rare reach of praise into ordinary life.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem celebrates the king's swift victory over an invader

comparisons.tenor: the speed of the king's battle

title: இருபாற்பட்ட ஊர்!
reading: A woman in love with Killi says she fears her mother if her bangles slip for this young bull of a man with ankleted feet and dark beard, and is ashamed before the assembly to embrace his conquering shoulders; she wishes that this bewildered town, split two ways and never on one side, may tremble with longing as she does.
nuance: Her own split (between fear of her mother and shame before others on one side, desire on the other) is set against a town split into two sides; 85 suggests the town is divided as the crowd at a contest, so her curse wishes her inner division onto the spectators. The exact sense of இருபாற் பட்ட is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: a one-sided longing held back by fear and shame, with no answering love

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the woman speaks of herself and wishes her longing on the town; no addressee is named

title: புற்கையும் பெருந்தோளும்!
reading: She says her lord has great shoulders though he eats coarse gruel, while she, kept outside his enclosure, has turned the colour of gold; when he goes out to fight, he is to the swaggering warriors of the noisy festive town like a ford the salt-carriers dread.
nuance: Two concessions run in parallel (he eats gruel yet is broad-shouldered; I am shut out yet golden), and பொன் here is the gold of பசலை, the pallor of longing, not wealth. Line 1's என்ஜ is a corrupt spelling of என்னை, my lord.

thinai_evidence.note: the woman stays outside and grows pale for a man who does not answer

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the hearer is not named

comparisons.tenor: the king in battle, to the warriors who meet him

title: யான் கண்டனன்!
reading: Because this is not her lord's own town or country, one side of the crowd says he is winning and the other says he is not; she finds both words good, for she ran with her anklets ringing, stood against the palmyra by her house, and saw for herself that he won.
nuance: The poem does not say what the contest is; ஆடு is read as victory. A stranger's contest splits the crowd, and the woman, who has no claim on him, settles the dispute only for herself by looking.

thinai_evidence.note: a woman with no tie to him watches his contest from her own house

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the hearer is not named

title: கல்லளை போல வயிறு!
poet: காவற் பெண்டு காதற்பெண்டு எனவும் பாடம். பாடப்பட்டோன்
tamil: யாண்டு உளனோ? என வினவுதி; என் மகன்
reading: Asked, as she holds the fine post of her small house, where her son is, a mother says she does not know where he is, but the womb that bore him is like a rock den a tiger has left: he will show himself on the battlefield.
nuance: The empty den carries the whole boast: the womb is a lair, the son a tiger, and his absence from home is the proof of his nature. The small house (சிற்றில்) sets her poverty against her pride.

thinai_evidence.note: a mother's pride in her son's valour, the household valour of the mullai thurais of vaakai

comparisons.tenor: the mother's womb, and the son who has gone from it

title: எம்முளும் உளன்!
reading: Enemies, beware of entering the battlefield: among us is a warrior like the wheel that a carpenter, who makes eight chariots a day, spent a month making.
nuance: The vehicle is about care, not size: a craftsman who turns out eight chariots a day gave a whole month to this one wheel, so the warrior is the most thoroughly made thing in the army.

thinai_evidence.note: a warning to the enemy before battle, the boast of an army

title: எவருஞ் சொல்லாதீர்!
reading: Whoever you are, mighty ones, do not boast that you will fight us with your rear and van until you have seen my lord, the great chief of the Mazhavar with the gleaming long spear, his broad chest bright with fine ornaments and his drum-like shoulders, a fighter who stands above the festival.

thinai_evidence.note: a warning to foes who boast of fighting

title: என்னையும் உளனே!
tamil: பொருநரும் உளரோ, நும் அகன்றலை நாட்டு? என,
reading: To a warlike king who keeps asking whether there are fighters in her broad land, the dancer answers that there are young warriors like snakes that do not fear the striking stick, and besides, her lord, who on hearing the wind strike the taut drum hanging in the common hall says 'that is war!'.
nuance: The lord's eagerness is shown by a mistake: he takes the wind on a drum for a call to battle. The dancer's answer turns the king's taunt into a threat.

thinai_evidence.note: a challenge before battle answered with a boast of the army

title: புலியும் மானினமும்!
reading: Can deer herds stand where a fierce tiger rages on the slope scented with kaandhal like broken bangles and wild jasmine? Can darkness stay when the sun grows angry? Is there a ford the proud bullock cannot cross as it drags a laden cart over sand and stone? So, lord of the Mazhavar with arms like a gate-bar, are there foes who can stand once you enter the field?
nuance: Three rhetorical questions from three orders (beast, sky, labour) all expect 'no', and only the fourth names the king, so the answer is already given before he appears.

thinai_evidence.note: the king's irresistibility in battle

comparisons.tenor: the king entering battle, and the foes as the deer
the king for whom no obstacle is impassable

title: எமக்கு ஈத்தனையே!
reading: Avvai blesses Anji, lord of the Athiyar, with his true sword, anklet and golden garland, that he may last like the blue-throated one whose head shines with the milk-white crescent, because he gave her the sweet fruit of the small-leaved nelli taken from a hard crag of an ancient mountain, without telling her what it would do, so that she might escape death.
nuance: The gift is in what he withheld: by keeping the fruit's virtue to himself (ஆதல் நின்னகத்து அடக்கி) he made sure she would eat it, and so gave up long life for a poet. The blessing matches the gift: life for life, and from the god who survived the poison.

thinai_evidence.note: a blessing on a patron for his gift, which is praise rather than battle

title: மழலையும் பெருமையும்!
reading: A child's prattle does not keep to the lute, does not suit the hour and carries no sense, yet it moves fathers to tenderness; Avvai says her own words are like that, since Neduman Anji, who crossed many guarded walls of his enemies, receives them with grace.
nuance: Modesty and praise are one move: by calling her poem prattle she makes the patron a father, so his favour is love, not judgement of merit.

thinai_evidence.note: the poet praises the patron's grace toward her poems

comparisons.tenor: the poet's words to her patron

title: பெருந்தகை புண்பட்டாய்!
tamil: நீழ் கழல் மறவர் செல்வுழிச் செல்க! என
reading: Avvai asks what is left of going to war with drums booming, since the kings who could not even meet the van and ran would have died of sickness and been laid by the four-Veda priests on darbha grass and cut with a sword, so as to go where heroes go; they escaped that rite because they fell on your field, great one, where you crushed the elephants and took a noble wound.
nuance: The poem records a rite: a body that died of disease was laid on darbha grass and cut with a sword so that it could go where those who died in battle go. A death without a wound needed a wound. The turn on உய்ந்தனர் (they escaped) is ironic: being killed by Anji saved them from that disgrace. The syntax of lines 2 to 11 is compressed and the reading is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: the king's victory and his noble wound

title: சிறுபிள்ளை பெருங்களிறு!
reading: To us you are gentle, great one, like the big bull elephant that lies in the ford while the village boys wash its white tusks; to your enemies you are harsh, like its musth that no one can come near.
nuance: One elephant gives both halves: the same animal is a children's plaything and a terror, so the king's two faces are one nature, not a mask.

thinai_evidence.note: the king's excellence, mild to his own and terrible to foes

comparisons.tenor: the king to his own people

title: புதியதும் உடைந்ததும்!
reading: These spears, decked with peacock feathers and garlands, their thick shafts trimmed and oiled, sit in a guarded mansion; those, their points and edges broken from stabbing enemies, lie in the smith's small shed: they are the sharp spears of our lord, head of the kin of the poor, who gives food when he has it and shares the meal when he has none.
nuance: The praise of the other armoury is the insult: spears kept beautiful have never been used. The broken spears and the shared hunger are one portrait: what Anji has is always in use, by his army or his dependants.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the patron's spears and his sharing

title: அவன் செல்லும் ஊர்!
tamil: ‘விழவு இன்று ஆயினும், படு பதம் பிழை யாது,
reading: Two enmities have risen against my young lord with the thumbai on his broad chest and his long, thick arms: one has seized the women who looked at him, whose flower-like eyes grow pale and shoulders thin; the other is the town he goes to, which resents his lodging, asking whether, though there is no festival, his mutton-fed retinue will miss no meal and his elephants will take the water of the ford.
nuance: The 'enmities' are a joke of praise: one is the love-sickness he causes, the other the dread of feeding his following, so beauty and power are both counted as trouble he brings. The hosts' complaint in lines 6 to 8 is compressed and its sense is not sure.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a young prince through the effects he has on women and towns

title: மூதூர்க்கு உரிமை!
tamil: களிறே, எழூஉத் தாங்கிய கதவம் மலைத்து, அவர்
அவன் தானும், நிலம் திரைக்கும் கடல் தானைப்
கழற் கனி வகுத்த துணைச் சில் ஓதிக்
reading: Anji's swords lost their shape plunged in flesh as he broke his foes' guarded walls, his spears are loose in their sockets from crushing the toddy-rich lands of fort-holders, his elephants have shed their thick bands battering gates, his horses' hooves are bloodied from trampling warriors' gold garlands, and he himself is like a shield pierced by arrows; so, if you want your old town of rich paddy, pay him tribute, for he will not give way, and if you will not believe it, it will be no wonder if your soft-natured women lose their husbands' shoulders.
nuance: Each weapon is praised by its damage, ending with the king as a pierced shield; the threat is made through the enemy's women, whose loss is the last item of the catalogue.

thinai_evidence.note: a warning to enemies built on the army's battle wear, demanding tribute

title: வளநாடு கெடுவதோ!
reading: Seeing your elephants with battle-blunted tusks, your foes bar their fort gates; seeing your horses with bloodied hooves, they block the gaps with forked thorns; seeing your sheathed spear, they tighten their grip on their shields; seeing your scarred warriors, they bind up their arrow wounds; you are like the band that stands outside by old custom to carry off the wounded, undeterred even by the smoke of white mustard: so must their wide land, its fields where the bending ears touch the ridges and its great waters, perish while they grieve?
nuance: Each sight of Anji's army is answered by a defensive act, and the fourth turns to the wounded; the simile then makes Anji the death that waits outside the sickroom, against which the mustard smoke of the healing rite does nothing. The poem ends in pity for the enemy's rich land, the matter of கொற்றவள்ளை. The identity of the band in lines 15 to 17 is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: the closing lament for the enemy country about to be ravaged by the invader

comparisons.tenor: the king, who carries off the wounded foes

tamil: சென்று, அமர் கடந்து, நின் ஆற்றல் தோற்றிய
reading: Like your forebears of the ancient line, who honoured the gods, fed the sacrificial fire, brought here the sugarcane that is hard to obtain and ruled the sea-girt land with the wheel of command, you, with your giving anklets, palmyra garland, flowered groves and freshly bloodied spear, won without fault an undivided inheritance, yet were not content, but fought the seven kings with booming drums; even then you were beyond the singers, and now only Paranar could sing your shoulder that crushed proud Kovalur and bore the fort-breaking wheel.
nuance: The poem names another poet: Avvai places her patron beyond ordinary singers and hands the Kovalur victory to Paranar, which shows poets marking a deed as fit for a particular voice. The sense of எழுபொறி நாட்டத்து எழாஅத் தாயம் (line 7) and of பரணன் பாடினன் மற்கொல் (line 12) is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king's lineage and his victories

title: சினமும் சேயும்!
reading: Spear in hand, anklets on his feet, sweat on his body and a fresh wound on his throat, wearing in his curly hair the white leaf from the top of a young palmyra with vetchi and vengai flowers, he is like a mighty elephant that has fought a striped tiger; his rage has not yet cooled, those who fought him here did not escape, and the eyes that glared at his enemies stay red even as he looks at his own small son.
nuance: The last image tests the anger against the tenderest sight and the anger holds: the poem praises the hero and lets the cost show in the same line.

thinai_evidence.note: the victorious king fresh from battle

title: புறநானூறு 101-120
theme: Poems 101-120 move from Avvai's praise of Athiyaman and his son, the bard's trust in a patron and the warning not to slight a young king, to Kapilar on Pari: his giving, the siege of Parambu by the three crowned kings, and the laments of Pari's daughters and his poet after his death.
source_issues: 101, 113 and 117: the review's line table says sangamtamil.com lacks our opening line. In each our line 1 is needed for the sense (101: the first of the counted visits; 113: the toddy and the rams that the next line continues; 117: the first of the three omens), so the site has dropped or merged a line; all lines are marked.

116: the review's line table says we lack the site's line 10, after our line 9; the poem's middle (lines 9 to 14) does not read smoothly, consistent with a lost line. Marked as it stands and flagged uncertain.
116 line 9 (நோகோ யானே; தேய்கமா காலை!) is flagged as repeated in 234 line 1; it reads as a formula of grief shared by two laments, not a copying error.
110 line 2: கொள்ற்கு looks like a misprint for கொளற்கு (to take).

109: the colophon thurai மகண் மறுத்தல் is the sandhi spelling of மகள் மறுத்தல், as in 110 and 111; normalised in puram_thurai name. None of 109 to 111 mentions a daughter; the thurai comes from the tradition of the siege.
112: the colophon thurai is written கையறு நிலை, while 113 to 120 have கையறுநிலை; the same thurai.
117 line 8: முள் லெயிறு is முள்ளெயிறு (sharp tooth) split at an odd point.
102: the poem names no one; the patron Pokuttezhini is known only from the colophon.
113 to 120: the colophon patron is None, though every poem is about Pari; the poems name him (116, 118) or call him the girls' father (117, 120).

title: பலநாளும் தலைநாளும்!
reading: Avvai tells her own heart that Athiyaman greets a bard on the hundredth visit, even with a crowd, as eagerly as on the first, so whether the gift comes late or soon it is as sure as the food-ball an elephant holds between its tusks, and the heart need not fret.
nuance: The colophon files it as a demand for the gift (பரிசில் கடா நிலை), but the poem turns the demand inward: the one being urged to wait is the poet's own hungry heart. The food-ball is in the elephant's own keeping and already between its tusks, so the image says the gift is decided and only the moment is open. Line 9 (அருந்தே மாந்த) can be divided more than one way; the sense of a heart greedy for its meal is the likeliest.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem is a bard reassuring herself about a patron's gift

comparisons.tenor: the gift the patron has already resolved to give

title: சேம அச்சு!
reading: The prince is compared to the spare axle that salt-carters tie under a heavily loaded cart drawn by young, unbroken bulls, for the climbs and drops of the road, and to the full moon, so that no darkness can come to those who live in his shade.
nuance: The first image is of a prince who is not yet needed: a spare axle does nothing until the young bulls stumble and the main axle breaks, so the praise is that of a son held in reserve during his father's reign. The poem names no one; the patron, Athiyaman's son Pokuttezhini, comes from the colophon.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises the prince as the people's reliable reserve

comparisons.tenor: the prince on whom his people fall back
the prince, who drives off darkness for his dependants

title: புரத்தல் வல்லன்!
reading: Avvai tells a viraliyar sitting at the start of the wasteland road, with a one-headed drum at one end of her pole and a small hollow drum at the other, asking who will turn up her upturned bowl, that Anji is not far: he is in enemy country among his young elephants and the smoke of burning villages, and even in a dry season he can keep her bowl full of soft fat-rich food.
nuance: The patron is found not at home but at the front, so the bard is sent toward war smoke; the poem makes his generosity and his raids one fact, since the fat that fills her bowl comes from the enemy's land.

thinai_evidence.note: a performer is directed to a patron, the guide-poem situation

comparisons.tenor: the dark smoke of the burning war-front around his elephants

title: யானையும் முதலையும்!
reading: Avvai warns the enemy warriors: if you look down on my lord as a youth, not weighing his many subtle deeds, you will not win, for he is like the crocodile that drags down and kills an elephant in a foot-deep pool where village boys play.
nuance: The water is made as small as possible (foot-deep, a children's pool), so the crocodile's strength owes nothing to its ground: the image answers both the scorn of youth and the scorn of a small domain.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem asserts the king's martial worth against those who would scorn it

title: தேனாறும் கானாறும்!
reading: Kapilar tells a bright-browed viraliyar that she will win fine jewels if she goes singing to Pari, whose gentleness is sweeter than the water that, rain or no rain, comes down every peak of his ladder-hung hill, carrying the cool petals of bee-haunted lilies over the wide horse-gram fields.
nuance: The water flows whether it rains or not, which already says what the poem will say of the giver; the comparison is of degree (sweeter than), so Pari's manner outdoes the one thing in his land that never fails. Line 5 (உழைகால் ஆட) is hard to construe; the run of the water over the fields is the likely sense.

thinai_evidence.note: a performer is sent to the patron

title: தெய்வமும் பாரியும்!
reading: As the gods do not refuse even the erukkam, with its clustered blossoms and poor leaves, neither good nor bad, when people offer it, so Pari's open hand holds itself bound to give even when the foolish and the weak come to him.
nuance: The comparison reverses the usual direction: the giver is set in the place of the god who receives offerings, and the asker in the place of the poor flower, so to be given to by Pari is to be accepted by him. கடவன் makes the gift a debt he owes, not a favour.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem names the patron's giving as his defining nature

comparisons.tenor: the unworthy askers whom Pari still receives

title: மாரியும் பாரியும்!
reading: The fine-tongued poets praise one man, calling out 'Pari, Pari'; but Pari is not the only one: there is also the rain, which sustains this world.
nuance: It looks like a rebuke of the poets for flattering one man, and the rebuke is the praise: the only rival that can be found for him is the rain. The 'one' (ஒருவர், ஒருவனும்) is repeated so that the denial of uniqueness ends by granting it.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the patron in the form of mock blame

comparisons.tenor: Pari, whose giving keeps the world as rain does

title: பறம்பும் பாரியும்!
reading: Such is the Parambu the poets sing of: the dry-end firebrand a hill woman set burning is sandalwood, so its fragrant smoke drifts across to the flowering branches of the vengai on the slope; and Pari, having taken up virtue, would not say 'I will not come' if suppliants asked for him, but would be theirs.
nuance: In this land sandalwood is common firewood and its scent goes to the neighbouring tree unasked; the poem sets that scene beside the giver without saying they are alike, and leaves the reader to make the match. The last line goes past giving goods: asked for himself, he would go.

thinai_evidence.note: the patron's readiness to give even himself

title: மூவேந்தர் முன் கபிலர்!
tamil: நான்கே, அணிநிற ஒரி பாய்தலின், மீது அழிந்து,
வான் கண் அற்று, அதன் மலையே; வானத்து
மீன் கண் அற்று, அதன் சுனையே; ஆங்கு,
விரையொலி கூந்தல் நும் விறலியர் பின் வர,
reading: Kapilar tells the three crowned kings besieging Parambu that it is to be pitied: drums and all, they cannot starve it, for it has four yields no ploughman sows (bamboo rice, jackfruit, valli tubers and honey), its hill is like the sky and its springs like the stars; tie elephants to every tree, spread chariots over every field, they will not take it by effort and he will not yield it to the sword; but if they tune small lutes and come singing and dancing with their viralis, he will give land and hill together.
nuance: The poem ends a siege argument with a guide-poem: the one road into the fort is the bard's road, so the kings are mocked by being offered the only means they cannot use without ceasing to be kings. The colophon's thurai speaks of refusing a daughter, which the poem itself never mentions.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem is spoken from the besieged hill-fort against its besiegers

comparisons.tenor: the hill of Parambu, too vast to compass

title: யாமும் பாரியும் உளமே!
reading: Even if you three kings join your conquering armies in anger, Parambu is hard to take; its cool good country has three hundred villages and the suppliants have already received all three hundred; there remain only Pari and I, and the hill: come singing and they are yours.
nuance: The arithmetic is the point: nothing is left to conquer because everything has already been given, so the kings are told they arrive after the bards. Kapilar counts himself with Pari among what remains (யாமும் பாரியும்).

thinai_evidence.note: the besieged side answers the besiegers

title: விறலிக்கு எளிது!
reading: The great dark hill is to be pitied: to win it with the spear is hard even for kings, but it is easy for a kinai-drummer's daughter whose kohl-lined eyes are like a pair of blue lilies, if she comes singing.
nuance: அளிதோ (pitiable) is said of the hill, which can be had so cheaply by the humblest singer and is so costly to kings; the pity and the boast are the same word.

thinai_evidence.note: the defended hill set against the besiegers' spears

title: உடையேம் இலமே!
tamil: எந்தையும் உடையேம்; எம் குன்றும் பிறர் கொளார்;
reading: Pari's daughters say: that month, in that white moonlight, we had our father and no one had taken our hill; this month, in this white moonlight, kings with victorious drums have taken our hill, and we have no father.
nuance: The two halves use the same words in the same order, so the only change is the loss itself; திங்கள் is both the month and the moon, and the unchanging moonlight measures what has changed. The father is named first in the first half and last in the second.

thinai_evidence.note: a lament for a dead father and a lost home

title: பறம்பு கண்டு புலம்பல்!
tamil: மட்டு வாய் திறப்பவும், மை விடை வீழ்ப்பவும்,
அட்டு ஆன்று ஆனாக் கொழுந் துவை ஊன் சோறும்
நீர் வார் கண்ணேம் தொழுது நிற் பழிச்சிச்
கோல் திரள் முன்கைக் குறுந் தொடி மகளிர்
reading: Kapilar says to Parambu: once you were our friend, opening toddy jars, felling dark rams and giving rice with rich meat relish as much as anyone wished; now Pari is dead, and bewildered and helpless, with streaming eyes, we worship and praise you and go, seeking husbands for the girls with small bangles and fragrant dark hair.
nuance: The hill, not the dead man, is addressed and called a friend (நட்டனை), so the farewell is to the place that fed the bards; the last two lines give the reason for leaving, the duty to the daughters.

thinai_evidence.note: a lament at leaving the dead patron's hill

title: உயர்ந்தோன் மலை!
tamil: ஈண்டு நின் றோர்க்கும் தோன்றும்; சிறு வரை
reading: It can be seen from here and from the small hill beyond, surely: the hill of the tall one, where the courtyard runs wet with the dregs of pressed toddy, strewn like the food-balls an elephant chews and drops, and where chariots were given away from where he sat.
nuance: The hill is still visible from near and far, and that is the grief: the place stands while the giving is over. Only the colophon makes this a lament; the lines themselves are a picture of a feasting court.

thinai_evidence.note: a lament that looks back at the dead patron's hill

comparisons.tenor: the strewn dregs of pressed toddy

title: அந்தோ பெரும நீயே!
tamil: ஒரு சார் அருவி ஆர்ப்ப, ஒரு சார்
reading: On one side the waterfall roared, and on the other the clear honey-toddy, poured to fill the bards' bowls and spilled, ran washing over the stones: so it was once on the hill of the gentle one who was harsh to kings with many spears and great elephants.
nuance: மன்னே marks the whole scene as past; the toddy for bards is set as a second waterfall. The closing phrase, harsh to kings and sweet (இன்னான் ஆகிய இனியோன்), joins the two faces Pari showed to two kinds of visitor.

thinai_evidence.note: a lament for what the hill was

comparisons.tenor: the toddy poured for bards running over the stones

title: குதிரையும் உப்புவண்டியும்!
tamil: தீநீர்ப் பெருங் குண்டு சுனைப் பூத்த குவளைக்
ஏந்தெழில் மழைக் கண், இன் நகை, மகளிர்
புன் மூசு கவலைய முள் முடை வேலிப்,
பயில் பூஞ் சோலை மயில் எழுந்து ஆலவும்,
பயில் இருஞ் சிலம்பிற் கலை பாய்ந்து உகளவும்,
reading: Kapilar grieves that the girls with lily garlands and rain-dark eyes now climb a heap of eecham leaves by a little hut with a thorn fence to count the salt-carters' carts, when once, from the high hill of their father Pari of strong toddy and sharp spear, a hill of unfailing plenty where peacocks danced, stags leapt and trees bore fruit out of season, they counted the golden-saddled horses of kings who came to war not knowing his strength.
nuance: The poem is built on one act, counting, done in two places: then the girls counted enemy horses from a fort that could not be taken, now they count passing salt carts from a hut. Line 14 (வியன்மலை அற்றே) may be 'like the broad hill' or 'the broad hill is gone'; our text also lacks a line the other edition has after line 9, so the middle of the poem is not secure.

thinai_evidence.note: a lament over the dead patron's daughters

title: தந்தை நாடு!
reading: Even when Saturn smokes, comets appear and Venus runs to the south, the land of the father of the girls with fine bangles was a dry upland where rain never failed: fields filled, bush flowers bloomed, wild cows that had calved by the houses grazed in long herds on good grass, the worthy multiplied under a straight sceptre, and mullai budded like a kitten-civet's sharp teeth.
nuance: The three opening signs are omens of drought, and the poem says they had no power over this land because of its ruler's justice, so a lord of a hill is given the crowned king's rain-making sceptre. The lament is only in the past tense and in the phrase 'the father of the girls'.

thinai_evidence.note: a lament that praises the dead patron's land

comparisons.tenor: the pointed buds of the mullai

title: சிறுகுளம் உடைந்துபோம்!
tamil: எண் நாள் திங்கள் அனைய கொடுங் கரைத்
reading: The land of cool Parambu, of Pari who gave chariots and whose strong shoulders wielded sharp spears, is now seeing its little clear-water tank, with a curved bank like the eighth-day moon and a head where rocks and ridges meet, breaking.
nuance: With no one to keep it, the tank, the land's store of water, gives way; the poem lets the breach of one small tank stand for the end of the whole country. கீள்வது (is breaking, is splitting) is the one word that carries the lament, and its exact sense is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: a lament over the ruin of the dead patron's land

comparisons.tenor: the curved bank of the tank

title: வேந்தரிற் சிறந்த பாரி!
tamil: கார்ப் பெயல் தலைஇய காண்பு இன் காலைக்
reading: In the pleasant season after the rains, when therul blossoms open like the spots on an elephant's face and the red anthill holes turn sour with winged termites, the land rich in soft millet: will it last? It is the land of the generous one who, like a lone tree on a long shadeless road, gave to suppliants beyond what drum-rich kings would give.
nuance: நந்துங் கொல்லோ can be heard as 'will it still flourish?' or 'will it perish?', and the doubt is the lament. The lone tree is valued because nothing else on the road gives shade, so the simile measures Pari against the kings as the tree against the bare road.

thinai_evidence.note: a lament asking whether the dead giver's land can endure

comparisons.tenor: the giver, the only shelter suppliants had

title: கம்பலை கண்ட நாடு!
tamil: கார்ப் பெயர் கலித்த பெரும் பாட்டு ஈரத்துப்,
களை கால் கழாலின், தோடு ஒலிபு நந்தி,
மென் மயிற் புனிற்றுப் பெடை கடுப்ப நீடிக்,
ஆடு கழை நரலும் சேட் சிமைப், புலவர்
reading: On the red upland where the vengai grew, after the rains men ploughed again and again, sowed, harrowed and weeded until the millet rose tall like a peahen fresh from laying and bore grain top to bottom; then came the harvest of new varagu and millet, the bean pods ripe, buried toddy offered at every grass hut, and rice cooked with ghee and gram: will this effortless plenty last, the land of the father of the long-haired maidens, the war-hot lord of the high bamboo peaks whose quality poets never tire of singing?
nuance: The long account of farm labour ends in the word வருந்தா (without toil), so the plenty is called effortless just after the poem has shown the work; the lament turns on whether the work will still bear fruit without the lord. Several farm words (பல்லி, கவ்வை, பெருந் தோள் தாலம்) are rare and their sense is uncertain.

thinai_evidence.note: a lament asking whether the dead patron's land can endure

title: புறநானூறு 121-140
theme: Poems 121 to 140 are praise of three chiefs as givers: Malaiyaman Kari of Mullur (121 to 126), Ay Andiran of Pothiyil (127 to 136, 138) and the lord of Nanjil (137, 139, 140). They test what good giving is: judging rank, giving sober, giving without hope of a next-world return, and giving beyond what was asked.
source_issues: 127: the colophon patron reads வேள் ஆய் அரண்டின், a misprint for ஆய் அண்டிரன் (the poem names ஆஅய், and 128 to 136 give அண்டிரன்).

139 and 140: the colophon patron is ஆய் அண்டிரன், but both poems address the lord of Nanjil (நாஞ்சில் பொருந, 139 line 8; நாஞ்சில் பொருநன், 140 line 1), the patron of 137 (நாஞ்சில் வள்ளுவன்); the patron field looks carried over from the Ay poems before them.
123 line 5: பயன்கிழு looks like a misprint for பயங்கெழு (fruitful), the epithet spelt so in 135 lines 7 and 18.
126 line 13: நிறகப் is a misprint for நிற்கப் (பரந்து இசை நிற்கப் பாடினன், he sang so that the fame spread and stood).
137 line 4: அரியு மோனே reads best as அறியுமோனே (the one I know); ர for ற.
138 line 3: மீளினம் is very likely மீனினம் (shoals of fish), matching ஆனினம் and மானினம் in lines 1 and 2; marked as fish.
134 line 2: ஆ அய் is ஆஅய் split by a stray space.
127: the colophon thurai கடைஇநிலை is the lengthened spelling of கடைநிலை; puram_thurai name normalised.

122, 124, 126: the review's line table says sangamtamil.com lacks our opening line(s) (122 line 1; 124 lines 1-2; 126 line 1, and has two lines we lack). 122 line 1 and 124 lines 1-2 carry sense the following lines complete, so all our lines are marked; 126's opening was not compared against the site, as the brief forbids using it, and is marked as it stands.
137 line 1 is flagged as repeated in 270 line 2; it is a formula for the crowned kings' drums and elephants, not a copying error.

title: புலவரும் பொதுநோக்கமும்!
reading: Bards come from all four directions with one man in mind, so giving much is easy but knowing each one's due rank is hard; if the great giver understands this, he should stop looking at all poets with one undiscriminating eye.
nuance: Kapilar praises Kari by correcting him: the fault named is not meanness but indiscriminate giving, so generosity is assumed and judgment is what is asked. The poet's own interest is plain, since a poet of standing is the one who loses when all are treated alike.

thinai_evidence.note: counsel addressed to a named patron about how he gives, which is admonition (செவியறிவுறூஉ) under praise rather than a general truth

title: பெருமிதம் ஏனோ!
reading: Kari's land cannot be taken by the sea and enemies dare not attack it, yet it belongs to the fire-tending brahmins; the tribute the three crowned kings send him to win his help belongs to the bards who praise his clan; nothing is his own but the shoulders of his wife, chaste as the northern star, and still he holds himself proud.
nuance: The poem lists Kari's possessions only to give each away, so the praise is an inventory of dispossession. The one thing kept is his wife, set apart by her chastity; the closing word பெருமிதம் makes pride rest on what he has given, not what he holds.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a patron whose land and revenue are said to belong to brahmins and bards

title: மயக்கமும் இயற்கையும்!
reading: Anyone who drinks the morning's toddy and grows merry finds it easy to give away chariots, but the jewelled chariots that Malayan of unfading fame gave while sober outnumber the raindrops that fall on the heights of fertile Mullur.
nuance: The measure of the gift is not its size but the giver's state: a drunk man's chariot costs him nothing in judgment, a sober man's is chosen. The rain on Mullur, his own hill, makes the gifts as natural to the land as its weather.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a patron's sober giving

title: வறிது திரும்பார்!
reading: Those who sing Malayan of the mountain of loud waterfalls never go home empty-handed, even if they set out on an unlucky day, are held back by bad omens of birds, arrive at the wrong hour and speak without skill.
nuance: Every rule a suppliant was meant to keep (the right day, good omens, timing, skilful speech) is listed only to be cancelled by the patron's nature, so the poem praises him by making the bard's craft unnecessary.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a patron from whom no singer returns empty

title: புகழால் ஒருவன்!
tamil: பரூஉக் கண் மண்டை யொடு, ஊழ்மாறு பெயர
reading: The bard will feast on fat roast meat and drink by turns in Malayan's hall, where the toddy he relishes like nectar is a reward earned as the ploughing ox earns its straw; in the battle between two kings, the victor says Malayan made him win and the loser says that without Malayan victory would have been easy, so the strong hero of the high hill is the one man both sides name.
nuance: The praise is built from the testimony of both enemies: Malayan fought as an ally, and his worth is proven by the loser's complaint as much as by the winner's thanks. The ox simile turns the patron's drinking into wages for war-work, not indulgence.

thinai_evidence.note: the excellence of a warrior chief proven in battle on another king's side

comparisons.tenor: the white fat pieces of roast meat
Malayan drinking his toddy after the labour of war
Malayan, the hero of the high hill

title: கபிலனும் யாமும்!
tamil: இரந்து சென் மாக்கட்கு இனி இடன் இன்றிப்,
இன்மை துரப்ப, அசை தர வந்து, நின்
reading: Descendant of the hero who crowned bards with gold lotuses taken from enemy elephants' brow-plates, we are not skilled singers, yet poverty drove us to you: since Kapilar, the flawless brahmin, sang your fame so fully that no room is left for those who come asking, we are like other boats that cannot sail the sea lane the Chera's gold-laden ships have cut; lord of the land of palmyra groves who holds back hostile kings in battle.
nuance: A later poet admits he follows a master: Kapilar's praise has filled the space, and the ship simile makes poetic praise a trade route already taken. The modesty is itself a bid, since the bard binds himself to Kari's generosity rather than to his own skill.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard asking a patron for a gift

comparisons.vehicle: பொலந்தரு நாவாய் ஓட்டிய அவ் வழிப் பிறகலம் செல்கலாது
comparisons.tenor: the later bards after Kapilar's praise
the roar of the war drum

title: உரைசால் புகழ்!
tamil: பிறர்க்கு ஈவு இன்றித் தம் வயிறு அருத்தி,
reading: They say Ay's palace stands bare, since bards have led away its elephants and the forest peacocks flock to the empty tethering posts, with only its women left wearing the jewel that cannot be given; yet it is not like the cities of drum-owning kings who fill their own bellies with savoury food, give none away and lose their fame.
nuance: Poverty here is the proof of wealth: the emptied hall is set against the full but famous-less cities. The one thing not given, the women's jewel, is the marriage token, so the line marks the limit of a king's giving without saying so.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a patron whose giving has emptied his palace

comparisons.tenor: the black horn of the small lute

title: முழவு அடித்த மந்தி!
tamil: கழல் தொடி ஆஅய் மழை தவழ் பொதியில்;
reading: On Ay's cloud-wrapped Pothiyil, a female monkey on a branch of the jackfruit tree in the common ground beats the taut face of a drum the bards hung there, taking it for fruit, and the swan rises in answer and dances; only a dancing woman may approach that hill, and proud kings can hardly come near it.
nuance: The hill is open and closed at once: performers' drums hang in its common ground and a dancer may walk in, but kings cannot. The comic scene of the monkey and the swan shows a place so full of the bards' music that even the animals play it.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a patron's hill, open to performers and closed to kings

title: வேங்கை முன்றில்!
reading: Ay Andiran, war-winning lord of the great mountain of sweet jackfruit, where hill folk in low-eaved huts grow merry on toddy matured in bamboo and dance the kuravai in courtyards under the vengai: the elephants he gave to suppliants would match the stars only if the sky bloomed with stars everywhere, leaving no dark patch.
nuance: The hyperbole is hedged with a condition: the stars as they are fall short, so the sky must be imagined full. The kurinji scene of drinking and dancing is the patron's land, set out before his name.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a patron by the count of his gifts

title: சூல் பத்து ஈனுமோ?
reading: Ay of the bright jewelled ornament, does a young she-elephant in your land bear ten calves at a time? The noble elephants you gave gladly, without a grudging face, to those who come singing you and your mountain outnumber the spears the Kongar threw down when you drove them to the western sea.
nuance: The question is a joke that works as praise: so many elephants have been given that the herd must breed beyond nature. The comparison joins his giving to his war, counting gifts against an enemy's discarded spears.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a patron by the count of his gifts

title: காடும் பாடினதோ?
tamil: களிறு மிக உடைய இக் கவின் பெறு காடே?
reading: Did this lovely forest, so full of elephants, also sing the hill of Andiran, lord of the great cloud-resting mountain, who wears the vazhai flower and whose sword never fails?
nuance: The wit assumes the reader knows that singing Ay's hill earns elephants; the forest's wild herds are read as a bard's payment.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a patron through his reputation for giving elephants

title: போழ்க என் நாவே!
tamil: ஆழ்க, என் உள்ளம்! போழ்க என் நாவே!
பாழ் ஊர்க் கிணற்றின் தூர்க, என் செவியே!
reading: I thought of Ay only after others had thought of him first: may my heart sink, my tongue split and my ears silt up like a well in a deserted town; the Himalaya stands in the north, where the yak that grazed on fragrant naranthai grass drinks at the kuvalai pool and rests with its mate in the cool shade of the tagaram, and if Ay's clan did not stand in the south, this wide world would tip over.
nuance: The self-curse is the poet's apology for coming late to praise. The world-balance image sets a patron's family against the Himalaya as its counterweight, and the yak's ease in the north is drawn so fully that the south's single name has to outweigh a whole scene.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a patron's clan as the world's southern weight

comparisons.tenor: the poet's ears, deaf to praise

title: காணச் செல்க நீ!
tamil: காண்டல் சால வேண்டினை யாயின்- மாண்ட நின்
reading: Gentle dancer, you have only heard of his fame and never seen him; if you want to see him, go, your fragrant hair tossed by the mountain wind, moving lovely as a plumed peacock, to see Ay of the chariots, whose giving is like the rain.
nuance: The whole guide is a contrast of hearing and seeing: fame reaches the ear, but the gift is had only by going.

thinai_evidence.note: a performer directing another performer to a patron

title: இம்மையும் மறுமையும்!
reading: Ay is not a trader who buys virtue, saying that what is done in this life will pay in the next; his generous hand simply took the road that the worthy before him had travelled.
nuance: The poem names and rejects a motive for giving that was evidently current: giving as an investment in the next birth. What it puts in its place is not inner kindness but custom, the path the worthy have walked.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a patron's motive in giving

comparisons.tenor: one who gives for reward in the next life

title: காணவே வந்தேன்!
reading: I climbed the narrow, painful path of the high tiger-haunted mountain, my bangled dancer following wearily, my small lute with strings like drawn gold held to my side, and came thinking only of your fame, lord of the mountain land where the elephant flees with her calf when she sees bards in the common ground: I want no elephants, horses or chariots; let bards and singers take those as their own, and may your days go on with the wealth you never call yours; I came only to see you.
nuance: The elephant that runs from bards is a joke about how freely Ay gives them away. By refusing the usual gifts the poet asks for the patron's presence, a bid that flatters by claiming a higher kind of want.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard addressing a patron about the gift he seeks

title: வாழ்த்தி உண்போம்!
reading: Shall I call one enemy the lice and nits that cling in the seams of my many-patched rag, ribbed like the back of a lute? Another the hunger that wears down my many kin, flesh wasted and eyes brimming? Another the petty monkey-like robbers of the wooded slopes who swarm on me crying 'give what you have' without knowing my state? Trusting that Ay knows every enemy, praising your name, I crossed the sun-burnt wasteland: those who give to us give to others, and those who give to others give to themselves; I have said all this, so judge what suits you, give and send me off, and daily at Thuraiyur's ford we will eat your gift, praising you more times than its fine sands.
nuance: The catalogue of three enemies turns the bard's poverty into a war the patron is asked to win. The maxim in lines 20 and 21 is an argument, not a plea: a gift to the bard circulates, and in the end returns to the giver as fame.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard pressing a patron for the gift

comparisons.tenor: the number of the bard's praises

title: நின்பெற்றோரும் வாழ்க!
reading: I will no longer long for the three kings of the sea-bounded land with their roaring drums and herds of elephants; you are the one I know: in your land seed sown in the crowded pond does not die in drought but thrives like cane, flowers like eyes bloom even when summer dries the rain-water, and water like sapphire flows to the sea carrying the gold-like petals of the dark-stemmed vengai; lord of Nanjil of the red hills, ruler of the land of great rocks and small white falls, long may you live, and long live the father and mother who bore you.
nuance: The poet's renunciation of the three crowned kings is the measure of the small chief: a land that never fails in drought is a patron who never fails a bard. The blessing on the parents is a closing formula of praise.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a chief and his fertile land

comparisons.tenor: the seed that thrives in drought

title: நின்னை அறிந்தவர் யாரோ?
reading: Bard in rags, with your small lute of strong-voiced strings, who crossed many paths full of cattle, left behind hills full of deer and swam many fords full of fish to come here: do not worry; your lord will never say 'come back later', for the husband of the lady with thick dark hair is like the great ear of grain in the wide field the parrots frequent, so who would know beforehand that you were coming?
nuance: The image of the grain-ear the parrots feed on makes the patron a crop open to any bird that comes, so no appointment is needed. The poem names no patron; the colophon gives Ay.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard directing another bard to a patron

comparisons.vehicle: கிளி மரீஇய வியன் புனத்து மரன் அணி பெருங்குரல்
comparisons.tenor: the patron, open to all who come

title: சாதல் அஞ்சாய் நீயே!
reading: Young men with loads pressing their shoulders and dancers with slim waists whose feet ache from the long climb are with me, and to live I speak the truth, not lies: lord of Nanjil of the high peaks, the plough-hill no one ploughs, descendant of men who never turned back, this is no time to wait for the ripe moment; the king has not stopped giving, and you do not fear death for your king, so if one day a hard battle comes like the earth heaving up, my suffering troupe may come to grief.
nuance: The bard's argument for speed is the patron's courage: a man who will die for his king may not be there tomorrow. The pun of the unploughed plough (உழாஅ நாஞ்சில்) praises the hill and its lord in one phrase.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard urging a patron to give now

title: தேற்றா ஈகை!
reading: The lord of Nanjil with its wide-spreading jackfruit trees is surely a simpleton, red-tongued poets: when we asked for a little rice to go with the greens our bangled dancers had picked in the garden, he, knowing other kinds of due measure, weighed his own standing too and gave us a great elephant like a hill ringed by forest; is there any giving as unknowing as this? Do the great not keep watch over their own duty?
nuance: Praise disguised as blame: the patron is called foolish because he measured the gift by his own greatness rather than by the request. The closing question can be read as mock reproach (the great do not count the cost of their duty) or as a real one.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a patron through a gift far beyond the request

title: புறநானூறு 141-160
theme: Gift poems to the hill chieftains Pekan, Nalli, Ori, the lord of Konkanam, Erai and Kumanan: the guide poems, the cycle pleading with Pekan to return to his wife, the roll of seven dead givers, and the bard's starving household pressed on Kumanan.
source_issues: 141: the colophon thurai reads பாணாற்று படை, without the doubled ப் of பாணாற்றுப்படை (as in 155); name normalised in puram_thurai.

142: the review's line table says sangamtamil.com lacks our line 1; our line 1 (அறுகுளத்து உகுத்தும், அகல்வயல் பொழிந்தும்) is the first of the three places the rain falls and the simile needs it, so it is marked as part of the poem.

143 to 147: these are puram poems on akam matter (a patron's neglected wife), marked akam_puram mixed with thinai perunthinai, as their colophons have it; the bard who pleads is coded as paanan speaking to the thalaivan.
147: line 5 is flagged as repeated in 349 line 5 (a formula for a woman's eyes); line 6 has an edition variant noted in the flags, our reading kept.
148 line 3: கனிற்றொடு looks like a misprint for களிற்றொடு (with elephants); marked as elephant.
149: the colophon thurai is பரிசில், but the poem asks for nothing and states the effect of Nalli's giving, which fits இயன்மொழி (the review notes the site's Iyan Mozhi); colophon kept as is.
152 line 20: ழுறையுளிக் is a misprint for முறையுளிக் (in due order).
152 and 153: the colophon poet is spelt வண்பரணர், and 148 to 150 have வன்பரணர் / வன் பரணர்; likely one poet, spelt two ways.
154 line 13: கொண்டுபெருங்கானம் is very likely a misprint for கொண்பெருங்கானம், the name in 156 line 2.

155 line 7: கொண்பெருங்காலத்துக் is very likely a misprint for கொண்பெருங்கானத்துக் (the patron's land, as in 156); so no place entity is recorded for 155. Line 2 closes its quotation with ” after opening with ‘.
159 line 5: முதுர்வினள் looks like a misprint for முதிர்வினள் (aged).

160: the flags give four misprint candidates (line 6 குனிப்ப/குளிப்ப, line 10 கோடின்றாக/கேடின்றாக, line 14 நல்குவை/நல்குவன், line 21 வருங்கலம்/வறுங்கலம்); the reading follows the editions' வறுங்கலம் (empty pots) at line 21, and the review says our text lacks two lines of the site's (its 8 and 17). Marked uncertain; not compared against the site.

title: மறுமை நோக்கின்று!
tamil: படா அம் மஞ்ஞைக்கு ஈத்த எம் கோ,
reading: A bard resting on the road with his chariot unyoked, wearing a gold lotus and with his viṟali garlanded, answers a hungry bard who keeps asking who they are: before they saw Pekan they were poorer than he is, for Pekan, who gave a cloak to a peacock knowing it could neither wear nor wrap it, gives not with an eye to the next world but with an eye to other people's want.
nuance: The cloak given to a peacock is offered as proof of motive: a gift to a creature that can neither use it nor repay it cannot be a bid for merit, so Pekan's famous folly becomes the evidence that he looks only at others' need (வறுமை நோக்கின்று), not at the next world (மறுமை). The guide also admits that he was once poorer than the man he guides (நின்னினும் புல்லியேம்).

thinai_evidence.note: a guide's praise of a patron's giving, which is paadaan

comparisons.tenor: the rewarded bards resting at ease in the wild tract

title: கொடைமடமும் படைமடமும்!
reading: Like the rain that by its unbounded habit pours into the drained tank, over the broad field, and wastes itself on salt land where it helps no one, Pekan of the rutting elephant and warrior's anklet is foolish only in giving, never foolish in battle when other armies come at him.
nuance: கொடைமடம், folly in giving, is a fault named as praise: the poet concedes that Pekan gives without discrimination, as rain falls on salt land, then pairs it with the folly he lacks (படைமடம்), so the one fault becomes the measure of his greatness in the other field.

thinai_evidence.note: plain praise of a patron's giving and valour

comparisons.tenor: Pekan's giving, which falls on the deserving and undeserving alike

title: யார்கொல் அளியள்!
reading: Kapilar addresses Pekan, lord of a hill where the Kuravar, having made offerings to the god about the rain and rejoicing that it turned as they asked, eat their millet, and asks who that pitiable woman was who yesterday, in a small village by the waterfalls, when his hungry troupe stood at her door praising Pekan and his hill, could not stop her tears and wept aloud, wetting her breast, like a lamenting flute.
nuance: The poet never says the woman is Pekan's wife: the question யார்கொல் அளியள் leaves him to supply the answer, and it is the song in his praise that makes her weep, so the praise poem turns into the reproach. The hill people whose prayer was answered stand at the opening against a woman whose waiting is not.

thinai_evidence.note: a woman's weeping for an absent husband told to the man himself, which is the unmatched love of perunthinai

title: தோற்பது நும் குடியே!
tamil: கலுழ்ந்து, வார் அரிப் பனி பூண்அகம் நனைப்ப,
reading: Paranar tells Pekan that his want of pity is cruel: when the bards at nightfall played the sevvazhi mode and sang of his forest that meets the rains, a woman whose kohl-lined eyes outshone the neythal flower wept until her tears wet her ornaments, and when they bowed and asked whether she was kin to their patron she wiped her eyes with fingers like kaanthal buds and said she was not, only that he is said to drive there always in his loud chariot, desiring the beauty of a woman like her, to the good town fenced with mullai.
nuance: Asked whether she is his kin, she denies being his kin and names the other woman only as one 'like me', so the wife's restraint carries the rebuke the poet does not make himself. The cycle 143 to 147 shows several poets taking up one patron's domestic breach in turn.

thinai_evidence.note: a wife weeping for a husband who goes to another woman, told to him by the bards

comparisons.tenor: her kohl-lined eyes, more beautiful than the flower

title: அவள் இடர் களைவாய்!
reading: Paranar reminds Pekan, famed for giving a cloak to the peacock in pity lest it shiver, that the bards come neither from hunger nor with a burden to lay down: the gift they beg, playing the small lute until listeners tremble and crying 'do this dharma, lover of grace', is that he mount his chariot tonight and end the grief of the woman who lives in sorrow.
nuance: The peacock is turned against Pekan: if he pitied a bird that might be cold, he cannot leave a woman in sorrow. By declaring that they are not hungry, the bards empty the parisil form of its usual content and make it a plea for reconciliation.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife abiding in grief for an absent husband, which the bards plead for

comparisons.tenor: the dark stem of the small lute

title: தேர் பூண்க மாவே!
reading: Arisil Kizhar tells Pekan to keep his rare jewels and wealth: if, after the bard has sung his good hard-soiled land in the sevvazhi mode, he wishes to give a gift, let it be that his wife, who wastes away in grief at his neglect, may perfume her soft hair, thick as a peacock's gathered tail, with fragrant smoke and wear a cool garland, and that his horses be yoked to his tall chariot.
nuance: The gift is described entirely through the wife's toilet: the incense and the garland she has given up will come back when he does, so the poem asks for his return without stating it, and ends by commanding his horses rather than him.

thinai_evidence.note: a wife enduring her husband's neglect, the gift asked being his return

title: எம் பரிசில்!
reading: Perunkunrur Kizhar tells the lord of the Aviyar that he has crossed many hills of cave-fed falls playing the sevvazhi mode, and that the gift he asks is this: that the lovely woman with streaked, rain-dark eyes, who heard alone yesterday the sweet rumble of the dark clouds and lives in one corner in loneliness, should wash clean as an earth-dulled gem her dark hair left without oil and crowd it with fresh flowers, if he goes back today.
nuance: The rain-cloud heard 'yesterday' is the season of promised return, so the gift is set against a deadline already passed; hair left without oil (நெய்யொடு துறந்த) is the sign of a wife who has given up adornment while she waits, and the poet asks for it to be reversed today.

thinai_evidence.note: a wife living alone through the rains her husband was to return by

comparisons.tenor: her hair washed clean of its neglect

title: என் சிறு செந்நா!
reading: Nalli of the high hill loud with falls: having praised his tireless strength and the wealth people long for, the poet has been given daily, in his bright great house, fine jewels with elephants, gifts in full, so that his small red tongue no longer knows how to recite deeds never done in seeking praise from kings without merit.
nuance: The poem praises by renouncing a genre: Nalli's gifts have made flattery unnecessary, so the poet's honesty is counted among the things Nalli gave him. It also admits that bards did invent deeds for meaner patrons.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a patron's giving through its effect on the poet's speech

title: வண்மையான் மறந்தனர்!
reading: Long live Nalli: because of the generosity with which he has taken on the duty of keeping them, the poet's people have forgotten the order of their modes, playing marutham in the hushed evening and sevvazhi in the morning.
nuance: The praise is a joke against the bards: plenty has done what hunger never did and made them lose the clock of their own craft, since each mode had its hour. The poem asks for nothing, which is why the colophon's பரிசில் sits awkwardly on it.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a patron through what his giving has done to the bards

title: நளி மலை நாடன்!
reading: In a cloak torn like an autumn kite's dark wing, the poet lay at the foot of a jack tree, past caring for himself, when a strong-bowed hunter with a gem on his head and an anklet bloody from killing deer saw his weariness, made him sit as he rose to bow, roasted white fat on a fire he struck himself before his men caught up, and bade him eat with his kin; when the poet had eaten, drunk at the cool falls and made to leave, the hunter said a forest people have no other rare treasure and gave him the chain from his chest and the bracelet from his arm, told neither his country nor his name, and only from others did the poet learn that he was Nalli, lord of the hill guarded by Thotti.
nuance: The poem turns on what Nalli withholds, his country and his name, so the gift comes without the fame it usually buys, and the poet repays him by naming him in the last line. He cooks with his own fire before his attendants arrive. Line 25 plays on தோட்டி, an elephant goad and the name of the hill: a goad 'not forged of iron'.

thinai_evidence.note: a patron's giving told as an encounter, plain praise

comparisons.tenor: the white fat of the kill
the sweet water of the hill

title: அடைத்த கதவினை!
reading: The poet tells the young Vicchi lord why he embraced Kandeerakkon and not him: Kandeerakkon is of a house so generous that when the lord of the sky-touching hill is away even its women give jewelled young she-elephants to delight singers as of old; the Vicchi lord, kin of Nannan of the golden chariot, would also have deserved an embrace, but because of a door shut against singers the poet's people have shunned his fragrant great hill where the clouds pour.
nuance: An embrace was a public honour that a poet could give or withhold, and this poem justifies a public snub. Whose door was shut, the young lord's or his line's, is not certain from the text. The irrealis மன்னே ('you would have been fit') keeps the refusal courteous.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of one patron set against blame of another

title: பெயர் கேட்க நாணினன்!
tamil: வேட்டுவர் இல்லை, நின் ஒப் போர்’ என,
தான் உயிர் செகுத்த மான் நிணப் புழுக்கோடு,
reading: The poet tells how he met a hunter whose one arrow felled an elephant, passed through a gape-mouthed tiger, rolled a spotted stag, dropped a boar and lodged in an iguana in an anthill; guessing that this rich killer, plainly no man who sells, might be Ori, lord of the fruitful hill, he had his viṟali and troupe set up drum, lute, horn and pipes and played all twenty-one modes in order, and when they hailed him as 'king' the man was abashed because it was his own name and, not letting them go, gave them the meat of his kill, toddy like melted ghee and gold and gems from his hill, there in the wilderness: the lord of tall Kolli, eager for unguarded giving.
nuance: The single arrow through five beasts is the poem's credential for the man before he is named, and the bards test their guess by performance: hailed as கோ, he is abashed because it is his own name. As in 150, the patron is met as a hunter in the forest, not at court.

thinai_evidence.note: the patron's giving and the bard's dismissal with gifts

comparisons.tenor: the hunter, who does not look like one who sells his kill

title: கூத்தச் சுற்றத்தினர்!
reading: The poet's troupe of performers went to see the rain-like giving of Athan Ori, lord of the cloud-clad hill who daily gives jewelled elephants to suppliants, and received garlands of gold lilies on white fibre that no cold water ever bloomed, ornaments and herds of elephants; now, perhaps because they are no longer hungry, they will neither dance nor sing to their tight-strung drums.
nuance: The lilies 'that do not bloom in cold water' are gold work, so even the flowers are imperishable; and the closing joke, that the troupe stopped performing when it stopped being hungry, admits that the bards' art ran on need.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a patron through the wealth of his bards

title: இரத்தல் அரிது! பாடல் எளிது!
reading: Even beside the wave-beaten sea people ask someone they know for a little water to quench their thirst, and so poets, though they live among kings, go to the faultlessly generous; the poet therefore does not ask what he will get, but came because he thought of the patron: to say 'give' is hard, but whether he gives or not, singing his valour that does not run from thrown spears and his great forest of Konkanam, where cool falls come down like spread white cloth, is easy.
nuance: Kings are the sea, vast and undrinkable; the generous small lord is the little sweet water got from someone known. The poet separates what parisil poems usually join: asking is hard for him, praising is easy, so the praise is offered as free.

thinai_evidence.note: the poet's approach to a patron for a gift, parisil under paadaan

comparisons.tenor: poets who live among kings but go to the generous
the falls of the patron's forest

title: ஞாயிறு எதிர்ந்த நெருஞ்சி!
reading: Bard who hug the small curved-stemmed lute to your wasted side and cry out for someone to understand and end your distress, listen: as the pale white flower of the nerunchi in a deserted village opens to face the rising sun, the bowls of needy poets open in bloom when they face the cool-garlanded chest of the lord of Konperunkanam of shining fame.
nuance: The image is a weed of the deserted village that turns to the sun, so the poor are flowers of a ruined place and the patron is their sun; the flower's colour is பசலை, the word akam keeps for the pallor of lovesickness.

thinai_evidence.note: one bard directing another to a patron, aatruppadai under paadaan

comparisons.vehicle: நெருஞ்சிப் பசலை வான்பூ ஏர்தரு சுடரின் எதிர்கொண்டு
comparisons.tenor: the poor poets' bowls opening toward the patron

title: இரண்டு நன்கு உடைத்தே!
reading: Other hills have one good thing, but Konperunkanam always has two: it will lie open for the suppliants who come to it in desire to gather and eat, and besides that it has the lord who sends kings with numberless armies home after taking their tribute.
nuance: The poem counts a hill's goods like assets: the land itself feeds suppliants, and the lord feeds it with kings' tribute, so giving and conquest are two products of one place.

thinai_evidence.note: plain praise of a patron's land and conquest

title: ஏறைக்குத் தகுமே!
reading: Bearing with the faults of one's own kin, feeling shame at others' destitution, having a strength that never brings disgrace on the army, and walking tall in the assembly of kings are not fitting for your lords; they fit our Erai, chief of the Kuravar, with broad chest, killing spear and kodal chaplet, lord of the great hill on whose cloud-cleared heights, at dusk, a fine stag that has lost its herd and cannot find its lair calls to its young doe while the spotted tiger in the rock cave listens.
nuance: The virtues are those the Kural later files under shame and forbearance, claimed here by a woman poet of the Kuravar for her own hill chief against other men's lords. Who நும்மோர் ('your people') are is not certain. The closing scene of the stag, the doe and the listening tiger is left without comment.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a hill chief's virtues

title: உள்ளி வந்தெனன் யானே!
reading: Now that the seven are dead who fought and gave, Pari of Parambu, Ori who ruled Kolli, Malaiyan who rode Kari to victory, Ezhini of the horse held but not ridden, Pekan of the great hill guarded by a god, Ay whom Mosi sang, and Nalli who drove off his foes and gave without refusing, the poet has hurried here thinking of Kumanan to end the need of suppliants, and blesses the lord of Muthiram, where a male monkey that has eaten an old thorny jackfruit calls his soft-headed mate with his hand, that his spear may prevail over his enemies along with his famed generosity.
nuance: The roll of seven makes generosity a line of succession with a gap that Kumanan is invited to fill, so the praise is also a summons. Each giver gets one emblem, compressing whole poems into an epithet. 'The horse held but not ridden' (ஊராது ஏந்திய குதிரை) may be Ezhini's hill named Kuthirai; the text does not settle it.

thinai_evidence.note: a blessing on a patron, with a plea for gifts

title: கொள்ளேன்! கொள்வேன்!
tamil: தீர்தல்செல் லாது, என் உயிர்’ எனப் பலபுலந்து,
reading: The poet's mother, so old she complains that her life will not leave her, walks in short steps on a stick, hair like spread thread, never past the yard; his wife, pale and worn, her breasts dried by the many small children who knead and suck them, boils without salt the unripe shoots of rubbish-heap greens, forgets rice, eats the greens without buttermilk and, in soiled scant cloth, goes without and does not blame virtue; so that both their hearts and his hungry kin may rejoice, as cloud pours on a hunters' burnt clearing whose millet would not ear, he will not take a gift given grudgingly though it were a tusked killer elephant, but given gladly he will take even a kunri seed's worth, and asks Kumanan to grant it so.
nuance: After the longest picture of household hunger in the chapter, the demand is about manner, not size: an elephant given grudgingly is refused and a kunri seed given gladly accepted, so the bard puts the giver's gladness above his family's need. அறம் பழியா, his wife does not blame virtue though she starves, gives the household its own pride.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard pressing a patron for a gift, parisil kadaanilai

comparisons.tenor: the patron's gift reviving the starving household

title: புலி வரவும் அம்புலியும்!
tamil: இல் உணாத் துறத்தலின், இல் மறந்து உறையும்
reading: Told by Kumanan's praisers that this lord of Muthiram, who flings away hard-won gold vessels so that the bards' troupe may not fail, would revive him like rain on a sun-scorched forest with rich seasoned rice and ghee served in small gold dishes ringed like stars around the moon, the poet hurried, driven by his heart, from a house where his little tufted son sucks his mother's milkless breast and cries opening the empty pots, while she quiets him with the tiger and the moon and at last asks him to show how he sulks when he thinks of his father; and he asks to be sent off quickly with lasting wealth so that she who suffers in waking life may flourish, and will praise Kumanan's fame across the sea-girt earth.
nuance: Lines 1 to 14 quote the hearsay that brought him, so the poem holds Kumanan to a reputation. The mother uses the tiger and the moon, the props of nursery talk, in place of food. Four lines are flagged as possible misprints and the review finds two lines missing, so details of the household scene are not secure.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard pressing a patron for a quick gift

comparisons.vehicle: முளிபுல் கானம் குழைப்பக், கல்லென அதிர்குரல் ஏறோடு துளிசொரிந் தாங்கு
comparisons.tenor: Kumanan's food reviving a starving body
the small gold dishes ringed around the rice

title: புறநானூறு 161-180
theme: Poems 161-180 are almost all about giving and asking: Perunchiththiranar's and Saththanar's pleas to Kumanan and his gift of his own head, a bard's elephant tied in rebuke to a mean patron's tree, the hill chief Pittankotran praised by five poets as giver and as an anvil to his foes, the hunger-healer Pannan, and soldiers and small chiefs whose scars and spears feed the bards, with one brahmin sacrificer praised as a patron.
source_issues: 166: the colophon thurai reads பார்பபன வாகை, a misprint for பார்ப்பன வாகை; copied exactly in colophon and colophon_form, corrected in puram_thurai name.
172 line 5: வெண்டா looks like a misprint for வேண்டா (do not need to); the sense requires the negative.

171 line 13: உற்றாக reads as a wish that the thorn hurt the patron's foot, which contradicts the blessing; the sense needs a negative wish (as if உறாஅற்க), so the line looks corrupt. Marked uncertain.
162 line 5: கடுமரம் is read as கடிமரம், the guarded tree of a chief's town; the spelling may be a variant or a misprint.
163: the review's line table says sangamtamil.com lacks our line 1; line 1 begins the list of those to be given to and is needed by the syntax, so all nine lines are marked.
178: the colophon patron field carries a variant-reading note (பாண்டிக் குதிரைச் சாக்கையன் எனவும் பாடம்) after the name; 179's poet field likewise carries two variant names.
173 line 12 ends with a comma where the poem ends (எமக்கே,).

title: பின் நின்று துரத்தும்!
reading: Perunchiththiranar tells Kumanan, who is a height for him and for others as the clouds that gather from the sea fill the Ganga in the hot season, that his wife, sure he has died on the robber-haunted waste a year ago, should be dazed by the wealth of Kumanan's feet, so he asks to ride home on a tall tusked elephant with face-plate and bells, making kings ashamed, and asks Kumanan to measure him by his own greatness rather than by the bard's skill.
