reading: Where the aaral fish hides in the mud, the vaalai leaps at the surface and turtles turn up at the rasping taḍāri drum as fishermen trample the flame-flowered fields together and scoop up roe-swollen varaal and bright kayal, the lord of that wide land once ate his food in company with many; now, as he has gone to the high world, his young wife of restrained chastity and fine brow clears a small space with an ash-smeared winnowing basket and smears it with cow dung and with the tears of her eyes that will not stop weeping.
nuance: The abundance of the first seven lines and the shared meal of line 8 are set against the small cleared patch where the widow now eats alone: the poem turns on நெருநை (yesterday) and இன்றே (today). Line 11 is broken in our text, so what she does as he enters the high world is lost.

thinai_evidence.note: the widow's mourning rite after her husband's death

title: மனையும் மனைவியும்!
reading: The poet tells the prosperous mansion that it has become desolate: its gate once held back suppliants with rich, sizzling rice and relish and its cool fragrant pandal stopped the tears of patrons, and now, since the father of tuft-headed sons who hold white rice and ask for sweet milk has gone to the lonely burning ground, it holds a wife who has cut her hair, put off her small bangles and eats alli food.
nuance: The house is addressed, not the widow, and food runs through every stage: the feast that stopped suppliants at the gate, the widow's alli, and the small sons still asking for milk. The children, who do not yet know what has happened, carry the poem's last weight.

thinai_evidence.note: the house and wife after the householder's death

title: அவனும் இவனும்!
reading: The man who, in a spacious house like a painting, made doll-like girls with small bangles grow thin until their ornaments slipped, is seen now bathing in the waterfall of a tall hill of bamboo, tending a fierce red fire with wood the forest elephant brought, and drying the matted locks that hang down his back.
nuance: The poem is built on the before and after of one man, and the only detail of his former life is the women who pined for him. The same elephant-gathered firewood that lights the pyre in 247 here feeds the ascetic's sacrificial fire. Line 3's கண்டிக்கும் is unusual (the old first-person plural கண்டிகும், 'we have seen', is expected).

thinai_evidence.note: the victory of the ascetic's life (தாபத வாகை)

title: அவனே இவன்!
reading: The ascetic who now plucks soft-leaved thaali, his matted hair dulled and changed in colour like the thillai tree from standing under the roaring white waterfall, was once a hunter who snared, with a net of words, the gentle peacocks that move about the house.
nuance: The hunter is the past and the ascetic the present, so the poem reverses the moralist's suspicion that an ascetic may be a hunter in hiding. His weapon was speech (சொல்வலை), and the women are not named but drawn as peacocks of the house. Line 5 ends with a stray closing quotation mark.

thinai_evidence.note: the ascetic set against his former life as a seducer

comparisons.tenor: the man's former wooing of the women of the house

title: கூறு நின் உரையே!
reading: A wife speaks to her husband who has fallen in the wasteland: let him not grieve for her any more; since he came as the young men with strong-strapped garlands rejoiced, how is she to go among her kin raising an empty hand without bangles, pale as a young bamboo stripped of its sheath; let him tell her his word.
nuance: The bare arm is the public sign of widowhood, and her question is how to carry it among her people. Line 3 (நாகாஅல் என வந்த மாறே) is hard and the sense of her first line turns on it.

thinai_evidence.note: a wife alone after her husband's death on the road, the முதுபாலை of porul 2.24

title: ஆனாது புகழும் அன்னை!
reading: The speaker addresses the warrior who fell in the middle of the wasteland, not rising to meet the attack, his chest embracing the earth, while the young and old went off to other lands: if, raising her pale empty bangle-less hand among the kin, she carries the word that the young man has come to this, what will become of his mother, who daily, without tiring, praised him, saying that her son's wealth and greatness were to them like the bird-filled plenty of the fruiting banyan at the edge of the town.
nuance: Lines 3 to 4, on the pale empty hand raised among the kin, repeat 253 lines 4 to 6 almost word for word, so the bare arm raised among kin was a set image of this thurai. The grief is displaced onto the mother's praise, quoted in her own words: the banyan full of birds is a son who feeds many. The comparison's marker is the அற்று of தற்றே, an அன்ன-type form.

thinai_evidence.note: a death in the wasteland and the news that must be carried home

comparisons.tenor: the son's wealth and greatness to his family

title: முன்கை பற்றி நடத்தி!
tamil: ஐயோ! எனின் யான் புலி அஞ் சுவலே;
reading: A wife over her husband's body in the wilds says that if she cries out she fears the tiger and if she tries to embrace him she cannot lift his broad chest; she wishes on lawless Death, which did him this harm, a great trembling like her own, and asks him to take hold of her wrist with its wave-ridged bangles and walk a little, so they may reach the shade of the hill.
nuance: Each of the first two lines closes a way of grieving (crying aloud, embracing); the last asks the dead man to do the impossible, take her hand and walk. Death is called அறனில், without justice, a charge laid against Death itself rather than fate.

thinai_evidence.note: a wife alone with her husband's corpse in the wilds, the முதுபாலை

comparisons.tenor: Death, cursed to tremble as she does

title: அகலிதாக வனைமோ!
reading: A widow asks the potter of the wide old town to take pity on her too, who came with her husband through many wastelands like the small white lizard that clings to the spoke of an axled cart, and to make the burial urn in the wide grove of broad flowers wide enough for both.
nuance: The lizard on the spoke goes wherever the wheel turns without moving itself, which is how she describes her travels with him; the request is practical (make the urn wider), and the burial urn rather than the pyre is the rite named.

thinai_evidence.note: a widow who came through the wastelands with her husband asks to share his grave

comparisons.vehicle: அச்சுடைச் சாகாட்டு ஆரம் பொருந்திய சிறுவெண் பல்லி
comparisons.tenor: the wife who travelled with her husband

title: செருப்பிடைச் சிறு பரல்!
reading: Who is he, poor fellow, this man like a pebble in a sandal, with thick calves, a fine belly, a broad chest, fresh eyes, a beard of coarse hair set like rows of sticks, and cheek hair hanging below his ears, carrying a bow? He did not ride far from town in a chariot or take the forest as his fort, yet in the morning, watching the backs of the enemy's departing herd, he pointed with his hand, counted them slowly and turned them with his bow; and many though they are, what are they to him, who never hears the daily sound of the churning stick in a pot that shows no white?
nuance: The poem begins as if puzzled by a stranger (யார்கொலோ, அளியன்) and ends by showing why he is pitied: he takes herds by the score, yet his own pot never shows the white of curd, because he keeps none. The seizure is made without chariot or fort, by a man counting cattle on his fingers.

thinai_evidence.note: the seizure of the enemy's herd, the deed vetchi is named for

comparisons.tenor: the young raider, a constant vexation to the enemy
the coarse hair of his beard

title: தொடுதல் ஓம்புமதி!
reading: The sweet toddy, matured until it bursts like the old fruit of the thorny kaarai, was drunk first by the young man with the thin beard at the head of the gathered company; he ate raw meat, wiped his wet hand, greasy with fat, on the back of his bow and went into the empty land, and before one round can be drunk he will bring a great herd to fill the outskirts of the town; so the speaker tells the woman to keep the old-mouthed jar from everyone's touch, for that lover of toddy, dusty with eagerness, can also be fierce.
nuance: The toddy is not his pleasure but his advance pay: the jar is to be kept for him because he will bring back the herd before the others finish drinking. The comparison's marker is ஏய்ப்ப, a போல-type word. Line 10 (ஆதரக் கழுமிய துகளன்) is hard; the sense of eagerness is a guess.

thinai_evidence.note: a raider who will bring the herd home, honoured with the first toddy (உண்டாட்டு)

title: புனை கழலோயே!
reading: The speaker warns the warrior with the bright sword at his side and the wrought anklet not to go, not to go, without seeing the ambush of strong-bowed fighters who stayed hidden, heads covered, in the leafy great forest when the herd with its bulls was driven back: may his heart do well, though it is set on the cattle that leap and spring like an old possessed pulaitti.
nuance: The poem is a warning, not a praise: the recovered herd may be bait, and the hidden bowmen are the danger. What the simile compares is not certain: the leaping cattle, or the hero's eager rush toward them; முதுகுமெய் (possessed) is itself a rare compound.

thinai_evidence.note: the pursuit to recover a seized herd, the deed of karanthai

title: கேண்மதி பாண!
reading: The poet tells a bard whose tuning slips into the mourning mode, whose heart fails, who saw his wife's loosened hair as an omen, worshipped the god in the kalli shade of the salt waste and came hungry and weeping asking 'shall I not see him?', to hear how the prosperous one stands: whether he would have eaten under his protection or wakes at night in distress, both now lie close at hand; the hero appeared at the alarm of the near village, gathered his town's long herd, crossed the flood of arrows with the drum for a raft, won, killed, made the raiders let go, and as the moon escapes the sharp fang of the snake that seized it, the many cows with their calves escaped the raiders' hands and came back with his fame; then, like a snake shedding its skin, he went to the world hard to reach, his body stayed there shaking with arrows like a target post shaking with its pole on the steep bank of a forest stream, and his name, risen until high fame could hold no more, is on the stone in a narrow path no one else takes, under a cloth canopy, crowned with the fine feathers of the gentle peacock.
nuance: The hero is split three ways at his death: the self goes like a snake from its skin, the body stays behind shaking with arrows like a target post, and the name moves onto the stone. The bard's omens at the start (the slipping tune, the loosened hair) are confirmed rather than answered, and the poem gives the bard the hero-stone in place of a patron. The marker of the snake simile is மான, a போல-type word.

colophon.thurai: கையறுநிலை செருவிடை வீழ்தல்; கையறு நிலையுமாம்; பாண்பாட்டுமாம்; பாடாண் பாட்டுமாம்

thinai_evidence.note: the hero recovers the herd and dies, and is set up as a stone, the karanthai deed and its sequel

comparisons.tenor: the hero crossing the arrow-storm with only his drum
the herd escaping the raiders' hands
the hero leaving his body for the other world
the hero's body shaking with arrows

title: புறநானூறு 261-280
theme: Poems 261-280 are the hero-stone and battlefield poems: laments for cattle-defenders who became stones, the victory feast of the raiders, the nochchi of the fort's defenders, single warriors against armies, and the old mothers and wives who measure a death by its honour and its cost.
source_issues: 271 and 272: the colophon thinai reads நொட்சி, a misprint for நொச்சி; copied as it stands in colophon, inferred thinai nochchi.
280: the colophon thurai reads ஆந்தப் பையுள், a misprint for ஆனந்தப் பையுள்; corrected in puram_thurai name, colophon_form keeps the misprint.
276: the poet's name reads மாதுரைப் பூதன் இளநாகனார்; மாதுரை is likely a misprint for மதுரை.
262: the colophon thurai's alternative is written தலை தோற்றமுமாம், for தலைத்தோற்றமும் ஆம்; normalised in puram_thurai name.

275: the review's line table says sangamtamil.com lacks our opening line 1. Our line 1 (கோட்டம் கண்ணியும், கொடுந்திரை ஆடையும்) supplies the subjects that line 3 (ஒத்தன்று மாதோ, இவற்கே) completes, so it belongs to the poem; marked as it stands.
270 line 2 repeats purananuru:137 line 1 (இரங்கு முரசின், இனம்சால் யானை), flagged by show; read as a shared formula, not a corruption.
263: the poet is not recorded (poet None).
270: the colophon's thinai is karanthai, but nothing in the poem concerns the recovery of cattle; inferred pothuviyal.

title: கழிகலம் மகடூஉப் போல!
reading: A poet sees the ever-open house of his dead lord, once loud with toddy bowls, endless rice and meat frying in ghee for newcomers, now as useless as a ferry on a dried river and as bare as a widow with shorn head, because the young spearman who brought back the cattle and was crowned with karanthai has become a hero-stone.
nuance: The address shifts in mid-poem from the poet's own eyes (சோர்க, என் கண்ணே) to the house itself (பயந்தனை... புல்என் றனையால்), so the house is mourned as a person who has lost her husband. Lines 11 and 12 (the unlearned bowmen, the owl's call) are compressed and their syntax is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: the dead man is a cattle-recoverer crowned with karanthai, and the poem laments him as a hero-stone

comparisons.tenor: the lord's courtyard, now of no use
the hiss of meat frying in ghee

comparisons.vehicle: கொய்ம்மழித் தலையொடு கைம்மையுறக் கலங்கிய கழிகலம் மகடூஉப் போல
comparisons.tenor: the house stripped of its ornaments

title: தன்னினும் பெருஞ் சாயலரே!
reading: Draw the toddy, slaughter the ram, fill the leaf-roofed shed with fresh river sand: my lord is coming with the herd, having broken the enemy's front and guarded the rear, and those beside him are spent more than he.
nuance: The leader is both in front (முருக்கி) and behind (பின்நின்று): he breaks the enemy and then guards the retreat with the herd. Line 6 can be read as his companions being more worn than he, or gentler than he; either way the feast is ordered for them all.

thinai_evidence.note: the lord returns driving a captured herd, the cattle raid of vetchi

title: களிற்றடி போன்ற பறை!
reading: A bard with a one-faced drum like an elephant's footprint is told not to pass without worshipping the stone on this road: it stands for the man who turned back the stolen herd, stood fast when the untrained youths fled, and, sunk in arrows, held the enemy like a dam against a killing flood.
nuance: The poem is an instruction to a passing performer: the dead man's stone has become a place of worship on the road, which is how a lament turns into a cult. Line 4 (வண்டுமேம் படூஉம், இவ் வறநிலை யாறே) is hard: it may mean the road through dry land where bees swarm at the garlanded stone, or a path of virtue.

thinai_evidence.note: the dead man turned back a driven-off herd: the deed of karanthai

comparisons.tenor: the warrior holding back the enemy

title: இன்றும் வருங்கொல்!
reading: On the gravelly ground they have heaped the cairn, crowned it with a red flower garland bound with split maral fibre and with peacock feathers, carved his name and set up the stone; will the bards' troupe still come today, not knowing that the noble man who drove off the enemy and brought back the cows with their calves is gone?
nuance: The grief is measured from the bards' side: the rite is complete (cairn, garland, feather, name, stone) but the news has not travelled, so the performers who lived on his giving are still on the road to him. The order of the rite in lines 1 to 4 is itself a record of how a hero-stone was made.

thinai_evidence.note: the dead man brought back the milch cows with their calves

title: வென்றியும் நின்னோடு செலவே!
reading: On the old gravelly battlefield far beyond the town, the cowherds have crowned you with a garland of venkai blossom tied with palmyra leaf, and you have become a stone, prince of swift horses; and with you have gone not only the wealth of the bards who lived in the shade of your feet but the victory that made elephant-riding kings shrink.
nuance: The cowherds, not kings or priests, perform the crowning, with flowers of the hill (venkai) and leaf of the palmyra: the stone belongs to the people he protected. The last lines make the loss double, patronage and conquest at once, so the dead man's giving and his fighting are one reputation.

thinai_evidence.note: the cowherds honour the dead man at his stone, which places him as the defender of their cattle

comparisons.tenor: the patron's feet that sheltered bards

title: அறிவுகெட நின்ற வறுமை!
reading: The poet asks Chenni, lord of a land whose watered fields stay green even when the rains fail, to remove at once, as a plea made in the assembly of the wise is answered, the poverty that has risen in his body, ruining his understanding and making him hide from the very guests he longed for.
nuance: The snail pair mating in the shade of a lily leaf at midday, in a drought, shows a land so well watered that even the weakest creatures prosper; the poet's own house is the one place in it where the guest is avoided. The comparison makes relief a matter of justice, as in a court, rather than of favour.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises a king's land and presses him for relief from poverty

comparisons.vehicle: சான்றோர் இருந்த அவையத்து உற்றோன் ஆசாகு என்னும் பூசல்
comparisons.tenor: the poet's plea to the king

title: கருங்கை வாள் அதுவோ!
reading: After the warrior, his hair wreathed with loose athiral buds sharp as a koel's beak, has drunk the warm liquor once or twice from a new bowl, the drummer comes asking for pressed toddy, and he is given instead, it is said, this dark-handled sword, which cut down the bowmen who had seized the herd and drove them back while the kites cried over them.
nuance: Who says 'take this' in lines 7 and 8 (என்ப, 'they say') and what 'this' is are not settled by the syntax; read with the closing words இக் கருங்கை வாளே, the feast's answer to a request for drink is the sword's deed. Avvaiyar's poem keeps the feast and the slaughter in one sentence.

thinai_evidence.note: the feast follows a raid in which the sword beat back the karanthai men who tried to retake the herd

title: ஆண்மையோன் திறன்!
reading: Addressing the grey-haired mother of a great house, the poet says that even wheel-rolling emperors with drums and elephants meet in battle what they sought, and grieves while bidding her look at her son, who, after warriors stirred by the war drum fought a fearful battle, lies on the swords like a tree felled by an axe.
nuance: The poet's நோகோ யானே (I grieve) is set against நோக்குமதி நீயே (but you, look): the mother is asked to see valour where the poet sees loss. Lines 1 to 4 on the emperors are elliptical and their link to the son is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: a lament over a warrior dead in a pitched battle, with nothing of cattle recovery that karanthai needs

comparisons.tenor: the son lying on the swords

title: மைந்தன் மலைந்த மாறே!
reading: We once saw the bright nochchi leaves, grown where the ground never lacks water, worn as a girdle on the waists of jewelled women; now we have seen the same leaves, soaked in blood and shredded out of shape, carried off by a kite that took them for flesh, because the young warrior eager for battle wore them.
nuance: The warrior's death is never stated; it is told only through what happened to the leaf he wore, from women's ornament to carrion. The kite's mistake (ஊன்செத்து) makes the garland stand for his flesh.

thinai_evidence.note: the warrior wore nochchi, the flower of those who defend a fort

title: கிழமையும் நினதே!
reading: The poet praises the nochchi, its clusters like strung sapphires, as the best loved of flowering trees: it gives shade, lies on the waists of bangled women in the guarded mansion, and, because the enemy breached the guarded wall, it also wins the honour of crowning the noble man who would not yield the town's outskirts.
nuance: The tree is addressed as a person with rights (கிழமையும் நினதே): its last and highest claim is to the head of the defender at the moment the wall falls. The colophon's falling in battle is implied by the breach, not stated.

thinai_evidence.note: the defence of a walled town, whose sign is the nochchi

title: கூடல் பெருமரம்!
reading: A wife cries that her husband's horse has not come while everyone else's horses have returned, and asks whether it has perished like a great tree that lies across the meeting of two great rivers.
nuance: She asks only about the horse; the rider's fate is left unspoken, and naming him as the one who gave her a son puts the household's future into the question. The tree across the confluence fits a horse (and rider) that blocked two converging armies.

thinai_evidence.note: the horse fought in a pitched battle and has not returned

comparisons.vehicle: இருபேர் யாற்ற ஒருபெருங் கூடல் விலங்கிடு பெருமரம்
comparisons.tenor: the horse that stood across the enemy's onrush

title: நீலக் கச்சை!
reading: The great warrior in blue waistband, flowered cloth and peacock-feather crown hurled his spear at the oncoming elephant; now, as the foes with spears came on with their horses, he seems ready to hurl himself too, and seizing with his hand, embracing, lifting with his shoulder's strength, he took it upon his body.
nuance: With his spear gone, the warrior turns himself into the weapon (தன்னும் துரக்குவன்). What he seizes in lines 6 and 7 (an enemy's spear, or an enemy) is not stated, and the last verb can mean taking it bodily or taking it into his body.

thinai_evidence.note: a warrior facing elephants and horsemen in pitched battle

title: தன் தோழற்கு வருமே!
reading: His bent garland, his cloth of curling folds and his naming what he wanted as he went at the king all suit him: splitting the koovai so the ranks cried out, raising his spear at the front, crying 'hold here, hold here!' without guarding himself, his legs tangled in the guts of a chained elephant, he rushes like a cow to its calf toward the comrade who faced the first clash.
nuance: The simile of the cow running to its calf is a tender one inside a scene of entrails: the warrior's rush to his comrade is love, not only valour. Lines 3 and 4 (செற்றிய திணிநிலை, கூவை போழ்ந்து) are hard and the sense of the opening garland and cloth is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: a warrior challenging a king in open battle

comparisons.tenor: the warrior going to his comrade

title: குடப்பால் சில்லுறை!
reading: The beloved son of a red-skinned old woman, her white hair untended and her breasts dry and shrunk like dark seeds, became the ruin of a whole army, as a few drops of curd-starter flicked by a cowherd girl's nail turn a pot of milk.
nuance: The simile turns on size: a few drops change a whole pot. Taken from the dairy of mullai, it makes the hero's deed as quiet and certain as a daily chore, and sets the dried breasts of the mother against the milk.

thinai_evidence.note: one warrior against a whole army in battle

comparisons.vehicle: மடப்பால் ஆய்மகள் வள்உகிர்த் தெறித்த குடப்பால் சில்லுறை
comparisons.tenor: the one son who undid an army

title: சிதரினும் பலவே!
reading: When the old woman with hair white as the down of a fish-eating heron heard that her son had killed an elephant and fallen, her joy was greater than on the day she bore him, and her tears outnumbered the drops that hang on the swaying bamboo after rain.
nuance: The thurai's name, joy and weeping together, is the poem's structure: one sentence for each. The bamboo after rain is an image of plenty, so even her tears are counted as abundance.

thinai_evidence.note: the son died in battle after killing an elephant

comparisons.vehicle: நோன்கழை துயல்வரும் வெதிரத்து வான்பெயத் தூங்கிய சிதரினும்

title: பெரிது உவந்தனளே!
reading: Told by many that her son had broken and fled, an old woman with withered, veined arms swore in rage to cut off the breasts he had sucked, took a sword and searched the red field turning over the dead, and when she found her son lying hacked to pieces, she rejoiced more than on the day she bore him.
nuance: Her proof is in the wounds: a son cut to pieces (சிதைந்து வேறாகிய) could not have run, so the report of the many is refuted by what she sees. Her vow against her own breasts makes motherhood itself answerable for the son's courage.

thinai_evidence.note: a battlefield search by a mother for her son's body

title: செல்கென விடுமே!
reading: The poet, aghast, says this woman's resolve is fierce and worthy of an old warrior house: her elder kinsman died killing an elephant the day before yesterday, her husband died yesterday holding back the great herd, and today, hearing the war drum, she puts a spear in the hand of her only son, wraps him in white cloth, oils his tufted hair and sends him to face the battle.
nuance: கெடுக சிந்தை, the poet's opening curse on her (or his own) mind, is awe close to horror. The days are counted (மேல்நாள், நெருநல், இன்றும்) so the poem becomes a three-day ledger of loss; the only son (ஒருமகன் அல்லது இல்லோள்) is the last entry. Whether தன்னை here is her father or elder brother is not fixed by the poem.

thinai_evidence.note: the excellence of a woman of an old warrior house, the mark of vaakai's muuthin mullai

title: வழிநினைந்து இருத்தல் அரிதே!
reading: A wife beside her husband's wounded body lists the bad signs, the burning wounds, the bee buzzing at midnight, the lamps that go out, the owl's cry, the old woman's omen that does not come right, pities the drummer, bard and virali whose life here is over too, and says that for her, to sit like widows with shaven heads eating white water-lily seeds and think of the road he took will be harder still.
nuance: The first seven lines are a run of omens, each a short clause ending in a verb, so the poem enacts a night of watching. She foresees widowhood in the simile and judges it harder than his death. Line 12 (தொன்றுதாம் உடுத்த அம்பகைத் தெரியல்) is obscure.

thinai_evidence.note: a wife's lament at the death of her husband from wounds

comparisons.vehicle: சிறுவெள் ஆம்பல் அல்லி உண்ணும் கழிகல மகளிர்

title: புறநானூறு 281-300
theme: Poems of the fighting men and their households: the rites that guard a wounded man, the deaths of warriors from old martial houses, the mothers who weep and rejoice over sons, and the toddy, flowers and land a king owes those who go first.
source_issues: 282 line 4 is a dotted gap; the colophon has no thinai or thurai. Marked from the lines present.
283 lines 7 and 12 are gaps (line 12 is flagged for a word beginning with a dead consonant), and line 3 differs in another edition; the poem is marked uncertain.
284: the colophon thurai பண்பாட்டு looks like a misprint for பாண்பாட்டு, the thurai of 283 under the same thinai; puram_thurai name corrected.
285 lines 5 and 9 are gaps; line 12 ends தனனெ, likely a misprint for தனனே.
288 line 7 is a gap, which held who came to embrace the dead man.
289: the colophon has no thinai or thurai.

295 line 6: மாண்புகண் டருவி is கண்டு அருவி in sandhi; the karu form keeps the written டருவி. 295 line 7: வாடுமலை reads best as வாடுமுலை (withered breasts), the sense the mother's milk requires; மலை for முலை.

296: the colophon thurai எறான் முல்லை is a misspelling of ஏறாண் முல்லை; puram_thurai name corrected. The review's line table says sangamtamil.com lacks our line 1; it carries the neem-breaking that matches 281, so it is marked as it stands.

297: the colophon thurai இண்டாட்டு looks like a misprint for உண்டாட்டு, the vetchi thurai of the victors' toddy feast, which suits the poem's toddy (line 6); puram_thurai name corrected. The colophon has no poet.
298: the colophon's poet, thinai and thurai were filled from Duraisamy Pillai's edition; another edition gives the poet as ஆலியார்.

title: நெடுந்தகை புண்ணே!
reading: A woman calls her dear friend to come and guard the wound of the great man who took on the king's trouble: hang neem with iravam in the house, sound the lute and many instruments, smear the dark paste, scatter mustard, blow the ampal pipe, ring the bell, sing kaanchi and burn incense through the long house.
nuance: The whole poem is a list of household rites and only the last line says whose wound it is, so the wound is guarded as much by the women's noise and smoke as by medicine; ampal here is the pipe that is blown, not the water-lily.

thinai_evidence.note: the deed is guarding a wounded man's life with rites against harmful powers

title: புலவர் வாயுளானே!
reading: If you ask where the great doer is who paid his hard debt to the land with a spear through his chest, the answer is that holding the oncoming army he was cut down until neither body nor life could be seen, and nothing of him is left on the field but his split shield, yet he lives on, fame set far, in the mouths of poets.
nuance: The poem answers the question 'where is he?' twice: nowhere on the field, where even the body is gone, and in the poets' speech, so the poem itself is offered as the place where the hero now is.

thinai_evidence.note: a warrior's death holding back the oncoming army

title: அழும்பிலன் அடங்கான்!
reading: Through a broken text: after a scene of a cool pond where the vaalai fish and the otter take their daily prey and turn back from the crocodile, the poem names the unsubmitting Azhumbil man and the assembly of the Kosar, the women of soft shoulders playing with sand dolls, and a hero who wore the fragrant thumbai on his forehead.
nuance: Lines 7 and 12 are gaps and line 3 is read differently in another edition, so who the Azhumbil man is to the hero (enemy or lord) cannot be fixed; the Kosar, a people, are not one of the entity types and are noted here.

thinai_evidence.note: the hero wears the battle flower; the rest is too broken to decide on

title: பெயர்புற நகுமே!
reading: When the king's messengers cry everywhere 'let him come quickly', the man of an old fighting house comes alone on foot, garlanded, holds the hard battle, and while he straightens his bent sword against the tusk of the elephant he killed in front, he laughs at the back of the man who fled from him.
nuance: The elephant's tusk becomes a tool for mending the sword, so the kill is already work done; the laugh is the poem's last word and it is aimed at a back, the one part of a fighter that should not be seen.

thinai_evidence.note: a lone warrior holding a battle against an army

title: தலைபணிந்து இறைஞ்சியோன்!
reading: Through a damaged text: in the camp the drummer holds the spear and the bard the shield; a warrior with a faded garland, his chest pierced by a long spear, fell to the ground with his fat-smeared anklet, all who saw it praised him, and his lord bowed his head, because to this leader of a poor kin he had given only a small village of barren land and not the cool fields where the grain-ears sway.
nuance: On this reading the lord's bow is shame, not grief: the man's death exposes how little he was paid, so the poem judges the giver; with lines 5 and 9 broken, whether it was the lord who gave the barren village is the likeliest but not a certain reading.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem's event is a warrior's death in battle, which the lord's response follows

title: பலர்மீது நீட்டிய மண்டை!
reading: Avvaiyar's speaker sets her son, who held out his bowl above many, against the other youths who remain like rams of white goats, and says it has not laid him on a bier with bound feet and covered him in pure white cloth.
nuance: The closing negative can be read as a plain statement (he died on the field and was not even carried home and shrouded) or as an exclamation (has it not laid him on the bier!); either way the son who was first to the king's bowl is set apart from the youths who survive.

thinai_evidence.note: the shroud and bier make the poem about a son's death

comparisons.tenor: the other youths, many and alike and unharmed

title: காண்டிரோ வரவே!
reading: Speaking to the drum-beating pulaiyan, the poet says that warriors of pride who do not run though arrows hit like the seasonal rain, spears flash like kendai fish in the paddy and an elephant drives its tusk into them, care nothing for winning cool fields where vaalai fish roll at the granary's foot, since if they die they enjoy the weddings of flawless women in the high world; so watch the upstart king's army come from here.
nuance: The poem names the two rewards of the hero side by side and ranks them: land if he lives is waved aside with யாவது, and the reward that counts is in the high world, which is a Sangam poem itself making heaven, not only fame, the warrior's wage.

thinai_evidence.note: a boast made as an invading army approaches

title: மொய்த்தன பருந்தே!
reading: The drum covered with the unshaved hide of the winner of two bulls set to fight sounds in the middle ground; in the confused battle a long spear pierced the warrior's heart that knew shame, and on his blood-swaying chest the kites crowded so thick they left no room for an embrace.
nuance: The drum's hide is itself the trophy of a fight between bulls, so the poem opens on one victor's skin and ends on another's body; who came to embrace him was in the lost line 7, and the kites have taken that place.

thinai_evidence.note: a warrior's death in the press of battle

title: ஆயும் உழவன்!
reading: As a ploughman, even when the wet season has favoured him, looks among his many bulls for the best one, the king looks among the men of old fighting houses and says of the gold bowl raised for himself, 'give it to this one'; and more, hear, bard, the drummer in the camp crying 'today is the taking of flowers'.
nuance: The honour and the death are announced together: the bowl the king gives is the sign of who will go first, and the drum that follows calls the flower-taking for battle, so the chosen man is being picked as the ploughman picks the bull for the hardest furrow.

thinai_evidence.note: the drum announces the taking of the battle flowers before a fight

comparisons.tenor: the king choosing among the warriors

title: மறப்புகழ் நிறைந்தோன்!
reading: Give this man toddy before you drink, lord of war elephants: his father's father stood unblinking and died, like the hub the carpenter fits the spokes into, beside your father's father in battle, and this man too, full of martial fame, will cover you from the spear aimed at you like thatch in the rain.
nuance: The claim to the first cup rests on a debt between two lines, not on this man's own deeds, and the two similes are both household things (the wheel hub, the roof thatch), so the warrior is made part of the king's house.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a warrior's inherited excellence, spoken to his king

comparisons.tenor: the grandfather standing as the spears were driven into him
this warrior shielding the king from spears

title: மாலை மலைந்தனனே!
reading: The bard tells the children and drummers to keep the birds' clamour off the dark man lying under pure white cloth while she drives off the white jackal with the turning of a lament tune, and wishes on the king the same great trembling she feels, for he once put his own gem-like garland on the man who longed to die and wore the dead man's single-strand garland himself.
nuance: The exchange of garlands is the poem's charge against the king: by wearing the warrior's garland he took the warrior's place in a bond, so the mourner asks that he share the grief too; கொன்னும் makes the death look needless.

thinai_evidence.note: a lament sung over a dead warrior

title: சினவல் ஓம்புமின்!
reading: Do not be angry, petty men, that when the sweet cool toddy raised for the king was being mixed he stopped it and stood gripping his true sword: if he wants something, as he did here, he will not wait for his turn, and the manly one will stand there and stop the great army as it rises.
nuance: The speaker turns a breach of the feast's order into a promise: the same refusal to wait for his turn that offends at the toddy is what will hold the front, so his rudeness is offered as evidence of his courage.

thinai_evidence.note: the claim to the king's drink made at the feast before the army sets out

title: பூவிலைப் பெண்டு!
reading: If the summoning drum that the rider of the unflinching elephant beats against the hill-fort men sounds for men who know shame, the speaker asks, will the flower-selling woman, who has lost more of her beauty than we have, go into other people's houses as her trade: she is to be pitied.
nuance: The drum that sends men to take flowers for battle sends the flower-seller into houses that may soon be in mourning; who the 'we' are (the wives at home) and why she has lost more beauty than they is not said, so the pity may be for her poverty or for her trade in the flowers of the dead.

thinai_evidence.note: the war-drum's effect on those at home, seen through a poor woman

title: வம்மின் ஈங்கு!
reading: In the sea-like camp under the moon of the white umbrella, in a battle so confused that kin cannot be told from foe, your husband called out his lord's name and his own, 'come here, you who would cut short our men's days', and stood fighting apart, and no one came near him, as no one comes near the gem a serpent has spat out.
nuance: Naming his lord and himself is the point: in a battle where nobody knows who is who, he makes himself known and so becomes untouchable, like the serpent's gem that is treasure and danger at once; குமரிப்படை in line 3 is unclear.

thinai_evidence.note: a single warrior's stand in the press of battle

comparisons.tenor: the husband standing alone, whom no one approaches

title: ஊறிச் சுரந்தது!
reading: In the camp heaving like the sea, the young man of unretreating vow bit his lip, drove forward, split the oncoming army and lay broken apart in the middle of the press; seeing the glory of her excellent son, his mother's withered breasts welled and flowed.
nuance: The mother sees the body, not a report, and the response is in the body too: breasts long dry give milk again, as at his birth, so his death returns her to his infancy; the thurai's name holds joy and weeping together.

thinai_evidence.note: a son's death in battle and his mother's response

comparisons.tenor: the milk flowing from the mother's breasts

title: நெடிது வந்தன்றால்!
reading: Neem branches are broken, kaanchi is sung, mustard is smoked by ghee-smeared hands and every house is loud with it: is it that he fights on, burning with rage, that the great man's chariot is so long in coming?
nuance: The question in the last two lines is a hope disguised as a guess: the rites of 281 are already under way in every house, which suggests wounds, but the speaker reads the delay as rage still fighting.

thinai_evidence.note: the household rites that guard a fighter, with fear for his delay

title: தண்ணடை பெறுதல்!
reading: We do not want to seize this small village where the wild cow with her calf sleeps on a bed of threshed gram stalks whose pods are as long as a buffalo's horns; we want a grant, and blessing it with toddy from the jar it is right that cool fields by the ford where the waterhen lays her eggs be given to those who stand like the stiff-fronded palmyra, their chests pierced by the long spear.
nuance: The poem refuses plunder of a poor village and asks instead for a lawful grant, so it sets a limit on what the victors may take; the palmyra image gives the wounded men a standing posture even with spears in them.

thinai_evidence.note: the warriors' claim to the reward their wounds have earned

comparisons.tenor: the speared warriors who still stand

title: கலங்கல் தருமே!
tamil: வாய் மடித்து உரறி,’ நீ முந்து? என் னானே.
reading: The warrior complains of his king: he used to give us the dregs and drink the clear toddy himself, which was once his way; he is truly unkind, for now, besieging the enemy's strong fort, biting his lip and roaring, he does not say to me 'you go first'.
nuance: The grievance is not the poor drink but the denial of the vanguard: a warrior measures the king's favour by who is sent first to die, and மன் may mark the drinking order as a past custom now broken.

thinai_evidence.note: the setting is the siege of an enemy fort

title: கலம் தொடா மகளிர்!
reading: The horse of the chief of a small village fenced with cotton, slow-gaited from eating gram stalks, cleaved the battle-front like a boat driving into the sea, while the garlanded, ghee-fed, mane-clipped horses of the kings of rich fields held back, like women who may not touch the vessels in fearsome Murugan's shrine.
nuance: Every detail is set in pairs, cotton fence against cool fields, gram stalks against ghee, so the poem argues that feeding and finery do not make a warhorse; the second simile turns the rich horses' hanging back into a ritual bar rather than open cowardice, which makes the scorn sharper.

thinai_evidence.note: two sides' horses meeting at the battle-front

comparisons.tenor: the poor chief's horse cleaving the army
the rich kings' horses holding back

title: எல்லை எறிந்தோன் தம்பி!
reading: You cry 'give me a shield, give me a shield', but even with a shield behind a boulder you will not escape: the younger brother of the man you killed yesterday evening, his eyes whirling like kunri seeds dropped in a lamp, is searching for you as men search the great town for the one house where toddy was brewed.
nuance: The revenge is a kinsman's duty, so the killing of yesterday makes today's enemy; lines 5 and 6 also compare the search to a hunt for toddy, but the phrase ஓர் இல் கோயின் is unclear and is left out of the comparisons.

thinai_evidence.note: a taunt to an enemy warrior in battle

comparisons.tenor: the avenging brother's red whirling eyes

title: புறநானூறு 301-320
theme: Poems 301-320 move from the battle line to the warrior's house: horses and young riders, vows that frighten camps, a brahmin whose few words end a siege, warriors fallen with their elephants, and then the old houses and the able men of small villages, whose mothers assign duties, whose wives pray for guests at hero-stones, and whose lords pawn swords and promise gold to the bards.
source_issues: 302: the poet field carries an editor's variant note, வெறிபாடிய காமக் கண்ணியார் (காமக் கணியார் எனவும் பாடம்); copied as it stands.

306: line 6 is gapped after its first letter (ஒ .. ..), so the prayer for the husband is incomplete; the review's line table says sangamtamil.com lacks our line 1, which the poem needs (its fence and elephants set the village).
310, 314, 315, 316, 318: the review lists these among our poems with stray non-Tamil glyphs; the text as `show` prints it was read as it stands.
312: the poet, thinai and thurai are filled from Duraisamy Pillai's edition (FILLED_FROM_DURAISAMY_PILLAI); this poem is usually attributed with 310 to Ponmudiyar, as here.
313, 314, 315: the colophon thurai reads வல்லான் முல்லை; 316 to 320 read வல்லாண் முல்லை, the usual name; normalised to வல்லாண்முல்லை in puram_thurai.
317: lines 1, 5 and 6 are largely lost to gaps; the poet field reads மவேம்ப்ற்றூர்க் குமரனார், apparently a misprint for வேம்பற்றூர்க் குமரனார்.
319: line 4 reads கஃடு, read here as the toddy (கள்) that was drunk; lines 6 and 7 are hard to construe.
320: lines 17 and 18 repeat 329 lines 8 and 9 exactly (flag repeated_line).

title: அறிந்தோர் யார்?
reading: The speaker warns the many warriors in the thorn-fenced camp to guard their king and their elephants, for the hero opposite does not even go out to meet those who strike at him, no one knows what he intends, and having ridden off at night on his fine horse he looks like a man who will lift his spear only against the elephant the enemy king rides.
nuance: The threat lies in restraint: the hero's refusal to answer ordinary blows (எறிந்தோர் எதிர்சென்று எறிதலும் செல்லான்) is what makes him dangerous, because it shows he is saving his spear for the king's own elephant.

thinai_evidence.note: a warning across the battle line about one warrior's chosen target

comparisons.tenor: the thorn fence set round the camp
the short path the horseman rides, as if measuring the ground

title: வேலின் அட்ட களிறு?
poet: வெறிபாடிய காமக் கண்ணியார் (காமக் கணியார் எனவும் பாடம்)
reading: The horses leap and bound like a bamboo bursting; the village's flowers went to the women's hair and its narantham garlands to the bards; the poor small village on stony ground is never full, yet if one counted the elephants the young warrior killed with his spear they would outnumber the stars of the sky and the drops of the cool rain.
nuance: The poem sets the village's want (நிரம்பா இயல்பின் கரம்பைச் சீறூர்) against its giving: what little it has, flowers and garlands, has already gone to women and bards, and its only abundance is the count of its warrior's kills.

thinai_evidence.note: the count of elephants killed in battle

title: மடப்பிடி புலம்ப எறிந்தான்!
reading: A warrior speaks: the young rider who destroys his mockers is coming on a whirling horse that digs the ground with its hooves as if thrusting the earth back, to try his hot spear and scar the chest of me, who only yesterday, before famous kings, cut through their ranks like a boat through the sea and killed their tusked elephant so that its young cow mourned.
nuance: The colophon names the horse's valour, but the poem is spoken by the target: the older warrior describes the young rider's charge as a test he welcomes, and answers it with his own record of yesterday.

thinai_evidence.note: two warriors meeting in battle

comparisons.tenor: the horse's hooves tearing the ground
the speaker cutting through the kings' army

title: எம்முன் தப்பியோன்!
reading: The hero garlands the women, drinks strained toddy against the shivering cold, and hurries to harness his horse that outruns the wind; saying 'tomorrow I fight the younger brother of the man who escaped me yesterday', he will not even feed his lean belly but drives the strong horse hard, and when the victorious king's camp hears it, it trembles, because what he says does not come out two ways.
nuance: The enemy camp fears a sentence, not an army: its trembling rests on the hero's record that his word is never 'two' (இரண்டா காது), so the vow does the work of an assault.

thinai_evidence.note: a warrior's vow of battle and its effect on the enemy camp

title: சொல்லோ சிலவே!
reading: A lean, pale brahmin, his waist shrunk like a withered vayalai creeper, came at nightfall and went straight in; he spoke only a few words, and for them the siege ladders and the gate-bars were put away and the bells were taken off the well-trained war elephants.
nuance: The poem measures cause against effect: a frail man and a few words on one side, the whole apparatus of siege dismantled on the other; it never says what he said, which keeps the force on the brevity.

thinai_evidence.note: the brahmin's excellence is the war his words ended

title: ஒண்ணுதல் அரிவை!
reading: In a small village fenced with thorns that shake when elephants fight, where the well is hard to drink from, a woman with soft thick hair and bright brow worships the hero-stone with joined hands every day, praying that she may always have guests to receive and that her lord, [gap] with the king, may win a great war that brings land.
nuance: Her first request to the dead hero of the stone is guests, and only then her husband's war; hospitality and battle are asked of the same stone, and the war she wants is one that brings land (நாடுதரு), not one that merely brings fame.

thinai_evidence.note: a woman of a warrior house prays for guests and for her husband's war

title: யாண்டுளன் கொல்லோ!
reading: Where is my lord, our support? He fell with an elephant like a hill and lies like a stranger; see, the old ookam blossoms, like a summer squirrel's tail, settle on his long curled hair, and like a lame old bull the salt-carters abandoned without water or grass he still takes the lives of foes, so that the enemy king, seeing it, said there was nothing finer than to stay on this field and fell, his heart broken.
nuance: The image of the abandoned bull is pitiless: the support of the house (ஆசாகு எந்தை) lies like a beast left to die by a road, and yet the same lines give him the power to kill, so the lament and the boast share one figure.

thinai_evidence.note: a warrior fallen with the elephant he killed

comparisons.tenor: the elephant the hero fell with
the fallen hero lying alone on the field

title: நாணின மடப்பிடி!
reading: A woman of the warrior house tells the bard with the gold-stringed little lute that the small-village chief's little-leafed spear now stands in the face of the king's mounted elephant, while the spear the angry king threw passed through the chests of those around her lord; and when our hero raised the bright weapon and drove forward, all the bull elephants turned their backs, to the shame of their young cows.
nuance: A small village's chief (சீறூர் மன்னன்) against a crowned king's elephants is the poem's proportion; the shame is transferred to the cow elephants, who watch their males flee.

thinai_evidence.note: the deed told is a battle against a king's elephants, though the colophon files it as an old house's pride

title: என்னைகண் அதுவே!
reading: Smashing iron-faced shields and crossing a great battle of foes is easy for anyone; what belongs to my lord is the single shining tall victorious spear at whose mere report 'he is in the camp' matchless enemies take fright, as people fear an anthill where a cobra lives or a common where a killing bull roams.
nuance: The poem demotes the deed the thurai names (cutting through the ranks) as common to all, and claims for the lord only the fear his presence causes; both similes are of a place made dangerous by what lives in it, not of the creature itself.

thinai_evidence.note: a warrior's valour judged in battle

comparisons.tenor: the camp where the lord is present
the camp where the lord is present

title: உரவோர் மகனே!
reading: Once, when milk was brought to him he would not drink, and he fretted at the little stick she raised without anger; now the son of the strong man who fell the other day, having killed a spotted elephant, says he does not even feel the arrow in his wound, as he lies on the shield, his tuft like a horse's mane, his beard just coming.
nuance: The before and after are both about refusing: the child who would not drink milk and feared a raised stick is now the youth who will not notice an arrow; the speaker's tenderness never says whether he lives.

thinai_evidence.note: a youth killing an elephant in battle

title: சால்பு உடையோனே!
reading: Avvai speaks of a lord in a white cloth washed daily by the washerwoman in water from a well dug in saline ground, who sat in the pollen-strewn street and served the needs of many: in battle there is no one like him, the noble one who, when the honoured warriors' red eyes smoke with rage, covers them with his single shield.
nuance: The first half is all peace and humility: a plain washed cloth, sitting in the dust of the street, doing others' errands; the same man in battle is the one who hides others behind his shield, so his service does not change with the setting.

thinai_evidence.note: a hero praised for shielding others in battle

title: காளைக்குக் கடனே!
reading: To bear him and bring him up is my duty, to make him a worthy man is his father's, to forge and give him a spear is the smith's, to give him good conduct is the king's, and to cut through the hard battle with his shining sword, kill elephants and come back is the young man's duty.
nuance: Five duties are owed to the son by four givers, and the last, his own, is not to win but to return (பெயர்தல்) after killing elephants; the king's share is conduct (நன்னடை), not wealth.

thinai_evidence.note: a mother of a warrior house sets out each one's duty, ending in the son's

title: வேண்டினும் கடவன்!
tamil: எள் அமைவு இன்று, அவன் உள்ளிய பொருளே.
reading: The great hero of a land beside the wilderness has nothing in hand, yet if the suppliants who go longing to see him ask for elephants and tall chariots he is bound to give them; what he has in mind is as sure as the hill of salt the salt-carters with laden carts point to, without a sesame seed's doubt.
nuance: The word for his obligation is கடவ, 'bound to': giving is owed, not chosen, and the poem asserts it while saying in the same breath that he has nothing in his hand.

thinai_evidence.note: a chieftain's excellence in giving though he has nothing

title: மனைக்கு விளக்கு!
reading: The husband of the bright-browed woman, a lamp to his house, the tall noble with the conquering spear who is the boundary of the battle front, is alone the stay of the people of the small village of thin-stemmed nelli on hard ground beside the leaf-strewn field of standing hero-stones, and if his own lord falls, he alone is the dam for the army that breaks rank and flees with its banners.
nuance: The three metaphors share one function at three scales: lamp to a house, boundary to a front, dam to a broken army; the village of hero-stones beside him shows what that function has cost others before him.

thinai_evidence.note: one man's excellence in house and in war

comparisons.tenor: the warrior who stops the routed army

title: இல்லிறைச் செரீஇய ஞெலிகோல்!
reading: Avvai says of Neduman Anji: when he has, he can eat; he gives to suppliants even beyond those he is bound to; he is the joy and companion of simple folk; like the fire-drill stick tucked into the eaves of a house he can stay unseen, and like the roaring fire it gives off he can blaze out when he chooses to appear.
nuance: The two similes are one object in two states: the fire is already in the stick, so his restraint is not weakness but stored force, and the word வல்லன் (he can) is repeated for both eating, hiding and blazing.

thinai_evidence.note: a chieftain's excellence in giving and in timely force

comparisons.tenor: the patron when he shows his force

title: சீறியாழ் பனையம்!
reading: The bard says: he who sleeps late in the yard overgrown with scrub, drowsy from the toddy he praises day after day, is our lord and we are his bards; yesterday he pawned his old iron-bound sword for guests who came, today this black-necked little lute is the pledge; do not think he has nothing to give, but take it, so that your slim-waisted woman may wear bright jewels and we may sway with our toddy pots, and may he go and come back red-mouthed when the king with small-eyed elephants meets trouble.
nuance: The pledge passes downward: the lord pawns his sword for guests, and the bard then offers his own lute as surety to the toddy-seller, so the household's credit rests on the lord's coming war, which will redeem both.

thinai_evidence.note: a warrior who pawns his sword for guests and is ready for the king's war

title: யாதுண்டாயினும் கொடுமின்!
reading: [Line 1 gapped] Whatever there is, a hide, a mat, anything, give it quickly to the great reveller lying in the front yard; [lines 5 and 6 gapped] having given to us, to others, to everyone, he took to sleep.
nuance: What survives is a reversal: the man who gave to everyone has nothing left to lie on, and the speaker asks others to give him a hide or a mat.

thinai_evidence.note: the gaps leave only the spear and the giving; the colophon's warrior excellence is followed

title: பெடையடு வதியும்!
reading: The noble's town has gone hungry together with his dark woman of peacock grace, the plucked greens wilting and the gathered firewood drying unused; yet if the king meets trouble it becomes a place of plenty, where the house sparrow with its dark throat eats rice from the big fields and lives with its dull-backed hen in a nest woven of bards' lute-string fibres and plumes.
nuance: The village's plenty depends on its lord's distress turning into the warrior's opportunity (வேந்து விழுமுறின்): peace starves this house and war feeds it, so the sparrow's nest of bards' strings and plumes is a picture of the spoils to come.

thinai_evidence.note: a warrior house whose plenty comes from the king's wars

title: முயல் சுட்டவாயினும் தருவோம்!
reading: The wife of the small-village lord tells the old wise bard: the old jar in the yard of our small house, where a little reddish water from a well dug in red earth is poured, is clean and empty because we drank the toddy; it is too late to spread the millet out for the doves and quail; so though it is only roasted hare we will give it, come in and stay; our lord, whose boys yoke the trembling calf of the wild cow as if it were a calf of the house, went yesterday on the king's errand, and when he returns he will crown you with a lotus that never fades so that your paadini may wear a garland.
nuance: The wife offers what is gone (the toddy drunk, the millet unspread) before what she has (roasted hare), and pays the rest on credit against her husband's return: the unfading lotus is the gold the king's errand will bring.

thinai_evidence.note: a warrior's house receives a bard in his absence

comparisons.tenor: the wild cow's calf the boys yoke

title: கண்ட மனையோள்!
reading: In a yard where munjai and musundai creepers make a shade no pandal is needed for, a hunter sleeps; a lone stag frolics with the tame decoy doe, and his wife, seeing their happy union, stays still, afraid her husband might wake and afraid the stag might leave the doe, while jungle fowl and quail noisily eat the millet drying on a deerskin; so, bard, eat the roasted meat smelling of sandal-fire with your whole kin, stay and then go, for this town is guarded by the famed noble who always gives the suppliants the fine food the king gives him.
nuance: A love scene sits inside a puram poem: the wife holds still between two fears, for her husband's sleep and for the deer's union, and lets the birds eat the household's millet rather than break either; the poem then turns the same open-handedness on the bard.

thinai_evidence.note: a hunter-warrior's town where the bard is fed

title: புறநானூறு 321-340
theme: Poems 321-340 praise the small warrior villages of hard, dry land (vaakai: வல்லாண் முல்லை and மூதின் முல்லை), whose chiefs and wives give away even their seed grain and whose only god is the hero-stone, then turn to the magatpaal kaanchi poems, where a king's demand for a chief's daughter brings war on her town.
source_issues: 323, 327, 328, 333, 339 and 340: the poet is not recorded (poet None).
321 line 8, 323 line 3, 328 lines 1, 5, 7-9, 12-13, 333 lines 14-15, 334 lines 4-5 and 9, 335 lines 1-2, 337 line 4, 339 line 10 and 340 lines 3-6 have dotted gaps; marked as they stand.
323 line 3 and 334 line 9: show flags a word beginning with a dead consonant (க்கு, ப்); each is the tail of a word lost in the gap before it.
325: the review's line table says we lack the site's lines 14 and 15, but our text now has 15 lines ending வேந்து தலைவரினும் தாங்கும், / தாங்கா ஈகை, நெடுந்தகை ஊரே; the table row looks out of date.
336: the review says our colophon read பாற் பாற் காஞ்சி; show now prints மகட்பாற் காஞ்சி, so it appears corrected.

338: the review says the site lacks our line 1 (ஏர் பரந்த வயல், நீர் பரந்த செறுவின்); it begins the list of the town's wealth that போந்தை அன்ன (line 4) closes, so it belongs to the poem; marked as it stands.
321 is listed in the review among poems with stray non-Tamil glyphs; the text show prints has none.
331: the poet field carries a variant in brackets (உறையூர் முது கூற்றனார் எனவும் பாடம்).

title: வன்புல வைப்பினது!
reading: The bard is told that the town guarded by the battle-loving lord whose head bears sword scars lies in hard country, where a fighting quail snatches husked sesame drying on a winnowing tray and, chased by a rat with ears like a summer kongu bud, hides in the thick millet stalks.
nuance: The long opening shows a poor dry land where even a quail must steal grain and hide, so the town's strength is all in its lord: the poem turns from a small comic chase to the scarred head in the last two lines. Line 8 is broken, so what the bard is told to do on arrival (eat fruit and rest?) is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem ends on the lord's battle scars and love of war, the valour of a small-land chief

title: கண்படை ஈயான்!
reading: The spearman who denies sleep to the kings of the cool wet fields lives in hard country, where dull-headed boys leaning on cactus with thorns like an old plough-bull's worn horns watch for rats in the millet stubble and their shouts send a hare leaping across the common, breaking the black pots, while near by, when the sugarcane press groans, the vaalai fish leap.
nuance: Two economies sit side by side: boys hunting rats in a dry millet land, and the sugar mills and fish of the kings' watered fields next door. The hero belongs to the poor land, and his threat runs from it to the rich one.

thinai_evidence.note: the praise is of a spearman whose threat keeps kings awake

comparisons.tenor: the forked thorns of the cactus

title: உள்ளியது சுரக்கும் ஈகை!
reading: An old cow, her anger gone, suckles the calf of a wild cow that a tiger has taken, and (after a broken line) the poem praises the spearman's unguarded giving that flows to whatever is wished for, and his sword, which leaves its sheath only for elephants.
nuance: The image of a cow nursing an orphan of another kind is set before ஓம்பா ஈகை, giving that keeps nothing back; line 3, which would have joined them, is lost, so whether it was an open simile cannot be known.

thinai_evidence.note: generosity and a sword kept for elephants alone, the paired virtues of the small-land hero

comparisons.tenor: the hero's giving to those not his own

title: உலந்துழி உலக்கும்!
reading: In a small village on poor land, where hunters' boys with frightened eyes like a wild tomcat's and mouths smelling of bird meat bend their bows with thorn-tipped reed arrows to watch for rats at the cotton hedge, the modest noble man who sits with the bards by a herdsman's small fire is the heart-knowing companion of the victorious king, who will perish when the king perishes.
nuance: The hero is first shown at ease, modest among bards in a poor village; his value is stated only at the end and as a pledge, not a deed. Lines 9 and 10 (what spreads over the pandal) are obscure.

thinai_evidence.note: the hero is praised as the king's companion unto death

title: வேந்து தலைவரினும் தாங்கம்!
reading: In a dry settlement where cows take turns drinking the muddy seep of a dug pit after a stray rain has passed, where the porcupine hunters' share of fat burning on the firebrand scents the street and boys play at arrows under the jujube's swaying shade, stands the thorn-fenced town of the lord of unbounded giving, who will hold back even a king who comes at the head of a victorious army.
nuance: The pun in the last lines turns on one verb: தாங்கும், he holds back the king, and தாங்கா ஈகை, giving that cannot be held back. The rain is வம்ப, untimely, and leaves only a muddy pit, so the land is shown as poor in water before it is praised.

thinai_evidence.note: the lord resists kings and gives without limit

title: பருத்திப் பெண்டின் சிறு தீ!
reading: In a thorn-fenced village where a young hen, terrified by the wild cat that prowls the old hedge, cries until the cotton-spinning woman rises with her small lamp and it calms beside the crested cock, the wife longs to feast arriving guests and bards on curd-rice with iguana fat, and her husband, who shattered the enemy in hard battle, owns the great gift of the gold forehead plate from the leading elephant.
nuance: The frightened hen that quiets beside the cock may be read as a quiet figure of the village safe beside its warrior, though the poem draws no comparison. The wife's wish that the hunting boys not go far is a wish to have meat ready for guests, so even the hunt serves hospitality.

thinai_evidence.note: the old warrior house: the wife's hospitality and the husband's battle gift

title: வரகின் குப்பை!
reading: After the creditors took their share of a meagre millet crop threshed by hand without oxen and the hungry bards ate the rest, the noble man, to end his people's want, goes to the small farmers of his own town and begs millet face to face; and this is the strong man who holds back any king who comes.
nuance: The poem sets the begging and the valour in one sentence, so the man who stoops to ask small farmers for grain is the same man who will stand against a king; begging is not shame when it is for others.

thinai_evidence.note: the poor hero's begging for others and his strength against kings

title: ஈயத் தொலைந்தன!
reading: In a small village of poor land by the woods where no paddy grows and all its millet and thinai have gone in gifts to suppliants, the bard is told that the little king, though so reduced, will still cook dried meat and fresh rice in ghee for him and give him gifts if he goes singing to the yard where hares nibble the fragrant muññai.
nuance: Lines 1, 5, 7 to 9, 12 and 13 are broken; the sense of the whole (an empty granary, yet a feast promised) survives, but the details of the meal and of line 5 do not.

thinai_evidence.note: giving that outlasts the village's grain

comparisons.tenor: a dish of the meal; the tenor is lost in the gap of line 8

title: மாப்புகை கமழும்!
reading: Though the small village of a few houses that brew their own toddy sits at a dangerous frontier, where the hero-stone at its edge gets daily offerings, is bathed and lit with ghee and its dark smoke spreads like mist down the street, and though it is as hard to approach as an anthill where a striped cobra lives, the famed noble man who guards it gives to suppliants every day without stint.
nuance: The anthill simile faces two ways: to enemies the village is a snake's hole, to suppliants it is open every day. The phrase in line 7 about the patron's distress is not certain: it may mean that he gives without minding what giving costs him.

thinai_evidence.note: constant giving in a dangerous frontier village

comparisons.tenor: the frontier village, dangerous to approach

title: ஆழி அனையன்!
reading: When a king's army pressed in and broke the front, he stood alone with raised sword and stopped it from passing him, as the shore stops the great sea; and always, beyond what he gave those who came singing, his generosity keeps up the old name of a small village too poor to pay its levy.
nuance: ஆழி here is the shore or boundary that the sea cannot pass, so the army becomes the sea; the image measures one man against a whole host.

thinai_evidence.note: a single warrior's stand and his giving

comparisons.tenor: the lone warrior holding back the army

title: இல்லது படைக்க வல்லன்!
poet: உறையூர் முதுகூத்தனார் (உறையூர் முது கூற்றனார் எனவும் பாடம்)
reading: The strength of a small village that lives by the bow, with a well cut through rock, is a chief who, though very poor, can make what is not there, like an unlearned herdsman kindling a small fire on a cold evening; can measure out in order to a few, like a good housewife who serves a long pandal of guests from very little without saying they are too many; and, when he scatters gifts, can scatter them like the white rice of offering cast at the gates of guarding kings.
nuance: The three similes are a scale of giving: making something from nothing, sharing scarcity fairly, and pouring out freely. All three vehicles are humble or domestic, a herdsman and a housewife set beside the king's offering rice.

thinai_evidence.note: the poor chief's skill in giving

comparisons.tenor: the chief contriving what he lacks
the chief measuring out a little to many

title: வேல் பெருந்தகை உடைத்தே!
reading: Unlike other men's spears, this warrior's spear has its own greatness: sometimes it lies in the thatch of the hut with dust on its dark back; sometimes, garlanded among auspicious women, it is carried round the pond and the streets to the sound of drums and lutes till the land trembles; and it never stops short of the faces of the great elephants of kings whose armies are like the sea.
nuance: The spear is given three states, idle, honoured and in battle, and the repeated கிடக்கினும் கிடக்கும் and செல்லினும் செல்லும் make its indifference to the first two a mark of greatness.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the warrior through his spear

title: தங்கனிர் சென்மோ புலவீர்!
reading: Poets are urged to stay at a poor village where hares with eyes like raindrop bubbles leap in the bushes of the holed common, even though no one there knows how to say 'eat', for the housewife, her millet and thinai all given to suppliants and no loan coming back, has put the dried seed-millet into the mortar; and her lord, who would face a king with a new-decked elephant, eats only that and gives as gifts what he takes in battle.
nuance: Cooking the seed grain is the extreme of hospitality: it spends next year's crop on today's guest. Lines 14 and 15 are broken, and the closing lines (what the lord eats, what he takes as his gift) can be read more than one way.

thinai_evidence.note: the old warrior house that gives away even its seed and faces kings

title: தூவாள் தூவான்!
reading: Where hares with fur like the sedge flower hide in the thickets when boys shout on the common, the housewife never rests her hands from the clatter of feeding bards and keeping suppliants, and the young bull-like spearman never rests his either, giving away the gold ornaments taken from the faces of high-tusked elephants.
nuance: The poem rhymes the wife and the husband: கைதூ வாளே, she does not rest her hands, and கைதூ வானே, he does not rest his, which makes hospitality and battle-won giving one shared duty of the house. Lines 4, 5 and 9 are broken.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife and the warrior are equally unresting in giving

title: கடவுள் இலவே!
reading: In this land there are only four flowers (kuravam, ..., kuruntham, mullai), only four foods (millet, thinai, horsegram and beans), only four clans (the thudi drummer, the bard, the parai drummer and the kadamban), and no god worshipped with scattered paddy except the stone praised for the warrior who stood against the enemy, struck down a bright-tusked elephant and fell.
nuance: The fourfold lists read like a census of a whole way of life, and the last item overturns the pattern: not four gods but one, and that one a man. The first line and a half are broken, so one flower is lost.

thinai_evidence.note: the only god of the land is the fallen warrior's stone

title: பண்பில் தாயே!
tamil: அன்னோ, பெரும்பே துற்றன்று, இவ் வருங்கடி மூதூர்;
reading: The king who wants the girl is hot with anger and her father will not do what is due; the elephants have not yet been tied to the guarded tree, the spearmen who reached it are silent, and with drums sounding that even the musicians do not know, this ancient guarded town is in great turmoil; truly without virtue is the mother who, raising the girl's young breasts with the beauty of kongu buds on the vengai hill, raised enmity along with her.
nuance: The blame falls on the mother, not on the king or the father: her care in rearing the girl's beauty is said to have reared a war. Lines 4 and 5 (the guarded tree, the warriors' வாய்மூழ்த்தனரே) are hard, and the state of the siege is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: a king's demand for a daughter brings war on the town

title: இவர் மறனும் இற்று!
reading: Though the Chola lord is loud with power and suitors who rule the earth have come singing, she, like the cold spring on Pari's Parambu, has become hard to see, kept indoors in the tall fragrant house; kings keep coming, feeding paddy to their fierce elephants in every grove, while her brothers' heads are clotted with blood from their long spears, and the poet asks who will ever be the ones to press her young breasts.
nuance: Kapilar, Pari's own poet, uses his dead patron's hill spring as the measure of something precious and out of reach. The closing question is not a wish but a threat: given her brothers' spears, it is not clear anyone will live to marry her. Lines 3, 4 and 13 are obscure.

thinai_evidence.note: kings besiege a house to win a daughter her brothers guard

title: ஓரெயின் மன்னன் மகள்!
tamil: ஏர் பரந்த வயல், நீர் பரந்த செறுவின்,
நெல் மலிந்த மனைப், பொன் மலிந்த மறுகின்,
reading: Like Neduvel Aathan's Ponthai, rich in ploughed fields, paddy-filled houses, gold-filled streets and bee-loud groves, she is of great worth and hard to win: even if the victorious kings who wear neem, aar and palmyra bring gifts, the king of a single fort, which stands among the paddy fields like a stranded ship in the sea, will not give his one young daughter to any who do not bow as befits him.
nuance: The three garlands are the emblems of the Pandya, Chola and Chera, so the refusal is made to all the crowned kings at once by the lord of one fort. போந்தை is both the town of line 4 and the palmyra of line 6.

thinai_evidence.note: a small king refuses his daughter to the three crowned kings

comparisons.tenor: the single fort among the fields

title: வளரவேண்டும் அவளே!
reading: Where a long-horned bull rests in the shade, cowherds pluck crowded mullai flowers, a hare struck by a stick leaps among vaalai fish in the flood, and bangled women bathe in the sea, dive in ponds and pick neythal flowers from the backwater, she has grown, and the poet says she has taken and hidden in herself the fierce hearts of kings with winnow-eared elephants who are eager for hard battle.
nuance: The opening gathers three landscapes, pasture, wet field and shore, into one country, so the girl is the flower of a land that has everything; the comic hare among the fish marks the floods. Line 10 is lost, and the sense of line 12 is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: the girl draws kings to war

title: அணித்தழை நுடங்க!
reading: To one who asks about the young girl who runs, her leaf skirt swaying, to gather spotted kunri seeds, the speaker answers (through broken lines) that her father has set her apart for great kings whose elephants with trunks like dark palmyras trample the karanthai fields.
nuance: The child still playing with seeds is already the subject of kings' wars; the gaps in lines 3 to 6 hide who asks and whose father is meant, and வரைந்திருந்தனனே may mean he has promised her or has limited her to such kings.

thinai_evidence.note: the daughter's marriage is a matter between kings

title: புறநானூறு 341-360
theme: Poems 341 to 355 are magatpaal kaanchi: a chieftain refuses his daughter to kings, and the poet sees the town's groves, fords and walls about to be ruined by the war her beauty brings. Poems 356 to 360 are perunkaanchi: the burning ground outlives all rulers, so kings are told to give while they can.
source_issues: Purananuru 341 line 5 (அனரமண் இஞ்சி) looks corrupt, and line 6 is lost.
Purananuru 344 line 8 has a gap and line 9 (கணிமே வந்தவள்) is obscure.
Purananuru 346 line 1 and 347 line 8 are lost (347 line 9 is partial).
Purananuru 345 line 19 and 347 line 9 are the same formula (என்னா வதுகொல் தானே), flagged as a repeated line; it is a refrain of the magatpaal poems, not a copying error.
Purananuru 352 has gaps in lines 2, 8, 11, 12, 15 and 16, and 353 line 13 is lost.
Purananuru 355 has only four lines and no thurai, poet or patron in the colophon; Duraisamy Pillai's edition has two more lines before the gap.
Purananuru 357 line 6 is mostly lost and read differently by the two sources.
Purananuru 358's colophon thurai (மனையறம், துறவறம்) is not a thurai of the kaanchi list; the poem's content is renunciation only.
Purananuru 360 line 10 has a closing quotation mark with no opening one.

title: இழப்பது கொல்லோ பெருங்கவின்!
reading: A chieftain refuses his young daughter even to a king who pleads, calls his fierce kin to the flower-taking of war and wades into the pond, torn between wedding her tomorrow and entering the world of no return with a spear-scarred body; the poet fears the cool field-town will lose its beauty like a pool churned by fighting elephants.
nuance: The hero (குருசில்) is given the choice as a pair of 'one or the other' (ஒன்றோ ... ஒன்று): the wedding day and the warrior's death are set as equal outcomes, and the poet's own worry is for the town, not for either man.

thinai_evidence.note: a refused bride brings war, and the poem weighs death against the town's ruin

comparisons.tenor: the field-town about to be spoiled

title: வாள்தக உழக்கும் மாட்சியர்!
reading: Asked by an eager spear-bearing lord whose daughter the broad-shouldered girl with the dark flower garland is, the speaker answers that her beauty is for warriors alone: her father owns rich fields where heron chicks feed on fish eggs and prawn, and because kings could not win her, her brothers thresh the battlefield daily with swords, using heaped corpses as sheaves and broken elephants as oxen.
nuance: The heron chick that eats its fill and still finds eggs and prawn is a picture of the father's plenty; it is set against the brothers' harvest of corpses, so the poem's two 'fields' are the paddy land and the battlefield.

thinai_evidence.note: a girl withheld from kings and the war it causes

comparisons.tenor: the battlefield as a threshing floor, its corpses as sheaves and dying elephants as oxen

title: ஏணி வருந்தின்று!
reading: Musiri, where fish is bartered for paddy, pepper sacks crowd the houses and the gold brought by ships comes ashore by canoe, belongs to Kuttuvan who gives the goods of hill and sea to comers; even if wealth like Musiri is humbly offered, the father says she will not be married to those not his equal, and the poet asks whether the walled town, with the attackers' ladders against it and kites resting on the inner wall, will not suffer.
nuance: The bride-price is measured by a real port's trade, gold coming in and pepper going out; the father's refusal is framed as rank (புரையர்), not price, so no wealth can settle it.

thinai_evidence.note: bride-price refused and a siege ladder already raised

comparisons.tenor: the great wealth offered as bride-price
Musiri's roaring sea as its drum

title: இரண்டினுள் ஒன்று!
reading: The suitor will do one of two things, give a town of fields, where peacocks that ate red paddy fly up with the bangled women and settle on the marutham tree by the ford, together with great wealth, or spread smoky fire and enmity with graceless manliness; one of them is sure to come, because of the girl with the kaanchi-shoot garland and the lines on her waist.
nuance: The peacocks and the women rise together and settle in the marutham tree; whether the poet means them as one picture of the town's ease or likens the women to the birds is not fixed by the text.

thinai_evidence.note: the suitor's two courses, gift or war

title: பன்னல் வேலிப் பணை நல்லூர்!
reading: The groves are shaken by tethered elephants, the streets thick with chariot dust, the roads jammed with horses, the ford muddied by the washing of weapons, the ground bowed by the weight of fierce warriors: many new kings have come for the girl, and her lovers are to be pitied, for her brothers want war, not wealth, saying there is no giving to those out of line, and with shields, notched swords and blood-matted heads they are such men that the poet cries, what will become of this good town fenced with cotton?
nuance: The siege is told entirely through what it does to the town (grove, street, road, ford, ground) before the girl is named; lines 8 and 9 (the iron like a she-elephant's breath, the back like a painting) are obscure.

thinai_evidence.note: kings encamped around a town over a refused daughter

comparisons.tenor: the iron (bellows or goad) the hand grips

title: பாழ் செய்யும் இவள் நலினே!
