reading: The mother does not refuse her and the young man, strong and good with the bright spear, insists; if that comes true, the fallen will fall, the kin who remain will die with none to care for them, and the girl's beauty will make a great wasteland.
nuance: The last line makes the girl's beauty (நலன்) the grammatical agent of the ruin, the same move as 349's anangu.

thinai_evidence.note: a girl's beauty foreseen as the town's ruin

title: வேர் துளங்கின மரனே!
reading: Akuthai of fierce war, who drinks fragrant toddy, wears battle-withered thumbai and carries a spear notched in fight, holds a Koodal ringed by deep water, and the girl with heavy hair is likened to it; though the trees of our town are thick-trunked, they have shaken at the root since the kings tethered their trained elephants to them.
nuance: Line 8 is lost, so what the simile of Akuthai's Koodal is joined to cannot be read with certainty; the closing image of trees shaken at the root by tethered elephants recurs in 348.

thinai_evidence.note: kings' war elephants tethered in the girl's town

title: பெருந்துறை மரனே!
reading: The girl with kuvalai eyes is like Unur of truthful Thazhumban, where the drum of the rice reapers scares bees from the honey, toddy is strained in pots and the panar quarter scales fish; had her mother not borne her, the trees of our great ford would not suffer from long chariots standing in every shade and red-browed elephants tied at every place.
nuance: The counterfactual (had her mother not borne her) blames no one; the harm is told only through the trees, which is how the speaker can grieve without accusing the girl.

thinai_evidence.note: kings' chariots and elephants camped at the town for a girl

title: ஊர்க்கு அணங்காயினள்!
reading: The king wipes the sweat from his brow with his spear-point and speaks harsh words, and the father too speaks only proud words and never bows; that is their vow, so the girl with fine teeth and cool streaked eyes has become, like a small fire born in wood, a danger to the town she was born in.
nuance: The fire that is born in wood and burns the wood names exactly the girl's relation to her town; the poet calls her அணங்கு, a harmful power, not because of anything she does but because of two men's vows (படிவம்).

thinai_evidence.note: king and father both unbending over a daughter

comparisons.tenor: the girl who brings ruin on her own birthplace

title: வாயிற் கொட்குவர் மாதோ!
reading: The old town with its moat filled in, its battlements sagging and its wall broken cannot hold out; kings with drums like falling thunder and fast horses come at dawn and circle our tall gate and will not leave without a fight, all for the freckles budding on the breast of the young girl whose eyes are red like her brothers' spears.
nuance: The poem ends on the smallest thing in it, the freckles on a young girl's breast, as the cause of a siege; her eyes are said to be red like her brothers' spears, which ties her beauty to the men who will fight for it.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem is about a besieged town's failing walls and gate

title: தாராது அமைகுவர் அல்லர்!
reading: Kings whose army is as wide as the sea, with belled elephants, flag-topped chariots, horses and warriors, will never rest without taking the girl whose beauty is like the vaakai of generous Eyinan; what will become of this secure field-town where the red-striped heron, tired of the honeyed marutham's branch, sleeps in the lovely kaanchi?
nuance: Whether வாகை here is Eyinan's victory or a place called Vaakai is not settled by the line. The heron that leaves the marutham for the kaanchi tree to sleep is a picture of the town's safety (ஏமம்), set against the army that threatens it.

thinai_evidence.note: a refused girl and the town's fate

title: தித்தன் உறந்தை யன்ன!
reading: Through broken lines the poem sets milking, mullai picking with leaf cups and women with aambal-stalk bangles leaping into water beside a comparison with Uranthai of the great giver Thithan, ringed with white paddy; fine jewels like that town are offered and refused, and the girl's freckles shine like young vengai flowers.
nuance: So many lines are lost that who refuses the jewels and what the brothers do cannot be read.

thinai_evidence.note: bride-gifts offered and refused

title: 'யார் மகள்?' என்போய்!
reading: To the victorious lord who stopped his chariot, eyes pale, gazing at the girl in a gold-coin girdle and eekai garland, and keeps asking whose daughter she is, the speaker answers: she is the daughter of an old-line chieftain who never fails to feed the bowmen from grain heaps like hills, and her brothers, who answered the old kings who asked before with blood and still wear unchanged wound dressings, are men to fear.
nuance: The answer moves from the father's open-handed feeding of fighters to the brothers' wounds, so the girl's lineage is described as both generous and dangerous; line 13 is lost.

thinai_evidence.note: a king's question about a girl answered with her brothers' war record

title: நாரை உகைத்த வாளை!
reading: Spears that would not be stilled even if a king came against them are plunged in water, and the father turns back even worthy suitors; will the town, where the vaalai fish chased by the heron leaps from the field pond into the houses of bathing women, lose its beauty over the young girl's gaze, gentle as a doe's?
nuance: Lines 2 and 3 (spears plunged in water; the father 'turning back' even the worthy) admit more than one construction.

thinai_evidence.note: suitors turned back and the town's beauty at stake

title: ஊரது நிலைமையும் இதுவே?
reading: The fort has no battlements, its moat is so dry that calves graze and frisk in it; that is the state of the town; the rest is lost.
nuance: The calves playing in the dry moat make the town's helplessness almost comic; the colophon gives only the thinai and no thurai, poet or patron.

thinai_evidence.note: a fort's broken defences

title: காதலர் அழுத கண்ணீர்!
reading: The old misty burning ground, with its salt waste, spreading cactus, owls hooting by day, pyre lamps and ghoul-women with crooked teeth, is fearful; the tears of loving kin quench the white ash of its bone-strewn pyres, and having seen the backs of everyone and become the end for all mankind, it has never seen the back of anyone who would see its back.
nuance: 'Seeing someone's back' is to outlast them (they turn and go); the ground has seen everyone's, and no one has seen its own, so the cremation ground, not any king, is the true survivor.

thinai_evidence.note: the burning ground outlasts everyone

title: தொக்குயிர் வௌவும்!
reading: Even those who ruled without sharing the hill-bound earth that is common to three kings have seen their years end, and wealth was not what stayed as their support; when death takes life as kin weep, it is hard for those who let go of the raft to climb from this bank to the far one.
nuance: Line 6 is mostly lost, so what the raft (புணை) is, merit or giving, is inferred from the contrast with wealth in line 5.

thinai_evidence.note: death and what outlasts kingship

comparisons.tenor: the merit that carries one through death

title: விடாஅள் திருவே!
reading: This rich earth circled by the sun has had seven owners in a single day; weighed against austerity the world is not worth a mustard seed of it, so those who loved it let it go; therefore Fortune does not leave those who leave her, and those who will not leave are left by her.
nuance: The last two lines turn on one verb (விடு) four times, so that leaving and being left are the same act seen from Fortune's side; the poem praises renunciation in a book of kings.

thinai_evidence.note: the impermanence of rule weighed against austerity

title: நீடு விளங்கும் புகழ்!
reading: The burning ground of hooting owls, corpse-eating jackals with fat-shining teeth and ghoul-women who clasp the dead, eat pale flesh and dance on the salt waste by the pyre lamps, has received even conquerors of kingdoms, and your day too will come; blame stays and fame stays, so put away blame, seek fame, speak good without wanting, and give elephants, gold-trapped horses and tall chariots freely to suppliants, and your fame will shine here long after you go.
nuance: 'Blame stays and fame stays' (line 10) makes the counsel a choice between two lasting names, not between a name and oblivion.

thinai_evidence.note: counsel to give drawn from the burning ground

title: பலர் வாய்த்திரார்!
reading: Few have ruled this land as a shelter for others, men slow to anger, of few words and much learning, of fine understanding and great giving, who served cool liquor and rich food and helped many; even their wealth does not abide, so keep your conduct faultless and fill the hands of gift-seekers, for after the pulaiyan sets out the rice offering on grass in the vulture-haunted cremation ground and the body enters the fire, those who shared their food will not remain.
nuance: The last line (பலர்வாய்த்து இராஅர்) can be read as 'they do not stay' or as a claim about being in many mouths; the sense of the close, whether sharers are remembered or simply die like all, is not settled. Line 10 carries a stray closing quotation mark.

thinai_evidence.note: counsel on the impermanence of wealth

title: புறநானூறு 361-380
theme: Poems 361 to 380 move from death to the bard's reward. 361 to 367 are kaanchi counsel on impermanence: kings more than the sand have gone to the burning ground, so give, feast and act now (361 to 364, 366), or, in 365, the Earth herself weeps at being held by king after king. 368 to 373 are களவழி poems in which a drummer sings a king's battle as ploughing, sowing and threshing and asks for elephants as his share; 374 to 380 are kinai-drummers' praises of the givers Ay, Nalliyathan, Perunarkilli, Ilanchetchenni and the lord of Nanjil.
source_issues: 361: the colophon has no thinai, thurai, poet or patron.
361 line 9: கொன்றுதன் kept; another edition reads கொன்றதன் (flagged). The review's line table says we lack a final line (site line 23).
363 line 9 and 366 line 22 are the same line (மடங்கல் உண்மை மாயமோ அன்றே); a shared kaanchi refrain, not a copying error.

366: lines 7, 12, 16 and 21 are broken; editions differ on lines 16 and 21 (one fills the lacuna and adds a line, with lines 16 to 19 in another order). The review lists 366 among poems whose line breaks differ.
370 line 1 is lost except its last syllable; the review says lines 1 and 2 read differently in another edition. 370 line 27 repeats 373 line 39, a closing formula of the களவழி poems.
370: the colophon patron reads செரப்பாழி இறிந்த, a misprint for எறிந்த (378's colophon has செரப்பாழி எறிந்த).
371: the review's line table says our text lacks the poem's first two lines (it starts at its third). Line 11 is broken. Line 21 களிற்றுக்கோட்ட டன்ன has a doubled ட (களிற்றுக்கோட்டன்ன).
372: the colophon thurai மறக்கள வேள்வி is normalised as மறக்களவேள்வி.

373: lines 9, 13, 14, 18, 22, 23, 27 and 32 are broken; lines 18 and 23 begin with a dead consonant (lost letters); the review lists 373 among poems with stray non-Tamil glyphs and lines 13, 18, 22 reading differently. Line 11 நெடுங்சுவர் is a misprint for நெடுஞ்சுவர்.
374 line 4 repeats 383 line 2, and line 6 repeats 397 line 10: formula lines of the kinai poems. The review says line 10 reads differently in another edition.
374 and 375: the poet is spelt உறையூர் ஏணிச்சேர் முடமோசியார் in 374 and உறையூர் ஏணிச்சேரி முடமோசியார் in 375.
377: lines 23 and 26 are broken; line 8 has a stray opening quotation mark; the review says the site lacks our line 22 and we lack two of its lines (line breaks differ).
378: the review says we lack a line (site line 17).

379: line 14 is broken; the review says lines 14 and 15 read differently in another edition. The colophon patron ஓய்மான்வில்லியாதன் lacks a space; the poem names வில்லி யாதன் (line 7). 376's colophon gives the same poet's patron as ஓய்மான் நல்லியாதன்.
380: lines 3, 8 and 13 are broken; the colophon fields were filled from Duraisamy Pillai's edition.

title: முள் எயிற்று மகளிர்!
reading: The poet tells Death, who roars like thunder before the rains and is never sated with lives, that this king does not fear its coming: he has poured gifts with water for learned sacrificing brahmins, given like a mother to many, given elephants to those who sing him and chariots to those who come to his feet, drunk the toddy his women held to his lips like nectar, and needs no one to tell him that the world does not last, for he learned it long ago.
nuance: The poem is addressed to Death, not to the king, and turns the kaanchi lesson round: the counsel that the world is unstable is declared unnecessary, because a life of giving and enjoying has already answered it. The colophon has no thinai, thurai or poet.

thinai_evidence.note: impermanence is the theme, set against a life of giving

title: உடம்பொடுஞ் சென்மார்!
reading: A king with a gem necklace like the sun and moon on his chest, a drum fed with offerings in his camp and an army dreadful as a demon, mighty as Death, having cleared his confusion, pours gift-water wide as the sea, gives land, rice and splendid jewels, and then, while his kin go home from the burning ground of small white bones, where crows and owls call even by day, saying 'he is no more', goes on with his body to the land of the high ones.
nuance: Lines 8 to 10 contrast what a brahmin's four Vedas aim at with aram and with substance (பொருள்); their syntax is hard and the reading here is tentative. The closing image, going to the high world with the body, makes the gifts the king's last act rather than his reward, and the burning ground is drawn with the same small-white-bone detail the kaanchi poems share.

thinai_evidence.note: a king's last giving before death, with the burning ground described

comparisons.tenor: the gift-water poured from his hand

title: உடம்பொடு நின்ற உயிரும் இல்லை!
reading: The kings who ruled the sea-girt earth alone, sharing it with none, are more than the sand the waves heap up, and all went to the burning ground and died while others took their lands; so listen: no life stays with the body for ever and death is no illusion; before the bitter day when, in the burning ground of cactus, you eat with the earth for your plate the saltless boiled rice that a man of low birth hands over without looking back, do the work you intended, renouncing the whole sea-bounded world.
nuance: The humiliation is precise: the funeral offering is boiled without salt, handed over by an outcaste who does not turn to look, and eaten off the ground. The king who held the world 'with no share to others' ends taking food from the lowest. What the deed to be done is (giving, or renunciation) is left open by செய்ந்நீ முன்னிய வினையே.

thinai_evidence.note: impermanence of kings argued to move a king to act

comparisons.tenor: the number of kings who have died

title: மகிழகம் வம்மோ!
reading: Let the bard-woman wear the unfading gold garland and the bard the gold lotus that blooms in no pool; let us roast the black ram on the red fire, turn the tongue over the spiced fat chunks in a toddy-reddened mouth, eat, devour and give to those who ask, and rejoice, warrior; for it will be hard, great one, when we have reached the great burning ground of urns, where the owl hoots suddenly from the hollow of an old tree with many roots split into the earth.
nuance: Kaanchi here means feasting, not renouncing: the same knowledge of death that makes 363 urge the king to give up the world makes this poet urge him to eat, drink and give now. The poet's name, கூகைக் கோரியார், is taken from the owl of line 12.

thinai_evidence.note: enjoy and give before the burning ground

title: நிலமகள் அழுத காஞ்சி!
reading: The wise say there is also a kaanchi in which the Earth, with the clouded sky for her face and the two moving lights for her eyes, wept: 'The ancestors who rolled the golden wheel of diamond hub and gem spokes before every battle and found no equal have gone, yet I do not go, and many still claim to be over me like a woman whose beauty is bought; I do not wish to live.'
nuance: The kaanchi is told from the side of the land, not the king: kings pass while the Earth stays, and her lament is not for their deaths but for being possessed by one after another, which she likens to a courtesan's lot. The poem presents itself as a report of a known kaanchi (உண்டென உரைப்பரால்), a poem about a genre.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem names its own kind as kaanchi: the earth's lament over passing kings

comparisons.tenor: the Earth claimed by many kings

title: மாயமோ அன்றே!
reading: Even the great ones who ruled alone, whose drum roared like snake-striking thunder with one command through the land, set up their fame and died; so, son of the wise one, lord of warriors, hear me: [the text is broken here] use the day for effort and the night for weighing what is to come, drink sweet toddy in fine vessels with red-eyed women like a great ox released from the plough, give food and rice without stint, fell bulls and share the roast in every grove on the sandy bank, for death is real and no illusion.
nuance: Four lines are broken (7, 12, 16, 21), so the order of counsel is partly lost. What remains balances work by day (ஞாயிற்று எல்லை ஆள்வினைக்கு உதவி) with feasting and giving, and ends on the same line as 363. The colophon's patron தருமபுத்திரன் answers the poem's address அறிவோன் மகனே.

thinai_evidence.note: kings' deaths used to counsel a living king

comparisons.tenor: the king at his ease after labour

title: வாழச் செய்த நல்வினை!
reading: Avvaiyar tells three crowned kings seated together, fair as the three sacred fires of the twice-born: the lands you hold do not go with you but stay for others; so pour flowers and gold with water into brahmins' hands, drink the toddy women bring in gold cups, scatter jewels to suppliants and live the days allotted, since only the good done while living is a raft when you sink; and may your days outnumber the stars and the raindrops.
nuance: Blessing and warning are one poem: the kaanchi doctrine that possessions stay behind is the reason given for the court's pleasures and gifts, and the blessing that closes it counts days, not conquests. The kings are not named; the colophon gives no patron.

thinai_evidence.note: a blessing addressed to kings, with counsel inside it

comparisons.tenor: the round earth the kings hold
the good deed done while living

title: பாடி வந்தது இதற்கோ?
reading: A drummer tells the Chera that he came to scoop up elephants, but all fell to arrows like hills that stop the clouds; chariots, but they lie broken on the ground; horses, but they lie dead and wounded in the flood of blood like ships becalmed; so on this cruel field where beggars grieve with nothing to take, ploughman whose plough is the sword, all his singing was to ask for the gem necklace on the king's chest.
nuance: The poem praises by complaint: the king's battle was so destructive that there is no war booty left to give, so the bard asks for the necklace he wears. The request formula முகக்குவம் எனின் (if we would scoop) frames the whole poem, as 372 and 371 use முகவை.

thinai_evidence.note: the king's victory sung by a bard at the battlefield

comparisons.tenor: the dead horses sunk in blood

title: போர்க்களமும் ஏர்க்களமும்!
reading: The bard sings the Chera's battle as a season of rain and tillage: elephants for clouds, swords for lightning, the drum for thunder, horses for wind, arrows for rain; chariots plough the wet field from dawn, spears sow it, fallen heads are the green crop, corpses the stacked sheaves that the demon-woman holds, jackals and ghouls thresh and spirits guard the heap; and he asks the lord of this field for a gift of elephants, cows like the gold-peaked Himalaya and their calves.
nuance: This is the fullest form of the ploughing figure that 368 compresses into one epithet and 373's colophon names ஏர்க்கள உருவகம். The bard's request is placed exactly where a harvest's share would fall, after the threshing, so the allegory carries a claim: the drummer is owed a portion of this crop as a labourer is of grain.

thinai_evidence.note: the king's battle as harvest, with the bard's claim

title: பழுமரம் உள்ளிய பறவை!
reading: With his large family starved to eating fibre and bark, the drummer crossed the parched long road where the owl's call answers the kite's mate in the uzhinjil fork and the bamboo has dried, and came like a bird to a fruiting tree to the field where weapons rained down fruit, blood flooded the ground, corpses were reaped, heaped and threshed with elephants for oxen; praising the field, he asks for elephants with iron-capped tusks, while the demon-woman dances decked in entrails and vultures circle.
nuance: The bard's hunger and the field's plenty are set side by side: the starving family of the opening is fed, in the figure, by the harvest of corpses. The first line is lost, and the review notes the opening lines read differently in another edition.

thinai_evidence.note: the battlefield praised as a harvest by a bard seeking a gift

comparisons.tenor: the bard coming to the king

title: பொருநனின் வறுமை!
reading: Finding no patron in the wide world, sleeping hungry under trees, his hair dressed with alari flowers tied on fibre, carrying his drum-bag and a useless broken pot with no rice in it, the drummer crossed the hard way to the camp, remembering the fame of the king's bow-plough that heaps headless corpses and threshes them with the elephant for ox; beating his moon-like drum he has come for an elephant, while the demon-woman, tasting fat and garlanded with entrails, blesses the giver of such plenty to live longer than the stars.
nuance: The demon-woman's blessing (வாழியர் ... பல) is the bard's own blessing displaced: the creature fed by the battle thanks the king, and the drummer, fed by nothing yet, asks to be next. According to the review's line table our text begins at the poem's third line.

thinai_evidence.note: the king's battle as threshing, with the bard's request

comparisons.tenor: the gleam of the iron weapons
the years wished for the king

title: ஆரம் முகக்குவம் எனவே!
reading: The drummer says all his praise was to ask for the king's moon-bright necklace: the king performed a sacrifice in the battlefield, where swords flashed and arrows rained, with enemy heads for the hearth, vilva wood for fuel and a vanni ladle, the demon who never bore a child stirring the pot, the cook holding up the lump of flesh, and the blessing 'may the ghoul-water poured in hot mouths fill all the new guests of this wedding feast'.
nuance: The sacrifice is a full parody of a Vedic rite and of a wedding feast at once, with every ritual item replaced by a battle one. Mangudi Kizhar uses the same figure of a feast cooked on crowned heads in 26 for the same king; here it is the preface to a request.

thinai_evidence.note: the king's battle as a field-sacrifice, praised by a bard

title: நின்னோர் அன்னோர் இலரே!
reading: The poet hails the victorious Chola who defeated the Kongu people: drums roared like thunder, war elephants were clouds, chariots and horses rain; swords dripped blood as if wrung; women left their high-walled houses; enemy kings turned their backs; mansions fell in flames like hills struck by thunder; he made the courtyard of Vanji a threshing floor and threshed the fearless warriors there; others came to every king's field for elephants, and he too, beating his drum for love, has come to this lord of the fearful field.
nuance: Eight lines are broken (9, 13, 14, 18, 22, 23, 27, 32), so the sequence of siege, sack and request is only partly recoverable. The colophon's second thurai, ஏர்க்கள உருவகம், names the ploughing figure that 368 to 372 share.

thinai_evidence.note: a city taken, its sack sung as threshing, with the bard's request

title: அண்டிரன் போல்வையோ ஞாயிறு?
reading: At dawn in the cold dew, his thin hair damp like the gold-lit forehead of a blackbuck, leaning on the hill by the jackfruit of the common ground, the drummer sang the kurinji melody so that the stags listened, in the land where tiger-toothed boys and deer-eyed women heap porcupine meat, ripe sandal and elephant tusks on tiger skins as tribute; and he asks the sun whether it too has the generosity of Ay Andiran, or whether it shines in the sky for nothing.
nuance: The standard praise likens a giver to the sun or rain; this poem turns the measure round and finds the sun wanting. The colophon's பூவைநிலை usually names comparison of a king to a god; here the comparison is put as a challenge to the sky.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a patron's giving by a challenge to the sun

title: பாடன்மார் எமரே!
reading: Lodging in a corner of a ruined common hall with leaning pillars, his drum bundled with palmyra fibre and strips, never entering the ploughmen's households and asking who will take on his wretched life of begging by turns, the drummer came to Ay of unfailing giving thinking of him alone, as great rain spreads over the sea; so may Ay live on earth as the poets' home, and in a world empty of him let there be no patrons, lest our people sing kings of meritless wealth who understand nothing.
nuance: The close is a curse on the alternative more than a blessing: if Ay goes, the poet would rather there were no patrons than have his people praise kings who, told great things, grasp not even small ones. Lines 17 and 18 can be read otherwise, and the reading of நிலவன்மாரோ புரவலர் is uncertain.

thinai_evidence.note: praise and blessing of a patron by a needy bard

comparisons.tenor: the bard coming to Ay alone

title: கிணைக்குரல் செல்லாது!
reading: Just after sunset the drummer, holding his drum with its torn straps, stood at the granary of the patron's rich house; as the moon rose and drove off the dark, the great one saw his strange gaunt shape and his cloth worn to holes, called him a pitiable guest, stopped his song, and that same night gave him toddy fierce as an angry snake and roast meat and cleared his hell-like want; since that day he has not thought of begging, and his little drum has never sounded at the gates of other givers.
nuance: The gift is praised by its consequence: one night's giving ended a career of asking. The patron interrupts the song before it is sung (நின்ற முரற்கை நீக்கி), so the giving is not a payment for praise.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard's report of a patron's gift

title: நாடு அவன் நாடே!
reading: In the dewy watches of the night, his hair wet, the drummer came to the palace where the king slept and sang 'may the gods guard him, may the righteous one live'; the king, whom men call the one comparison for others with none for himself, saw him and called the far-travelling drummer his patron, and gave him, as if in a dream but awake, gems from the hills, gold from the forests, pearls from the sea, fine cloth and pots of toddy; and the poet blesses the victorious lord of the sea-loud army to last long.
nuance: Lines 10 and 11 state a theory of praise inside a praise poem: the king is the standard others are compared to, and nothing is his standard. The king's calling the bard 'patron to us' (நீ புரவலை எமக்கு) inverts the roles of giver and receiver. Two lines are broken.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a king's giving to a drummer

title: எஞ்சா மரபின் வஞ்சி!
reading: In the Chola's palace, with stucco terraces like the new moon and a long hall cool as a pool, the drummer sang the vanji theme and the king showered on him more precious jewels than were ever meant for such as he; his long-starved kin put finger rings on their ears and ear rings on their fingers, waist chains on their necks and neck chains on their waists, like the red-faced monkey clan that found the jewels Sita dropped when the demon carried her from Rama, and had unending laughter; after great suffering he has become head of a large clan.
nuance: The Ramayana is cited for comedy: the monkeys decking themselves with Sita's jewels are the bard's family who have never owned ornaments. It is one of the few Sangam references to the Rama story, and it presupposes that the jewel episode was well known to the audience.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a king through the bard's report of his gift

comparisons.tenor: the bard's kin wearing the jewels wrongly

title: இலங்கை கிழவோன்!
reading: Let me have life in the shade of his feet and let him have my tongue's praise: hearing your drummer say 'we are drummers of Villiyathan, lord of Ilangai of rich paddy, where reapers whose sickles blunt whet them on the curved back of a mud tortoise taking it for a stone; our lord melts fragrant ghee and gives daily rice and knows how to end hunger', my longing did not abate, and leaving the sky-touching hills behind I came like a child to its mother to that rich town whose fragrant smoke veils the streets like rain-mist.
nuance: The poem is built on report: the patron's fame reaches the poet through another drummer's speech, which the poem quotes, so one bard's praise becomes another bard's road. The tortoise mistaken for a whetstone makes the land's fertility comic and exact. Line 8 is obscure and line 14 broken.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a patron by a bard who comes to him

comparisons.tenor: the bard coming to the patron
the fragrant smoke over the streets

title: சேய்மையும் அணிமையும்!
reading: The lord of Nanjil of the sweet jackfruit, a strong warrior of the Pandya, who wears pearls of the southern sea and sandal of the northern hill, in whose land rain becomes pearl in the sea and fragrant wild flowers flourish, is far beyond thought to those who meet him in enmity and close as the palm to those who come in friendship; because he is such, though this land should fall into want, the loneliness of the poet's family is gone and it has blossomed.
nuance: Three lines are broken (3, 8, 13), and line 12 mentions a Kandan of the strong spear whose relation to the patron is lost. The colophon fields were filled from Duraisamy Pillai's edition.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a chief through what he has done for the bard's family

title: புறநானூறு 381-400
theme: The last twenty poems of the Purananuru are almost all bards' gate poems (கடைநிலை, இயன்மொழி, வாழ்த்தியல், பரிசில் விடை): a kinai or thadari drummer comes at dawn to a chief's gate, often driven by famine (Venus in the south), sings, and is answered by the same ritual of rags exchanged for fine cloth, toddy, meat and rice, after which he swears to sing no other patron. Their argument is that giving is the giver's glory and the bard's memory its return.
source_issues: 381: the poet field reads புறத்திணை நன்னகனார் while 384, by the same poet for the same patron, reads புறத்திணை நன்னாகனார் (the flag notes the tvu reading நன்னாகனார்); line 6 has a closing quotation mark with no matching opening.
382 line 10 is the edition variant the flag records; line 12 யங்கேள் and line 13 கட்கேள்விக் look corrupt; the review's table says our text lacks a line the site has (site line 11).
383: lines 14, 15, 19 and 20 are gaps; we have 23 lines against 25 in Duraisamy Pillai's edition, and the review notes the site breaks the lines differently.
384: lines 5, 10 and 13 are gaps (line 5 is full in one edition); line 10 repeats in 396 line 14; the review notes the site breaks the lines differently.
386 line 12: a stray space before the comma (புறவே ,); the review's table says our text lacks a line the site has (site line 21).
390 line 26 is a full-line gap.
393 line 22 has a gap and is read differently in each edition; line 2 is the edition variant the flag records (கூமை against கூர்மை).
395 line 25 has a gap.
396 lines 21 and 22 have gaps.

397: the patron field reads கோழன் குளமுற்றத்துத் துஞ்சிய கிள்ளி வளவன், a misprint for சோழன்; the colophon thurai has two thurais (பரிசில் விடை; கடைநிலை விடையும் ஆம்), recorded as two puram_thurai items.
398 line 2 has a gap; line 28 ends with a full stop in the middle of the sentence.
399: the poet field ஐயூற் முடவனார் is a misprint for ஐயூர் முடவனார்; line 8 has a gap.
400 lines 12 and 18 have gaps.
381 and 388: the thurai is spelt இயன் மொழி in 381 and இயன்மொழி elsewhere; puram_thurai name normalised to இயன்மொழி.

title: கரும்பனூரன் காதல் மகன்!
tamil: சிறுநனி, ஒருவழிப் படர்க’ என் றோனே - எந்தை,
reading: After the bards had feasted long on meat and sweet milk-and-jaggery drinks and asked leave to go home, the chief of Venkatam, the son of the Karumban town man, afraid of their parting, told the kinai player that he would end his poverty and set him a sign to come back by after the summer rains, which the poet praises as a ferry that carries great and small in turn.
nuance: The chief fears the bard's leaving (எம்பிரிவு அஞ்சி), the word akam uses for lovers' separation, so the host-guest bond is spoken of as a bond of love. The opening quotation marks are unbalanced, so where the chief's speech begins (line 5 or line 15) is uncertain, and the simile of rain on a barren tangle (lines 8 to 10) may describe the wasted wealth of misers or the bard's wasted waiting.

thinai_evidence.note: a chief's speech of giving to a departing bard, told in praise of him

comparisons.tenor: the bard's labour at the gates of rich kings who do not give
the chief who carries great and small alike without forgetting

title: கேட்டொறும் நடுங்க ஏத்துவேன்!
tamil: நினதே, முந்நீர் உடுத்த இவ் வியன் உலகு, அறிய;
reading: The porunar declare they want only Nalankilli of the cool Chola land and will sing no other patron; fed and freed from hunger, the bard asks leave to go, saying the sea-girt world is the king's but his own part is to praise him in other kings' courts with his drum, so that his enemies tremble each time they hear it as the drumstick quivers each time it strikes.
nuance: The bard sells a service, not only thanks: praise sung in rival courts is to frighten the king's enemies. Lines 10 to 15 (the children who left, the snake shedding its skin) are hard to construe and one edition reads line 10 differently.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard at a king's gate praising him and asking leave

comparisons.tenor: the clear eye of the kinai drum
the king's enemies trembling at each hearing of his praise

title: வெள்ளி நிலை பரிகோ!
tamil: பிறர், பாடுபுகழ் பாடிப் படர்பு அறி யேனே;
reading: Rising at cockcrow in the cold dawn, the bard beat his small drum at the long gate, blessed the bullocks and praised the chief, who clothed him in cloth fine as a snake's slough; reborn as it were, he will sing no other patron, since he has one man, Aviyan of the tall chariot, and need not fear whatever the drought-star Venus portends.
nuance: அழித்துப் பிறந்தனென் (line 16): the gift is felt as a second birth. The last line ties the bard's security to the patron against the omen of Venus, a motif this chapter repeats (384, 386, 388).

thinai_evidence.note: a bard at the gate who rests his life on one patron

title: நெல் என்னாம்! பொன் என்னாம்!
reading: The kinai player describes the chief's land, where the heron sleeps on the vanji branch and the hare starts among the millet and farmers' bowls hold fish and toddy without a festival, and says that though he tried to stop him the chief kept giving paddy, gold and toddy, feeding with fat rice and ghee for fame; such a protector he had, so he knew only the day that came and never counted what was spent, whatever Venus foretold.
nuance: The colophon's thurai, கையறுநிலை, makes this a lament for a dead patron; the poem itself has only the past tense புரந்தோன் and அன்னோனை உடையேம் என்ப, which allows it but never says he is dead. The opening sets the soft wet land (மென் பாலான்) against the hard dry land (வன் பாலான்), both rich.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a chief's unstinting giving in a bard's voice

title: காவிரி அணையும் படப்பை!
reading: The bard had not even come to his gate, but hearing his drum at another man's door at dawn, the lord of Ambar took pity, stripped off his earth-eaten rags, dressed him in white and ended his hunger; the poet wishes good Aruvanthai more years than the raindrops on Pulli's Venkatam.
nuance: The gift came unasked: the chief heard the drum at someone else's gate and called the bard in. புல்லிய (line 10) can be read as 'of Pulli', naming the chief of Venkatam whom akam poets also name, or as an epithet; the link to Akananuru 61 takes the first reading.

thinai_evidence.note: a blessing for a patron who gave without being asked

comparisons.vehicle: வேங்கட விறல்வரைப் பட்ட ஓங்கல் வானத்து உறையினும் பலவே

title: வேண்டியது உணர்ந்தோன்!
reading: Killi Valavan gave so that his bards ate ghee-fried meat and milk food and knew the sweat of hot eating but never the sweat of work; his land holds paddy fields, herds with no bandits, ships counted under the punnai and salt traders on the backwaters, and his bards, who never fight, wish long life to the feet of the one who knew their want, whichever way Venus moves.
nuance: The four lands (வயலே, புறவே, கடலே, கழியே) are listed as one king's territory, a whole landscape in a single puram catalogue. பொரா அப் பொருநரேம், porunar who do not fight, plays on பொருநர் as both bard and warrior.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king's gifts and the lands that feed them

comparisons.tenor: the ghee spattering from the frying meat

title: சிறுமையும் தகவும்!
reading: The bard sang Chelvakkadungo Vazhiyathan as the king whose elephants break enemy walls and bring tribute that ends his supplicants' poverty; the king did not look down on the singer's smallness but gave by the measure of his own greatness elephants, horses, herds and fields so many that they seemed a dream given in waking, and the poet wishes him years more than the Porunai's sand and the paddy of its fields.
nuance: The poem names its own principle of measure: the gift is sized by the giver's greatness, not by the receiver's smallness (lines 20, 21). The list of gifts asked as questions (என்கோ) recurs in 396.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard's praise and blessing of a Chera king's gift

comparisons.tenor: the years wished on the king

title: நூற்கையும் நா மருப்பும்!
reading: When Venus stood in the south and the fields withered in a barren season, the drummer went to Pannan of Sirukudi, who saw his state and gave until his trouble fled; the bard swears that if he fails to sing Pannan every day, may the protection his kin have from Vazhuthi, the Pandya of the elephant army, fail.
nuance: The closing oath stakes the protection of a Pandya king on the bard's loyalty to a village landholder, so the small patron's gift binds the bard as firmly as a king's. Lines 8 to 11 (the tongue as ploughshare, the plough and the drum) can be construed more than one way.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard's report of a landholder who fed him in famine

comparisons.tenor: the tongue of truthful speech used as a ploughshare

title: நெய்தல் கேளன்மார்!
reading: Athanungan, lord of Venkatam where elephant calves are tied in the village common while their mothers grieve, gave to the young porunan asking only to be remembered when the drought dries the palmyra and the neem; the bard asks the patron he now addresses to give like Athanungan and end his family's hunger, so that the women of his house never hear the dirge at his gate.
nuance: The giver asks the receiver to remember him (எம்மும் உள்ளுமோ), so the patron himself treats the bard's memory as the return on the gift. The colophon names Athanungan as patron, though the poem holds him up as a model to a second patron it does not name.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard holds up one giver's words as a model to another patron

title: காண்பறியலரே!
reading: At the guarded house that only well-wishers approach, the poet beat her drum for days; on the night she arrived the chief called the poor bard in, stripped the rag like old pond moss from her waist, dressed her in new cloth, served toddy and meat rice in silver vessels, sent red paddy in stacks to her family resting at the village common and told her to take it as plunder; kings with elephants do not even know such feeding.
nuance: கொண்டி, the word for war booty, is used for a gift: the bard is told to carry off the paddy as soldiers carry off plunder. The closing sets the chief above crowned kings, who cannot know such hunger-ending. The colophon gives Athiyaman; the poem does not name him, and lines 1 and 2 and the gap at line 26 are hard.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard's account of a chief's feeding at his gate

comparisons.tenor: the yard of the chief's house

title: வேலி ஆயிரம் விளைக!
reading: When the northern land of Venkatam, rich in paddy and toddy feasts, fell into famine, the bard brought his large family south and asked in the old town for the house that relieves want; those who knew the chief recognised him as the poor porunan who had come before, so he has come to see the chief, and wishes him sweet sleep with his wife in his house among the punnai where herons roost, and fields that yield a thousandfold.
nuance: The bard's credentials are his known poverty: those who know the chief vouch for him because he came before and is still poor (lines 11 to 13). The blessing of rain at its time (துளிபதன் அறிந்து) answers the famine that drove him south.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard arrives at a patron's gate and blesses him

title: அமிழ்தம் அன்ன கரும்பு!
reading: At dawn at the gate of Ezhini of the Athiyar, the poet beat her one-eyed drum and hailed him as the daily ploughman who yokes donkeys on the bloody fields of conquered forts and sows white varagu and horse-gram; that day he took off her rags, clothed her in fine cloth, poured aged toddy into golden cups and gave food and a guest's share, the descendant of the one who brought sugarcane here like heaven's ambrosia.
nuance: The conqueror's destruction is sung as farming: donkeys plough the ruined fort and poor men's grains are sown where a city stood, a curse dressed as praise of his diligence (வைகல் உழவ). The sugarcane brought from heaven is the Athiyar house's own legend.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard at the gate of a conqueror, praised and fed

comparisons.tenor: the king who lays waste enemy forts

title: பழங்கண் வாழ்க்கை!
reading: Wandering with his kin, their pots long empty and no one in other lands who knows the duty of feeding them, the bard came thinking of Killi Valavan's fame and asks him to end his family's hunger with fat meat heaped like summer cotton bales, to strip his rags and dress him in cloth like a new pakanrai flower and give lasting wealth, promising to beat his moon-white drum and sing the sword-true Valavan of the Kaviri land.
nuance: குடிமுறை பாடி (line 3): the bard's family sings lineages by inherited order, so asking is a hereditary office, not a lapse. Line 22 has a gap and is read differently in other editions.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard's request for gifts at a king's gate

comparisons.vehicle: கோடைப் பருத்தி வீடுநிறை பெய்த மூடைப் பண்டம்
comparisons.tenor: the white fat meat asked for

title: என்றும் செல்லேன்!
reading: The poet warns other poets not to set their hopes on Kuttuvan, however the world praises his generosity: when he sang the king's father's war-song, Kuttuvan gave him a killer elephant; when the terrified bard sent it back, the king, ashamed it had seemed too small, gave a bigger one; so the bard will never go to his land again, however his family suffers.
nuance: Praise by mock complaint: the warning to poets is a boast that the gift outran anything a bard could use. The king reads the return of his gift as a judgment that it was too small (சிறிதென உணர்ந்தமை நாணி), so the giver's shame, not the receiver's need, sets the size of the second gift. வாடா வஞ்சி (line 9) names what the bard sang, a war-march song.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a patron's giving in the mock form of a warning

title: அவிழ் நெல்லின் அரியல்!
reading: After a picture of Pidavur's rich fields, where farmers eat old rice with hare and fish and women drive off parrots, the bard says he is of Sathan's kin: arriving at dusk after a day on the hot road, he was given rare vessels at once, without delay or long speech, and the chief showed his wife and told her to care for him as for himself; since then the bard thinks of no one else, for even in drought the house keeps feeding him.
nuance: The chief makes his wife the bard's keeper (என்போல் போற்று), so the gift becomes a standing place in the household. The phrase 'not stopping, not saying much' (lines 27, 28) makes speed and few words part of the gift. The drought images of lines 33 to 35 show the giving does not depend on the season.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard at a patron's gate recounts how he was received

comparisons.tenor: the long grains of cooked rice

title: பாடல்சால் வளன்!
reading: In Vattaru, where fish move in the low water and flowers like eyes bloom on the high, birds are driven off with drums and the Kosar dance the kuravai over toddy, Ezhiniyathan is strength to the weak and kin to the kinless; his kinai players list his roasts, toddy, hare-fat rice and open stores, say there is no bound to their wealth, and wish his fame to shine like the moon among the stars.
nuance: 'Strength to those without strength, kin to those without kin' (lines 10, 11) gives the chief's charity a social reach beyond bards. The list of foods in question form (என்கோ) is the same device as 387. Lines 21 and 22 have a gap.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard's praise of a chief's land and table

comparisons.tenor: the flowers on the upper water

comparisons.vehicle: மீன் நாப்பண் விரி கதிர வெண் திங்களின்

title: தண் நிழலேமே!
reading: At dawn in the guarded war camp, when Venus rose and birds called and drums and conch sounded, the bard beat his drum and bade the garlanded king wake; pleased, Valavan gave him fried meat, fragrant toddy, cloth like a snake's slough and rare jewels, pouring like rain to end his summer heat, so the bard fears nothing even if the sea runs dry or the sun rises in the south, living in the cool shade of his feet.
nuance: The dawn song is a wake-up call in a war camp (ஏமப் பாசறை), so the bard serves the king's day as well as his fame. The final boast sets the patron's protection against cosmic upheaval, a claim of security that the ethics books would deny any wealth.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard's wake-up song in a camp and the gift that answered it

comparisons.tenor: the sacrificial fires of the brahmins
the protection of the king's feet

title: துரும்புபடு சிதா அர்!
reading: At dawn, as the moon hid and Venus rose, cocks cried and bards played their lutes, the poet came to Vanjan of true word, whose old town is open to friends and shut to enemies like a cave where tigers sleep, and beat his drum asking that the king stay unfailing for them; glad at the small offering, the king took off the bard's rags, dressed him in cloth like rising smoke, filled a bowl like spat fire with clear toddy, fed his kin deer meat and rice, and gave the flowered cloth and gem necklace from his own body.
nuance: 'Rejoicing greatly at a small thing' (line 17) turns the usual scale: the king is grateful for the bard's coming. The cloth from the king's own body (புரையோன் மேனிப் பூந்துகில்) is the most intimate gift of the chapter. Line 2 has a gap, and பாயல் in the last line may be a place name.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard's account of a Chera chief's dawn reception

comparisons.tenor: the town that enemies cannot approach

title: கடவுட்கும் தொடேன்!
tamil: பகடே அத்தை யான் வேண்டிவந் தது’ என,
reading: After a picture of the rich Kaviri gardens of Killi Valavan, where field workers eat fish curry and boiled rice, the bard says he would go to no other face; living on bitter-gourd gruel his drum-wife cooked with fish from his own line, he sat apart in ruin, until, restringing his broken drum, he sang Thonrikkon as the most righteous and most valiant and asked only for a strong bullock for his cart, and before he had finished wanting it the chief gave a herd of many colours like stars with a cart.
nuance: The bard's own catch and his wife's gruel are counted as ruin (அழிவுகொண்டு), so living by one's own labour is the state the patron's gift rescues him from. How the opening picture of Valavan's land joins the gift of Thonrikkon is unclear (lines 12 to 14, a gap at line 8, line 26).

thinai_evidence.note: a bard's request and its fulfilment by a hill chief

title: உலகு காக்கும் உயர் கொள்கை!
reading: In the last watch of the night at full moon, the bard sounded his drum, round like the moon seen over the sea, and sang the king's lineage; the king, who stays awake while others sleep to guard the world, heard it and, still not satisfied, took away his old rag and gave fine vessels and cloth, so the bard is drunk on fresh toddy every day and has lost count of time; he drives off not only his own enemies but the hunger of those who come to him, lord of the town where ships are tied at every ford to the sacrificial post.
nuance: 'Hunger-enemy' (பசிப்பகை) sets the king's charity beside his wars as a second campaign of the same kind. The ships moored to the sacrificial post join trade and Vedic ritual in one image. Lines 12 and 18 have gaps.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a king's watchfulness and giving

comparisons.vehicle: வெண் திங்கள் மூ வைந்தான் முறை முற்றக், கடல் நடுவண் கண்ட

comparisons.tenor: hunger as an enemy to be driven off

title: திருமுருகாற்றுப்படை
theme: Thirumurugatruppadai is a guide poem in which one who has received the god's grace directs another seeker to Murugan: after a 66-line opening sentence that ends in the promise that the seeker will have what he wants, it describes the god at six places (Parankunram, Alaivay, Avinankudi, Eragam, every hill, and Pazhamudircholai with all the places of his worship), each with its own worshippers, and closes by scripting the seeker's praise, the god's appearance and his gift, and the waterfall of his hill.
structure_note: Six sections, each closing on a refrain of right (உரியன், அதாஅன்று; நின்றதன் பண்பே). Twelve of the 21 core units were moved to sentence breaks inside the sections, giving 18 units.
source_issues: Throughout the text the comitative ending -ஒடு after ய and some other letters is printed -அடு (தெய்வ வுத்தியடு 23, ஓடையடு 79, கூகையடு 49, வள்ளியடு 102, மடந்தையடு 175, குளவியடு 191, கொடியடு 219, 227, தொகுதியடு 212, அருவியடு 240, மஞ்சளடு 235): this looks like an encoding loss of the vowel sign ொ, like the TSCII repairs flagged at lines 39, 285 and 291. Karu forms are copied as printed.
Line 173 மருங்கிந்தம் looks like a misprint for மருங்கில் தம்.
Line 188 பெரிந்துஉவந்து looks like a misprint for பெரிது உவந்து.

Line 295 prints நல்கும்;அதி, which reads more naturally as one word with the particle -மதி (நல்குமதி); the semicolon may be an editorial or encoding error. The sentence break used for the units (after பரிசில் நல்கும்) does not depend on it.
Line 314 கருந்கோட்டு has an irregular nasal (expected கருங்கோட்டு).

unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 1-16: the opening description of the god closes at மார்பினன் in line 11, and line 12 turns to his hill and its women.
reading: The god's far-reaching brightness is first likened to the sun that the world praises, rising out of the sea; then he is named by his works, feet that bore up those who came to him and a great hand that wore down his foes, as the husband of a bright-browed woman of spotless chastity, wearing on his chest a cool rolling garland from the kadamba of a forest freshly soaked by the first rains.
nuance: Lines 4 and 5 are built as a pair (உறுநர்த் தாங்கிய ... நோன்றாள், செறுநர்த் தேய்த்த ... தடக்கை): the same god is shelter to those who come and ruin to those who oppose, which is the whole promise the guide will make. The consort of line 6 is not named.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the god's form and deeds: கடவுள் வாழ்த்து, under paadaan (porul 2.27)

comparisons.tenor: the great hand that wore down his enemies

unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 1-16, 17-32 and 33-48: lines 12 to 44 are one description of the hill's women and the god's garland. This unit takes the women's adornment to line 37, where they toss the vila shoots, before the song they sing in line 38.
reading: On the god's high hill, women with anklets on small red feet, cloth as red as the cochineal insect and girdles strung with coins dress their parted hair with vetchi and kuvalai petals, set a tilakam on the brow, tuck in champak and marutham clusters, hang pindi shoots in their ears, smear their young breasts with sandal paste and vengai pollen, and pluck and toss the tender leaves of the vila tree.
nuance: The women are not named until line 41 (சூரர மகளிர், the fearsome maidens of the hill), so this long toilet scene is a description of goddesses of the slope, not of mortal girls; the flowers they wear are of every land, and the poem does not comment on it.

thinai_evidence.note: a description of the god's hill and its women inside the praise; no love situation is stated

comparisons.tenor: the scent of the sandal paste

unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 33-48 and 49-66: begins with the women's song in line 38 and ends at line 66, where முன்னிய வினையே closes the poem's first sentence.
reading: The women sing 'long live the victorious cock banner' and dance in a grove on a slope so dense even the female monkey does not know it; the god wears on his head a cool garland of kaanthal that bees do not swarm, and with his long bright spear entered the cold old sea and cut down Sur at the root, while a dread demoness with dry hair and rolling eyes, owl and snake hanging from her ears, held up a skull and danced the thunangai of the battlefield; this red-speared god of flawless victory is the one, the guide says, that you will reach at once if your heart desires to go to his red feet.
nuance: The poem's first sentence runs 66 lines before its main verb: the sunrise, the hill, the women and the war on Sur all lead to the promise இன்னே பெறுதி நீ முன்னிய வினையே (66), so the whole description serves as the guide's grounds for that promise. Lines 57 and 58 (இருபே ருருவின் ஒருபே ரியாக்கை / அறுவேறு வகையின்) are hard: whether the great body of two forms is Sur's or the god's, and what the six ways are, I cannot settle from the words alone.

thinai_evidence.note: the god's victory over Sur, praised; the battle is the god's deed, so the thinai stays paadaan

reading: He also has a right to dwell on the hill west of Koodal, the city of crowded mansion streets whose gate, hung with tall war banners, ball and doll, has worn down its enemies; there bees sleep in the thorny-stemmed lotus of the wide muddy fields, hum on the honeyed neythal at dawn, and when the sun is up swarm humming round the pool flowers that open like eyes on the hill.
nuance: The bees' day, from field lotus to dawn neythal to the hill pool, joins the city's farmland to the god's hill: the shrine is placed by walking the eye from the walled city out to the slope, and the war-scarred gate of Koodal is the first thing the seeker passes.

thinai_evidence.note: the first of the god's dwelling places, praised; the refrain உரியன் names his right to each

comparisons.tenor: the pool flowers opening at sunrise

unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 78-90 and 91-108: the six faces (91 to 102) belong with the faces introduced in line 90, and line 103 (ஆங்குஅம் மூவிருமுகனும்) sums them up and turns to the twelve hands.
reading: At Alaivay he rides an elephant fast as the wind and irresistible as Death, its scarred, striped brow carrying an unfading garland and frontlet and bells ringing at its sides; gems of five kinds flash like lightning in his crown, gold earrings shine like stars clasping the moon, and each of his six faces does a work: one spreads rays so the dark world shines, one gladly grants boons to those who praise, one watches over the sacrifices of brahmins who keep the mantra rule, one lights the directions like the moon as it searches out the meanings left over, one crushes enemies in battle with a wrathful heart, and one smiles with Valli, the young kuravar girl with a waist like a creeper.
nuance: The six faces are a list of offices (light, boon, sacrifice, knowledge, war, love) rather than a portrait; only the last face is turned toward one person, Valli, and she is placed among the kuravar of the hill, not among the gods.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the god's form and deeds: கடவுள் வாழ்த்து, under paadaan (porul 2.27)

comparisons.tenor: the flashing of the crown's gems
the gold earrings shining around the face
the face that lights the directions

unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 91-108 and 109-125: begins at line 103, which sums up the six faces and turns to the twelve hands, and ends at the Alaivay refrain in line 125.
reading: As the six faces keep their order, each of the twelve hands does its part: one raised for the sages who travel the sky, one at the waist, one on the thigh, one driving the goad, two whirling shield and spear, one at the chest, one with the garland, one swinging the bangle aloft, one ringing the bell, one pouring rain from the blue sky, one crowning the heavenly women with the wedding garland; and with the sky's instruments, horns, white conches and thunder-voiced drums sounding and the peacock crying on his victory banner, he goes swiftly by the sky road to Alaivay, which the world praises: dwelling there is his settled nature.
nuance: Where the faces were given offices in the world, the hands are given gestures, and two of them (rain, line 116; the wedding garland, line 117) reach out to the sky and its women. The god reaches his sea shrine by the sky road (விசும்பு ஆறாக), not over land.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the god's form and deeds: கடவுள் வாழ்த்து, under paadaan (porul 2.27)

unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 126-142 and 143-159: the sages (126 to 137) and the musicians with their women (138 to 147) are one procession that closes at விளங்க in line 147; line 148 begins the first of the three great gods.
reading: At Avinankudi the sages go first: clothed in bark, hair white as the valampuri conch, bodies shining, deerskin on chests where the flesh has wasted, bones showing, fasting for many days, minds rid of hostility and hatred, knowing what the learned do not and themselves the limit of the learned, having cast out lust and fierce anger and knowing no distress; after them come musicians in spotless clothes like smoke, their gentle hearts trained to the lute, plucking its sweet strings, with flawless women whose bodies glow like mango shoots and whose skin is spotted like gold on a touchstone.
nuance: The sages are described almost wholly by what they have removed (flesh, food, hostility, lust, anger, distress), and that list is what gives them the right to walk in first, ahead of the gods of the next lines.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the ascetic's excellence in his own calling, the தாபதப் பக்கம் of vaakai (porul 2.16)

comparisons.tenor: the spots on the women's skin

unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 143-159: begins at line 148, where the three great gods begin, after the sages' procession closes at 147; ends at line 159 with the third god (செல்வனும்).
reading: Then come three lords, each known by banner, mount and deed: the rich one whose long banner bears the many-striped bird that strikes down the snake with venomous fangs and fire-hot breath; the one with the white bull raised on his banner, Uma beside him, three unwinking eyes, who destroyed the three walled cities; and the one with a thousand eyes, who completed a hundred sacrifices, mounted on the neck of the four-tusked elephant.
nuance: None of the three gods is named; they are identified by emblem and deed, and all three come as visitors to the younger god's shrine.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the god's form and deeds: கடவுள் வாழ்த்து, under paadaan (porul 2.27)

reading: With those three famed lords, who guard the world from their good cities, at their head, and with the four-faced one born of the lotus in mind, the thirty-three gods of four kinds and the eighteen companies, bright as stars in bloom, swift as rising wind, strong as fire in wind and loud as thunder, whirl through the sky and come together to see him and win what they need; and with his flawless consort he rests some days at Avinankudi.
nuance: Lines 160 to 168 are hard: why the four-faced one is 'pointed to' (நான்முக ஒருவற் சுட்டி) and what high state the gods seek (உயர்நிலை பெறீஇயர்) are not said. One later reading takes it as the gods coming to ask for Brahma's release; the words here say only that they come with a need (உறுகுறை).

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the god's form and deeds: கடவுள் வாழ்த்து, under paadaan (porul 2.27)

reading: At Eragam, the twice-born of many ancient families, never failing in the six duties, who spent forty-eight years of youth in study, devoted to dharma and rich in the three fires, chant at the proper hours; wearing the fine thread of three strands of nine, their wet cloth drying on them, hands joined above their heads, they praise him, recite with their tongues the rare hidden mantra of six letters, and holding fragrant flowers rejoice; and there he dwells.
nuance: Every number in the passage (six duties, 'the two', forty-eight years, three fires, nine threads, six letters) marks the brahmins' order, and the six-letter mantra (ஆறெழுத்து, line 186) is the only place the idyll names a mantra. இருவர்ச் சுட்டிய (178) is obscure to me: it may mean families traced from both parents.

thinai_evidence.note: the brahmin's six duties praised: the பார்ப்பனப் பக்கம் of vaakai (porul 2.16)

reading: On the hills the velan wears a garland of green naRai pods with wild jasmine and white koothaalam, his chest smeared with fragrant sandal; the hunters with their cruel bows, drinking with their kin in the small hill village the toddy matured in long bamboo, dance the kuravai to the small thondagam drum; and the women, their hair bound with flowers from deep pools, kulai leaves and the white clusters of red-stemmed kadamba, wearing skirts of cool leaves strung for the bees, walk with the soft gait of peacocks.
nuance: This is the only section of the idyll where the worshippers are the people of the land itself, the velan, the hunters and their women, drinking and dancing, rather than sages, gods or brahmins.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill people's festival for the god, inside the praise

reading: The god himself is red, in red clothes, with tender seyalai shoots swaying at his ears, wearing waistband, anklets and a garland of red ixora, with flute, horn and many small instruments, the ram and the peacock, and the flawless cock on his banner; tall, with bangled shoulders, among women whose voices are sweet as plucked strings, wearing a fine cloth that reaches the ground, he takes the many soft-shouldered does in his drum-like arms and leads them: dancing on every hill is his settled nature.
nuance: The god is described in the same list form as the hill people of the previous lines, with the same red garland, instruments and women: on the hills he is one of the dancers, leading the kuravai, not a figure carried through the sky as at Alaivay.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the god's form and deeds: கடவுள் வாழ்த்து, under paadaan (porul 2.27)

comparisons.tenor: the women he leads in the dance

unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 218-233: lines 218 to 226 list the places of his worship, ending at கந்துடை நிலையினும்; line 227 begins the rite itself, which runs to line 249.
reading: He is found wherever he is worshipped: at the festivals each town holds, where small millet is mixed with flowers, a kid is cut and the cock banner is set up; wherever devotees praise him; at the veri ground the velan prepares; in forests, groves and lovely river islets, at rivers and tanks and many other places, at crossroads and junctions and under fresh-flowered kadamba, in the common ground, the hall and at the sacred post.
nuance: The list moves from the town's festival to the open country, the crossroads and a single kadamba tree: the god's places are not only the named shrines but any spot where he is called, which is why the guide will say 'whatever the place may be' (ஆண்டாண்டு ஆயினும் ஆக, line 250).

thinai_evidence.note: the places of the god's worship listed, inside the praise

unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 218-233 and 234-249: begins at line 227, where the rite begins after the list of places, and ends at line 249, which closes places and rites with அறிந்த வாறே.
reading: There the rite is performed: the place is washed with a fine banner raised, smeared with ghee and white mustard, words murmured and bows made, rich flowers scattered, two clothes of contrasting colour worn, a red thread tied, white puffed rice strewn, pure white rice mixed with the blood of a strong fat ram set out in small offerings in many baskets, turmeric and fragrant water sprinkled, cool oleander garlands cut in pairs and hung, the hill town praised, incense raised and the kurinji tune sung; with waterfall and instruments sounding, flowers scattered so that all fear, and red millet spread with blood, the kuramagal sets up Murugu's music in the dread great house where the god is brought, horns are blown and curved bells rung, the unyielding elephant is praised, and those who seek obtain what they sought; so it is known that he dwells in each place.
nuance: முருகாற்றுப் படுத்த (244), 'where Murugu is guided in', uses the same verb as the poem's own title: the priestess guides the god to the worshippers just as the poem guides the worshipper to the god. The rite is presented as effective without qualification (வேண்டுநர் வேண்டியாங்கு எய்தினர், 248).

thinai_evidence.note: the worship rite that brings the god, inside the praise

reading: Whatever the place, when you first see him, praise him with a glad face, worship with joined hands, bow to touch his feet, and say: lord of six dwellings, born of the six, whom one of the five took into his palm at the blue pool on the high peak; son of the god of the banyan; son of the mountain's daughter; Death to enemies; child of victorious Kotravai; infant of the jewelled ancient one; leader of the army of the gods; garlanded chest; poet who knows the texts; unmatched in war; warrior of peerless strength; wealth of the brahmins; mountain of the words of the wise; husband of the women; bull among men; great lord with the spear in your hand.
nuance: The guide gives the seeker the very words to say: the poem turns from description to a script of address. The epithets of birth name three mothers in a row (the mountain's daughter, Kotravai, the ancient one), and the six of his birth and the six of his dwelling are set side by side (அறுவர் பயந்த ஆறமர் செல்வ).

thinai_evidence.note: praise and supplication (பரவல், புகழ்ச்சி), paadaan (porul 2.22)

comparisons.tenor: the god as destroyer of his enemies
the god's store of the words of the wise

unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 266-275 and 276-291: the string of epithets ends at குரிசில் in line 276, closed by எனப்பல; line 277 turns to the seeker's own words.
reading: ...of undiminished victory, who killed the mountain; lord of kurinji with its sky-touching peaks; bull among poets of praised good speech; Muruga, of great name and rare lineage; famed one who satisfies those who long; red one of gold ornament who gives to the afflicted; tall Vel who shelters suppliants on your fearsome chest that won great wars; god of great name whom the great praise; mighty one whose strength cut down Sur; warrior great in battle; chief!
nuance: The god is praised in the words a bard uses of a patron: one who satisfies those who long (நசையுநர்க்கு ஆர்த்தும்), gives to the afflicted, and shelters suppliants (பரிசிலர்த் தாங்கும்). The puram patron's praise is carried over whole to a god, and he is also made a poet himself (புலவர் ஏறே).

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the god as warrior and as giver to suppliants, paadaan

unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 276-291 and 292-307: the god's reply that begins in line 291 (அஞ்சல் ஓம்புமதி) runs to the gift in line 295 (பரிசில் நல்குமதி); the waterfall's sentence begins with பலவுடன் at the end of line 295 and is taken whole into the next unit.
reading: Praising him tirelessly as far as you know, say: 'Since it is hard for living beings to know you to your measure, I have come thinking of your feet, wise one who has no equal'; and before you finish what you meant, his many small attendants of many forms will appear at the festival ground and say, 'Great one, a poor old-mouthed suppliant has come, longing for your generous fame,' praising many sweet and good things; and he, coming in a sky-high form full of divine power, will take his awesome high place, show the young beauty of his fragrant ancient godhead, say 'Fear not; I knew of your coming,' speak kind words lovingly, and give you the rare gift that makes you stand alone in the dark-sea-girt world.
nuance: The scene follows the bard's arrival at a king's court step by step: the suppliant (இரவலன்) is announced by attendants, praised to the patron, reassured, and given a gift; only the gift is different, since it makes him unique in the world rather than rich. நின்னளந்து அறிதல் மன்னுயிர்க்கு அருமையின் (278) gives the reason for coming to the feet at all: the god cannot be known, only approached.

thinai_evidence.note: the guide's promise of the patron's gift, the core of the ஆற்றுப்படை, paadaan

unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 292-307 and 308-317: begins at line 296, where the waterfall's sentence starts after பரிசில் நல்குமதி in line 295, and runs to the end of the poem, since lines 296 to 317 are one sentence ending in மலைகிழவோனே.
reading: The poem closes on the god's waterfall: swaying like many different cloths, carrying agil, rolling whole sandal trunks, tearing up bamboo with its flowered branches, breaking the cool fragrant honeycombs that hang like the sun's disc from the sky-touching peak, mixing in old jackfruit segments, shedding fragrant naga flowers, chilling langur and monkey, drenching the great she-elephant, sweeping along the pearl-bearing tusk of the great tusker so that gold and gems gleam, felling banana trunks and coconut clusters, bending pepper vines, scattering peacocks and the jungle hen, driving the boar and the bear with fur like palmyra fibre into the rock clefts and making the wild bull bellow, it roars down from afar: he is the lord of the hill of Pazhamudircholai.
nuance: The last sentence (296 to 317) is a single torrent through every native thing of the hill, trees, fruit, beasts and birds, and only its last line names the god as lord of the hill: the poem ends by showing the seeker the god's land in motion rather than the god.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the god's form and deeds: கடவுள் வாழ்த்து, under paadaan (porul 2.27)

comparisons.tenor: the round honeycombs on the peak

title: பொருநராற்றுப்படை
theme: Porunaratruppadai: a bard who has been rewarded by Karikal Valavan guides another bard to him, describing the lute and its singer, his own reception, feast and parting gifts, the king's birth and victory at Venni, and the Chola land where the five landscapes mingle and the Kaveri does not fail.
structure_note: The idyll is one long address. Lines 1-59 hail the bard and describe the lute and the paadini; 60-129 tell the guide's own reception; 130-148 praise the king; 149-177 promise the gifts; 178-248 describe the land. Fourteen of the sixteen core units were re-cut at sense breaks into thirteen adjusted units (fifteen units in all); 189-207 and 208-217 are unchanged.
source_issues: Line 168 prints முறையுழிக்; tamilvu reads முறையுளிக் (flag r11). The sense (in due order) is the same; our reading kept.
Line 73 prints ஓன்றியான் with a long initial vowel; ஒன்றியான் (or ஒன்று யான்) is expected.
Line 97 prints கண்டோட்; கண்டோர் (those who see) is the expected form.
Line 123 prints அகறி ரொவெம், which reads as அகறிரோ எம்; the short ொ for ோ looks like a misprint.
Line 145 prints ஒங்கிருஞ் with a short initial vowel; ஓங்கிருஞ் is expected (as line 206 was repaired, flag r7).
Lines 129 and 177 each end with the first word of the next sentence (வென்வேல், நொல்லென); units cannot split a line, so these words stay in the earlier unit.
Line 228 is printed ஒரு குடையா னென்று கூற; the sense (they say: one umbrella) takes it as ஒரு குடையான் என்று.

unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 1-14 and 15-29: the description of the lute runs from line 4 to பாலை in line 22, and line 23 turns to how it is played and to the singing woman.
reading: The guide hails a skilled porunan who, once the festival of a great town of unfailing plenty is over, cares nothing for its leftover food and sets out for another land, and describes his lute part by part: a bowl forked like a hoofprint, a covering skin the colour of lamp flame stitched with a seam like the line of down on a young pregnant woman's belly, pegs like the eyes of a crab in its hole, a mouth shaped like the eighth-day moon, a stem rising like a snake's raised hood, bands like the bangles on a dark woman's forearm, strings fine as pounded millet, the whole like a bathed and fragrant bride, a paalai lute so sweet that it makes the robbers who waylay travellers drop their weapons and turn back.
nuance: Almost every part of the lute is likened to a woman's body or ornament (the down on a pregnant woman's belly, a dark woman's bangles, a bathed bride), so the instrument is already a body before the singing woman of the next unit is described. The power of the paalai tune over robbers (lines 21 and 22) is the first proof that this bard's art protects him on the road.

thinai_evidence.note: a performer addresses a fellow bard to direct him to a patron: the guide poem (ஆற்றுப்படை) under paadaan

comparisons.tenor: the forked bowl of the lute
the colour of the skin stretched over the bowl

comparisons.vehicle: எய்யா விளஞ்சூற் செய்யோ ளவ்வயிற் றைதுமயி ரொழுகிய தோற்றம் போல
comparisons.tenor: the seam of the stitched cover
the pegs that close the holes
the tight bands on the stem

unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 15-29 and 30-48: the playing begins at line 23, and the description of the paadini closes at பெருந்தகு பாடினி in line 47.
reading: Playing the lute in all its ways and scattering fine words with the music, the bard is accompanied by his paadini, described from head to foot: hair like rippled sand, brow like the crescent, brows like a killing bow, mouth red as the silk-cotton petal, teeth like pearls, ears hung with swinging earrings, neck bent with modesty, shoulders like swaying bamboo, fingers like the kaanthal of the high hills, nails like a parrot's beak, breasts so close a split rib cannot pass between, navel like an eddy, a waist one hardly knows is there, a girdle of strands like rows of bees, thighs like a she-elephant's trunk, and small feet like a panting dog's tongue, blistered like ripe marul fruit from walking on ground red as melted lac, so that at midday she stops on the road, like a peahen.
nuance: The head-to-foot description ends not on beauty but on injury: the feet like a panting dog's tongue are soft because they are hurt, and the blisters are the road's mark on her. The ideal body and the poverty of the journey are drawn in one sentence, which is the guide poem's whole case for going to the patron.

thinai_evidence.note: the companion of the bard on the guide's road; the description belongs to the guide poem under paadaan

comparisons.tenor: the many strands of her girdle

unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 30-48 and 49-59: line 48 (the singing to the beat) begins the clause that closes at நோற்றதன் பயனே in line 59.
reading: Singing to the beat day after day, halting in forest tracks where tuskers roam, bearing the hardship of thin, net-like shade under the leafless maraa, and making the due offering to the god who dwells in the forest, the leader of the performers with his lute, which looks like the three drum-thundering kings seated together in council, is told that having strayed from the way he did not know, meeting the guide on the road is the fruit of his past penance.
nuance: What the simile of the three kings in council (lines 53 to 55) describes is not fixed by the words: it may be the lute, held up as a court in itself, or the gathered company of performers. 'நோற்றதன் பயனே' (line 59) makes the chance meeting a reward for past austerity, the first of the poem's comparisons between the bard's luck and the fruit of tapas (see lines 91 and 92).

thinai_evidence.note: the guide hails the wandering performer and turns him toward the patron

comparisons.tenor: the thin shade of the leafless tree

comparisons.vehicle: மூவருங் கூடி அரசவை யிருந்த தோற்றம் போல
comparisons.tenor: the lute that carries the song (or the company of performers)

unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 60-75: the bard's arrival and playing end with the time of day in line 72; from line 73 the patron's welcome begins.
reading: Listen well, the guide says, you who excel in fame: if you want to end the long hunger of your large kin, worn by wasting hunger, rise without delay, master of the seven strings; for I too, like a bird that thinks of a fruiting tree, entered unannounced the wide humming palace whose great gate stops no one who comes in need, weary in body, to end my distress, and beat my wide drum, its face stained by the hand like the spots on a cobra's spread hood, to a double beat in the depth of night as Venus rose.
nuance: The open gate 'that does not bar those who come in need' (line 66) is what makes the fruit-tree simile work: a fruiting tree in the open is free to every bird. The guide's argument is his own story, told in the first person, so the promise rests on testimony rather than on the patron's reputation.

thinai_evidence.note: the guide urges the hungry bard to go to the patron, offering his own arrival as proof

comparisons.tenor: the hungry bard going to the patron's house
the hand-stains on the drum's face

unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 60-75, 76-94 and 95-117: the welcome begins at line 73 and the sentence of the first night closes at மாழாந்து எழுந்து in line 95.
reading: Before I could say what I wanted, the patron, wishing to take me as kin, spoke words of welcome, seated me close where his eyes could reach me, looked at me without tiring as if drinking me in, so that my bones cooled as if melting, had my rags, sweat-soaked, patched with other threads and full of lice and nits, stripped off and gave me cloth fine as a snake's slough that the eye cannot see through, and had jewelled, smiling women pour drink again and again into golden cups in his cloud-high mansion until my weariness ended; so I stayed in a corner of his palace like ascetics who gain the fruit of their penance without leaving the body, and rose free of every care except the drowsy tremor of drink.
nuance: The patron gives before he is asked (line 73), and the comparison in lines 91 and 92 makes the bard's ease the reward that ascetics get only after death, here received in the living body. The removal of the patched rags is the first act, before food: the bard is re-dressed as a guest of rank.

thinai_evidence.note: the patron's reception of the bard, told as the guide's own experience

comparisons.vehicle: தவஞ்செய் மாக்கள் தம்முடம் பிடாஅ ததன்பய மெய்திய வளவை மான
comparisons.tenor: the bard's ease in the palace

unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 95-117 and 118-127: the morning begins at line 96, and the image of the blunted teeth closes with மழுங்கி in line 118.
